# keta — full documentation

> keta is a finite-element kernel for bar structures and bridges, written in C++20 and driven from Python: a script describes the structure, runs the analyses and processes the results.

Source: https://pavlishenku.github.io/keta/


# Python API User Manual

# Chapter 1 Overview of keta

## 1.1 Introduction

keta is a structural analysis kernel written in C++. It handles three-dimensional or plane bar
structures, slabs and walls modelled as thin or thick shells, and two- and three-dimensional
continua. It is mainly intended for the analysis of bridges and civil engineering frames.

The kernel is driven from the Python language by the `keta` module. A model is
described by a script: creation of the nodes, materials, sections, elements, supports and loads,
then running of the analyses and processing of the results. All the features of the Python
language (loops, functions, lists, numerical computation) serve to parametrise the structure and
to process the results; there is no data language specific to keta.

The main features available from Python are the following:

- the description of bar structures (Timoshenko beams with 12 degrees of freedom, truss bars,
cables as elastic catenaries), with offsets, hinges, section orientation, Winkler elastic
foundation and links between nodes;

- triangular flat shell facets (membrane and bending, orthotropy, laminates), plane,
axisymmetric and solid continuum elements;

- sections from the European catalogue (IPE, HEA, HEB, HEM), parametric sections and directly
given section properties;

- fixed loads (self-weight, nodal loads, loads on bars, temperatures, support displacements,
surface loads, hydrostatic pressures) and their combinations;

- prestressing by tendons (friction, anchorage draw-in, time-dependent losses) and staged
construction with creep, shrinkage and relaxation according to the main code laws;

- live loads by influence lines and surfaces: load models of EN 1991-2 (road, rail, fatigue),
load systems of Fascicule 61 Titre II, arbitrary vehicles;

- dynamics: mode shapes, spectral analysis, harmonic response, power spectral density, linear
and nonlinear time-history analyses, passage of high-speed trains;

- wind: profiles, turbulence, response to turbulent wind, equivalent static loads,
flutter;

- stability: linear buckling, imperfections, second order, large displacements, arc length and
collapse load;

- nonlinear link laws (tension only, gap, tabulated laws), soil springs and earth
pressure;

- fire analysis of reinforced concrete bars (temperature field in the section, hot stiffnesses,
search for equilibrium) and the properties of materials at high temperature;

- section checking tools (reinforced concrete, shells, composite beams).

The results are returned as Python numbers, tuples and lists. They lend themselves directly to
the production of tables, the writing of files or the plotting of curves with the usual
libraries.

## 1.2 Characteristics of the kernel

The kernel uses the exact solution of the chosen mechanical model wherever one is available. This
applies to the internal forces at the output stations of Timoshenko beams, which are recomputed by
equilibrium, to the elastic catenary of cables, to the integration of distributed loads and to the
search for extreme combinations. An unsupported configuration raises an error; it is not replaced
by an approximation without the user's knowledge.

The analyses are deterministic: the same script produces the same numbers, bit for bit, from one
run to the next and whatever the number of threads used by the solver. The outputs of the
examples reproduced in this manual can therefore be obtained again without any difference.

## 1.3 Limits

The number of nodes, bars and load cases is limited only by the available memory. Linear
systems are solved by a supernodal sparse factorisation; the size of the models commonly handled
(a few tens of thousands of degrees of freedom) poses no difficulty.

The Python module exposes only part of the features of the C++ kernel. Functions that do not yet
have a Python interface are flagged in the text by a “Pending” box; Appendix C lists them. They
cannot be used from a script.

**Pending.**

Example of a box: a feature flagged in this way exists in the calculation kernel but is
not yet accessible from Python. The text describes its principle; the syntax will be documented
when the interface is available.

## 1.4 Writing conventions

### 1.4.1 Command syntax

Each command is presented in a syntax box, followed by a table describing its parameters, by
notes and by an example. In the boxes:

- `m` denotes a model created by `m = keta.Model()`; `r`,
`case_` or `res` denote results objects;

- parameters written in the form `name=value` are optional; the value shown is the
default value. Parameters without a value are mandatory;

- the arrow `→` indicates the returned value;

- optional parameters are preferably given by name
(`m.add_udl(b, wz=-10e3, case=2)`), which makes the script readable and independent of
the order of the arguments.

Syntax

```python
m.add_udl(bar, wx=0.0, wy=0.0, wz=0.0, case=1, frame='global')
```

In the parameter table, the “Unit” column gives the expected SI unit and the “Default” column
the value taken when the parameter is absent; a dash marks a mandatory parameter.

### 1.4.2 Notes

Throughout the manual, notes are presented as follows:

**Note.**

Note: usage detail or additional information.

**Important.**

Important note: a point whose omission leads to a wrong result or to an error.

### 1.4.3 Examples

The examples are complete scripts, provided in the directory
`examples/manual` of the repository (`examples/manuel` for the French edition).
Each has been run with the version of the module described by this manual; the output reproduced
below the listing is the output actually obtained. The script `executer_tous.py` of the
same directory re-runs all the examples and checks that their outputs are unchanged (Chapter 2). When a closed form
exists, the example prints it next to the keta result, or checks it with an `assert`
statement.

Numbers are written with a decimal point, in the text as in the scripts and outputs; the scripts
and outputs follow Python notation (decimal point, `1e-3` for 10-3).

## 1.5 Error detection

Errors are reported by Python exceptions, which stop the script at the faulty line with an
explicit message:

| Exception | Cause |
|---|---|
| `KeyError` | non-existent identifier: node, bar, load case, combination, cable, catalogue section, mode shape, etc. |
| `ValueError` | invalid data (unknown keyword, value out of range, incompatible number of parameters) or impossible analysis (unstable structure, lack of convergence, analysis not applicable to the model). |
| `TypeError` | argument of an unexpected type (list instead of a number, etc.), reported by Python itself. |

The method `m.validate()` checks a model without analysing it and returns the list of
problems found (an empty list for a consistent model). These messages, written in English, are
those of the calculation kernel.

Example `examples/manual/ex_erreurs.py`

```python
# Error detection: missing identifier (KeyError), invalid data or analysis (ValueError).
import keta

m = keta.Model()
a, b = m.add_node(0, 0, 0), m.add_node(6, 0, 0)
beam = m.add_beam(a, b, m.add_section_rect(0.2, 0.4), m.steel())
m.add_point_load(b, fz=-1e3)

try:
    m.add_section("IPE999")
except KeyError as e:
    print("KeyError:  ", e)

try:
    m.add_udl(beam, wz=-1.0, frame="oblique")
except ValueError as e:
    print("ValueError:", e)

try:
    m.analyze()                    # no support: mechanism
except ValueError as e:
    print("ValueError:", str(e).splitlines()[0])

m.fix(a)
r = m.analyze()
try:
    r.case(2)
except KeyError as e:
    print("KeyError:  ", e)

m2 = keta.Model()
m2.add_node(0, 0, 0)
m2.add_beam(1, 7, 1, 1)            # non-existent references
print("validate():", m2.validate())
```

Output

```text
KeyError:   "unknown profile 'IPE999'"
ValueError: frame must be 'global' | 'local' | 'projected', got 'oblique'
ValueError: solver: factorization failed (singular or structurally deficient stiffness)
KeyError:   'no load case 2'
validate(): ['model: unknown node id 7']
```

**Note.**

An exception can be caught by `try … except` to continue a script, for example in
a parametric study or when a lack of equilibrium has a physical meaning (collapse of a structure in
fire, Chapter 18).

# Chapter 2 Installation

## 2.1 Principle

The Python module `keta` is a compiled extension: the calculation kernel, written in C++,
is delivered with its Python binding in a single package. It can be installed in three ways, from
the simplest to the most complete: a prebuilt wheel (`.whl` file), the source archive
compiled by `pip`, or a direct build from the repository.

The package depends on no other Python library; it is used with Python 3.10 or later, under
Windows, Linux or macOS.

## 2.2 Installation with pip

### 2.2.1 Prebuilt wheel

When a wheel matches the system and the Python version, installation is immediate. It is
advisable to work in a virtual environment specific to the project:

```text
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate            (Windows)
source .venv/bin/activate         (Linux, macOS)
pip install keta-1.0.0-cp313-cp313-win_amd64.whl
```

The file name gives the Python version (`cp313`: Python 3.13) and the platform
(`win_amd64`, `manylinux`, `macosx`). The wheels are produced for each
published version by the continuous integration of the repository; the `dist` directory
of the sources receives, for each version, the Windows one.

### 2.2.2 Source archive

Failing a wheel, `pip` compiles the package itself from the source archive or from the
repository; it downloads CMake and Ninja if necessary. A C++20 compiler is all that is needed: under
Windows, the Visual Studio 2022 “Build Tools” (workload “Desktop development with C++”); under
Linux, GCC 13 or later.

```text
pip install keta-1.0.0.tar.gz        (source archive)
pip install .                       (at the root of the repository)
```

The full compilation of the kernel takes ten to twenty minutes.

## 2.3 Building from the repository

To follow development or run the tests, the module is built with CMake:

```text
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build --target _keta
```

The build writes the package to `build/python/keta`. It is made visible to Python
through the `PYTHONPATH` variable:

```text
export PYTHONPATH=/path/to/keta/build/python      (Linux, macOS)
set PYTHONPATH=C:\path\to\keta\build\python       (Windows)
python -c "import keta; print(keta.__version__)"
```

| CMake option | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `-DKETA_PYTHON=ON\|OFF` | ON | builds the Python module or not |
| `-DKETA_NATIVE=ON` | OFF | optimises for the processor of the build machine; the module can then be used only on compatible processors |
| `-DPython3_EXECUTABLE=…` | — | selects the target Python interpreter when several are installed |

**Important.**

The compiled module can be used only with the Python version that was used to build it:
the name of the library carries this version (for example
`_keta.cpython-313-x86_64-linux-gnu.so` or `_keta.cp313-win_amd64.pyd`).

## 2.4 Code editor

The package contains the full description of its types (`.pyi` files): an editor
such as Visual Studio Code, with the Python extension, therefore provides completion of the methods,
shows their documentation on hover and flags misnamed arguments before any run.

## 2.5 Checking the installation

The examples of this manual serve to check the installation. The following script runs
each of them and compares its output, character by character, with the output reproduced in the
manual; it uses the installed module, or the one in the directory given by `--module`:

```text
python3 examples/manual/executer_tous.py
```

Each conforming example is reported by `OK`; the script ends with the number of
conforming examples and returns a zero exit code if all of them conform. A discrepancy is shown as
a line-by-line difference.

The smallest possible analysis confirms that the module works correctly:

Example `examples/manual/ex_console.py`

```python
# First analysis: 4 m IPE 300 steel cantilever loaded at its tip.
import json
import keta

m = keta.Model()
a = m.add_node(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)            # fixed support
b = m.add_node(4.0, 0.0, 0.0)            # free end
steel = m.steel()                        # E = 210 GPa, nu = 0.3
ipe = m.add_section("IPE300")
beam = m.add_beam(a, b, section=ipe, material=steel)
m.fix(a)
m.add_point_load(b, fz=-10e3)            # 10 kN downwards (case 1)

res = m.analyze()
case_ = res.case(1)
ux, uy, uz, rx, ry, rz = case_.displacement(b)
print(f"tip deflection     uz = {uz * 1e3:.4f} mm")
print(f"tip rotation       ry = {ry * 1e3:.4f} mrad")
node, (fx, fy, fz, mx, my, mz) = case_.reactions()[0]
print(f"reaction at node {node}: Fz = {fz / 1e3:.3f} kN, My = {my / 1e3:.3f} kN.m")

# Check: bending + shear (Timoshenko beam), with the properties
# actually used for the section (JSON model)
p = json.loads(m.to_json())["sections"][0]["props"]
E, G = 210e9, 210e9 / (2 * 1.3)
w = -10e3 * 4.0**3 / (3 * E * p["Iy"]) - 10e3 * 4.0 / (G * p["Avz"])
print(f"closed form        uz = {w * 1e3:.4f} mm")
assert abs(uz - w) < 1e-9 * abs(w)
```

Output

```text
tip deflection     uz = -12.3958 mm
tip rotation       ry = 4.5590 mrad
reaction at node 1: Fz = 10.000 kN, My = -40.000 kN.m
closed form        uz = -12.3958 mm
```

## 2.6 Run-time parameters

The factorisation of large systems can be distributed over several processor cores. The
number of threads is a global setting of the process:

Syntax

```python
keta.set_solver_threads(n)
keta.solver_threads()  →  int
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `n` | — | 1 | number of threads of the supernodal factorisation: 1 = sequential, 0 = all available cores |

The results are identical bit for bit whatever the number of threads. Parallelism is useful
only for large models.

## 2.7 Rebuilding this manual

This document is produced from its HTML sources by:

```text
python3 tools/build_manuel_python.py --module build/python --lang en
```

The script first checks all the examples (the build stops if one of them fails or if its
output has changed), then lays out the document with the Chromium browser, driven by Playwright from
Node.js. The result is written to `docs/keta_python_manual.pdf`. The option
`--doc principes` builds the manual of calculation principles in the same way
(`docs/keta_calculation_principles.pdf`), and `--doc tous` both.

# Chapter 3 Units, axes and sign conventions

## 3.1 Units

keta works exclusively in the International System. All data are supplied and all results are
returned in the following units, without implicit conversion:

| Quantity | Unit | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| length, coordinate, displacement | m | thickness 0.25 m; deflection −0.0124 m |
| angle, rotation | rad | `beta=math.pi / 2`; `math.radians(30)` |
| force | N | 10 kN is written `10e3` |
| moment | N·m | 40 kN·m is written `40e3` |
| distributed load per unit length | N/m | 25 kN/m is written `25e3` |
| pressure, stress, modulus | Pa | E = 210 GPa is written `210e9`; 5 kN/m² is written `5e3` |
| density | kg/m³ | concrete 2500 |
| mass, mass moment of inertia | kg, kg·m² | point mass of 20 t: `20e3` |
| temperature, gradient | K (or °C for fire), K/m | ΔT = 30 K |
| time | s; days for staged construction and creep; minutes for fire | stage date 28 (days) |
| frequency | Hz; angular frequency in rad/s |  |
| spring stiffness | N/m; N·m/rad |  |
| subgrade reaction modulus (elastic foundation) | N/m per m (= Pa) | soil modulus × width |

The acceleration of gravity is g = 9.80665 m/s². The self-weight is computed from the density of
the materials; a zero density gives a material without mass and without weight.

**Note.**

Python scientific notation (`3.5e-3`, `210e9`) avoids errors in the
power of ten; the `_` separators are also accepted
(`10_000`).

## 3.2 Global axes

The global coordinate system is a right-handed orthonormal system (O, X, Y, Z). The Z axis is
vertical, pointing upwards: gravity acts along −Z. Node coordinates, nodal loads, nodal
displacements and support reactions are expressed in this system.

**Figure 3.1** — Global axes and local axes of a bar

A plane structure is described in a plane of the global system, by restraining the out-of-plane
degrees of freedom (Section 3.4); there is no separate plane analysis option.

## 3.3 Local axes of bars

Each bar carries a local coordinate system (x, y, z):

- the x axis lies along the bar, from the origin node `n1` to the end node
`n2`;

- for a non-vertical bar, the y axis is horizontal (y = Z ∧ x, normalised) and the z axis, lying
in the vertical plane that contains the bar, points upwards (z = x ∧ y). For a bar parallel to the
X axis of the global system, the local and global axes coincide;

- for a vertical bar (component of x along Z greater than 0.99999 in absolute value), the y axis
is the global Y axis and z = x ∧ y. For a column pointing upwards, z = −X;

- the angle `beta` (parameter of `add_beam`) then rotates the y and z axes
about x, in the positive (right-handed) sense.

The y and z axes are the principal axes of the section: `Iy` is the bending second
moment of area about y (bending in the xz plane), `Iz` the second moment of area about z
(bending in the xy plane). For a rectangular section `add_section_rect(b, h)`, the width
b is measured along y and the depth h along z: a horizontal rectangular beam is therefore bent
vertically through its strong-axis second moment of area b h³/12.

**Important.**

The rule for choosing the local axes changes in the vicinity of the vertical. A nearly
vertical bar (slightly inclined by a geometric imperfection, for example) receives a horizontal y
axis perpendicular to its projection, whereas a vertical bar receives y = Y. In a column
in which some bars are vertical and others very slightly inclined, the second moments of area Iy
and Iz can then be swapped from one bar to the next. For a column with an unsymmetrical section
whose geometry is perturbed along Y, the section is oriented by `beta` so that the
bending under study occurs along X (example in Chapter 16).

## 3.4 Degrees of freedom

Each node has six degrees of freedom, expressed in the global system and identified by a
component index from 0 to 5:

**Figure 3.2** — Degrees of freedom of a node

This order (dx, dy, dz, rx, ry, rz) is that of all the tuples of displacements, reactions and
nodal loads, and of the index `comp` of the functions that target a component
(influence lines, adjustments, time-history analyses, etc.).

Unused degrees of freedom are restrained automatically: rotations of nodes that carry only truss
bars, rotations and out-of-plane translation of the nodes of plane continuum elements. For a plane
bar structure, the out-of-plane degrees of freedom are restrained explicitly by
`add_support` (for example dy, rx and rz for a structure in the XZ plane).

## 3.5 Internal forces and stresses

The internal forces at the output stations of a bar are expressed in its local axes. They are
the forces exerted on the part of the bar located on the origin side by the part located on the end
side (forces on the face with normal +x):

**Figure 3.3** — Sign conventions for internal forces in a bar

- **N**, axial force, positive in tension;

- **Vy, Vz**, shear forces, components along y and z of the force on the +x face
(Vz = dMy/dx);

- **T**, torsional moment about x;

- **My**, bending moment about y, positive when it puts the fibre z > 0 in tension;

- **Mz**, bending moment about z, positive when it compresses the fibre y > 0.

The normal stress at a point (y, z) of the section is:

σ = N / A + My · z / Iy − Mz · y / Iz

For a horizontal beam loaded downwards (−Z), whose local z axis is vertical upwards, the span
moment is negative (bottom fibre in tension) and the moment over an intermediate support is
positive (top fibre in tension).

**Note.**

The end forces `end_forces` (12 components) are, by contrast, the forces and
moments exerted by the nodes on the bar, in the local axes and in the order (Fx, Fy, Fz, Mx,
My, Mz) at the origin node then at the end node. At the origin, they are of opposite sign to the
internal forces defined above; at the end, they are of the same sign.

## 3.6 Reactions and loads

Nodal loads and support reactions are expressed in the global system, positive in the direction
of the axes. A reaction is the force exerted by the support on the structure: for a beam carrying a
downward load, the vertical reaction is positive. The sum of the reactions balances the sum of the
applied loads.

Distributed loads on bars are given in the global axes (default), in the local axes of the bar
or in projection (Chapter 11). Imposed support displacements are expressed in the global
system.

# Chapter 4 Organisation of an analysis

## 4.1 Course of a script

A keta analysis is a Python script that chains four steps:

**Figure 4.1** — The four steps of a calculation script

- **import of the module**: `import keta`;

- **description of the model**: creation of a `keta.Model()` object, then calls to its
`add_…` methods to define nodes, materials, sections, elements, supports, links and
loads;

- **running of one or several analyses**: `m.analyze()` for linear statics,
`m.modal()`, `m.buckling()`, `m.phased()`, etc. Each analysis returns
an independent results object; the model is not modified;

- **processing of the results**: reading of displacements, reactions and internal forces through
the methods of the results objects, printing, additional calculations in Python.

The steps can be repeated: a model can be completed after a first analysis and then analysed
again, several models can coexist in the same script, and a model can be built by a parametrised
Python function (Chapter 21).

## 4.2 Identifiers

All the `add_…` methods that create an object return its **identifier**, an
integer. Identifiers are assigned automatically, in the order of creation, separately for each
family of objects: the first node has number 1, the first bar number 1, the first material
number 1, etc. These identifiers are kept in Python variables or lists for later
use:

```text
a = m.add_node(0, 0, 0)                 # a == 1
b = m.add_node(6, 0, 0)                 # b == 2
steel = m.steel()                       # material 1
beam = m.add_beam(a, b, m.add_section("IPE300"), steel)    # bar 1
```

The separately numbered families are: nodes, bars (beams and trusses), cables, materials,
sections, links, shells, continuum elements, tendons, combinations. It is not possible to choose a
number oneself; the correspondence with an external numbering is made with a Python
dictionary.

**Important.**

Identifiers are integers without geometric meaning. An identifier of one family must not be
used for another (a node number instead of a bar number): depending on the case, the error is
reported (`KeyError`) or applies to another existing object.

## 4.3 Load cases

Loads are grouped into **load cases** identified by an integer number chosen by the user and
passed through the `case` parameter of the loading methods (default value 1). A case is
created by the first load that refers to it; it can be named by `m.name_case`. The cases
are analysed together, in a single factorisation of the stiffness matrix. Linear combinations of
cases are defined by `m.add_combination` (Chapter 19).

**Note.**

`m.harmonic` and `m.psd` (Chapter 14) designate the case by its number
with the argument `case_id`; their argument `case` gives its **rank** (0 for
the first case in increasing order of numbers).

## 4.4 Results

Each analysis returns an object specific to the analysis. Linear statics returns a
`Results` object, which gives access to the results of each case (`r.case(i)`)
and of each combination (`r.combo(j)`) in the form of `CaseResult` objects. The
main reading methods are common to most static analyses:

| Method | Result |
|---|---|
| `displacement(node)` | tuple (dx, dy, dz, rx, ry, rz), global axes |
| `reactions()` | list of (node, (Fx, Fy, Fz, Mx, My, Mz)) of the supported nodes |
| `sum_reactions()` | resultant (Fx, Fy, Fz) of the reactions |
| `bar_forces(bar)` | list of (x/L, N, Vy, Vz, T, My, Mz) at the output stations |
| `end_forces(bar)` | the 12 end forces, local axes |
| `max_displacement()` | largest nodal translation (norm) |

Chapter 20 describes all the results objects and Appendix B the format of each.

## 4.5 Annotated example

The example below illustrates the organisation of a complete script: a two-span continuous beam
on an elastic central support, whose reaction is compared with the closed form.

Example `examples/manual/ex_appuis.py`

```python
# Rigid and elastic supports: continuous beam of 2 x 8 m, elastic central support.
import keta

L, q, ks = 8.0, -30e3, 20e6          # span [m], load [N/m], stiffness [N/m]
m = keta.Model()
n = [m.add_node(L * i, 0.0, 0.0) for i in range(3)]
sec = m.add_section_props(sx=0.05, iy=2.0e-3, iz=1.0e-3, ix=1.0e-3)   # rigid in shear
mat = m.add_material(e=30e9, nu=0.2)
b = [m.add_beam(n[i], n[i + 1], sec, mat) for i in range(2)]

m.add_support(n[0], dx=True, dy=True, dz=True, rx=True)   # pinned support (rotations ry, rz free)
m.add_support(n[1], dy=True, kz=ks)                       # elastic vertical support
m.add_support(n[2], dy=True, dz=True)                     # sliding support
for bi in b:
    m.add_udl(bi, wz=q)

case_ = m.analyze().case(1)
for nd, (fx, fy, fz, mx, my, mz) in case_.reactions():
    print(f"node {nd}: Fz = {fz / 1e3:9.3f} kN")
w1 = case_.displacement(n[1])[2]
print(f"settlement of the elastic support: {w1 * 1e3:.3f} mm")

# Check (closed form): R1 = (5 q (2L)^4 / 384 EI) / (1/ks + (2L)^3 / 48 EI)
EI, Lt = 30e9 * 2.0e-3, 2 * L
R1 = (5 * -q * Lt**4 / (384 * EI)) / (1 / ks + Lt**3 / (48 * EI))
print(f"expected reaction: {R1 / 1e3:.3f} kN")
assert abs(dict(case_.reactions())[n[1]][2] - R1) < 1e-8 * R1
assert abs(w1 + R1 / ks) < 1e-12
```

Output

```text
node 1: Fz =    95.094 kN
node 2: Fz =   289.811 kN
node 3: Fz =    95.094 kN
settlement of the elastic support: -14.491 mm
expected reaction: 289.811 kN
```

The script creates three nodes (`n` is the list of their identifiers), a section
defined by its properties and a material, then two bars. The left support restrains the three
translations and torsion; the central support restrains the transverse translation dy and carries
a vertical spring `kz`; the right support slides along X. A vertical distributed load is
applied to both bars in case 1, the default case. After the analysis, the loop over
`case_.reactions()` prints the vertical reactions; the reaction of the elastic support is
then checked against the closed form.

# Chapter 5 General commands

## 5.1 Importing the module

Syntax

```python
import keta
keta.__version__  →  str
```

All classes and functions are accessible in the `keta` namespace. The attribute
`__version__` gives the version of the module. If the compiled extension cannot be
found, the import fails with a message reminding the user to build the `_keta` target
and to complete `PYTHONPATH` (Chapter 2).

## 5.2 Creating a model

Syntax

```python
m = keta.Model()  →  Model
```

Creates an empty model. A script can create as many models as necessary; they are
independent. The following attributes give information on the size of the model:

Syntax

```python
m.node_count  →  int
m.bar_count  →  int
repr(m)  →  str
```

`node_count` and `bar_count` give the number of nodes and of bars
(beams and trusses, cables excluded). The representation `repr(m)`, also obtained by
`print(m)`, summarises the model: number of nodes, bars, cases and combinations.

## 5.3 Checking a model

Syntax

```python
m.validate()  →  list[str]
```

Checks the consistency of the model without analysing it: references to non-existent nodes,
materials or sections, bars of zero length, non-finite values, thermal action on a material without
a coefficient of thermal expansion, etc. Returns the list of problems found, empty if the model is
sound. The check stops at the first problem encountered: the list contains at most one message.

**Note.**

Each analysis performs this check itself and raises a `ValueError` if there is a
problem; `validate()` allows it to be done separately, for example before a loop of
analyses. An unstable structure (mechanism) is detected only during the analysis, at the
factorisation.

## 5.4 Saving and reloading a model

A model can be saved as text in JSON format, then rebuilt
identically:

Syntax

```python
m.to_json()  →  str
keta.Model.from_json(text)  →  Model
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `text` | — | — | JSON string produced by `to_json` |

The JSON text contains the nodes, materials, sections (with their computed properties), bars,
cables, supports, skew supports, rigid and elastic links (with their laws), linear relations,
slabs, shells, continuum elements, point, nodal and bar masses, tendons, load cases and
combinations. It
is written to a file by the usual Python means (`open(...).write(m.to_json())`).
The reloaded model keeps the numbering: identifiers created afterwards follow the largest existing
identifiers.

The JSON content is also the means of knowing the properties actually used by the kernel (shear
areas of the sections, for example, Chapter 6):
`json.loads(m.to_json())["sections"]`.

**Important.**

The time-dependent laws of the materials (`set_concrete_law` and
`set_concrete_law_functions`, Chapter 7) are not part of this save: they must be
defined again after reloading. Tapered bars (`set_tapered`) and composite bars cannot be
saved: `to_json` refuses a model that contains them rather than write it without
them.

## 5.5 Exporting as a script

Syntax

```python
m.export_script(results=None, stations=11)  →  str
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `results` | — | None | `Results` object of a static analysis: the produced script then checks that it finds the same values |
| `stations` | — | 11 | number of output stations per bar for the check analysis |

Returns a stand-alone Python script that rebuilds the model and analyses it again. This script
serves to archive an analysis in a readable form, to pass on a model or to build a non-regression
test when the argument `results` is supplied.

Example `examples/manual/ex_modele_json.py`

```python
# General commands: description, validation, saving and reading back of a model.
import json
import keta

m = keta.Model()
n = [m.add_node(5.0 * i, 0.0, 0.0) for i in range(3)]
s = m.add_section_rect(0.30, 0.60)
c = m.concrete()
b = [m.add_beam(n[i], n[i + 1], s, c) for i in range(2)]
for nd in n:
    m.add_support(nd, dy=True, dz=True, rx=True)
m.add_support(n[0], dx=True)
m.add_udl(b[0], wz=-20e3, case=1)
m.name_case(1, "span 1 loaded")

print(m)                                   # model summary
print("nodes:", m.node_count, " bars:", m.bar_count)
print("problems detected:", m.validate())

text = m.to_json()                         # full model in JSON
d = json.loads(text)
print("JSON sections:", sorted(k for k in d if d[k]))
m2 = keta.Model.from_json(text)            # reading back
r1 = m.analyze().case(1).displacement(n[1])[4]
r2 = m2.analyze().case(1).displacement(n[1])[4]
print(f"rotation over support: {r1:.6e} rad (original), {r2:.6e} rad (read back)")
assert r1 == r2

script = m.export_script()                 # the model as a Python script
print("exported script:", len(script.splitlines()), "lines; start:")
print("\n".join(script.splitlines()[:3]))
print("module version:", keta.__version__)
```

Output

```text
<keta.Model: 3 nodes, 2 bars, 1 cases, 0 combos>
nodes: 3  bars: 2
problems detected: []
JSON sections: ['bars', 'cases', 'materials', 'nodes', 'sections', 'supports']
rotation over support: -2.922746e-04 rad (original), -2.922746e-04 rad (read back)
exported script: 49 lines; start:
# Generated by keta v1.0.0
#
# TWO FORMATS, ONE MODEL:
module version: 1.0.0
```

See Section 2.6: `keta.set_solver_threads(n)` and
`keta.solver_threads()`.

## 5.7 Online help

Each method and each function carries a description (in English) accessible through the Python
`help` function, which gives the signature, the default values and the accepted
keywords:

```text
help(keta.Model.add_beam)
help(keta.Model.phased)
```

# Chapter 6 Description of the geometry

The geometry of the structure is defined by the description of:

- the nodes;

- the rigid, elastic or skew supports;

- the bars (beams and trusses), their orientation, their offsets and their hinges;

- the sections and materials (Chapter 7) of the bars;

- where applicable, the elastic foundation of bars on soil, the links between nodes, the point
masses, the cables, the shells and the continuum elements.

The methods can be called in any order, provided that the referenced objects exist (a bar
refers to two nodes, a section and a material already created).

## 6.1 Nodes

Syntax

```python
m.add_node(x, y, z)  →  int
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x, y, z` | m | — | coordinates of the node in the global axes |

Creates a node and returns its identifier. Two nodes may occupy the same position (links between
coincident nodes, zero-length springs): they are not merged.

Series of nodes are generated with Python loops and lists. The identifiers are kept in a list
(a row of nodes), a list of lists (a grid) or a dictionary indexed by
position:

Example `examples/manual/ex_noeuds.py`

```python
# Generation of nodes and bars by Python loops.
import math
import keta

m = keta.Model()
# 1) A line of 11 nodes every 2 m along X (numbers 1 to 11)
line_x = [m.add_node(2.0 * i, 0.0, 0.0) for i in range(11)]
# 2) A circular arc of radius 15 m, 9 nodes, in the XZ plane
R, angle = 15.0, math.radians(80)
arc = []
for i in range(9):
    t = -angle / 2 + angle * i / 8
    arc.append(m.add_node(10.0 + R * math.sin(t), 8.0, R * math.cos(t) - R * math.cos(angle / 2)))
# 3) A grid of 4 x 3 nodes (numbered row by row)
grid = [[m.add_node(3.0 * i, 20.0 + 2.5 * j, 0.0) for i in range(4)] for j in range(3)]

steel, sec = m.steel(), m.add_section("HEA200")
bars_x = [m.add_beam(line_x[i], line_x[i + 1], sec, steel) for i in range(10)]
bars_arc = [m.add_beam(arc[i], arc[i + 1], sec, steel) for i in range(8)]
print("first and last node of the line:", line_x[0], line_x[-1])
print("nodes of the arc:", arc)
print("row 2 of the grid:", grid[1])
print("bars of the arc:", bars_arc)
print(m)
```

Output

```text
first and last node of the line: 1 11
nodes of the arc: [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20]
row 2 of the grid: [25, 26, 27, 28]
bars of the arc: [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18]
<keta.Model: 32 nodes, 18 bars, 0 cases, 0 combos>
```

**Note.**

The order of creation of the nodes has no influence on performance: the solver renumbers
the unknowns to minimise the fill-in of the factorised matrix.

## 6.2 Rigid supports

Syntax

```python
m.fix(node)
m.pin(node)
m.add_support(node, dx=False, dy=False, dz=False, rx=False, ry=False, rz=False,
              kx=None, ky=None, kz=None, krx=None, kry=None, krz=None)
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `node` | — | — | identifier of the supported node |
| `dx, dy, dz` | — | False | restraint of the translations along X, Y, Z (global axes) |
| `rx, ry, rz` | — | False | restraint of the rotations about X, Y, Z |
| `kx, ky, kz` | N/m | None | stiffness of a translational spring (Section 6.3) |
| `krx, kry, krz` | N·m/rad | None | stiffness of a rotational spring (Section 6.3) |

`fix` creates a fixed support (six degrees of freedom restrained), `pin` a
hinge (three translations restrained, rotations free). `add_support` restrains the
chosen components, expressed in the global axes.

**Figure 6.1** — Types of supports

**Note.**

Several supports can be declared on the same node; their restraints are cumulated. This is
the usual way of restraining the out-of-plane degrees of freedom of a plane structure:
`for n in nodes: m.add_support(n, dy=True, rx=True, rz=True)`.

**Important.**

At least one of the supports must prevent each rigid-body motion of the structure,
otherwise the analysis fails (“factorization failed (singular or structurally deficient stiffness)”).

## 6.3 Elastic supports

A spring is declared by the parameters `kx` to `krz` of
`add_support`. It acts along the corresponding component of the global axes, between the
node and a fixed point.

**Note.**

A spring placed on a restrained component has no effect: the rigid restraint prevails. A
single declaration can combine restraints and springs on different components
(`m.add_support(n, dy=True, kz=20e6)`).

A spring oriented in an arbitrary direction, or a spring with a nonlinear law, is obtained by an
elastic link to a fixed node (Section 6.11 and Chapter 17). The example of Section 4.5 (beam on an
elastic central support) illustrates a vertical elastic support.

### 6.3.1 Elastic supports with a full matrix, unilateral supports and uplift

Syntax

```python
m.set_support(node, uplift=None, decol=None, stiffness=None, rot=0.0, cap=None)
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `node` | — | — | supported node (the support is created if it does not exist) |
| `uplift` | — | None | unilateral support: dict(component=sign), for example dict(dz=+1); +1: the reaction must remain positive or zero, −1: negative or zero. The component must be restrained by `add_support` |
| `decol` | — | None | “all or nothing” uplift: (axis, sign), axis 'x', 'y' or 'z' global; when the reaction on this axis changes sign, all the components of the support are released |
| `stiffness` | — | None | stiffness matrix of the support in its own axes: 6 diagonal terms, or 21 terms of the lower half-matrix row by row (dx, dy, dz, rx, ry, rz) [N/m, N·m/rad] |
| `rot` | rad | 0 | rotation of the support axes about global Z (positive sense) |
| `cap` | N, N·m | None | force cap of a restrained component (yielding of a bearing): dict(component=Rmax), for example dict(dz=2e6); beyond it, the support carries ±Rmax and the node moves. The component must be restrained by `add_support` |

These options complement a support; they are given by name. The `stiffness` matrix is added to the springs
declared by `add_support`. For 21 terms, the order is that of the lower half-matrix read
by rows: k11; k21 k22; k31 k32 k33; …; k61 … k66.

**Important.**

A unilateral support, a support with uplift or a capped support makes the analysis nonlinear: each load case is
solved separately by an active-set method, and the results can no longer be superposed. A
combination of cases (`add_combination`) adds the results of the cases; it does not
represent the analysis under the sum of the loads. To study a combination, a load case is created
that contains all its factored loads. The unilateral conditions are taken into account by linear
statics `analyze` and by staged construction `phased`; the second-order,
large-displacement and link-law analyses treat the support as bilateral.

Example `examples/manual/ex_appuis_unilateraux.py`

```python
# Unilateral supports, lift-off and elastic support with a full matrix:
# two-span beam of 5 m spans, only the first span loaded.
import math
import keta

Ls, q, EI = 5.0, 10e3, 210e9 * 1e-4

def make_beam():
    m = keta.Model()
    st = m.add_material(e=210e9, nu=0.3, rho=0.0)
    s = m.add_section_props(sx=0.01, iy=1e-4, iz=1e-4, ix=1e-4)
    n = [m.add_node(Ls * i / 4, 0, 0) for i in range(9)]
    b = [m.add_beam(n[i], n[i + 1], s, st) for i in range(8)]
    m.add_support(n[0], dx=True, dy=True, dz=True, rx=True)
    m.add_support(n[4], dy=True, dz=True)
    m.add_support(n[8], dy=True, dz=True)
    for bi in b[:4]:
        m.add_udl(bi, wz=-q)
    return m, n

for option in (None, "uplift", "decol"):
    m, n = make_beam()
    if option == "uplift":
        m.set_support(n[8], uplift=dict(dz=+1))      # vertical reaction >= 0 only
    elif option == "decol":
        m.set_support(n[8], decol=("z", +1))         # the whole support is released if it lifts off
    case_ = m.analyze().case(1)
    R = dict(case_.reactions())
    Rb = R.get(n[8], (0.0,) * 6)[2]
    print(f"{str(option):6}: reactions A = {R[n[0]][2] / 1e3:7.3f}, B = {R[n[4]][2] / 1e3:7.3f}, "
          f"C = {round(Rb / 1e3, 3) + 0.0:7.3f} kN; uz(C) = {case_.displacement(n[8])[2] * 1e3:7.3f} mm")
print(f"expected free uplift: theta_B L = q L^3 / (24 EI) x L = {q * Ls**4 / (24 * EI) * 1e3:.3f} mm")

# Elastic support defined by its matrix (6 diagonal terms), rotated by 90° about Z:
# the "x" spring of the support acts along global Y
m = keta.Model()
st = m.add_material(e=210e9, nu=0.3, rho=0.0)
a, b = m.add_node(0, 0, 0), m.add_node(2, 0, 0)
m.add_truss(a, b, m.add_section_props(0.01, 1e-4, 1e-4, 1e-4), st)
m.fix(a)
m.add_support(b, dz=True, rx=True, ry=True, rz=True)
m.set_support(b, stiffness=[5e6, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], rot=math.pi / 2)
m.add_point_load(b, fx=2e3, fy=1e3)
d = m.analyze().case(1).displacement(b)
print(f"rotated support: uy = {d[1] * 1e3:.4f} mm (1 kN / 5 MN/m = 0.2000 mm), ux = {d[0] * 1e6:.4f} µm (elongation of the bar)")
```

Output

```text
None  : reactions A =  21.875, B =  31.250, C =  -3.125 kN; uz(C) =   0.000 mm
uplift: reactions A =  25.000, B =  25.000, C =   0.000 kN; uz(C) =  12.401 mm
decol : reactions A =  25.000, B =  25.000, C =   0.000 kN; uz(C) =  12.401 mm
expected free uplift: theta_B L = q L^3 / (24 EI) x L = 12.401 mm
rotated support: uy = 0.2000 mm (1 kN / 5 MN/m = 0.2000 mm), ux = 1.9048 µm (elongation of the bar)
```

Under the load on the first span, the bilateral end support holds the beam down (negative
reaction of −3.125 kN). Made unilateral, it lifts off: the two spans then behave as a statically
determinate beam with a cantilever and the end rises by θB·L.

## 6.4 Skew supports

Syntax

```python
m.add_skew_support(node, axes, dx=False, dy=False, dz=False, rx=False, ry=False, rz=False)  →  int
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `node` | — | — | supported node |
| `axes` | — | — | 3 × 3 matrix given by rows: unit vectors of the local x, y, z axes of the support, expressed in the global axes (orthonormal basis) |
| `dx … rz` | — | False | restrained components, in the support axes |

The skew support restrains components expressed in an arbitrary coordinate system: roller on an
inclined plane, support of a skew bridge. Its reactions are read by `skew_reactions()`,
which returns for each skew support the triplet (node, reaction in the support axes, reaction in
the global axes).

Example `examples/manual/ex_appui_biais.py`

```python
# Skew support: roller inclined at 30° in the XZ plane at the end of a beam.
import math
import keta

m = keta.Model()
a, c = m.add_node(0, 0, 0), m.add_node(6, 0, 0)
m.add_beam(a, c, m.add_section("IPE400"), m.steel())
m.add_support(a, dx=True, dy=True, dz=True, rx=True)
t = math.radians(30)
axes = [[math.cos(t), 0.0, math.sin(t)],        # local x: free direction of the roller
        [0.0, 1.0, 0.0],                          # local y
        [-math.sin(t), 0.0, math.cos(t)]]         # local z: normal to the rolling plane
m.add_skew_support(c, axes, dy=True, dz=True)     # restrains local y and z
m.add_point_load(c, fz=-50e3)

case_ = m.analyze().case(1)
node, loc, glob = case_.skew_reactions()[0]
print(f"node {node}: local reaction  Rz' = {loc[2] / 1e3:.3f} kN")
print(f"        global reaction Rx = {glob[0] / 1e3:.3f} kN, Rz = {glob[2] / 1e3:.3f} kN")
print(f"reaction of the fixed support: Rx = {case_.reactions()[0][1][0] / 1e3:.3f} kN")
assert abs(loc[2] - 50e3 / math.cos(t)) < 1e-6 * 50e3
```

Output

```text
node 2: local reaction  Rz' = 57.735 kN
        global reaction Rx = -28.868 kN, Rz = 50.000 kN
reaction of the fixed support: Rx = 28.868 kN
```

## 6.5 Bars

Syntax

```python
m.add_beam(n1, n2, section, material, beta=0.0, ecc=None)  →  int
m.add_truss(n1, n2, section, material)  →  int
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `n1, n2` | — | — | origin and end nodes; the local x axis runs from n1 to n2 |
| `section` | — | — | identifier of the section (Section 6.9) |
| `material` | — | — | identifier of the material (Chapter 7) |
| `beta` | rad | 0 | rotation of the local y and z axes about x (Section 6.6) |
| `ecc` | m | None | offset (ex, ey, ez) of the bar axis with respect to the line of the nodes, global axes (Section 6.7) |

`add_beam` creates a two-node spatial Timoshenko beam with twelve degrees of freedom:
tension-compression, Saint-Venant torsion, bending in two planes with shear deformation (taken into
account through the shear areas of the section). A section without shear areas gives an
Euler-Bernoulli beam. `add_truss` creates a pin-ended bar that works only in
tension-compression.

A bar is straight and of constant section. A curved beam or a beam with variable second moment of
area is modelled by a succession of bars.

### 6.5.1 Bars with variable section

Syntax

```python
m.set_tapered(bar, law, orig, ext, mid=None)
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bar` | — | — | bar concerned |
| `law` | — | — | law of variation: 'lin_y' or 'lin_z' (rectangle whose dimension along y, or along z, varies linearly: linear area and shear areas, cubic or linear second moments of area depending on the axis); 'para' (the inverse of each property varies along the parabola through the three sections) |
| `orig, ext` | — | — | section at the origin and at the end: section identifier or dict(A, Avy, Avz, Iy, Iz, J) |
| `mid` | — | None | section at mid-length, mandatory for 'para' |

The stiffness matrix and the equivalent loads of the bar are exact for the given variation of
section: they are obtained by integrating the flexibility along the bar. The internal forces at the
output stations are obtained by equilibrium. A shear area absent from the dictionary
(`Avy` or `Avz`) makes the bar infinitely stiff for the corresponding shear
force. The other properties (`A`, `Iy`, `Iz`, `J`) are
mandatory and strictly positive, otherwise a `ValueError` is raised.

**Important.**

`set_tapered` is called once the nodes, orientation, offsets and material of the
bar are final. The bar must carry no hinge. Its mass and geometric stiffness remain those of its own
section (that of `add_beam`): the mode shapes and the buckling of a variable bar are
computed with this mean section.

Example `examples/manual/ex_sections_variables.py`

```python
# Bar with variable section: cantilever of 8 m with linearly varying depth (1.0 -> 0.5 m),
# then inverse parabolic second moment of area; comparison with the integral of M m / EI(x).
import keta

E, L, P, b = 30e9, 8.0, 100e3, 0.3

def cantilever(law, orig, ext, mid=None, n=1):
    m = keta.Model()
    c = m.add_material(e=E, nu=0.2, rho=0.0)
    s = m.add_section_props(sx=0.3, iy=0.025, iz=0.002, ix=0.005)    # "mean" section of the bar
    nd = [m.add_node(L * i / n, 0, 0) for i in range(n + 1)]
    bars = [m.add_beam(nd[i], nd[i + 1], s, c) for i in range(n)]
    m.fix(nd[0])
    m.set_tapered(bars[0], law, orig, ext, mid)
    m.add_point_load(nd[-1], fz=-P)
    return m.analyze().case(1).displacement(nd[-1])[2]

def rect(h):                                    # properties of a b x h rectangle (no shear)
    return dict(A=b * h, Iy=b * h**3 / 12, Iz=h * b**3 / 12, J=0.1 * b**3 * h)

def simpson(f, a, c, n=2000):
    step = (c - a) / n
    return step / 3 * sum((1 if i in (0, n) else 4 if i % 2 else 2) * f(a + i * step) for i in range(n + 1))

w = cantilever("lin_z", rect(1.0), rect(0.5))
h = lambda x: 1.0 + (0.5 - 1.0) * x / L
wref = simpson(lambda x: P * (L - x) ** 2 / (E * b * h(x) ** 3 / 12), 0, L)
print(f"linear depth: uz = {w * 1e3:.5f} mm; integral of M m / EI = {-wref * 1e3:.5f} mm")

I0, Im, I1 = 0.025, 0.012, 0.004
w = cantilever("para", dict(A=0.3, Iy=I0, Iz=0.002, J=0.005), dict(A=0.2, Iy=I1, Iz=0.002, J=0.005),
               dict(A=0.25, Iy=Im, Iz=0.002, J=0.005))
inv = lambda t: (1 / I0) * 2 * (t - 0.5) * (t - 1) - (1 / Im) * 4 * t * (t - 1) + (1 / I1) * 2 * t * (t - 0.5)
wref = simpson(lambda x: P * (L - x) ** 2 * inv(x / L) / E, 0, L)
print(f"inverse parabolic: uz = {w * 1e3:.5f} mm; integral = {-wref * 1e3:.5f} mm")

# the same cantilever split into 8 prismatic bars of mean depth
m = keta.Model()
c = m.add_material(e=E, nu=0.2, rho=0.0)
nd = [m.add_node(i * 1.0, 0, 0) for i in range(9)]
for i in range(8):
    hm = h(i + 0.5)
    m.add_beam(nd[i], nd[i + 1], m.add_section_props(sx=b * hm, iy=b * hm**3 / 12, iz=hm * b**3 / 12, ix=0.01), c)
m.fix(nd[0])
m.add_point_load(nd[-1], fz=-P)
print(f"8 prismatic bars: uz = {m.analyze().case(1).displacement(nd[-1])[2] * 1e3:.5f} mm")
```

Output

```text
linear depth: uz = -37.21745 mm; integral of M m / EI = -37.21745 mm
inverse parabolic: uz = -31.57333 mm; integral = -31.57333 mm
8 prismatic bars: uz = -37.46347 mm
```

A single variable bar gives the value of the Mohr integral; the subdivision into eight prismatic
bars of mean depth gives a deflection approximate to within 0.7 %.

## 6.6 Orientation of sections

The default orientation of the local axes is described in Section 3.3. The parameter
`beta` of `add_beam` rotates the y and z axes by an angle β about the x axis,
in the positive sense. It serves to place the strong axis of a rolled section in the desired plane
or to orient the section of a column.

Example `examples/manual/ex_orientation.py`

```python
# Section orientation (angle beta): the same IPE 300 cantilever bent
# about its strong axis (beta = 0), then about its weak axis (beta = pi/2).
import math
import keta

def z(x):                     # removes the displayed negative zero
    return 0.0 if abs(x) < 1e-6 else x

for beta in (0.0, math.pi / 2):
    m = keta.Model()
    a, b = m.add_node(0, 0, 0), m.add_node(3, 0, 0)
    m.add_beam(a, b, m.add_section("IPE300"), m.steel(), beta=beta)
    m.fix(a)
    m.add_point_load(b, fz=-5e3)
    case_ = m.analyze().case(1)
    uz = case_.displacement(b)[2]
    x, N, Vy, Vz, T, My, Mz = case_.bar_forces(1)[0]
    print(f"beta = {beta:.4f} rad: uz = {uz * 1e3:8.3f} mm, My(0) = {z(My) / 1e3:7.3f} kN.m, Mz(0) = {z(Mz) / 1e3:7.3f} kN.m")

# Local axes of a vertical bar and of an inclined bar (read through the deflection under a load)
m = keta.Model()
a, b = m.add_node(0, 0, 0), m.add_node(0, 0, 4)
m.add_beam(a, b, m.add_section_rect(0.3, 0.5), m.concrete())
m.fix(a)
m.add_point_load(b, fx=10e3)          # horizontal force at the column head
x, N, Vy, Vz, T, My, Mz = m.analyze().case(1).bar_forces(1)[0]
print(f"column, base: Vy = {z(Vy) / 1e3:.3f} kN, Vz = {Vz / 1e3:.3f} kN, My = {My / 1e3:.3f} kN.m, Mz = {z(Mz) / 1e3:.3f} kN.m")
```

Output

```text
beta = 0.0000 rad: uz =   -2.654 mm, My(0) =  15.000 kN.m, Mz(0) =   0.000 kN.m
beta = 1.5708 rad: uz =  -35.554 mm, My(0) =   0.000 kN.m, Mz(0) = -15.000 kN.m
column, base: Vy = 0.000 kN, Vz = -10.000 kN, My = 40.000 kN.m, Mz = 0.000 kN.m
```

For β = π/2, the IPE 300 cantilever is bent about its weak axis: the deflection is multiplied by
the ratio of the second moments of area (apart from shear deformations) and the moment appears on
the Mz component. For the vertical column, the local z axis points along −X: a force along +X
produces a negative shear force Vz and a positive moment My at the base.

## 6.7 Offsets

The parameter `ecc = (ex, ey, ez)` shifts the axis of the bar with respect to the line
joining its nodes, by the same vector at both ends, expressed in the global axes. The nodes are
connected to the bar axis by infinitely rigid arms. This arrangement serves to model a beam under a
slab, a composite deck or an offset crosshead.

**Figure 6.2** — Offset bar: rigid arms between the nodes and the ends of the bar

Example `examples/manual/ex_excentrement.py`

```python
# Offsets: schematic composite deck, beam offset by 0.6 m below the node line.
import keta

def z(x):                     # removes the displayed negative zero
    return 0.0 if abs(x) < 1e-6 else x

L = 10.0
for e in (0.0, -0.6):
    m = keta.Model()
    a, b = m.add_node(0, 0, 0), m.add_node(L, 0, 0)
    beam = m.add_beam(a, b, m.add_section("HEB500"), m.steel(), ecc=(0.0, 0.0, e))
    m.add_support(a, dx=True, dy=True, dz=True, rx=True)
    m.add_support(b, dy=True, dz=True)
    m.add_point_load(b, fx=-200e3)                  # horizontal thrust on the movable support
    case_ = m.analyze().case(1)
    st = case_.bar_forces(beam)
    print(f"e = {e:5.2f} m: N = {st[5][1] / 1e3:8.2f} kN, My(mid) = {z(st[5][5]) / 1e3:8.2f} kN.m, "
          f"ux(B) = {case_.displacement(b)[0] * 1e3:7.4f} mm, ry(B) = {z(case_.displacement(b)[4]) * 1e3:7.4f} mrad")
```

Output

```text
e =  0.00 m: N =  -200.00 kN, My(mid) =     0.00 kN.m, ux(B) = -0.3991 mm, ry(B) =  0.0000 mrad
e = -0.60 m: N =  -200.00 kN, My(mid) =  -120.00 kN.m, ux(B) = -3.5981 mm, ry(B) = -2.6658 mrad
```

When the beam is offset 0.6 m below the line of the nodes, the horizontal thrust applied on
this line creates a constant moment N·e = 120 kN·m in the beam and a rotation of the
supports.

**Note.**

The internal forces at the output stations are those of the bar, referred to its own axis;
the reactions and displacements are those of the nodes.

### 6.7.1 Offsets specific to each end

Syntax

```python
m.set_eccentricity(bar, origin=(0, 0, 0), end=(0, 0, 0))
m.add_beam(n1, n2, section, material, ecc=None, ecc_end=None)  →  int
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bar` | — | — | identifier of the bar |
| `origin, end` | m | (0, 0, 0) | shift of the origin and of the end of the bar with respect to their nodes, global axes |
| `ecc_end` | m | None | in `add_beam`: shift of the end when it differs from `ecc` |

The bar then connects the point $\mathbf{x}_i + \mathbf{e}_O$ to the point
$\mathbf{x}_j + \mathbf{e}_E$; it can therefore be inclined with respect to the line of its
nodes, like a beam of variable depth placed under a horizontal line of nodes. The rigid arms
transmit the forces: a force $H$ applied at the node reaches the end of the bar accompanied by
the moment $H\,e$.

Example `examples/manual/ex_liberations.py`

```python
# Offsets specific to each end, translation and torsion releases.
import keta

def z(x):
    return 0.0 if abs(x) < 1e-9 else x

# 1) 6 m cantilever whose axis is raised by 0.4 m at both ends: H in the line of the nodes
L, e, H = 6.0, 0.4, 100e3
m = keta.Model()
a, b = m.add_node(0, 0, 0), m.add_node(L, 0, 0)
sec = m.add_section_props(sx=0.3, iy=0.01, iz=0.05, ix=0.01)
mat = m.add_material(e=30e9, nu=0.2)
beam = m.add_beam(a, b, sec, mat)
m.set_eccentricity(beam, origin=(0, 0, e), end=(0, 0, e))
m.fix(a)
m.add_point_load(b, fx=H)
case_ = m.analyze().case(1)
ux = case_.displacement(b)[0]
print(f"ux(B) = {ux * 1e3:.4f} mm  (H L/EA + H e2 L/EI = {(H * L / (30e9 * 0.3) + H * e * e * L / (30e9 * 0.01)) * 1e3:.4f} mm)")
print(f"My in the bar = {case_.bar_forces(beam)[5][5] / 1e3:.2f} kN.m  (H e = {H * e / 1e3:.2f})")

# 2) same cantilever, only the end is raised: the bar is inclined
m.set_eccentricity(beam, end=(0, 0, e))
case_ = m.analyze().case(1)
print(f"clamping moment = {z(case_.reactions()[0][1][4]):.2f} N.m, "
      f"moment at the bar end = {case_.bar_forces(beam)[-1][5] / 1e3:.2f} kN.m")

# 3) two aligned bars clamped at both ends; the first one released in dx and rx at its end
m = keta.Model()
n = [m.add_node(5.0 * i, 0, 0) for i in range(3)]
s = m.add_section_rect(b=0.3, h=0.5)
b1 = m.add_beam(n[0], n[1], s, m.concrete())
m.add_beam(n[1], n[2], s, m.concrete())
m.fix(n[0]); m.fix(n[2])
m.set_releases(b1, end="dx rx")
m.add_point_load(n[1], fx=10e3, mx=2e3)
for nd, r in m.analyze().case(1).reactions():
    print(f"node {nd}: Fx = {z(r[0]) / 1e3:7.2f} kN, Mx = {z(r[3]) / 1e3:6.2f} kN.m")
```

Output

```text
ux(B) = 0.3867 mm  (H L/EA + H e2 L/EI = 0.3867 mm)
My in the bar = -40.00 kN.m  (H e = 40.00)
clamping moment = 0.00 N.m, moment at the bar end = -40.00 kN.m
node 1: Fx =    0.00 kN, Mx =   0.00 kN.m
node 3: Fx =  -10.00 kN, Mx =  -2.00 kN.m
```

With the same shift at both ends, the displacement of the free node adds to the elongation
$HL/EA$ the rotation of the bar multiplied by the arm,
$He^2L/EI$. With a shift at the end only, the force passes through the fixed support: the
fixed-end moment is zero, and the bar receives the moment $He$ at its end.

## 6.8 Hinges

Syntax

```python
m.set_releases(bar, ry_or=False, rz_or=False, ry_ex=False, rz_ex=False)
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bar` | — | — | identifier of the bar |
| `ry_or, rz_or` | — | False | release of the rotation about y, about z at the origin of the bar |
| `ry_ex, rz_ex` | — | False | release of the rotation about y, about z at the end of the bar |

Releases the bending rotations at the ends of a bar (hinge). The released components are
condensed in the bar matrix; the corresponding moment is zero there and the nodes remain connected
to the other bars.

**Important.**

Each call replaces the hinges previously declared for the bar: all the desired releases are
given at once. A release that leaves a node free in rotation (all the bars hinged at the same node,
without a support) causes an instability.

Example `examples/manual/ex_articulations.py`

```python
# End hinges: two-span beam of 6 m spans, continuous, then made
# statically determinate by a hinge (ry) at the start of the second span.
import keta

L, q = 6.0, -10e3

def z(x):                     # removes the displayed negative zero
    return 0.0 if abs(x) < 1e-6 else x

def two_span(hinge):
    m = keta.Model()
    n = [m.add_node(L * i, 0, 0) for i in range(3)]
    sec, mat = m.add_section("IPE330"), m.steel()
    b = [m.add_beam(n[i], n[i + 1], sec, mat) for i in range(2)]
    m.add_support(n[0], dx=True, dy=True, dz=True, rx=True)
    m.add_support(n[1], dy=True, dz=True)
    m.add_support(n[2], dy=True, dz=True)
    for bi in b:
        m.add_udl(bi, wz=q)
    if hinge:
        m.set_releases(b[1], ry_or=True)   # rotation ry released at the start of bar 2
    case_ = m.analyze().case(1)
    return case_.bar_forces(b[0])[-1][5], dict(case_.reactions())[n[1]][2]

for hinge in (False, True):
    My, R = two_span(hinge)
    print(f"hinge = {hinge!s:5}: My over central support = {z(My) / 1e3:7.3f} kN.m, reaction = {R / 1e3:7.3f} kN")
print(f"Euler-Bernoulli: -q L²/8 = {-q * L * L / 8 / 1e3:.3f} kN.m; reactions 10 q L/8 = {-10 * q * L / 8 / 1e3:.3f} kN and 2 q L/2 = {-q * L / 1e3:.3f} kN")
```

Output

```text
hinge = False: My over central support =  44.532 kN.m, reaction =  74.844 kN
hinge = True : My over central support =   0.000 kN.m, reaction =  60.000 kN
Euler-Bernoulli: -q L²/8 = 45.000 kN.m; reactions 10 q L/8 = 75.000 kN and 2 q L/2 = 60.000 kN
```

The continuous beam (without hinge) differs slightly from the Euler-Bernoulli closed forms
(44.53 instead of 45.00 kN·m): shear deforms the IPE 330 section and relieves the central support.
With the hinge, the two spans become statically determinate.

### 6.8.1 Release of all components

Syntax

```python
m.set_releases(bar, ry_or=False, rz_or=False, ry_ex=False, rz_ex=False, origin='', end='')
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `origin, end` | — | '' | components released at the origin, at the end, among `dx dy dz rx ry rz` (local axes), separated by spaces |

The keywords `origin` and `end` complement the four booleans: they also
release the translations and torsion. A bar released in `dx` at one end no longer
transmits axial force (sliding bearing of a deck, expansion joint); released in `rx`, it
no longer transmits torsional moment. In the third part of the example above, the axial force and
the torque applied at the central node are carried entirely by the right-hand fixed support.

## 6.9 Sections

A section is created once and can be assigned to several bars. It carries the area A, the bending
second moments of area Iy and Iz, the torsion constant J and the shear areas Avy and Avz.

### 6.9.1 Catalogue sections

Syntax

```python
m.add_section(designation)  →  int
keta.section_props(designation)  →  dict
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `designation` | — | — | designation of a European rolled section: IPE 80 to IPE 600, HEA, HEB and HEM 100 to 1000 (EN 10365); case, spaces and hyphens are ignored (“HEB 300”, “heb-300”) |

The properties take account of the web-flange root fillets. An unknown designation raises
`KeyError`. The function `section_props` returns, without creating a section,
the dictionary of the catalogue properties: `A`, `Iy`, `Iz`,
`J`, `Iw` (warping constant), `Asy`, `Asz` (code shear
areas of the rolled section).

### 6.9.2 Parametric sections

Syntax

```python
m.add_section_rect(b, h)  →  int
m.add_section_tube(d, t)  →  int
m.add_section_i(h, b, tw, tf)  →  int
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `b, h` | m | — | solid rectangle: width along local y, depth along local z |
| `d, t` | m | — | circular tube: outer diameter, thickness |
| `h, b, tw, tf` | m | — | doubly symmetric (welded) I-section: depth, flange width, web thickness, flange thickness |

### 6.9.3 Directly given properties

Syntax

```python
m.add_section_props(sx, iy, iz, ix, sy=None, sz=None, name=None, iw=0.0, beta_x=0.0)  →  int
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sx` | m² | — | area of the section |
| `iy, iz` | m⁴ | — | bending second moments of area about the local y and z axes |
| `ix` | m⁴ | — | Saint-Venant torsion constant |
| `sy, sz` | m² | None | shear areas along y and z; None: section infinitely stiff in shear (Euler-Bernoulli) |
| `name` | — | None | name of the section (carried into the JSON) |
| `iw` | m⁶ | 0 | warping constant, read by `warping` and `lateral_buckling` (Section 16.8) |
| `beta_x` | m | 0 | Wagner coefficient of the section, read by the same analyses |

### 6.9.4 Shear areas

For parametric and catalogue sections, keta computes by default the shear areas consistent with
the strain energy of Saint-Venant flexure, for the Poisson's ratio of the material of the bar. They
are determined when the first bar that uses the section is created. The classical convention of
shape factors (5/6 for a rectangle, 0.9 for a circle, web area for a rolled section) can be chosen
instead:

Syntax

```python
keta.set_shear_areas(convention)
keta.shear_areas()  →  str
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `convention` | — | 'energy' | 'energy': energy-based areas; 'shape_factor': classical shape factors |

The setting is global to the process and applies to bars created afterwards.

**Important.**

The shear areas returned by `section_props` are those of the catalogue; under the
default convention, the bar uses the energy-based area, which differs (for the IPE 300,
Avz = 20.8 cm² instead of 25.7 cm²). The values actually used can be read in the JSON model, as in
the example of Section 5.5 and below.

Example `examples/manual/ex_sections.py`

```python
# Sections: catalogue, parametric sections and direct properties.
import json
import keta

for name in ("IPE300", "HEA400", "HEB1000"):
    p = keta.section_props(name)
    print(f"{name:8} A = {p['A'] * 1e4:8.2f} cm2  Iy = {p['Iy'] * 1e8:10.1f} cm4  "
          f"Iz = {p['Iz'] * 1e8:9.1f} cm4  J = {p['J'] * 1e8:7.2f} cm4")

m = keta.Model()
steel = m.steel()
ids = {
    "catalogue HEB 300": m.add_section("heb 300"),          # case and spaces tolerated
    "rectangle 0.4 x 0.8": m.add_section_rect(b=0.4, h=0.8),
    "tube 323.9 x 10": m.add_section_tube(d=0.3239, t=0.010),
    "welded I 1200 x 400": m.add_section_i(h=1.2, b=0.4, tw=0.012, tf=0.030),
    "direct properties": m.add_section_props(sx=0.25, iy=0.02, iz=0.01, ix=0.015, sy=0.2, sz=0.2,
                                            name="box"),
}
# the shear areas of the parametric sections are fixed when the first bar is created
# (they depend on the Poisson's ratio of the material)
n0 = m.add_node(0, 0, 0)
for i, s in enumerate(ids.values()):
    m.add_beam(n0, m.add_node(1.0, i, 0), s, steel)
props = {s["id"]: s["props"] for s in json.loads(m.to_json())["sections"]}
for name, s in ids.items():
    p = props[s]
    print(f"{name:27} A = {p['A']:.5e}  Iy = {p['Iy']:.5e}  Avz = {p['Avz']:.5e}  J = {p['J']:.5e}")
print("shear area convention:", keta.shear_areas())
```

Output

```text
IPE300   A =    53.81 cm2  Iy =     8356.1 cm4  Iz =     603.8 cm4  J =   19.92 cm4
HEA400   A =   158.98 cm2  Iy =    45069.4 cm4  Iz =    8563.8 cm4  J =  193.17 cm4
HEB1000  A =   400.05 cm2  Iy =   644748.3 cm4  Iz =   16275.8 cm4  J = 1267.08 cm4
catalogue HEB 300           A = 1.49078e-02  Iy = 2.51657e-04  Avz = 3.22611e-03  J = 1.89178e-06
rectangle 0.4 x 0.8         A = 3.20000e-01  Iy = 1.70667e-02  Avz = 2.66541e-01  J = 1.17085e-02
tube 323.9 x 10             A = 9.86146e-03  Iy = 1.21583e-04  Avz = 4.93898e-03  J = 2.43167e-04
welded I 1200 x 400         A = 3.76800e-02  Iy = 9.69674e-03  Avz = 1.39206e-02  J = 7.85664e-06
direct properties           A = 2.50000e-01  Iy = 2.00000e-02  Avz = 2.00000e-01  J = 1.50000e-02
shear area convention: energy
```

### 6.9.5 Sections of arbitrary shape

Syntax

```python
keta.section_polygon(outer, holes=[], nu=0.2, mesh_size=0.0, materials=[], regions=[])  →  dict
m.add_section_polygon(outer, holes=[], name=None, exact=True, nu=0.2, mesh_size=0.0)  →  int
keta.section_stress(outer, actions, points=[], holes=[], nu=0.2, mesh_size=0.0, materials=[], regions=[])  →  dict
keta.import_dxf(text, scale=1.0, arc_sagitta=0.0, is_path=False)  →  dict(outer, holes)
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `outer` | m | — | outer contour, list of points (y, z) in counterclockwise or clockwise order |
| `holes` | m | [] | voids, each described like the outer contour |
| `nu` | — | 0.2 | Poisson's ratio used for the shear areas |
| `mesh_size` | m | 0 | size of the elements of the section mesh (0: one twentieth of the largest dimension) |
| `exact` | — | True | computation of torsion and shear areas by finite elements; False: area and second moments of area only |
| `materials, regions` | — | [] | composite section: materials [dict(E, nu=0.3)] and regions [dict(outline, material)]; a region gives its material (index in materials) to the elements it contains, the rest keeps material 0 |
| `actions` | N, N·m, N·m² | — | actions dict(N, Vy, Vz, T, My, Mz, B) at the elastic centroid and at the shear centre; absent keys are 0 |
| `points` | m | [] | points (y, z) where the stresses are read, in the axes of the contour |
| `text, is_path` | — | —, False | text of a DXF drawing (ASCII), or path of the file if is_path |
| `scale, arc_sagitta` | — | 1, 0 | factor from the drawing unit to the metre (1e-3 for millimetres); maximum sagitta of the chords that replace the arcs, in drawing units (0: one thousandth of the radius) |

The area and second moments of area are computed by integration over the contour (Green's theorem).
The torsion constant, the warping constant, the shear centre and the shear areas come from the
solution, by six-node triangular finite elements, of the Saint-Venant warping problem,
$\Delta\omega = 0$ in the section with
$\partial\omega/\partial n = z\,n_y - y\,n_z$ on the contour. The returned dictionary contains
`A`, `yc`, `zc` (centroid), `Iy`, `Iz`,
`Iyz`, the principal second moments of area `I1`, `I2` and their angle
`phi`, `J`, `Iw`, the shear centre `ys`,
`zs`, the areas `Avy`, `Avz` and the distances to the extreme fibres
`ymax`, `zmax`.

A composite section is described by its materials and by the regions they occupy. Its properties
are those of the section transformed to the modulus of material 0, `E_ref`: `A`
remains the geometric area, `EA_ref` is the transformed area $\sum (E_i/E_{ref})\,A_i$,
and the centroid, the second moments of area, the torsion and the shear areas are weighted in the
same way. The Poisson's ratios are then those of the materials.

`section_stress` computes the stresses in the section under given actions. At each
requested point it returns `sigma`, `tau_y`, `tau_z`,
`tau` and `von_mises`. It also gives `sigma_min` and
`sigma_max`, each in the form (value, y, z), which are the extremes of the normal stress
due to N, My and Mz, reached on the contour, and `von_mises_max`, taken at the nodes of
the mesh. The normal stress is $N/A + M_y z/I_y - M_z y/I_z$ about the centroid,
multiplied by $E_i/E_{ref}$ in material i of a composite section; the warping stress due to
the bimoment B is added to it. The shear stresses due to Vy, Vz and T come from the Saint-Venant fields computed by
finite elements. A point outside the section is rejected.

`import_dxf` reads the contour of a section in a drawing: closed polylines, with
their arcs, and circles. The largest closed contour is the outer contour, the others its voids;
all are returned in counterclockwise order, ready for `section_polygon` and
`add_section_polygon`.

**Important.**

In a model, the axes of the polygon must be its principal axes of inertia ($I_{yz} = 0$):
an arbitrary contour is first rotated or re-centred by the user.

Syntax

```python
keta.thinwall_section(nodes, walls)  →  dict
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nodes` | m | — | nodes of the mid-line of the walls, (y, z) |
| `walls` | — | — | walls (node a, node b, thickness t [m]), or (node a, node b, t_a, t_b) for a thickness varying linearly from a to b; nodes numbered from 0 |

The open parts follow Vlasov theory ($J = \sum b\,t^3/3$), the closed cells Bredt theory,
whatever their number ($J = 4A^2 / \oint \mathrm{d}s/t$ for one cell). The result also
contains `J_open`, `J_closed`, the number of cells and the elastic section
moduli.

A wall of linear thickness is treated by the same formulas, the thickness remaining under the
integral: $\oint \mathrm{d}s/t$ is $L \ln(t_b/t_a)/(t_b - t_a)$ on the wall, the open
term $L\,(t_a + t_b)(t_a^2 + t_b^2)/12$, and the shear flow becomes cubic along the
wall.

Example `examples/manual/ex_section_polygone.py`

```python
# General sections: polygon with a void (section finite elements) and thin walls.
import math
import keta

# solid rectangle 0.8 x 0.4 m: torsion compared with the Saint-Venant series
b, h = 0.8, 0.4
rect = [(-b / 2, -h / 2), (b / 2, -h / 2), (b / 2, h / 2), (-b / 2, h / 2)]
p = keta.section_polygon(rect, mesh_size=0.02)
series = sum(math.tanh(k * math.pi * b / (2 * h)) / k**5 for k in range(1, 200, 2))
J = b * h**3 / 3 * (1 - 192 / math.pi**5 * h / b * series)
print(f"A = {p['A']:.4f} m2, Iy = {p['Iy']:.6f} m4 (b h3/12 = {b * h**3 / 12:.6f})")
print(f"J = {p['J']:.6f} m4 (series: {J:.6f}), Avz = {p['Avz']:.4f} m2")

# hollow box: the kernel computes J, Iw and the shear centre
void = [(-0.3, -0.1), (0.3, -0.1), (0.3, 0.1), (-0.3, 0.1)]
q = keta.section_polygon(rect, [void], mesh_size=0.02)
print(f"box: A = {q['A']:.4f} m2, Iy = {q['Iy']:.6f} m4, J = {q['J']:.6f} m4")

# thin walls: square box of 1 m, thickness 10 mm (Bredt: J = a3 t)
a, t = 1.0, 0.01
c = keta.thinwall_section([(0, 0), (a, 0), (a, a), (0, a)], [(0, 1, t), (1, 2, t), (2, 3, t), (3, 0, t)])
print(f"Bredt: J = {c['J']:.6f} m4 (a3 t = {a**3 * t:.6f}), {c['cells']} cell")

# polygonal section in a model: cantilever in torsion
m = keta.Model()
s = m.add_section_polygon(rect, mesh_size=0.02)
n1, n2 = m.add_node(0, 0, 0), m.add_node(4, 0, 0)
m.add_beam(n1, n2, s, m.add_material(e=30e9, nu=0.2))
m.fix(n1)
m.add_point_load(n2, mx=1e3)
rx = m.analyze().case(1).displacement(n2)[3]
print(f"torsional rotation = {rx * 1e6:.4f} microrad (T L / G J = {1e3 * 4 / (12.5e9 * J) * 1e6:.4f})")
```

Output

```text
A = 0.3200 m2, Iy = 0.004267 m4 (b h3/12 = 0.004267)
J = 0.011709 m4 (series: 0.011709), Avz = 0.2583 m2
box: A = 0.2000 m2, Iy = 0.003867 m4, J = 0.009992 m4
Bredt: J = 0.010000 m4 (a3 t = 0.010000), 1 cell
torsional rotation = 27.3305 microrad (T L / G J = 27.3306)
```

Syntax

```python
keta.thinwall_from_quads(contour, walls, snap=0.0)  →  dict(nodes, walls)
keta.thinwall_from_nodes(contour, nodes, branches)  →  dict(nodes, walls)
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `contour` | m | — | points of the contour of the section, (y, z), outer and inner contours one after the other |
| `walls` | — | — | thinwall_from_quads: one wall per quadruplet of points (p, q, r, s) taken going round it, p→q and s→r being its two faces |
| `snap` | m | 0 | distance below which two wall ends are the same node (0: 1e-6 of the extent of the contour) |
| `nodes` | — | — | thinwall_from_nodes: for each junction, the list of the contour points attached to it (at least two) |
| `branches` | — | — | walls (node a, node b) between these junctions |

These two functions derive the mid-line and the thicknesses from a contour; their result is
passed as is to thinwall_section. With quadrilaterals, the mid-line of a wall joins the midpoints of
its two short sides p-s and q-r, and the thickness at an end is its short side projected on the
normal to the mid-line: for a corner cut on the skew, this gives the actual thickness and not the
length of the diagonal. With
nodes and branches, the spread of the points of a node across a branch gives its thickness at that
end, and each node is placed at the intersection of the mid-lines of its branches. A wall whose two
ends do not have the same thickness becomes a wall of linear thickness. The ratio of the two
thicknesses is free: a cantilever slab that goes from 0.50 m to 0.20 m is described by a single
wall. A wall without a determinate mid-line (zero length or thickness, or, with quadrilaterals, two
faces whose lengths differ by more than half the longer one) is rejected.

Example `examples/manual/ex_morphologie.py`

```python
# Simplified bridge box girder given by its outline: top slab of 12 m x 0.25 m, webs of
# 0.40 m, bottom slab of 0.30 m. The mid-line and the thicknesses are derived from the outline
# by nodes and branches, then the section is analysed as thin-walled.
import keta

contour = [
    (-6.0, 0.0), (6.0, 0.0), (6.0, -0.25), (3.0, -0.25),       # 0 to 3: top surface and right cantilever slab
    (3.0, -3.0), (-3.0, -3.0), (-3.0, -0.25), (-6.0, -0.25),   # 4 to 7: webs, soffit, left cantilever slab
    (-2.6, -0.25), (2.6, -0.25), (2.6, -2.70), (-2.6, -2.70),  # 8 to 11: cell void
    (-3.0, 0.0), (-2.6, 0.0), (2.6, 0.0), (3.0, 0.0),          # 12 to 15: top surface above the webs
]
nodes = [
    [0, 7],             # 0: left edge
    [12, 13, 6, 8],     # 1: junction of the top slab and the left web
    [14, 15, 9, 3],     # 2: junction of the top slab and the right web
    [1, 2],             # 3: right edge
    [5, 11],            # 4: bottom left corner
    [4, 10],            # 5: bottom right corner
]
branches = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (1, 4), (4, 5), (5, 2)]

g = keta.thinwall_from_nodes(contour, nodes, branches)
print("mid-line nodes:", [(round(y, 3), round(z, 3)) for y, z in g["nodes"]])
print("thicknesses:", [round(ta, 3) for _, _, ta, _ in g["walls"]])
p = keta.thinwall_section(g["nodes"], g["walls"])
print(f"A = {p['A']:.3f} m² (outline: {12 * 0.25 + 2 * 0.40 * 2.45 + 6 * 0.30:.3f} m², the junctions are "
      f"counted twice), zc = {p['zc']:.3f} m")
print(f"Iy = {p['Iy']:.2f} m4, J = {p['J']:.2f} m4, {p['cells']} cell")
# by hand: Bredt on the mid-line cell 5.6 x 2.725 m
Am, contour_ds_t = 5.6 * 2.725, 5.6 / 0.25 + 5.6 / 0.30 + 2 * 2.725 / 0.40
print(f"Bredt by hand: closed J = {4 * Am ** 2 / contour_ds_t:.2f} m4 (computed {p['J_closed']:.2f})")
```

Output

```text
mid-line nodes: [(-6.0, -0.125), (-2.8, -0.125), (2.8, -0.125), (6.0, -0.125), (-2.8, -2.85), (2.8, -2.85)]
thicknesses: [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.4, 0.3, 0.4]
A = 6.860 m² (outline: 6.760 m², the junctions are counted twice), zc = -1.225 m
Iy = 9.59 m4, J = 17.06 m4, 1 cell
Bredt by hand: closed J = 17.03 m4 (computed 17.03)
```

Syntax

```python
keta.resal_web_shear(A, Iy, Iz, chords, N=0.0, Vy=0.0, Vz=0.0, My=0.0, Mz=0.0)  →  dict
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `A, Iy, Iz` | m², m⁴ | — | area and principal second moments of area of the whole section, at the cut |
| `chords` | — | — | chords: (area, y, z, dy/dx, dz/dx), position of the centroid of the chord from that of the section and slopes of its line along the bar |
| `N, Vy, Vz, My, Mz` | N, N·m | 0 | actions on the section (convention of the bar results) |

This function evaluates the Résal effect in a beam of variable depth. Each chord carries its axial force
$N_f = \sigma_f A_f$ along its inclined line, with
$\sigma_f = N/A + M_y z_f/I_y - M_z y_f/I_z$. The transverse component of these forces is
subtracted from the shear force, $V_{z,\text{web}} = V_z - \sum N_f\,\mathrm{d}z_f/\mathrm{d}x$
(EN 1992-1-1, 6.2.1(1)). The result gives the shear force left to the web (`Vy`,
`Vz`), the part carried by the chords (`relief_y`, `relief_z`)
and the factors of the section, that is, the part carried per unit of (N, My, Mz). For two equal
chords at a distance h apart, the lower one inclined at α, under a moment M alone, the web keeps
$V - (M/h)\tan\alpha$. The values are raw: their sign shows whether the chords relieve
the web or load it.

Example `examples/manual/ex_resal.py`

```python
# Box girder of variable depth near a support: horizontal top chord (0.60 m²),
# bottom chord (0.35 m²) inclined at 8 % (the depth increases towards the support), 2.60 m between the
# centroids of the chords at the cut. Negative moment of 30 MN.m (top fibre
# in tension), shear force of 4 MN, prestressing axial force of -12 MN.
import keta

A, Iy, Iz = 1.45, 1.92, 3.4            # whole section at the cut
z_top, z_bot = 1.05, -1.55             # chords, from the centroid
chords = [(0.60, 0.0, z_top, 0.0, 0.0), (0.35, 0.0, z_bot, 0.0, 0.08)]
N, Vz, My = -12e6, -4e6, 30e6

r = keta.resal_web_shear(A, Iy, Iz, chords, N=N, Vz=Vz, My=My)
print(f"total shear force {Vz / 1e6:.2f} MN, carried by the chords {r['relief_z'] / 1e6:.3f} MN, "
      f"left to the web {r['Vz'] / 1e6:.3f} MN")
# by hand: force in the bottom chord, then its vertical component
N_bot = 0.35 * (N / A + My * z_bot / Iy)
print(f"by hand: N_bot = {N_bot / 1e6:.3f} MN, N_bot x 0.08 = {N_bot * 0.08 / 1e6:.3f} MN")
kN, kMy, kMz = r["factors_z"]
print(f"section factors: {kN:.5f} per N, {kMy:.5f} 1/m per My")
```

Output

```text
total shear force -4.00 MN, carried by the chords -0.910 MN, left to the web -3.090 MN
by hand: N_bot = -11.373 MN, N_bot x 0.08 = -0.910 MN
section factors: 0.01931 per N, -0.02260 1/m per My
```

## 6.10 Bars on elastic foundation

Syntax

```python
m.set_soil(bar, kfx=0.0, kfy=0.0, kfz=0.0, kmx=0.0)
```

| Parameter | Unit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bar` | — | — | bar resting on the soil |
| `kfx, kfy, kfz` | N/m per m | 0 | distributed subgrade reaction moduli along the local x, y, z axes (soil modulus multiplied by the bearing width) |
| `kmx` | N·m/rad per m | 0 | distributed torsional stiffness |

The bar rests on a bed of continuous springs (Winkler model), expressed in its local axes. In
linear statics, a frame bar without release or shear area is computed from the exact solution of the
beam on elastic foundation (transfer functions in series): the displacements and internal forces do
not depend on the mesh, and the internal forces at the output stations include the soil reaction. A
Timoshenko bar or a bar with a release, and the other analyses (modes, buckling, nonlinear), use a
