$\left[\begin{smallmatrix}2 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{smallmatrix}\right]$, $I_p$ being the
polar moment of inertia ($I_y + I_z$ by default). The lumped matrix places $\rho A L/2$ on
each translation and $\rho I_p L/2$ on each torsional rotation. A truss bar receives the
consistent mass of linear interpolation on its three translations. Rigid arms transform the mass as
they do the stiffness. This matrix is not exact: subdividing the bar is necessary in dynamics, as
chapter 15 explains.

## 3.10 Scope and limits

The keta beam element is exact, in the sense of beam theory, for the linear statics of a
prismatic bar or a bar with variable cross-section under the loads described above. Its limits are
as follows:

- the bar is straight; a curved beam is represented by a sequence of bars;

- the shear centre coincides with the centroid, and the axes of the cross-section are its
principal axes: an asymmetric cross-section must be described in its principal axes, with the angle
$\beta$ orienting them;

- torsion is uniform; restrained warping is covered in chapter 19;

- the mass and the geometric stiffness are consistent approximations (chapters 15 and 17), and
remain those of the constant cross-section on a bar with variable cross-section;

- a bar of zero length, a beam bar with a zero second moment of area, an offset truss bar or a
truss bar on elastic foundation, a bar with variable cross-section fitted with releases, a release
that turns the bar into a mechanism, a load outside the bar, a thermal load on a material without a
coefficient of thermal expansion and any non-finite input are refused by an error that names
them.

# Chapter 4 Assembly, solution and recovery

This chapter follows a linear static analysis from start to finish: the numbering of the unknowns
and the elimination of the supports, the assembly of the sparse stiffness matrix, the treatment of
rigid links and linear relations, the factorisation of the matrix and its use as a diagnostic, then
the passage from the nodal displacements to the quantities the engineer works with: reactions,
internal forces and displacements along the bars, stresses. The same tools serve the other
analyses, which call on them at each of their steps: chapter 15 adds the mass, chapter 17 the
geometric stiffness and the Newton iterations, chapter 10 the succession of stages. The elements
whose matrices are assembled are described in chapters 3 (bars), 6 (supports and elastic links), 24
and 25 (shells and continuum elements).

## 4.1 Assumptions

- the problem is linear: the stiffness matrix depends neither on the displacements nor on the
loads, and the results of several cases can be superposed;

- all the load cases of an analysis act on the same structure: same elements, same supports, same
links; they therefore share the same matrix;

- supports are bilateral. Unilateral and capped supports, which make each case nonlinear, are
dealt with in chapter 6;

- rigid links are exact (no penalty stiffness) and rotations in them are small.

## 4.2 Numbering and elimination of the supports

The global displacement vector stores the six components of each node in the order in which the
nodes were created: component $c$ of the node of rank $n$ occupies position $6n + c$.
The degrees of freedom restrained by a rigid support are removed from this vector; the others,
called free, are renumbered in the same order. Partitioning the unknowns into free $f$ and
restrained $s$, equilibrium reads

$$ \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{K}_{ff} & \mathbf{K}_{fs}\\ \mathbf{K}_{sf} & \mathbf{K}_{ss}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{u}_f\\ \bar{\mathbf{u}}_s\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{F}_f\\ \mathbf{F}_s + \mathbf{R}_s\end{bmatrix}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{K}_{ff}\,\mathbf{u}_f = \mathbf{F}_f - \mathbf{K}_{fs}\,\bar{\mathbf{u}}_s $$ (4.1)

where $\bar{\mathbf{u}}_s$ is zero except for an imposed support displacement (settlement,
support rotation) and $\mathbf{R}_s$ denotes the reactions. Only the matrix
$\mathbf{K}_{ff}$ is assembled and factorised; it does not depend on the imposed displacements,
which move to the right-hand side. The product $\mathbf{K}_{fs}\,\bar{\mathbf{u}}_s$ is computed
element by element, without forming $\mathbf{K}_{fs}$. A displacement can be imposed only on a
degree of freedom restrained by a rigid support, and only once per case: otherwise the calculation
stops.

Elastic supports add their stiffness to the diagonal of $\mathbf{K}_{ff}$, or a full
$6\times6$ matrix to the block of the node for a coupled elastic support (chapter 6). Their
degrees of freedom remain unknowns.

### 4.2.1 Automatic restraints

A degree of freedom that receives strictly no stiffness from any element, any elastic support or
any link is eliminated as if it were restrained, and reported in the list of automatic
restraints:

$$ \sum_e k^{(e)}_{ii} = 0\quad\text{and}\quad k^\text{support}_{ii} = 0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad u_i \text{ eliminated} $$ (4.2)

Since the diagonal terms of the element matrices are positive or zero, the sum is zero only if no
element restrains this degree of freedom. The typical case is that of the rotations of a node that
carries only truss bars or cables, or of an isolated node. The criterion is an exact zero: it does
not detect a stiffness that is non-zero but insufficient (for example a rotation restrained in a
single direction that is not a global axis). Such cases are caught by the pivot check described
further on. No reaction is returned on an automatic restraint, since it transmits no force.

## 4.3 Assembly

The global matrix is the sum of the contributions of all the elements, each placed in the rows and
columns of its free degrees of freedom:

$$ \mathbf{K}_{ff} = \sum_{e} \mathbf{A}_e^\mathsf{T}\,\mathbf{K}_e\,\mathbf{A}_e + \mathbf{K}_\text{supports} + \sum_\ell \mathbf{B}_\ell^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{k}_\ell\,\mathbf{B}_\ell,
\qquad \mathbf{F}_f = \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\Big(\mathbf{F}_\text{nodes} + \sum_e \mathbf{A}_e^\mathsf{T}\,\mathbf{T}_e^\mathsf{T}\,\tilde{\mathbf{f}}^0_e\Big) $$ (4.3)

$\mathbf{K}_e$ is the matrix of the element in global axes, with hinges condensed and rigid
arms and elastic foundation included (chapter 3); $\mathbf{B}_\ell$ and $\mathbf{k}_\ell$
are the deformation operator and the stiffness of an elastic link between two nodes (chapter 6);
$\tilde{\mathbf{f}}^0_e$ are the condensed equivalent nodal forces of the span loads. Since a
node is coupled only to its neighbours, the matrix is sparse: keta stores only its non-zero terms,
column by column. The order of assembly is fixed (bars, then shells, continuum elements, elastic
supports and links, each in order of creation), which makes the matrix identical, bit for bit, from
one calculation to the next.

Cables cannot be assembled into a linear matrix: a model that contains them is refused by the
linear analyses, which point to the cable analysis of chapter 7 or to replacing the cables with bars
of equivalent stiffness.

## 4.4 Rigid links and linear relations

Three types of kinematic conditions relate degrees of freedom to one another: rigid links (a
master node and slave nodes that follow its rigid-body motion), general linear relations and skew
supports (chapter 6). All are eliminated by substitution, with no penalty stiffness and no
multiplier in the system. For a rigid link, each linked component of a slave $s$ is expressed
in terms of its master $m$ by the rigid-body relation:

$$ \mathbf{u}_s = \mathbf{u}_m + \boldsymbol{\theta}_m \times (\mathbf{x}_s - \mathbf{x}_m),\qquad \boldsymbol{\theta}_s = \boldsymbol{\theta}_m $$ (4.4)

A mask restricts the link to certain global components (a floor diaphragm links only
$u_X$, $u_Y$ and $\theta_Z$, for example). A general linear relation
$\sum_k c_k\,u_k = 0$ eliminates its first term,
$u_1 = -\sum_{k>1} (c_k/c_1)\,u_k$. A skew support restrains an arbitrary direction; the
global component with the largest coefficient that is still free is eliminated. Chains (a slave that
is the master of another) are resolved step by step; a component linked twice, a supported slave
component or a cycle of links is refused.

Together these relations read $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{T}\,\mathbf{u}_r + \mathbf{u}_0$, where
$\mathbf{u}_r$ collects the degrees of freedom not eliminated and $\mathbf{u}_0$ the part
due to the imposed displacements of supported masters. The system solved is

$$ \mathbf{T}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{T}\;\mathbf{u}_r = \mathbf{T}^\mathsf{T}\left(\mathbf{F} - \mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{u}_0\right) $$ (4.5)

The matrix and the forces remain assembled in the unreduced space, which leaves assembly and
recovery unchanged; only the factorisation works on the reduced matrix. The forces transmitted by a
link are deduced from the out-of-balance $\mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{F}$ at the degrees of
freedom it eliminates: that of a slave is transferred to the degrees of freedom of its master, and
becomes a reaction if the master is supported. For a linear relation, the multiplier $\mu$ such
that $\mathbf{K}\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{F} = \mu\,\mathbf{c}$ is returned as the force of the
relation. Rigid links are accepted by linear statics, by modal, spectral and linear time-history
analyses (starting from rest), by influence lines, buckling, staged construction and
large-displacement static analysis. The analyses that do not handle them refuse them with a message:
nonlinear dynamics, staged construction in large displacements and plasticity of continuum
elements, for example.

## 4.5 Factorisation

### 4.5.1 LDLᵀ decomposition

The reduced matrix is symmetric. keta factorises it in the form

$$ \mathbf{P}\,\mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{P}^\mathsf{T} = \mathbf{L}\,\mathbf{D}\,\mathbf{L}^\mathsf{T} $$ (4.6)

where $\mathbf{P}$ is a permutation of the unknowns, $\mathbf{L}$ a unit lower
triangular matrix and $\mathbf{D}$ a diagonal matrix, whose terms $d_k$ are the pivots.
The factorisation is performed without numerical pivoting: the elimination order is fixed in advance
by $\mathbf{P}$, and each pivot may be negative. This form suits the positive definite matrices
of statics, and also the indefinite matrices of stability and eigenvalue analyses, whose negative
pivots it counts. Solving a load case is then a forward substitution
$\mathbf{L}\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{P}\mathbf{F}$, a division by $\mathbf{D}$ and a back
substitution.

### 4.5.2 Reordering

The cost of the factorisation depends on the elimination order. Eliminating a node couples all of
its remaining neighbours to one another: the zero terms of $\mathbf{K}$ that become non-zero in
$\mathbf{L}$ form the fill-in. keta chooses the order by the approximate minimum degree (AMD)
algorithm, which at each step eliminates the least connected unknown. Beyond 10,000 unknowns, it also
computes a nested dissection order: the graph is cut by a separator (a level of a breadth-first
search from a pseudo-peripheral vertex, the smallest level that leaves between 35 % and 65 % of the
vertices on each side), the two halves are treated recursively down to 64 vertices, and the
separators are eliminated last. For each of the two orders, keta computes the factorisation work by
a symbolic elimination,

$$ W = \sum_j c_j^2 $$ (4.7)

where $c_j$ is the number of non-zero terms in column $j$ of $\mathbf{L}$, and
keeps the dissection if it requires less than 90 % of the work of the AMD order. The graphs of decks
and frames, which are nearly planar, generally stay with the AMD order; space frames and solid meshes
benefit from dissection. Both algorithms are deterministic.

**Figure 4.1** — Effect of the elimination order on fill-in: graph of the nodes of a 6 × 4 node grillage (schematic)

### 4.5.3 Simplicial and supernodal factorisation

Below 10,000 unknowns, the factorisation is simplicial: column by column. Above, it is supernodal
and multifrontal. Columns with the same structure below the diagonal are grouped into supernodes;
each supernode forms a dense frontal matrix, which receives the terms of $\mathbf{K}$ and the
update matrices of its children in the elimination tree, and is then factorised by dense block
operations. Partitioning the frontal matrix between the columns of the supernode (index 1) and the
remaining rows (index 2),

$$ \mathbf{F}_{11} = \mathbf{L}_{11}\mathbf{D}_1\mathbf{L}_{11}^\mathsf{T},\qquad
\mathbf{L}_{21} = \mathbf{F}_{21}\,\mathbf{L}_{11}^{-\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{D}_1^{-1},\qquad
\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{F}_{22} - \mathbf{L}_{21}\mathbf{D}_1\mathbf{L}_{21}^\mathsf{T} $$ (4.8)

the pivot block being factorised densely without permutation, the panel $\mathbf{L}_{21}$
obtained by a triangular solve and the update matrix $\mathbf{U}$, passed to the parent, by
matrix products. The computation is the same as the simplicial factorisation, up to rounding errors;
it is merely organised around dense matrix products. Independent subtrees and the 256-row blocks of a
large front can be processed in parallel, in a fixed order of operations: the result is identical,
bit for bit, whatever the number of cores.

### 4.5.4 Reuse of the factorisation

All the load cases of a static analysis are solved with a single factorisation: the right-hand
sides are stored in a matrix and solved together,

$$ \left[\mathbf{u}^{(1)}\ \cdots\ \mathbf{u}^{(n)}\right] = \mathbf{K}^{-1}\left[\mathbf{F}^{(1)}\ \cdots\ \mathbf{F}^{(n)}\right] $$ (4.9)

by one forward and one back substitution per case. Analyses that factorise similar matrices
several times (staged construction, nonlinear iterations, influence lines) reuse what can be reused,
at three levels: if the matrix is identical, term by term and bit for bit, to the previous one, the
factorisation is kept; if only its structure is identical, the symbolic analysis (order and structure
of $\mathbf{L}$) is kept and only the numbers are recomputed; otherwise, everything is redone.
The comparison is made on the arrays of the matrix themselves, not on a hash.

## 4.6 Inertia and mechanism checks

### 4.6.1 Sylvester's law of inertia

The factorisation also provides a diagnostic at no extra cost. By Sylvester's law of inertia, a
symmetric matrix and the diagonal matrix of an $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{L}^\mathsf{T}$
decomposition have the same numbers of positive, zero and negative eigenvalues:

$$ \nu_-(\mathbf{K}) = \operatorname{card}\{k : d_k < 0\},\qquad
\nu_0(\mathbf{K}) = \operatorname{card}\{k : d_k = 0\} $$ (4.10)

A stable structure has a positive definite matrix: all its pivots are positive. A zero pivot
reveals a mechanism; the factorisation then stops with an error. Stability and large-displacement
analyses also count the negative pivots of $\mathbf{K} + \mathbf{K}_g$ to detect that a critical
load has been passed (chapter 17); applied to $\mathbf{K} - \sigma\,\mathbf{M}$, the same rule
counts the natural modes whose squared circular frequency is below $\sigma$ (chapter 15).

### 4.6.2 Ratio of pivot to diagonal term

Because of rounding errors, the pivot of a mechanism is often not exactly zero: three aligned
hinges, a chain of bars free to rotate, a node rotation restrained in an oblique direction only. The
factorisation then succeeds, and the solution would return huge displacements of arbitrary sign. In
linear statics, keta therefore compares each pivot with the diagonal term $a_{kk}$ of the
assembled matrix for the same unknown, and refuses the calculation if

$$ \min_k \frac{\lvert d_k \rvert}{\lvert a_{kk} \rvert} < 10^{-13} $$ (4.11)

The ratio $d_k/a_{kk}$ measures the part of the stiffness of unknown $k$ that remains
when the unknowns eliminated before it are free to adjust; for a mechanism, only rounding remains,
of the order of $10^{-16}$. A sound model stays far above the threshold, unless two stiffnesses
that follow each other in the same chain differ by more than thirteen orders of magnitude, a case
that is also refused because the solution would no longer have any significant digit. The error
message gives the value of the ratio, but does not locate the degrees of freedom involved.

The check is made on the matrix, before any solution: a mechanism is refused even if the loads do
not excite it. This is the case, for example, of the end node of an inclined bar hinged in bending
at that node and whose torsion is retained, when the node is connected to nothing but translational
supports: the torsion of the bar restrains the rotation of the node only about the axis of the bar,
and the perpendicular rotation, which is not zero component by component, is restrained by nothing.
The ratio is then about $3\cdot10^{-16}$. The torsion must also be released at that end (the
rotation of the node then receives no stiffness at all and is eliminated automatically), or the
rotation restrained by a support.

**Note.**

The threshold applies to the ratio of stiffnesses in series, not to their absolute
difference. A steel bar connected to a support of stiffness $10^{25}$ N/m passes the check,
because the pivot of that support remains equal to its diagonal term. On the other hand, two truss
bars in series whose axial stiffnesses differ by a factor of $10^{11}$ give a displacement with
a relative error of $3\cdot10^{-6}$, the relative error being of the order of rounding
multiplied by the contrast; with a contrast of $10^{14}$, the calculation is refused. An
“infinitely stiff” bar is better modelled by a rigid link, with no fictitious stiffness, than by an
inordinate modulus.

## 4.7 Reactions

Once the displacements are known, the reactions are obtained at the supported nodes as the
out-of-balance between the forces that the elements exert on the node and the loads applied to
it:

$$ \mathbf{R} = \sum_e \mathbf{A}_e^\mathsf{T}\,\mathbf{K}_e\,\mathbf{u}_e - \mathbf{F}_\text{nodes} - \sum_e \mathbf{A}_e^\mathsf{T}\,\mathbf{T}_e^\mathsf{T}\,\tilde{\mathbf{f}}^0_e $$ (4.12)

The last term removes the equivalent nodal forces of the span loads: the reaction of a simply
supported beam under a uniform load is indeed $qL/2$. $\mathbf{R}$ is the force that the
support exerts on the structure, in global axes, on the six components of the node; on a free
component of a partially supported node, it is zero to within rounding. On a free component
restrained by an elastic support, it equals $-k\,u$, the force of the spring on the structure.
The forces transmitted by rigid links to supported masters are included; skew supports return their
reaction in their own axes (chapter 6). Modelling restraints, which do not represent a bearing
(out-of-plane degrees of freedom of a plane model, for example), return no reaction. By
construction, the sum of the reactions balances the sum of the applied loads to within rounding,
which is the first check of a model.

## 4.8 Internal forces between the nodes

### 4.8.1 End forces

For each bar, the local end displacements are $\mathbf{u}_\ell = \mathbf{T}_e\,\mathbf{u}_e$,
completed by the released displacements (3.15). The end forces are then

$$ \mathbf{f} = \mathbf{k}\,\mathbf{u}_\ell - \mathbf{f}^0 $$ (4.13)

with the matrix $\mathbf{k}$ of the bar alone (not condensed, without the elastic foundation,
whose reaction is returned separately as a soil pressure) and the sum $\mathbf{f}^0$ of the
equivalent nodal forces of all its span loads.

### 4.8.2 Equilibrium of the segment

The internal forces at a section of abscissa $x$ are obtained by writing the equilibrium of
the segment $[0, x]$ under the end forces at $i$ and the loads it actually carries, without
any interpolation. With the convention of chapter 2, and writing $p_x, q_y, q_z$ for the local
distributed loads (point loads appearing in them as Dirac distributions) and $m_x, m_y, m_z$
for the distributed and point moments:

$$ \begin{aligned}
N(x) &= -f_1 - \int_0^x p_x\,\mathrm{d}\xi, &
T(x) &= -f_4 - \int_0^x m_x\,\mathrm{d}\xi,\\
V_y(x) &= -f_2 - \int_0^x q_y\,\mathrm{d}\xi, &
M_z(x) &= -f_6 + f_2\,x + \int_0^x (x - \xi)\,q_y\,\mathrm{d}\xi - \int_0^x m_z\,\mathrm{d}\xi,\\
V_z(x) &= -f_3 - \int_0^x q_z\,\mathrm{d}\xi, &
M_y(x) &= -f_5 - f_3\,x - \int_0^x (x - \xi)\,q_z\,\mathrm{d}\xi - \int_0^x m_y\,\mathrm{d}\xi
\end{aligned} $$ (4.14)

**Figure 4.2** — Equilibrium of the segment [0, x] in the xz plane

The integrals are computed in closed form for uniform, linear and parabolic loads. A point load
located exactly at the abscissa of an output section is counted in the segment $[0, x]$: the
shear force returned is the one just after the load. The only exception is the section
$x = L$, which returns the value just before a load placed on the end, since that load acts on
the node. These internal forces satisfy equilibrium at every section and do not depend on the number
of output sections: the moment of a simply supported beam under a uniform load is
$q\,x(L-x)/2$ at every section, even if the beam is represented by a single bar. On a 10 m beam
carrying a linear load from 10 to 30 kN/m between 2 and 7 m and a 50 kN force at 4.5 m, the moment
returned at 3.7 m, 272.108 kN·m, agrees with the statics calculation to within $10^{-12}$.

Bars with variable cross-section and bars on exact elastic foundation follow the same principle,
with their own end forces; the bar on foundation also derives the soil reaction along the bar
(chapter 6).

## 4.9 Displacements between the nodes

### 4.9.1 Integration of the curvature

The displacements at the output sections are obtained by integrating the strains of the bar,
known at every section from the internal forces (4.14) and the constitutive laws of
chapter 3. In each bending plane, the rotation of the cross-section and the deflection satisfy

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}\theta_z}{\mathrm{d}x} = \frac{M_z}{EI_z} - \kappa_z^*(x),\qquad
\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = \theta_z + \frac{V_y}{GA_{vy}} $$ (4.15)

and likewise in the $xz$ plane, with $\mathrm{d}\theta_y/\mathrm{d}x = M_y/EI_y - \kappa_y^*$
and $\mathrm{d}w/\mathrm{d}x = -\theta_y + V_z/GA_{vz}$; $\kappa^*$ is the imposed
curvature (thermal, shrinkage, creep). The double integration starts from the start of the bar; its
two constants are fixed by the transverse displacements of the two ends, which also suits hinged
bars, whose end rotations are recomputed. The rotation of the cross-section returned is the rotation
of end $i$ plus the integral of the curvature; the shear strain is not a rotation and does not
enter it. The axial displacement is obtained in the same way from $u' = N/EA + \varepsilon_0^*$,
and the twist from $\theta_x' = T/GJ + \kappa_x^*$, anchored on its two end values.
Dislocations add their jumps at their abscissa.

### 4.9.2 Numerical method

Each interval between two output sections is cut at the point loads and at the ends of the
distributed loads it contains. On each piece, the curvature is a polynomial of degree at most 4 (the
moment under a parabolic load), and the integration

$$ v(b) = v(a) + (b - a)\,v'(a) + \int_a^b (b - s)\,\kappa(s)\,\mathrm{d}s + \int_a^b \frac{V(s)}{GA_v}\,\mathrm{d}s,\qquad
v'(b) = v'(a) + \int_a^b \kappa(s)\,\mathrm{d}s $$ (4.16)

is carried out by a three-point Gauss quadrature, exact up to degree 5. The axial displacement and
the twist are integrated by Simpson's rule on the same pieces, which is exact for their integrands.
The displacements are therefore exact at every section, for all the loads of chapter 3: a simply
supported beam represented by a single bar gives the deflection (1.3) at midspan, to
machine precision. For a bar with variable cross-section, the integrand is no longer polynomial: each
piece is integrated by an adaptive Gauss quadrature, subdivided as long as two evaluations differ by
more than $10^{-14}$ in relative terms (24 levels at most). Truss bars interpolate the
displacements of their ends linearly.

**Figure 4.3** — Moment and deflection of a 10 m beam represented by a single bar (partial linear load and 50 kN force), computed by keta

## 4.10 Stresses at the stress points

Each parametric cross-section carries named stress points: the four corners and the centre of a
rectangle, the flange tips and the web of an I-section or a box, the four cardinal points of a circle
or a tube, the vertices of a polygonal section. At each of them, keta returns the normal stress
(2.15), an estimate of the shear stress and the von Mises equivalent stress:

$$ \tau = \phi_y\,\frac{V_y}{A_{vy}} + \phi_z\,\frac{V_z}{A_{vz}} + \frac{T\,r}{J},\qquad
\sigma_\text{VM} = \sqrt{\sigma^2 + 3\,\tau^2} $$ (4.17)

where $\phi_y$, $\phi_z$ equal 1 at the points where the corresponding shear force is
carried (centre of the rectangle, web, points of the circle lying on the neutral axis of the bending
considered) and 0 elsewhere, and $r$ is the distance from the point to the centroid. This
estimate is an average value: $V/A_v$ underestimates the maximum of the actual distribution
(1.5 $V/A$ at the centre of a rectangle, against 1.2 $V/A$ with $A_v = 5A/6$), and the
torsion term $Tr/J$ is exact only for circular sections. For the exact stresses at any point of
an arbitrary cross-section, chapter 20 solves the Saint-Venant torsion and flexure problems on the
meshed cross-section.

## 4.11 Output sections

Internal forces, displacements and stresses are returned at the output sections of each bar. By
default, there are eleven, equally spaced, ends included:

$$ x_k = \frac{k}{n - 1}\,L,\qquad k = 0, \dots, n - 1,\qquad n = 11 $$ (4.18)

The number can be changed for all bars, and each bar can receive its own list of abscissae,
sorted, in metres from its start. Since the internal forces and displacements are exact at every
section, the choice of output sections affects only where the results are read, not their value: it
is enough to place a section at the points of interest (under a point load, at a change of
cross-section, at the point of maximum moment). Combinations of cases (chapter 5) are formed section
by section and therefore assume the same output sections for all cases.

## 4.12 Scope and limits

- the solution assumes a stable structure: a mechanism, even unloaded, and a contrast of
stiffnesses in series greater than $10^{13}$ are refused before any solution;

- a displacement imposed on a degree of freedom that is not restrained, or imposed twice in a case,
is refused;

- cables, which are nonlinear, are refused by the linear analyses (chapter 7); rigid and elastic
links are accepted only by the analyses that handle them;

- a model with unilateral or capped supports is solved case by case by an active-set method
(chapter 6): its results cannot be superposed and combinations are refused for it;

- the shear stress at the stress points is an estimate; exact stresses are the subject of
chapter 20.

# Chapter 5 Combinations and envelopes

A structure is never verified under a single load case. Self-weight, superimposed dead loads,
support settlements, traffic, temperature and wind act together, each with its design value, and the
engineer looks, at each section, for the most unfavourable effect of their combination. This chapter
describes how keta forms these combinations from the computed load cases: linear combinations, the
EN 1990 combinations that the kernel can generate, the search for the extremum of a response among
all admissible combinations, then envelopes, which keep at each point the bounds of a family of
states, and concomitant forces, which restore the whole state behind each bound. It ends with the
output sections, the points of the bars where these results are evaluated. Moving loads, whose
extreme effect is read on an influence line, are the subject of chapters 11 and 12; combinations of
modal responses, of chapter 15.

## 5.1 Assumptions

- the results combined are those of linear analyses: the superposition principle applies, and the
response to $\lambda_1 F_1 + \lambda_2 F_2$ is $\lambda_1 R_1 + \lambda_2 R_2$;

- each load case is computed once, on the same structure (same supports, same active bars): all
the results combined have the same shape, node by node and section by section;

- a nonlinear result (unilateral supports, pseudo-plastic soil, links with a nonlinear law,
cables) cannot be superposed: keta marks it as such and refuses to combine it;

- the partial factors $\gamma$ and the combination factors $\psi$ are input data: the predefined sets
take the values of the French National Annex for bridges, and each value can be replaced;

- envelopes and combinations are formed at the output sections of the bars, at the nodes, at the
supports and at the centre of the shell facets; nothing is interpolated between these points.

## 5.2 Linear combination of cases

A combination is a list of (factor, case) pairs. Its result is the weighted sum of the results of
the cases, field by field:

$$ R_c = \sum_{i} c_i\,R_i $$ (5.1)

for the nodal displacements, the support reactions (including the reactions of skew supports and
the forces of linear relations), the end forces of the bars, the internal forces, deflections and
rotations at the output sections, the soil pressures, the forces and deformations of elastic links
and the stress resultants of shells. Since the internal forces at an output section are exact for
each case (chapter 4), they remain so for the combination.

Only the tensor components of a shell are superposed: $n_x, n_y, n_{xy}, m_x, m_y,
m_{xy}, q_x, q_y$. The principal moments of the combination are recomputed from the combined
moments,

$$ m_{1,2} = \frac{m_x + m_y}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{m_x - m_y}{2}\right)^2 + m_{xy}^2} $$ (5.2)

and are not themselves combined, which would be wrong as soon as the principal directions of the
cases differ. The same applies to the principal membrane forces.

The calculation refuses a combination that refers to a case that does not exist, to results of
different shapes, or to a result that cannot be superposed. A model with unilateral supports or
supports with a force cap is computed case by case (chapter 6) and its combinations are refused:
each combination must then be computed as a case, with all its loads.

## 5.3 EN 1990 combinations

### 5.3.1 Expressions

The combinations of actions of EN 1990 (§6.4.3.2 for ultimate limit states, §6.5.3 for
serviceability limit states, annex A2 for bridges) read, with $G_{k,j}$ the permanent actions,
$Q_{k,1}$ the leading variable action and $Q_{k,i}$ the accompanying variable actions:

$$ \text{ULS (6.10)}\qquad \sum_j \gamma_{G,j}\,G_{k,j} + \gamma_{Q,1}\,Q_{k,1} + \sum_{i>1} \gamma_{Q,i}\,\psi_{0,i}\,Q_{k,i} $$ (5.3)

$$ \begin{aligned}
\text{ULS (6.10a)}\qquad & \sum_j \gamma_{G,j}\,G_{k,j} + \sum_{i} \gamma_{Q,i}\,\psi_{0,i}\,Q_{k,i}\\
\text{ULS (6.10b)}\qquad & \sum_j \xi_j\,\gamma_{G,j}\,G_{k,j} + \gamma_{Q,1}\,Q_{k,1} + \sum_{i>1} \gamma_{Q,i}\,\psi_{0,i}\,Q_{k,i}
\end{aligned} $$ (5.4)

$$ \begin{aligned}
\text{characteristic}\qquad & \sum_j G_{k,j} + Q_{k,1} + \sum_{i>1} \psi_{0,i}\,Q_{k,i}\\
\text{frequent}\qquad & \sum_j G_{k,j} + \psi_{1,1}\,Q_{k,1} + \sum_{i>1} \psi_{2,i}\,Q_{k,i}\\
\text{quasi-permanent}\qquad & \sum_j G_{k,j} + \sum_{i} \psi_{2,i}\,Q_{k,i}
\end{aligned} $$ (5.5)

The “+” sign means “to be combined with”: each permanent action takes its unfavourable value
$\gamma_{G,\text{sup}}$ or its favourable value $\gamma_{G,\text{inf}}$, and a favourable
variable action is omitted. Prestress has no category of its own in these combinations: it is
described as a permanent action, with its own factors.

### 5.3.2 Generation of combinations

The keta generator adds explicit linear combinations to the model, each variable action becoming
the leading action in turn. The permanent actions all take the same pair of factors
$(\gamma_{G,\text{sup}}, \gamma_{G,\text{inf}})$, by default $(1.35, 1.0)$: the generator
does not set one favourable permanent action against another unfavourable one. Each variable action
carries its factors $\gamma_Q$, $\psi_0$, $\psi_1$, $\psi_2$; four sets are
predefined.

| Predefined action | $\gamma_Q$ | $\psi_0$ | $\psi_1$ | $\psi_2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| road traffic, group gr1a | 1.35 | 0.75 | 0.75 | 0 |
| wind | 1.5 | 0.6 | 0.2 | 0 |
| temperature | 1.5 | 0.6 | 0.6 | 0.5 |
| snow (on a bridge) | 1.5 | 0.8 | 0 | 0 |

For $n$ variable actions, the generator produces the following combinations.

| State | Combinations per leading action | Number |
|---|---|---|
| ULS, 6.10 | $\gamma_{G,\text{sup}}$ then $\gamma_{G,\text{inf}}$ on all the permanent actions; leading action at $\gamma_Q$, the others at $\gamma_Q\psi_0$ | $2n$ |
| ULS, 6.10a and 6.10b | 6.10a once, with no leading action, all variable actions at $\gamma_Q\psi_0$, with $\gamma_{G,\text{sup}}$ then $\gamma_{G,\text{inf}}$; 6.10b per leading action with $\xi\gamma_{G,\text{sup}}$ then $\gamma_{G,\text{inf}}$ | $2 + 2n$ |
| SLS characteristic | leading action at 1, the others at $\psi_0$ | $n$ |
| SLS frequent | leading action at $\psi_1$, the others at $\psi_2$ | $n$ |
| SLS quasi-permanent | all variable actions at $\psi_2$ | 1 |

With no variable action, the generator combines only the permanent actions: two combinations at
ULS (with $\gamma_{G,\text{sup}}$ then $\gamma_{G,\text{inf}}$), one at serviceability
limit states. A variable-action term with a zero factor is not written. Several features of this
generator should be known before using it:

- in the 6.10b combinations, the factor $\xi$ (0.85 by default) multiplies only
$\gamma_{G,\text{sup}}$: the combination in which the permanent actions are favourable takes
them at $\gamma_{G,\text{inf}}$, as provided by table A2.4(B) of EN 1990;

- the “traffic gr1a” set applies the same $\psi$ to the tandem and to the distributed load;
table A2.1 of EN 1990 gives $\psi_0 = \psi_1 = 0.40$ for the distributed load of load model 1,
against 0.75 for the tandem. The predefined set is therefore on the safe side for the distributed
load; to respect the distinction, describe the two parts of load model 1 as two actions, with their
own factors;

- the “snow” set is that of snow on a bridge (table A2.1, $\psi_0 = 0.8$).

Accidental and seismic combinations are not generated: they are written as linear combinations.
The combination of the directions of an earthquake (30 % rule of EN 1998-1) is described in
chapter 15.

### 5.3.3 Extremum of a response

Generating every explicit combination soon becomes impractical: with exclusive traffic groups,
settlement variants and permanent actions that are favourable or unfavourable separately, their
number grows as the product of the choices. keta therefore turns the problem round. For a given
scalar response (a moment at a section, a reaction), the effect $e_a$ of each action $a$
with a unit factor is known. The maximum (or the minimum) of

$$ E = \sum_a f_a\,e_a,\qquad f_a \in \mathcal{F}_a(\text{state}, \text{variant}, L) $$ (5.6)

is sought over all admissible factors $f_a$, the set $\mathcal{F}_a$ depending on the
limit state, on the variant (6.10, 6.10a or 6.10b) and on the leading action $L$.

| Category | ULS | SLS |
|---|---|---|
| permanent | $\{\gamma_{G,\text{sup}}, \gamma_{G,\text{inf}}\}$; in 6.10b $\{\xi\gamma_{G,\text{sup}}, \gamma_{G,\text{inf}}\}$ | $\{1\}$ |
| settlement | $\{\gamma_{\text{set,sup}}, \gamma_{\text{set,inf}}\}$, by default $\{1.2, 0\}$ | $\{1, 0\}$ |
| leading variable | $\{\gamma_Q, 0\}$ (none in 6.10a) | charact. $\{1, 0\}$, freq. $\{\psi_1, 0\}$ |
| accompanying variable | $\{\gamma_Q\psi_0, 0\}$ | charact. $\{\psi_0, 0\}$, freq. and q.p. $\{\psi_2, 0\}$ |

An exclusivity label groups actions of which at most one acts: the traffic groups gr1a and gr5,
the variants of a settlement, several arrangements of the same load. For exclusive permanent
actions, exactly one acts. Actions without a label each form a one-member group. Once the variant
and the leading action are fixed, the sum (5.6) is a sum of contributions from
independent groups: each group contributes its best by choosing, on its own, the member and the
factor that maximise $s\,f_a\,e_a$ ($s = \pm 1$ depending on whether the maximum or the
minimum is sought), or nothing in the case of a variable or settlement group that any contribution
would make favourable. The extreme value is therefore

$$ E^{*} = s\,\max_{\text{variant},\,L}\ \sum_{g} \max_{a \in g,\ f \in \mathcal{F}_a} s\,f\,e_a $$ (5.7)

and this maximum is attained, without approximation: the maximum of a sum of independent terms is
the sum of their maxima. The cost is proportional to the number of actions times the number of
possible leading actions. The result carries its provenance: the limit state, the variant, the
leading action and the list of the actions retained with their factors, whose sum gives back the
value. An action can be declared unable to be the leading action.

Example: two permanent actions with effects 1.0 and 0.5, a settlement with effect 0.2, two
exclusive traffic groups (load model 1 with effect 1.0, special vehicle with effect 0.8, both with
$\gamma_Q = 1.35$ and $\psi_0 = 0.75$), temperature (0.3; $\psi_0 = 0.6$) and wind
(0.4; $\psi_0 = 0.6$). At ULS with the 6.10a and 6.10b pair, keta retains the 6.10b combination
with load model 1 as the leading action:

$$ E^{*} = 0.85 \times 1.35\,(1.0 + 0.5) + 1.2 \times 0.2 + 1.35 \times 1.0 + 1.5 \times 0.6\,(0.3 + 0.4) = 3.941 $$

against 3.908 for the best 6.10a, in which all variable actions are taken at
$\gamma_Q\psi_0$:

$$ 1.35\,(1.0 + 0.5) + 1.2 \times 0.2 + 1.35 \times 0.75 \times 1.0 + 1.5 \times 0.6\,(0.3 + 0.4) = 3.908 $$

Enumerating all admissible combinations gives the same value.

Applied field by field (each component of displacement, of reaction, of end force, of internal
force and deflection at the output sections, each shell component), the same calculation gives the
envelope of the EN 1990 combinations. Each bound refers to the combination that produces it; the
distinct combinations thus found are stored once each, with their terms. Two components of the same
section may come from different combinations: they are bounds, not a state.

**Figure 5.1** — ULS envelope of the moments of a 25 + 30 + 25 m continuous beam: permanent actions (200 kN/m), distributed traffic by spans (60 kN/m, seven exclusive arrangements) and temperature gradient; extremum computed section by section

## 5.4 Envelopes

### 5.4.1 Component-by-component envelope

The envelope of a set of results $R^{(1)}, \dots, R^{(n)}$ (cases, combinations, states)
keeps, for each scalar component $k$, its two bounds and the index of the source that reaches
them:

$$ R_k^{\max} = \max_i R_k^{(i)},\qquad R_k^{\min} = \min_i R_k^{(i)},\qquad i_k^{\max} = \arg\max_i R_k^{(i)} $$ (5.8)

The components enveloped are the six displacements of each node, the six components of each
reaction, the twelve end forces of each bar, the six internal forces, the three deflections and the
three rotations of each output section, and twelve quantities per shell facet
($n_x, n_y, n_{xy}, m_x, m_y, m_{xy}, q_x, q_y, m_1, m_2, n_1, n_2$). The principal values are
enveloped as independent quantities; their angles have no meaning on a bound and are set to zero. In
case of a tie, the first source prevails. A non-finite value stops the calculation, as do sources of
different shapes.

An envelope bound is not a state of equilibrium: the maximum moment and the maximum shear force at
a given section generally come from different sources. For a verification that combines several
internal forces (bending with axial force, interaction of shear and torsion), the concomitant state
is needed.

### 5.4.2 Concomitant forces

A driving quantity is chosen, an internal force at an output section, a reaction component or a
nodal displacement, and keta looks for the source that makes it extreme:

$$ i^{*} = \arg\max_i\, p\!\left(R^{(i)}\right),\qquad R^{\text{conc}} = R^{(i^{*})} $$ (5.9)

The state restored is the whole result of this source: all the displacements, all the reactions,
all the internal forces at all the sections. It is an actual state of the structure, which satisfies
equilibrium. The figure below shows, for a section close to a pier, the pairs ($V_z$,
$M_y$) of a set of combinations: the envelope box contains corners that no state reaches.

**Figure 5.2** — States (Vz, My) of a section and box of the component-by-component envelope

### 5.4.3 Envelope of factored cases

A variant assigns to each case an interval of factors $[c_i^{\min}, c_i^{\max}]$, for
example $[1.0, 1.35]$ for a permanent action or $[0, 1.5]$ for a variable action. Each
case is then taken alone, with the factor from its interval that makes it most unfavourable, and the
envelope is the most unfavourable of the sources:

$$ R_k^{\max} = \max_i\ \max\!\left(c_i^{\min} R_k^{(i)},\ c_i^{\max} R_k^{(i)}\right) $$ (5.10)

This is not a combination: the cases are not added. For the effect of simultaneous actions, use a
combination, the extremum of (5.7) or the envelope with bounded factors described
next.

### 5.4.4 Envelope of combinations with bounded factors

The general case is that of sources acting together, each with a factor free within its interval.
At a given point, the driving quantity $p$ is linear in these factors; its maximum over the box
of factors is attained at a corner, chosen source by source:

$$ p^{\max} = \max_{c_i \in [c_i^{\min}, c_i^{\max}]} \sum_i c_i\,p_i = \sum_i \max\!\left(c_i^{\min} p_i,\ c_i^{\max} p_i\right) $$ (5.11)

The factor $c_i^{*}$ retained for each source being known, keta rebuilds the whole state at
the same corner,

$$ R^{\max} = \sum_i c_i^{*}\,R^{(i)} $$ (5.12)

which is a linear combination in the sense of (5.1), hence a consistent state: the
concomitant forces at a section never mix independent extremes. The minimum is treated in the same
way with its own corner. A reaction component can be enveloped at the same time as the driving
quantity, with its own corner.

A source may also be a set of possible states, for example the two bounds of an envelope already
computed. It then contributes through the most unfavourable of its alternatives, never through their
sum: this is how an envelope of envelopes is formed. In a simple envelope over alternatives, an
alternative whose value is zero at the section does not compete, unless all of them are zero; at
reactions, all of them compete.

### 5.4.5 Driving quantities

The driving quantity of an envelope with bounded factors is one of the following.

- An internal force at an output section, $N, V_y, V_z, T, M_y$ or $M_z$, or a nodal
displacement.

A normal stress at an extreme fibre of the cross-section,

$$ \sigma = \frac{N}{A} + \frac{M_y\,z}{I_y} - \frac{M_z\,y}{I_z} $$ (5.13)

- evaluated at $y = v_y$ or $-w_y$, $z = v_z$ or $-w_z$, or at the four corners
$(\pm, \pm)$. The distances to the extreme fibres come from the stress points of the
cross-section; failing those, from the elastic section moduli ($v_z = w_z = I_y/W_{el,y}$). A
cross-section that has neither is refused.

A generalised stress, a linear combination of the six internal forces plus a constant,

$$ \Sigma(x) = c_N N + c_{V_y} V_y + c_{V_z} V_z + c_T T + c_{M_y} M_y + c_{M_z} M_z + c_0 $$ (5.14)

whose coefficients are given per bar, constant, linear between the start and the end, or parabolic
through the start, the middle and the end:

$$ c(\xi) = 2\,(c_\text{start} - 2c_\text{mid} + c_\text{end})\,\xi^2 + (-3c_\text{start} + 4c_\text{mid} - c_\text{end})\,\xi + c_\text{start},\qquad \xi = x/L $$ (5.15)

- The constant $c_0$ applies to load cases, not to the effects of moving loads read on an
influence line. The coefficients may be written in the keta convention or in the
compression-positive convention ($N$, $M_y$, $M_z$ with their signs changed).

- A soil pressure $p_x, p_y, p_z$ or a soil moment $m_x$, on bars resting on an elastic
foundation (chapter 6).

The envelope can be evaluated at one section, or at all the output sections of all the bars; the
bars where the quantity does not exist (no soil, no generalised stress defined) are then skipped.
Envelopes over the steps of staged construction, with their own factors for prestress, are
described in chapter 10.

## 5.5 Output sections

The internal forces, deflections and rotations of a bar are returned at a finite number of
sections, the output sections. Unless otherwise specified, each bar receives eleven, equally spaced,
ends included (chapter 4). Arbitrary abscissae can also be given, bar by bar; a bar that receives
them loses its regular grid, the others keep theirs. The value at each section is exact (chapter 4);
envelopes and combinations are formed at these sections and are not interpolated between them. A
support section, the point of application of a point load or a section where the reinforcement
changes must therefore be declared if their extremes are wanted.

These abscissae are described in blocks. In this description, every bar carries by default a
section at each end. An ordinary block starts again from these default sections and adds its own to
them (earlier additions are forgotten); an “additional” block is added to what exists; an “only”
block replaces everything, default sections included. Each line of a block targets a list of bars
(or all of them) and gives absolute or relative abscissae, or else a step over an interval
$[x_a, x_b]$ (the whole bar by default). An absolute step $h$ places the sections
$x_a + k h$ and adds the end $x_b$ if the step does not fall on it. A relative step must be
the inverse of an integer of the form

$$ h = \frac{1}{n},\qquad n = 2^a\,5^b $$ (5.16)

so that the relative abscissae are terminating decimals: 1/2, 1/4, 1/5, 1/10 are accepted, 1/3 or
1/7 are refused. It must also divide the interval into a whole number of steps. Two sections less
than $10^{-9}\max(L, 1\ \text{m})$ apart are merged. Each section carries an indication of the
family of results it serves (internal forces and stresses, or displacements and soil pressures);
keta always returns both families at each section, and the indication only serves to restrict the
grid if requested.

The abscissae are measured from the start of the bar along its axis, that is from one offset end
to the other (chapter 3):

$$ L = \left\|(\mathbf{x}_j + \mathbf{e}_j) - (\mathbf{x}_i + \mathbf{e}_i)\right\| $$ (5.17)

so that a relative abscissa falls exactly where the recovery of internal forces expects it. An
abscissa outside $[0, L]$, an empty list or a step longer than the interval is refused.

## 5.6 Scope

The combinations and envelopes of this chapter apply to linear results computed on the same
structure. The results of nonlinear analyses are not combined: there, each combination is a load
case. The EN 1990 combination generator covers the fundamental ultimate limit states (6.10, or 6.10a
and 6.10b) and the three serviceability combinations; it applies a single pair of factors to all the
permanent actions and has the particular features noted above (same $\psi$ for the tandem and
the distributed load of traffic). The exact extremum of a response is free of these limits: each
permanent action in it is favourable or unfavourable independently, and the factor $\xi$ affects
only the unfavourable value. Accidental and seismic combinations are not generated. Envelopes see
only the declared output sections.

# Chapter 6 Supports, links and soils

A structure stands on its supports and on the ground, and its parts are connected to one another
by links: laminated elastomeric bearings, seismic stoppers, expansion joints, closure hinges, partial
fixities, footings and piles. This chapter describes how keta represents these boundary conditions
and devices: rigid, elastic or skew supports, supports that can only push or that cap their force,
rigid links and linear relations between degrees of freedom, springs between nodes, linear or with a
nonlinear law, and soil, whether distributed under a bar (Winkler foundation, zoned soil,
pseudo-plastic soil) or lumped into springs (earth pressure, pile curves). For each device, we state
which problem is solved, by which method, and which results are returned. The elimination of degrees
of freedom and the computation of reactions are described in chapter 4; the combination of nonlinear
results, in chapter 5.

## 6.1 Assumptions

- displacements are small: supports, links and springs act in their initial position, and their
axes do not rotate with the structure;

- a support or a link acts at a node; Winkler soil acts along a bar, at each point, in proportion to
the local displacement of that point, with no interaction between neighbouring points;

- the linear devices (rigid and elastic supports, rigid and elastic links, linear relations, elastic
soil) keep the problem linear and superposable;

- the nonlinear devices (unilateral supports, force caps, link laws, pseudo-plastic soil) are
handled in statics, one load case at a time; their results are not superposable;

- the nonlinear laws are piecewise linear; they are elastic (without memory), except for the staged
analysis with loading history described further on;

- friction, damping and the time dependence of the devices are not represented here (link damping
enters dynamics, chapters 15 and 16).

## 6.2 Rigid supports and imposed displacements

A rigid support restrains one or more of the six components of a node in the global axes. The
restrained degrees of freedom $s$ are eliminated from the system; an imposed displacement
$\bar{\mathbf{u}}_s$ (settlement, support rotation) moves to the right-hand side:

$$ \mathbf{K}_{ff}\,\mathbf{u}_f = \mathbf{F}_f - \mathbf{K}_{fs}\,\bar{\mathbf{u}}_s,\qquad
\mathbf{R}_s = \mathbf{K}_{sf}\,\mathbf{u}_f + \mathbf{K}_{ss}\,\bar{\mathbf{u}}_s - \mathbf{F}_s $$ (6.1)

The matrix does not depend on the imposed displacement: a settlement is a load case like any
other, and it can be combined. Imposed displacements apply only to rigidly restrained components.
The reaction $\mathbf{R}_s$ is the force that the support exerts on the structure; the reactions
together balance the applied loads.

Some components are restrained for modelling purposes rather than by a device: the out-of-plane
degrees of freedom of a plane model, for example. These restraints return no reaction, so that an
envelope over the construction stages does not pick up the zero reaction of a deactivated bearing.
A component that receives no stiffness is restrained automatically, and a warning is issued.

## 6.3 Elastic supports

### 6.3.1 Stiffness per degree of freedom

A support spring of stiffness $k$ (N/m or N·m/rad) on component $c$ of a node adds
$k$ to the corresponding diagonal term of the stiffness matrix. The component stays free, and the
reaction returned is the force of the spring on the structure,

$$ K_{cc} \leftarrow K_{cc} + k,\qquad R_c = -k\,u_c $$ (6.2)

obtained from the equilibrium of the node, with no special treatment. A component that is both
restrained and fitted with a spring is eliminated: the spring then has no effect and does not enter
the reaction.

### 6.3.2 Coupled 6 × 6 matrix

A general elastic support is a symmetric matrix $\mathbf{K}_s$ of dimension
$6\times 6$, expressed in support axes rotated by an angle $\alpha$ about $Z$. It is
given by its lower triangle (21 terms; 6 terms for a plane model, on
$u_x, u_y, \theta_z$) or by its diagonal alone. With
$\mathbf{R} = \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{R}_z(\alpha), \mathbf{R}_z(\alpha))$, which takes the
components from the global axes to the support axes, the assembled matrix is

$$ \mathbf{K}_g = \mathbf{R}^\mathsf{T}\,\mathbf{K}_s\,\mathbf{R} $$ (6.3)

A spring along the $x$ axis of a support rotated by $90°$ thus becomes a spring along
$Y$. A negative diagonal term is rejected. This matrix adds to the springs per degree of freedom
and, like them, returns the reaction $-\mathbf{K}_g\,\mathbf{u}$. It represents an elastomeric
bearing (shear and compression stiffnesses), a short condensed pier, or a foundation whose static
impedance matrix is known.

## 6.4 Skew supports

A skew support restrains components in arbitrary axes, given by its three orthonormal axes
$\mathbf{a}_x, \mathbf{a}_y, \mathbf{a}_z$: a bearing sliding along the axis of a curved bridge,
an oblique guide. Each restrained local component is a linear relation on the translations (or the
rotations) of the node,

$$ \mathbf{a}_k\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0 $$ (6.4)

keta eliminates one global component for each of them: the relations of a given node are put in
reduced row echelon form, taking as pivot the largest component still free, so that two restrained
directions (a guide and a longitudinal stopper) do not produce a cyclic chain. The reaction is
returned in the support axes and in the global axes:

$$ \mathbf{R}_\text{global} = \sum_{k\ \text{restrained}} \mu_k\,\mathbf{a}_k $$ (6.5)

where $\mu_k$ is the local component of the reaction. A component for which no free global
component remains to be eliminated is rejected.

## 6.5 Unilateral supports and force caps

### 6.5.1 Contact conditions

A bearing sitting on a pier can push the deck upwards but cannot hold it down. For each unilateral
component, the Kuhn-Tucker conditions are imposed, with $\sigma = +1$ if the admissible reaction
is positive and $-1$ if it is negative:

$$ \sigma R \ge 0,\qquad \sigma u \ge 0,\qquad R\,u = 0 $$ (6.6)

The support is either active ($u = 0$, reaction of the right sign) or lifted off
($R = 0$, displacement moving away from the support). A variant acts as a block: the criterion
bears on a global axis, and when it is crossed, all the components of the support are released
together (a support that lifts off no longer holds either the horizontal forces or the moments). The
two variants cannot be combined on the same support, and a unilateral component cannot be combined
with a $6\times 6$ support matrix (block lift-off, for its part, allows it).

### 6.5.2 Force cap

A restrained component may be given a cap $R_{\max}$: the support stays restrained as long as
$|R| \le R_{\max}$; beyond that, it yields and transmits exactly

$$ R = \pm R_{\max}\quad\text{as long as the node penetrates the support} $$ (6.7)

with the sign of the reaction that made it yield. The behaviour is rigid-plastic. On a unilateral
component, the cap acts on the admissible side. For a continuous beam of two 10 m spans, only one of
which carries 10 kN/m, the reaction at the intermediate pier is $10qL/16 = 62.5$ kN for an
Euler-Bernoulli beam (slightly less with shear deformation); capped at 60 kN, it is 60 kN, and the
equilibrium of the remaining beam gives 45 kN at the loaded support and $-5$ kN at the other
end: this is what keta returns.

### 6.5.3 Active-set method

keta solves these conditions by an active-set method. It starts with all supports active; at each
iteration, the structure is solved with the current set, the lifted-off supports being removed and
the yielded supports replaced by their force $\pm R_{\max}$. Each component is then examined,
and it changes state according to the tests

$$ \begin{aligned}
&\text{active} \to \text{lifted off} && \text{if } \sigma R < -10^{-9}\,(1 + |R|)\\
&\text{active} \to \text{yielded} && \text{if } |R| > R_{\max}\,(1 + 10^{-12})\\
&\text{lifted off} \to \text{active} && \text{if } \sigma u < -10^{-12}\ \text{m (the node passes through the support)}\\
&\text{yielded} \to \text{active} && \text{if } s\,u > 10^{-12}\ \text{m (the node no longer penetrates)}
\end{aligned} $$ (6.8)

where $s$ is the sign of the reaction that made the support yield. The analysis stops when no
component changes state. The matrix is refactorised at each iteration. The number of iterations is
limited to $18\,n_a + 10$, $n_a$ being the number of supports; beyond that, the analysis
stops with an error. A support whose components are all released stays in the list of reactions,
with a zero reaction.

The result depends on the load: each case is solved on its own, its results are flagged as not
superposable, and the model's combinations are rejected (chapter 5). A combination must be described
as a case, with all its loads.

## 6.6 Kinematic links

### 6.6.1 Rigid links

A rigid link connects one or more slave nodes to a master node as if they belonged to the same
rigid body: a pier head, a very stiff diaphragm, the connection of a deck to its axis. For the coupled
components (a mask in global axes), the displacement of the slave is

$$ \mathbf{u}_s = \mathbf{u}_m + \boldsymbol{\theta}_m \times (\mathbf{x}_s - \mathbf{x}_m),\qquad \boldsymbol{\theta}_s = \boldsymbol{\theta}_m $$ (6.9)

The slave degrees of freedom are eliminated without approximation, $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{T}\,\mathbf{u}_r$, and
the system solved is $\mathbf{T}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{T}\,\mathbf{u}_r =
\mathbf{T}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{F}$ (chapter 4). Chains (the slave of one link being the master of
another) are resolved; a cyclic chain, a component constrained twice and a supported slave are
rejected: the master is supported instead, or the support is connected through an elastic link. By
releasing the three rotations of the mask, a spherical hinge of zero length is obtained; since the
mask is in global axes, a single bending rotation in a local frame cannot be released in this way.

### 6.6.2 Linear relations

A general linear relation ties components of arbitrary nodes:

$$ \sum_k c_k\,u(n_k, j_k) = 0 $$ (6.10)

The component of the first term is eliminated,
$u_1 = -\sum_{k>1} (c_k/c_1)\,u_k$; it must be free, carry no other relation and have a
non-zero coefficient. These relations join the same reduction as the rigid links. keta returns for
each of them its multiplier $\mu$: the force it exerts on the structure is
$-\mu\,c_k$ on each of its degrees of freedom.

## 6.7 Elastic links

### 6.7.1 Spring between two nodes

An elastic link is a symmetric $6\times 6$ spring $\mathbf{k}$ located at the point
$P = \mathbf{x}_i + s\,(\mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{x}_i)$, which the two nodes reach through rigid
arms ($s = 0.5$ by default). The relative displacement at point $P$ is

$$ \mathbf{d} = \left(\mathbf{u}_j + \boldsymbol{\theta}_j \times (P - \mathbf{x}_j)\right) - \left(\mathbf{u}_i + \boldsymbol{\theta}_i \times (P - \mathbf{x}_i)\right),\qquad \Delta\boldsymbol{\theta} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_j - \boldsymbol{\theta}_i $$ (6.11)

so that a rigid-body motion of the pair does not deform the spring. Expressed in the axes of the
link, $(\mathbf{d}, \Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbf{B}\,\mathbf{u}_e$, it gives the element
matrix

$$ \mathbf{K}_e = \mathbf{B}^\mathsf{T}\,\mathbf{k}\,\mathbf{B} $$ (6.12)

The force on node $j$ is $-\mathbf{k}\,(\mathbf{d}, \Delta\boldsymbol{\theta})$; the
axial component is positive in tension when the $x$ axis runs from $i$ to $j$. The axes
of the link are either given explicitly or taken as those of a bar from $i$ to $j$ (with its
roll angle); for two coincident nodes, they are the global axes. A link between two coincident nodes
is an elastic hinge: partial fixity, semi-rigid closure hinge, bearing between deck and pier. The
results of a link are its deformation and its force, in its own axes.

**Figure 6.1** — Elastic link: spring at point P reached by two rigid arms

### 6.7.2 Nonlinear link laws

Each component of a link may follow a nonlinear law $F(d)$ in place of its stiffness term (it
must then have no coupling term with the other components). The law is piecewise linear, defined by
points $(d_i, F_i)$ with strictly increasing abscissae and non-decreasing forces; beyond the end
points, the end segments are extended. Four laws are predefined: tension only, compression only, a
gap $g$ on either side before the stiffness $k$ acts, and elastic-perfectly plastic
($k$ up to $|F| = F_y$, then a slope $k_p \ge 0$). The force at zero displacement may
be non-zero: a preloaded spring, earth pressure at rest.

**Figure 6.2** — Predefined link laws (F > 0 in tension)

A non-decreasing law derives from a convex potential $\Psi_j(d) = \int_0^d F_j$. Equilibrium is
then the minimum of the potential energy

$$ \Pi(\mathbf{u}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{u}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{f}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{u} + \sum_j \Psi_j\!\left(\mathbf{b}_j^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{u} + d_{0,j}\right) $$ (6.13)

where $\mathbf{K}$ is the stiffness of the linear part (rigid links eliminated),
$\mathbf{b}_j$ the operator that gives the deformation of component $j$, and $d_{0,j}$
the part of that deformation due to imposed displacements. keta minimises $\Pi$ by Newton's
method, with the tangent matrix
$\mathbf{K} + \sum_j k_{t,j}\,\mathbf{b}_j\mathbf{b}_j^\mathsf{T}$ ($k_{t,j}$ being the
slope of the current segment), and a line search that halves the step as long as the energy does not
decrease. Since the potential is piecewise quadratic, the full step gives the solution as soon as
every law is on its final segment: the analysis ends in a finite number of iterations, with no
tolerance on the laws and no penalty. It stops when the full step is accepted and the norm of the
residual is below $10^{-11}$ times the largest load (or the round-off error of
$\mathbf{K}\mathbf{u}$), within a limit of 200 iterations. A decreasing law is rejected, and a
mechanism (a node held only by the slack component of a link) stops the analysis.

For a simply supported 20 m beam, of midspan stiffness $k_b = 48EI/L^3$, resting at midspan on
a link of stiffness $k$ with gap $g$, under a force $P$, equilibrium is
$w = -(P + k g)/(k_b + k)$ once the gap has closed: keta finds it in two iterations, as it does
for the tension-only, compression-only and elastic-plastic cases.

### 6.7.3 Softening laws and moment-rotation laws depending on axial force

A hinge whose moment decreases after the peak (the ASCE 41 backbone curves, for example) no longer
derives from a convex potential. keta then follows the equilibrium path under control of a
displacement $u_c$: the unknowns are $(\mathbf{u}, \lambda)$ and the bordered system

$$ \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{f}_\text{perm} + \lambda\,\mathbf{f} - \mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{u} - \sum_j \mathbf{b}_j\,F_j(\mathbf{b}_j^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{0},\qquad u_c = u_c^\text{target} $$ (6.14)

is solved by Newton's method with the exact tangent, in 20 steps per branch of the imposed path, at
most 50 iterations and a tolerance of $10^{-10}$, the step being halved in case of failure (at
most ten times). Permanent loads may be applied first, at $\lambda = 0$. To get past a reversal
of the controlled displacement, the path can be followed by arc length, from event to event (a change
of segment in a law), each point of the path being an equilibrium state. A rotation component may
follow a family of laws $M(\theta)$ tabulated for several axial forces
$N_0 < N_1 < \dots$ of the same link: the law at $N$ is the linear interpolation, point
by point, of the two laws that bracket it, and the tangent includes the term
$\partial M/\partial N$; an axial force outside the table stops the analysis.

### 6.7.4 Elastic-plastic loading history

The longitudinal resistance of ballast, a friction bearing or a fuse retain a plastic slip from one
loading step to the next. For these components, keta uses an elastic-plastic law with linear
kinematic hardening: elastic stiffness $k$, threshold $F_y$, post-yield slope $k_p$
($0 \le k_p < k$), plastic slip $u_p$ and back force $\beta$:

$$ F = k\,(d - u_p),\qquad |F - \beta| \le F_y,\qquad H = \frac{k\,k_p}{k - k_p} $$ (6.15)

A step adds the loads of a case in equal increments (ten by default). Over an increment, the
return mapping (implicit Euler) turns each component into a piecewise linear law of its final
deformation, of slope $k$ between $(d^-, \beta - F_y)$ and $(d^+, \beta + F_y)$,
$d^\pm = u_p + (\beta \pm F_y)/k$, and of slope $k_p$ beyond: the increment is the convex
problem (6.13), solved as above, after which $u_p$ and $\beta$ are updated.
Between two steps, the law of a component may change (ballast unloaded, then loaded under the train):
the force is preserved and the new law starts from that force; a force above the new threshold is
brought back to it, and the out-of-balance is absorbed by the next step. A committed state may serve
as the starting point of several loading sequences (each position of a train from the same thermal
state, chapter 13).

## 6.8 Soils

### 6.8.1 Winkler elastic foundation

A Winkler soil exerts on the bar, at each point, a reaction proportional to the local displacement
of that point. The moduli are given in the local axes of the bar, per unit length:
$k_{fx}, k_{fy}, k_{fz}$ in N/m per m (Pa) and $k_{mx}$ in N·m/rad per m. With an
Euler-Bernoulli bar, the equations solved are

$$ EI\,w'''' + k\,w = q(x),\qquad EA\,u'' - k_{fx}\,u = -p_x(x),\qquad GJ\,\theta'' - k_{mx}\,\theta = -m_x(x) $$ (6.16)

the first one for each bending plane. The characteristic length $\ell = 1/\beta$, with
$\beta = (k/4EI)^{1/4}$, measures the reach of the effect of a concentrated load: under a force
$P$ at the middle of an infinite beam,

$$ w(x) = \frac{P\beta}{2k}\,e^{-\beta|x|}\left(\cos\beta x + \sin\beta|x|\right),\qquad M(x) = \frac{P}{4\beta}\,e^{-\beta|x|}\left(\cos\beta x - \sin\beta|x|\right) $$ (6.17)

The soil reaction is returned at the study sections, $p = k\,u_\text{local}$: it has the sign of
the local displacement, and the force of the soil on the bar is $-p$.

**Figure 6.3** — Beam on elastic soil

### 6.8.2 Exact element for a bar on soil

In linear statics, a bar on uniform soil without release, without shear deformation and of
constant cross-section is handled by an exact element. Without shear deformation means that the
shear areas of the section are zero: a parametric section, which carries them by default
(chapter 3), keeps the consistent bed described below unless they are set to zero. The exact element
is built on the solutions of (6.16) themselves. Following the note by A. L. Millan (Annales
de l'ITBTP no. 408), keta uses the transfer functions

$$ f_p(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \left(-\frac{k}{EI}\right)^{n} \frac{x^{p+4n}}{(p+4n)!},\qquad g_p(x) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \left(\frac{k}{EA}\right)^{n} \frac{x^{p+2n}}{(p+2n)!} $$ (6.18)

($f_p' = f_{p-1}$) in bending and in tension or torsion; their power series remains valid as
$k \to 0$, with no discontinuity. The functions $f_4, f_5$ ($g_2, g_3$) give the
particular solution for linearly distributed loads; concentrated loads and imposed strains (thermal
expansion, curvature) are also taken into account. A transfer matrix over a long, strongly supported
bar grows as $e^{\beta L}$ and becomes ill-conditioned. keta therefore divides the bar into
pieces of length $l \le (EI/k)^{1/4}$ ($l \le \sqrt{EA/k}$ in tension and torsion), builds
the exact stiffness and the fixed-end forces of each piece, then condenses the interior nodes: the
result remains the exact solution of the equation, with no discretisation error, whatever
$\beta L$.

A single bar is enough, and the internal forces at the study sections include the soil reaction.
For a 66 m beam ($\beta L = 20$) loaded at its middle and represented by one bar, the deflection
and the moment under the load differ from (6.17) by $6 \times 10^{-9}$ in relative
terms, a difference that is due to the finite length.

**Figure 6.4** — Beam on elastic soil under a force of 1 MN (EI = 1.5 GN·m², k = 50 MPa): one exact keta bar and the infinite beam

### 6.8.3 Consistent Hermite bed

When the exact element does not apply (Timoshenko bar, release, variable section), and in the
dynamic, stability, nonlinear and influence-line analyses, the soil stiffness is the consistent
matrix

$$ \mathbf{k}_\text{soil} = \int_0^L \mathbf{N}^\mathsf{T}\,k\,\mathbf{N}\,\mathrm{d}x $$ (6.19)

built on the shape functions of the element: cubic Hermite functions in bending, linear functions
in tension and torsion. It is added after the condensation of releases (a hinge releases the moment of
the bar, not the soil reaction). At the nodes, the solution converges to that of (6.16) as
the fourth power of the bar length; inside a bar, the internal forces returned do not include the soil
reaction. For the beam of the previous figure, handled with this consistent bed and divided into bars
of length $h$, the error in the deflection under the load is:

| $\beta h$ | 5 | 2.5 | 1.25 | 0.625 | 0.3125 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| relative error | 37 % | 10 % | 0.97 % | 0.063 % | 0.004 % |

The bars must therefore be appreciably shorter than $1/\beta$: $\beta h \le 0.5$ gives
the deflection to within one part in a thousand.

### 6.8.4 Zoned soil

The modulus may vary along a bar by zones: each zone carries its moduli
$k_{fx}, k_{fy}, k_{fz}, k_{mx}$ and the abscissa $x_z$ of its end; the last zone extends to
the end of the bar, whatever abscissa is given. The consistent matrix of the bar is the sum of the
integrals (6.19) over each zone,

$$ \mathbf{k}_\text{soil} = \sum_z \int_{x_{z-1}}^{x_z} \mathbf{N}^\mathsf{T}\,\operatorname{diag}\!\left(k_{fx}, k_{fy}, k_{fz}, k_{mx}\right)_z\,\mathbf{N}\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad x_0 = 0 $$ (6.20)

computed by an 8-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature, exact for these polynomials of degree 6 at most.
When the exact element applies to every bar on soil, each zone becomes a zone of the exact
element.

### 6.8.5 Pseudo-plastic soil and tensionless soil

Real soil does not pull, and its reaction is bounded. For each bar and each component, a threshold
$f_f$ (a force per unit length, N/m, or a moment per unit length) and a unilaterality may be
given: the soil reacts only where $p = k\,u$ is positive, or only where it is negative. The
reaction becomes

$$ r(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } p(x) \text{ does not have the admissible sign}\\ \operatorname{clamp}\left(k\,u(x),\ -f_f,\ f_f\right) & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$ (6.21)

The threshold is an intensity per unit length: a limit pressure must be multiplied by the width of
the footing or the diameter of the pile, as the modulus is. keta solves this problem by an active set
on sub-segments: each zone is divided into ten sub-segments (an adjustable number), and the state of
each sub-segment and each component is decided by the mean reaction over the sub-segment. When
elastic, the sub-segment keeps its modulus; when capped, it loses its modulus and receives a constant
distributed load of intensity $f_f$ opposing the motion; when lifted off, it carries nothing. The
structure is solved again until no state changes any more, in at most 50 iterations. A capped or
lifted-off sub-segment becomes elastic again only once it has clearly returned to the admissible
domain (a band of $10^{-8}$ in relative terms), which prevents oscillation between two states.
The yield front is located to within one sub-segment.

By default, each bar on soil is the exact element with the moduli of its states (zero where the soil
is capped or lifted off), and the mean reaction of a sub-segment is the integral of the exact
deflected shape. Unlike linear statics, this analysis uses the exact element even when the section
carries shear areas: shear deformation is then neglected. If a bar on soil carries a release or a
variable section, the whole model uses the consistent matrix (6.19); the bars must
then be finely divided. For the previous beam, divided into eight bars and capped at 100 kN/m, the
soil reaction is 100 kN/m under the load and its resultant equals the applied force to within
round-off.

**Figure 6.5** — Soil reaction under the previous beam (F = 1 MN): elastic soil and soil capped at 100 kN/m

The results of a unilateral or capped soil are not superposable; combinations are formed only if no
soil in the model is nonlinear. Zoned and pseudo-plastic soils are also available in the staged
analysis (chapter 10).

### 6.8.6 Nonlinear soil springs

The soil around a retaining wall or a pile can also be represented by springs lumped at the nodes:
a zero-length link between the node and a fixed node created at its position, whose axis is the
direction of action and whose law is one of the nonlinear laws above. They are solved by the
minimisation (6.13).

For earth pressure on a wall, each soil layer gives the effective vertical stress
$\sigma_v(y) = \sigma_{v,0} + \gamma\,(y_\text{top} - y)$ and, from the coefficients
$K_a, K_0, K_p$ and the cohesion,

$$ p_0 = K_0\,\sigma_v,\quad p_a = \max(0,\ K_a\,\sigma_v - K_{ac}\,c),\quad p_p = K_p\,\sigma_v + K_{pc}\,c,\qquad
p(d) = \operatorname{clamp}\left(p_0 - k_h\,d,\ p_a,\ p_p\right) $$ (6.22)

where $d$ is the displacement of the wall towards the excavation (the active direction) and
$k_h = A + B\,(y_\text{top} - y)^\kappa$ the modulus of subgrade reaction. The pressures are
distributed to the nodes of the wall consistently: each characteristic level of a node is the integral
of the field multiplied by the linear shape function of the node, over the part of its two segments
lying within the layer, then multiplied by the width. The sum of the plateau forces is then the exact
thrust, $K_a\,(qH + \gamma H^2/2)$ for a homogeneous layer. A lumped distribution (the field at
the level of the node multiplied by its tributary length) is also offered. The usual coefficients are
provided: Rankine, $K_a = \tan^2(\pi/4 - \varphi/2)$ and $K_p = \tan^2(\pi/4 + \varphi/2)$;
Jaky, $K_0 = 1 - \sin\varphi$; Coulomb for a vertical wall and a horizontal backfill, with the
wall friction $\delta$,

$$ K_a = \frac{\cos^2\varphi}{\cos\delta\left(1 + \sqrt{\dfrac{\sin(\varphi+\delta)\,\sin\varphi}{\cos\delta}}\right)^{2}} $$ (6.23)

and the same expression with a minus sign inside the square for $K_p$.

**Figure 6.6** — Total earth pressure on a 10 m wall (q = 10 kPa, γ = 18 kN/m³, Ka = 1/3, K0 = 0.5, Kp = 3) as a function of its displacement, computed by keta

For piles, keta builds the API RP 2A curves (21st edition, §6.7 and 6.8), per unit length of pile
(to be multiplied by the tributary length of the node): $p\text{-}y$ curves for soft clays
(Matlock), stiff clays above the water table (Welch and Reese) and sands
($p = A\,p_u \tanh(k X y / A p_u)$), $t\text{-}z$ curves for shaft friction and
$q\text{-}z$ curves for end bearing (compression only). Curves defined by a formula are sampled
on the curve and joined by chords (16 segments by default). The post-peak loss of friction of the
$t\text{-}z$ curves is not represented: a decreasing law would break the convexity of the
problem, and the peak is retained.

### 6.8.7 Edge springs

A shell edge resting on an elastic support, or a semi-rigid joint between two slabs, is a line of
springs of stiffness $\mathbf{k}$ per unit length (a $6\times 6$ matrix in the axes of each
segment: $x$ along the segment, $z$ upwards). keta represents it by node-to-node elastic
links; each node receives half of each of its two segments,

$$ \mathbf{K}_\text{node} = \sum_{\text{adjacent segments}} \frac{L_s}{2}\,\mathbf{R}_s^\mathsf{T}\,\mathbf{k}\,\mathbf{R}_s $$ (6.24)

which is exact for a relative displacement that is uniform along the line, and a discretisation of
the line of springs otherwise. Without an opposite line, each node is connected to a fixed node
created at its position. A hinge line is obtained by doubling the nodes, coupling their translations
by rigid links and adding, if needed, a rotational spring.

## 6.9 Scope

All the devices of this chapter act under small displacements and in their initial axes. Unilateral
supports, force caps and link laws are static analyses case by case, not superposable; the linear
analyses (eigenmodes, buckling, influence lines) reject links with a nonlinear law and treat a
unilateral support as bilateral. Imposed displacements apply only to rigidly restrained components.
The plastic slip of a support is carried from one case to the next only by elastic-plastic links
loaded in steps, not by the supports of the model. The exact element for a bar on soil is restricted
to the linear statics of prismatic Euler-Bernoulli bars without release; everywhere else, the
consistent matrix requires a division with $\beta h \le 0.5$. The pseudo-plastic soil locates
its front to within one sub-segment and decides the state of a sub-segment from its mean reaction.

# Chapter 7 Cables

This chapter deals with heavy cables stretched between two nodes of the frame: stays, main cables
and backstays of suspension bridges, ties, cable nets. The problem is the static equilibrium of the
assembly formed by the frame and its cables, under the loads of a case. A cable is not a bar: it
works in tension only, sags under its own weight and stiffens as its tension increases. Its stiffness
therefore depends on the state being sought, and the problem is no longer linear.

Prestressing tendons, which lie inside the concrete and transfer forces to it by friction and
deviation, are the subject of chapter 8. The dynamic behaviour of cables is dealt with in chapter 16,
and their role in large-displacement analysis in chapter 17.

## 7.1 Assumptions

The cable is represented by a single elastic catenary between its two attachment nodes, without
subdivision into elements. The assumptions are those of Irvine's theory:

- the cable is perfectly flexible: it has neither bending nor torsional stiffness, and carries no
compression;

- the material is linearly elastic, with a constant axial rigidity $EA$;

- the only distributed load is the self-weight, uniform, $w$ per unit unstressed length; the
other loads are applied at the nodes;

- under its weight, the cable stays in the vertical plane that contains its chord; a vertical chord
is not allowed;

- the strains of the cable remain small (the elongation is limited to a few per cent); its
displacements, on the other hand, may be large: the geometry of the cable is recomputed at each
iteration from the position of its ends.

The frame that carries the cables remains, in the coupled analysis of this chapter, under small
displacements. The large-displacement analysis of the whole (chapter 17) uses the same
catenaries.

## 7.2 Equations of the elastic catenary

The origin is placed at end 1 of the cable. In the vertical plane of the chord, $\ell$ denotes
the horizontal projection of the chord and $h$ its vertical projection, positive upwards from
end 1 to end 2. The cable has an unstressed length $L_0$, and a point of the cable is located by
its unstressed arc length $s$, from 0 to $L_0$. No horizontal load acts between the ends:
the horizontal component $H$ of the tension is constant. The vertical component increases with
the weight carried:

$$ V(s) = V_1 + w\,s,\qquad V_2 = V(L_0) = V_1 + w\,L_0,\qquad T(s) = \sqrt{H^2 + V(s)^2} $$ (7.1)

With the conventions of the figure, $(H, V_1)$ and $-(H, V_2)$ are the forces that the
cable exerts on its nodes 1 and 2. A cable that descends from end 1 has $V_1 < 0$; the low
point, if there is one, lies at $s = -V_1/w$.

**Figure 7.1** — Elastic catenary between two nodes: notation (computed geometry, equal scales in both directions)

The tangent to the cable is carried by the tension, $\mathrm{d}z/\mathrm{d}x = V(s)/H$, and the
element $\mathrm{d}s$ elongates by $T\,\mathrm{d}s/EA$ (Hooke's law). Integrating
$\mathrm{d}x = (H/T)(1 + T/EA)\,\mathrm{d}s$ and $\mathrm{d}z = (V/T)(1 + T/EA)\,\mathrm{d}s$
from 0 to $L_0$ gives the two projections in closed form:

$$ \ell = \frac{H L_0}{EA} + \frac{H}{w}\left[\operatorname{arsinh}\frac{V_2}{H} - \operatorname{arsinh}\frac{V_1}{H}\right] $$ (7.2)

$$ h = \frac{L_0}{EA}\left(V_1 + \frac{w L_0}{2}\right) + \frac{T_2 - T_1}{w} $$ (7.3)

The first term of each equation is the elastic elongation, the second the geometry of the
inextensible catenary. The tension is greatest at the higher end: on an inextensible catenary,
$T = T_1 + w\,(z - z_1)$.

A zero weight makes these expressions indeterminate. keta then replaces $w$ by a tiny weight,
$10^{-9}\,EA/L_0^2$, with no measurable effect on the result; the form finding of suspension
bridges (section 7.8) uses a form of the same integrals that admits a zero weight.

### 7.2.1 Solution for given end positions

When the positions of the two ends are known, (7.2) and (7.3) are two
