equations in $(H, V_1)$. keta solves them by Newton's method. The Newton matrix is the
flexibility of the cable, the derivative of the projections with respect to the forces:

$$ \mathbf{F} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial \ell}{\partial H} & \dfrac{\partial \ell}{\partial V_1} \\[2mm]
\dfrac{\partial h}{\partial H} & \dfrac{\partial h}{\partial V_1} \end{bmatrix},\qquad
\begin{aligned}
F_{11} &= \frac{1}{w}\left[\operatorname{arsinh}\frac{V_2}{H} - \operatorname{arsinh}\frac{V_1}{H}\right] - \frac{1}{w}\left(\frac{V_2}{T_2} - \frac{V_1}{T_1}\right) + \frac{L_0}{EA} \\
F_{12} &= F_{21} = \frac{H}{w}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right) \\
F_{22} &= \frac{1}{w}\left(\frac{V_2}{T_2} - \frac{V_1}{T_1}\right) + \frac{L_0}{EA}
\end{aligned} $$ (7.4)

Each iteration corrects the forces by

$$ \begin{bmatrix}\Delta H \\ \Delta V_1\end{bmatrix} = -\,\mathbf{F}^{-1}
\begin{bmatrix}\ell(H, V_1) - \ell_\text{target} \\ h(H, V_1) - h_\text{target}\end{bmatrix} $$ (7.5)

the step being halved as long as $H$ would become negative. The starting point depends on the
state of the cable. A cable longer than its chord $c$ starts from a parabola of sag
$f = \sqrt{3\,\ell\,(L_0 - c)/8}$, that is $H = w\ell^2/(8f)$. A cable shorter than its
chord starts from a tension directed along the chord, $T_0 = EA\,(c - L_0)/L_0$. The iterations
stop when the error on both projections is below $10^{-13}$ times the largest of the lengths
$\ell$, $|h|$, $L_0$, or below the round-off noise of the integrals, which grows with
the tension.

## 7.3 Tangent stiffness of the cable

The inverse of the flexibility (7.4) is the tangent stiffness of the cable in its
plane:

$$ \mathbf{K}_\text{plane} = \mathbf{F}^{-1} = \frac{1}{F_{11}F_{22} - F_{12}^2}
\begin{bmatrix} F_{22} & -F_{12} \\ -F_{12} & F_{11} \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} K_{xx} & K_{xz} \\ K_{xz} & K_{zz} \end{bmatrix} $$ (7.6)

It relates a small relative displacement of the ends, horizontal and vertical in the plane of the
cable, to the change in the forces $(H, V_1)$. Out of its plane, a cable displaced laterally by
an amount $\delta$ swings about its chord like a pendulum: the horizontal component of the
tension produces a restoring force $H\,\delta/\ell$. With $\mathbf{e}_h$ the horizontal unit
vector of the chord, $\mathbf{e}_z$ the vertical and
$\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{e}_h \times \mathbf{e}_z$ the horizontal normal to the plane of the cable,
the stiffness of one node relative to the other is

$$ \mathbf{k} = K_{xx}\,\mathbf{e}_h\mathbf{e}_h^\mathsf{T}
+ K_{xz}\left(\mathbf{e}_h\mathbf{e}_z^\mathsf{T} + \mathbf{e}_z\mathbf{e}_h^\mathsf{T}\right)
+ K_{zz}\,\mathbf{e}_z\mathbf{e}_z^\mathsf{T} + \frac{H}{\ell}\,\mathbf{n}\,\mathbf{n}^\mathsf{T} $$ (7.7)

and the matrix of the cable, on the translations of its two nodes, is that of a two-node
element:

$$ \mathbf{K}_c = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{k} & -\mathbf{k} \\ -\mathbf{k} & \mathbf{k} \end{bmatrix} $$ (7.8)

The cable contributes no rotational stiffness. A node that carries only cables must therefore have
its rotations restrained by a support or by another bar.

## 7.4 Unstressed length

The unstressed length $L_0$ defines the cable. It may be given directly, or determined in the
initial geometry of the model from a tension. In both cases, it is computed once, in the undeformed
geometry, and does not change afterwards, whatever the displacements of the frame.

### 7.4.1 Imposed horizontal tension

The root sought is that of

$$ H(L_0) - H_\text{target} = 0 $$ (7.9)

where $H(L_0)$ is the horizontal tension of the catenary of length $L_0$ stretched
between the two ends, obtained by the solution of the previous section. $H$ decreases as
$L_0$ increases: the root is unique. keta brackets it starting from
$[c/2,\ 3c/2]$, widened if needed, then narrows it by bisection until
$|H - H_\text{target}| < 10^{-10}\,H_\text{target}$.

### 7.4.2 Tension imposed at one end

The tension at one end is not monotonic in $L_0$:

$$ T_2(L_0) = \sqrt{H(L_0)^2 + \bigl(V_1(L_0) + w\,L_0\bigr)^2} $$ (7.10)

When a taut cable is lengthened, its tension first decreases, like that of a tie; then the cable
takes on sag, its weight increases with its length, and the tension rises again. The same tension
may therefore correspond to two lengths, one on the taut branch, the other on the slack branch
(figure 7.2).

**Figure 7.2** — End tension of a stay as a function of its unstressed length (ℓ = 200 m, h = 80 m, EA = 1.2 GN, w = 600 N/m)

keta keeps the root on the taut branch, the only one that suits a stay. The search starts from
$L_0 = c/(1 + 0.045)$, that is an elongation of 4.5 %, and proceeds in steps of 5 % until the
root is bracketed, followed by a bisection down to $10^{-12}\,T_\text{target}$. A tension higher
than that of this starting point would require an elongation beyond the elastic range and is
rejected; a tension below the minimum of the curve has no root on the taut branch and is rejected
too. The tension may be prescribed at either end.

## 7.5 Equilibrium of the frame and cables

The unknown is the vector $\mathbf{u}$ of the displacements of all the nodes. Each cable is
evaluated at the displaced position of its two nodes: its catenary is solved, which gives the forces
$\mathbf{q}(\mathbf{u})$ that it exerts on them. Equilibrium reads

$$ \mathbf{r}(\mathbf{u}) = \lambda\,\mathbf{F} + \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{u}) - \mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0} $$ (7.11)

where $\mathbf{K}$ is the linear stiffness of the frame, $\mathbf{F}$ the loads of the
case and $\lambda$ the fraction applied. The self-weight of the cables is always present, in
full, since it is contained in $\mathbf{q}$.

### 7.5.1 Newton's method

At each iteration, the system solved is

$$ \Bigl(\mathbf{K} + \sum_c \mathbf{K}_c(\mathbf{u})\Bigr)\,\Delta\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{r}(\mathbf{u}) $$ (7.12)

where the sum runs over the matrices (7.8) of the cables in the current state. The
step is followed by a line search: the update kept is $\mathbf{u} + s\,\Delta\mathbf{u}$ with
$s = 1, \tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{4}, \dots$, the first value for which

$$ \|\mathbf{r}(\mathbf{u} + s\,\Delta\mathbf{u})\|_\infty < \|\mathbf{r}(\mathbf{u})\|_\infty $$ (7.13)

A step for which a cable finds no catenary (chord become vertical, ends further apart than the
admissible tension allows) is rejected in the same way. After thirty unsuccessful halvings, the
analysis stops with an error. The matrix of each iteration has the same sparsity pattern as the
previous one: the reordering and the symbolic analysis of the factorisation (chapter 4) are done
once.

### 7.5.2 Convergence criterion

The analysis stops when each component of the residual satisfies

$$ |r_i| - 8\,\varepsilon \sum_j |K_{ij}\,u_j| \;\le\; 10^{-10}\,
\max\Bigl(\|\lambda\mathbf{F}\|_\infty,\ \|\mathbf{K}\mathbf{u}\|_\infty,\ \max_c T_c\Bigr) $$ (7.14)

with $\varepsilon$ the machine precision. The tension of the cables enters the scale because a
cable net without external load has a zero residual at equilibrium, while its cables are in tension.
The term subtracted on the left is the round-off error of the product $\mathbf{K}\mathbf{u}$: on
a very stiff member, a pylon for example, the terms $K_{ij}u_j$ are large and cancel out, and the
residual cannot fall below their round-off error. Without this term, Newton's method would iterate on
noise.

### 7.5.3 Load increments

The loads of the case may be applied in $n$ increments,

$$ \mathbf{r}(\mathbf{u}_m) = \lambda_m\,\mathbf{F} + \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{u}_m) - \mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{u}_m = \mathbf{0},\qquad \lambda_m = \frac{m}{n},\quad m = 1, \dots, n $$ (7.15)

each increment starting from the equilibrium $\mathbf{u}_{m-1}$ of the previous one. This is
useful when the final state is far from the initial state (a cable very slack at the start, a large
displacement of a saddle). The number of iterations is limited to sixty per increment.

### 7.5.4 Results

The displacements, internal forces and stresses of the frame are recovered as in linear statics
(chapter 4), from $\mathbf{u}$. For each cable, keta gives the horizontal tension $H$ and
the largest tension $\max(T_1, T_2)$. The support reactions include the pull of the cables
anchored at supported nodes:

$$ \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{q}(\mathbf{u}) - \mathbf{F} $$ (7.16)

**Note.**

The results of an analysis with cables are not superposable: each combination must be
analysed as a case, with all its loads. Imposed support displacements are not allowed in this
analysis.

## 7.6 Ernst equivalent stiffness

The linear analyses (statics, eigenmodes, response spectrum) cannot handle a catenary. Each cable is
then replaced by a straight bar with the same chord, whose stiffness accounts for the sag: this is
Ernst's method. A cable of chord length $L_c$ and horizontal projection $\ell$, under a mean
tension $T$ along the chord, has the axial stiffness

$$ \frac{1}{k} = \frac{L_0}{EA} + \frac{(w\,\ell)^2\,L_c}{12\,T^3},\qquad T = \frac{H L_c}{\ell} $$ (7.17)

The first term is the elastic flexibility, the second the flexibility that comes from the sag.
Written with the stress $\sigma = T/A$ and the unit weight $\gamma = w/A$, this result is the
classical equivalent modulus

$$ E_\text{eq} = \frac{E}{1 + \dfrac{(\gamma\,\ell)^2 E}{12\,\sigma^3}} $$ (7.18)

**Figure 7.3** — Ernst equivalent modulus of a stay (E = 195 GPa, γ = 78.5 kN/m³)

### 7.6.1 Range of the approximation

The approximation improves as the cable becomes tauter. Its relative error with respect to the
exact stiffness of the catenary is close to $\chi^2/5$, with the sag parameter

$$ \chi = \frac{w\,L_c\cos^2\alpha}{H},\qquad \cos\alpha = \frac{\ell}{L_c} $$ (7.19)

where $\alpha$ is the inclination of the chord. keta flags the cables for which
$\chi > 0.1$, that is an error above about 0.2 %: the catenary must then be kept. The sag term is
often found written as $w^2 L_c^3/(12H^3)$. This form is exact for a horizontal chord, but for an
inclined chord it multiplies the sag term by $1/\cos^5\alpha$, that is 2.05 at 30° and 32 at
60°: the stiffness is then underestimated, all the more as the sag weighs in the flexibility of the
cable.

### 7.6.2 Substitute model

From a state computed with the catenaries, keta builds a model in which each cable becomes a
pin-ended bar of stiffness $k$, placed on the geometry of the model. Its modulus and density
are chosen to reproduce the stiffness and the mass of the cable:

$$ E^* = \frac{k\,L_c}{A},\qquad \rho^* = \frac{w\,L_0}{g\,A\,L_c} $$ (7.20)

The tension of the state is retained on each bar. A modal analysis about this state accounts for
it through the geometric stiffness (chapter 17), which gives the stays their vibrating-string
stiffness $T/L_c$. The bars remain on the initial geometry: if the computed state has displaced
the anchorages by $u$, the chords rotate by about $u/L_c$, which gives the order of
magnitude of the error made.

## 7.7 Tension adjustment

Adjusting the stays of a bridge means finding the installation tensions that give, under permanent
loads, a chosen deck profile, a vertical pylon or chosen reactions. keta sets out this problem in two
ways.

### 7.7.1 Linear adjustment

The unknowns $x_j$ are load case coefficients, generally one unit pretension case per stay: an
imposed shortening $\varepsilon_0 = -1/EA$, which tensions the stay by 1 N if it is free to
shorten. Each target result $r_i$ (displacement, reaction, internal force in a bar or a link)
is an affine function of the unknowns:

$$ \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{x} $$ (7.21)

where $\mathbf{b}$ comes from the base cases and column $j$ of $\mathbf{A}$ from case
$j$, all obtained by a single solution with several right-hand sides. The objectives are
equalities, bounds or weighted least-squares terms; the unknowns may be bounded and penalised. The
problem

$$ \min_{\mathbf{x}}\ \sum_{i\,\in\,\text{fitted}} w_i\,(\mathbf{a}_i\mathbf{x} + b_i - t_i)^2 + \sum_j q_j\,(x_j - x_j^\text{ref})^2
\quad \text{subject to}\quad \mathbf{a}_i\mathbf{x} + b_i = t_i,\ \ \mathbf{a}_i\mathbf{x} + b_i \lessgtr t_i,\ \ x_j^- \le x_j \le x_j^+ $$ (7.22)

is a convex quadratic programme, solved exactly by the dual method of Goldfarb and Idnani. With as
many equalities as unknowns, it amounts to solving a square system; with more unknowns, the penalties
$q_j$ select the solution; with more objectives, these are fitted in the least-squares sense. If
the objective is not strictly convex on the unknowns that the equalities leave free, the analysis
stops with an error rather than choose a solution.

### 7.7.2 Nonlinear adjustment

The unknowns are the unstressed lengths of the cables and, if needed, the length defects of bars of
the frame (a bar fabricated too short by $\delta$ receives the imposed strain
$-\delta/L$). The results $\mathbf{r}(\mathbf{x})$ are those of the coupled analysis of
section 7.5, or of the large-displacement analysis of the whole. keta linearises them by central
differences,

$$ J_{ij} = \frac{r_i(\mathbf{x} + h_j\mathbf{e}_j) - r_i(\mathbf{x} - h_j\mathbf{e}_j)}{2\,h_j},\qquad h_j = 10^{-6}\,|L_{0,j}| $$ (7.23)

solves problem (7.22) for the step $\Delta\mathbf{x}$ with
$\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{J}$, repeats the coupled analysis at $\mathbf{x} + \Delta\mathbf{x}$,
and halves the step as long as the error on the equalities increases. For a length defect, the
difference step is $10^{-7}$ times the length of the bar. The analysis stops when each equality
is satisfied to within $10^{-9}$ and, if there are fitted or bounded objectives, when the step
itself has fallen below this tolerance; the error is measured relative to the largest of the target,
obtained and initial values; for a zero target displacement, the scale is the diagonal of the box
enclosing the model. When there are as many equalities as unknowns, keta computes the singular values
of their Jacobian. If the ratio of the smallest to the largest is below $10^{-10}$, two
objectives are dependent: the analysis stops, naming the objectives and the cables involved.

## 7.8 Suspension bridges

### 7.8.1 Form finding of the main cable

The main cable is the funicular of the loads transmitted to it by the hangers. Between two hangers,
it is an elastic catenary of constant horizontal tension. At the node of a hanger $k$, which
carries the downward load $P_k$, the tension of the cable jumps:

$$ V_{k+1} = V_k + P_k,\qquad H_{k+1} = H_k - P_k\,\frac{\Delta x_k}{-\Delta z_k} $$ (7.24)

where $(\Delta x_k, \Delta z_k)$ runs from the cable node to the attachment point of the hanger
on the deck ($\Delta z_k < 0$). For a vertical hanger, $\Delta x_k = 0$ and the
horizontal tension is the same over the whole span. An inclined hanger transmits a force directed
along its axis, which makes $H$ vary from one segment to the next; the force in the hanger
is

$$ S_k = P_k\,\frac{\sqrt{\Delta x_k^2 + \Delta z_k^2}}{-\Delta z_k} $$ (7.25)

**Figure 7.4** — Equilibrium of the main cable at the node of an inclined hanger

The abscissae of the cable nodes are given. The unknowns are the two components $(H, V_0)$ of
the tension in the first segment. From them, the computation marches from saddle to saddle. For each
segment $k$, the unstressed length $L_{0,k}$ that gives the required horizontal projection
is sought, and the difference in level follows:

$$ \ell_k(L_{0,k}) = x_{k+1} - x_k,\qquad z_{k+1} = z_k + h_k(L_{0,k}) $$ (7.26)

The first equation has a unique solution, since $\ell_k$ increases with $L_{0,k}$
($\mathrm{d}\ell/\mathrm{d}s = H/T_2 + H/EA > 0$); it is solved by a safeguarded Newton method.
The jumps (7.24) are then applied. Two conditions close the problem:

$$ r_1 = z_N(H, V_0) - z_\text{right saddle} = 0,\qquad r_2 = f(H, V_0) - f_\text{target} = 0
\ \ \text{(or } H - H_\text{target} = 0\text{)} $$ (7.27)

where $f$ is the sag, measured at the horizontal midpoint between the two saddles, from the
chord joining the saddles. These two equations are solved by Newton's method, with a Jacobian by
central differences. Without self-weight of the cable and with vertical hangers, the classical result
is recovered: under a uniform load $q$ over a span $L$,

$$ H = \frac{q\,L^2}{8\,f} $$ (7.28)

The catenary integrals are written here in a form that does not subtract two neighbouring
hyperbolic sine arguments, which allows a zero weight and avoids losing significant digits on short
segments.

### 7.8.2 Side spans and saddles

The cable may extend beyond a saddle to an anchorage. Two saddle behaviours bracket reality. On a
fixed saddle, the cable is clamped to the saddle: the horizontal tensions on the two sides are
independent, and their difference goes down the pylon as a horizontal force at its head,

$$ Q_\text{head} = H_\text{span} - H_\text{backstay} $$ (7.29)

the backstay being installed under a chosen horizontal tension (by default, that of the adjacent
span, which balances the saddle). On a free saddle, the cable slides without friction: the tension is
the same on both sides, as over a pulley, and the unstressed length of the backstay is computed to
obtain it:

$$ \sqrt{H_\text{span}^2 + V_\text{span}^2} = \sqrt{H_\text{backstay}^2 + V_\text{backstay}^2}\quad\text{at the saddle} $$ (7.30)

This behaviour is a condition of the permanent state: under live loads, the cable no longer slides
on the saddle. A saddle with finite friction, which satisfies $|\ln(T_1/T_2)| \le \mu\,\theta$
for a wrap angle $\theta$, lies between these two cases, and it is enough to compute both.

### 7.8.3 Flexible pylons

When the pylons are flexible, the saddles move under the permanent load, and the funicular must be
sought at their displaced position. keta alternates the form finding, with the saddles placed at
$\mathbf{u}_n$, and the analysis of the whole, which gives the displacement
$G(\mathbf{u}_n)$ of the pylon heads. The residual
$\mathbf{r}_n = G(\mathbf{u}_n) - \mathbf{u}_n$ is the error in the position of the saddles. The
iteration is accelerated by Aitken relaxation (Irons and Tuck):

$$ \theta_n = -\,\theta_{n-1}\,\frac{\mathbf{r}_{n-1}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_n - \mathbf{r}_{n-1})}{\|\mathbf{r}_n - \mathbf{r}_{n-1}\|^2},\qquad
\mathbf{u}_{n+1} = \mathbf{u}_n + \theta_n\,\mathbf{r}_n $$ (7.31)

with $\theta_0 = 1$ and $\theta_n$ bounded to $[0.05,\ 20]$. Without acceleration,
the iteration converges as $k_\text{cable}/(k_\text{cable} + k_\text{pylon})$ at each step, a
factor close to 1 when a taut backstay connects the pylon head elastically to the ground. The
analysis stops when the saddles move by less than $10^{-8}$ m.

### 7.8.4 Hanger lengths

A hanger that carries the tension $T$ is longer than its unstressed length: installed at its
geometric length, it would let the deck drop. For a hanger of geometric length $L$, rigidity
$EA$ and weight $w$ projected on its axis, the unstressed length is the root of

$$ L = L_0\left(1 + \frac{T}{EA}\right) + \frac{w\,L_0^2}{2\,EA}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_0 = \frac{2L}{a + \sqrt{a^2 + 2wL/EA}},\qquad a = 1 + \frac{T}{EA} $$ (7.32)

written in this form to avoid a subtraction. keta introduces it in the permanent case as a length
defect, that is the imposed strain

$$ \varepsilon_0 = -\,\frac{L - L_0}{L_0} $$ (7.33)

so that each hanger carries its form-finding tension and the deck hangs at its design level. This
is exact when the hanger loads are the reactions transmitted to them by the deck, that is for a deck
hinged at each hanger; a continuous deck retains the deflection due to the redistribution between its
supports.

### 7.8.5 Scope and verification

The form finding handles one cable plane at a time: a bridge with two cable planes is analysed
plane by plane, with the loads of each. The hangers are vertical or inclined in the plane of the
cable, and always in tension: a hanger whose attachment point does not lie below the cable node is
rejected. The shape found is checked by solving the permanent case on the assembled model: the same
horizontal tension and the same hanger forces must be recovered, together with a deck moment that is
negligible compared with that of the simply supported span,

$$ |M_\text{deck}| \ll \frac{q\,L^2}{8} $$ (7.34)

since the deck is suspended and does not carry the span.

# Chapter 8 Prestressing

This chapter deals with the prestressing tendons of a bar frame: internal tendons, bonded or not,
external tendons, and pretensioned strands. The tendon is a tensioned steel member that transfers a
force to the concrete through its anchorages, through its deviation in curves and through friction
against its duct. The problem is twofold. First, the force in the tendon must be known at each point,
allowing for friction, anchorage draw-in and the losses that follow stressing. Next, the effect of
this force on the structure must be known; keta represents it by a system of equivalent loads applied
to the bars and solved as an ordinary load case.

Time-dependent losses depend on the behaviour of concrete over time, described in chapter 9; their
computation through staged construction belongs to chapter 10. Stresses and losses at the level of a
cross-section, with several tendons and passive reinforcement, are dealt with in chapter 21. Stay
cables and suspension cables are the subject of chapter 7.

## 8.1 Assumptions

- the tendon is represented by its profile along a chain of consecutive bars, given by its
eccentricities $e_y(s)$ and $e_z(s)$ in the section axes of each bar, with the origin at the
centroid; $s$ is the abscissa along the chain;

- the tendon force is directed along the tangent to its profile; unless otherwise specified, the
slope of the tendon relative to the bar is assumed small: the axial force transmitted is $P$ and
not $P\cos\alpha$;

- friction follows the exponential law of EN 1992-1-1 §5.10.5.2, with coefficients constant along
the tendon;

- the prestressing steel is linearly elastic, of modulus $E_p$ and area $A_p$; a tendon
whose area is not given is a “force tendon”: it acts on the structure but undergoes neither anchorage
draw-in nor losses due to the deformation of the concrete;

- a bonded tendon follows the strain of the concrete at its level; an ungrouted tendon slides in its
duct (chapter 10);

- the geometry is that of the undeformed model: the equivalent loads are computed once and for all
on the initial profile.

## 8.2 Tendon profile

### 8.2.1 Description by segments

The profile is a sequence of contiguous segments $[s_0, s_1]$ along the chain. On each segment,
each eccentricity is a third-degree polynomial in $s$:

$$ e(s) = c_0 + c_1\,(s - s_0) + c_2\,(s - s_0)^2 + c_3\,(s - s_0)^3 $$ (8.1)

This form covers the straight line, the parabola and Hermite transitions. Two curves that are not
polynomials in $s$ are read on the curve itself: the parametric cubic
$(s, e_y, e_z)(u) = \sum_k \mathbf{p}_k\,u^k$, $u \in [0, 1]$, and the circular arc
$\mathbf{X}(\phi) = \mathbf{C} - R\cos\phi\,\mathbf{U} + R\sin\phi\,\mathbf{D}$. For a given
abscissa $s$, keta finds the parameter of the curve by Newton's method safeguarded by bisection,
then computes the derivatives from

$$ e' = \frac{Y'}{X'},\qquad e'' = \frac{Y''\,X' - Y'\,X''}{X'^3} $$ (8.2)

where $X$ is the component of the curve along the chain and $Y$ the eccentricity. The
curvature of the profile, which gives the radial thrust, is therefore that of the actual curve and
not that of an interpolation.

### 8.2.2 Usual profile constructions

The profile is built from design data in several ways:

- a polyline through given points, each side being a straight line;

- a parabola through three points, at abscissae $0$, $S/2$ and $S$ of the tendon
length $S$;

- a natural cubic spline through given points: continuity of slope and curvature at the interior
points, zero curvature at the ends;

- points with imposed slopes (angle in elevation, angle in plan) and straight alignments, each
interval being a parametric Hermite cubic whose tangents at the points are the imposed slopes, the
direction of the neighbouring alignments or, failing that, those of the $C^2$ spline;

- a polyline through vertices, each vertex given a radius receiving a circular fillet.

The parabola through the three points $e_0 = e(0)$, $e_m = e(S/2)$, $e_1 = e(S)$
reads

$$ e(s) = e_0 + \left(4 e_m - 3 e_0 - e_1\right)\frac{s}{S} + 2\left(e_0 + e_1 - 2 e_m\right)\frac{s^2}{S^2} $$ (8.3)

Its curvature is constant, $e'' = 4(e_0 + e_1 - 2e_m)/S^2$; for a tendon anchored at the
centroid at both ends with a sag $f$ at mid-length, $e'' = 8f/S^2$.

### 8.2.3 Circular fillets

At vertex $k$, the two alignments meeting there have the unit directions $\mathbf{d}_1$ and
$\mathbf{d}_2$, which make the angle $\theta = \arccos(\mathbf{d}_1\cdot\mathbf{d}_2)$. The
fillet of radius $R$ is the circular arc tangent to both alignments; its tangent points lie at
the distance

$$ T = R\,\tan\frac{\theta}{2} $$ (8.4)

from the vertex, $A = P_k - T\,\mathbf{d}_1$ and $B = P_k + T\,\mathbf{d}_2$, and the
alignments are shortened up to them. The arc is represented as such, in space. If $T$ exceeds
half of either alignment, keta reduces it to that half (the effective radius is then
$T/\tan(\theta/2)$) and issues a warning; a profile that turns back along the chain is rejected.
The points without a radius remain points of the spline, which is tangent to the neighbouring
alignments.

**Figure 8.1** — Circular fillet at a vertex of a profile

### 8.2.4 Translation, symmetry and copy

A profile may be shifted along its chain by a length $\Delta x$, or mirrored about the abscissa
$p$:

$$ e_t(s) = e(s - \Delta x),\qquad e_m(s) = e(2p - s) $$ (8.5)

Both transformations preserve the nature of the three types of segment: the cubic in $s$ is
re-expanded by the binomial formula, the parametric cubic is reparametrised by
$u \mapsto 1 - u$, and the circular arc has its centre reflected and its direction of travel
reversed. The half-profile completed by its mirror image is continuous at the pivot; it is
differentiable there only if $e'(p) = 0$, otherwise the kink of slope $2e'(p)$ is kept (a
deviator may lie at midspan). A tendon may also be copied, with its profile and its force, onto
another chain of bars of the same length, to within $10^{-9}$ in relative terms. The
anchorages, the imposed force profile, the free lengths and the live anchorage follow the
transformation.

### 8.2.5 Three-dimensional profiles and deviations

The tendon is a space curve with unit tangent

$$ \mathbf{t}(s) = \frac{(1,\ e_y'(s),\ e_z'(s))}{\sqrt{1 + e_y'^2 + e_z'^2}} $$ (8.6)

in the axes of the bar. The cumulative angular deviation $\theta(s)$ that enters friction is the
total angle swept by this tangent from the anchorage:

$$ \theta(s) = \int_0^s \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{t}}{\mathrm{d}\sigma}\right\|\mathrm{d}\sigma $$ (8.7)

It counts the curvatures in both elevation and plan, and remains correct for a steep profile, where
the sum of the $|e''|\,\mathrm{d}s$ would overestimate the angle by a factor $1 + e'^2$. keta
evaluates it by summing the angles between neighbouring tangents, sixteen per step of the
computation grid. A kink in the profile, that is a jump in $e_y'$ or $e_z'$ between two
segments (polyline, deviator), is a concentrated deviation: the angle
$\arccos(\mathbf{t}^-\cdot\mathbf{t}^+)$ is turned through over zero length.

The length of the tendon is its arc length, greater than that of the chain where the tendon is
inclined:

$$ \ell(s) = \int_0^s \sqrt{1 + e_y'^2 + e_z'^2}\;\mathrm{d}\sigma $$ (8.8)

computed by a three-point Gauss quadrature on eight sub-steps of each grid step. Wobble friction
and anchorage draw-in act over this length.

## 8.3 Force after friction

The tendon is stressed to the force $P_0$ at its live anchorage. Along the tendon, the force
decreases by friction against the duct according to EN 1992-1-1, expression (5.45):

$$ P(s) = P_0\;e^{-\mu\,(\theta(s) + k\,x(s)) - \varphi\,x(s)} $$ (8.9)

where $\mu$ is the coefficient of friction in curves [rad−1], $k$ the
unintentional angular displacement per unit length [rad/m] and $x(s)$ the arc length
(8.8) that rubs against the concrete. The term $\varphi$ [m−1] is a
friction per unit length independent of $\mu$, useful to reproduce data of the form
$e^{-(f\alpha + \varphi x)}$ with $f = 0$; it is zero by default. Over the free lengths of an
external tendon (the straight runs between deviators, where the tendon does not touch the concrete),
wobble friction does not act: $x$ is the arc length less these runs, while the deviations at the
deviators count in $\theta$.

The tendon may be stressed at its start, at its end or at both. Stressed at both ends, it carries at
each point the larger of the two friction curves, $\max(P_1(s), P_2(s))$. It may also start and
finish inside its bars: the force is zero outside the anchored interval $[s_b, s_e]$, and
friction runs from these anchorages.

keta evaluates the force on a grid of twenty intervals per metre of anchored length (at least
four), supplemented by each kink of the profile, entered twice (left and right limits) so that the
force drop $e^{-\mu\Delta\theta}$ of a concentrated deviation is a jump and not a ramp. The force
between two points is interpolated linearly. The default values are
$\mu = 0.19$ rad−1, $k = 0.01$ rad/m, an anchorage draw-in of 6 mm and
$E_p = 195$ GPa; they are to be replaced by the values of the technical approval of the
prestressing system.

Finally, the force may be given directly, point by point, along the chain: this imposed profile then
replaces friction and anchorage draw-in, which are deemed to be included in the values given. This is
the form taken by a pretensioned strand.

## 8.4 Anchorage draw-in

### 8.4.1 One live anchorage

At lock-off, the wedges slip and the anchorage moves back by a length $g$. The tendon shortens
near the anchorage; friction there reverses and now opposes this return. The force after lock-off
$P'(s)$ is the reflected friction curve: over the affected zone $[0, \lambda]$, the loss per
unit length is the same as at stressing, in the opposite direction. For the exponential law, this
reflection reads

$$ P'(s) = \min\!\left(P(s),\ \frac{C}{P(s)}\right),\qquad C = P(\lambda)^2 $$ (8.10)

On a logarithmic scale, $P'$ is the mirror image of $P$ about its value at
$\lambda$. The length $\lambda$ is set by compatibility: the shortening of the tendon over
the affected zone equals the movement of the anchorage,

$$ \int_0^{\lambda} \bigl[P(s) - P'(s)\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}\ell = g\,E_p\,A_p $$ (8.11)

keta solves this equation in $C$ by bisection (one hundred iterations), the integral being
computed on the grid with the change of sign of $P - C/P$ located linearly within its interval.
If the affected zone reaches the opposite anchorage, the same equation lowers the whole reflected
curve; if even a fully slack tendon cannot take up the movement, the force is zero. Anchorage draw-in
is computed only for a tendon whose area $A_p$ is given.

When friction is roughly linear near the anchorage, with slope $p = -\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}s$,
the classical form is recovered

$$ \lambda \approx \sqrt{\frac{g\,E_p\,A_p}{p}},\qquad \Delta P(0) \approx 2\,p\,\lambda $$ (8.12)

For the tendon of the figure below (a 30 m parabola with a sag of 0.6 m, $\mu = 0.19$,
$k = 0.005$ rad/m, $g = 6$ mm, $E_pA_p = 585$ MN, $P_0 = 4.185$ MN), equation (8.11) gives $\lambda = 21.1$ m and a loss of 332 kN at the anchorage; the
approximate form gives 20.7 m and 339 kN. The force computed by keta along the beam differs from the
reflection integrated on a very fine grid by less than $6\cdot 10^{-5}\,P_0$.

**Figure 8.2** — Tendon force after friction and after anchorage draw-in (keta computation)

### 8.4.2 Two live anchorages

A tendon stressed from both ends is locked off at one anchorage, then at the other, in the declared
order. Rule (8.10) is applied twice, the reference curve of each lock-off being the
friction curve issuing from the anchorage being released:

$$ P^{(1)}(s) = \min\!\left(P(s),\ \frac{C_1}{P_1(s)}\right),\qquad P^{(2)}(s) = \min\!\left(P^{(1)}(s),\ \frac{C_2}{P_2(s)}\right) $$ (8.13)

Each constant is set by (8.11), applied to the curve in place at the time of
lock-off. On a short tendon, the two affected zones overlap and the result depends on the order: the
second lock-off acts on a curve that has already been lowered (figure above, dotted curve: the force
at the end released second is lower than at the start).

## 8.5 Equivalent loads

### 8.5.1 Actions of the tendon on the concrete

The concrete is isolated: the tendon exerts on it the force of its anchorages, the pressure of its
curves and the friction along its duct. These actions form a self-equilibrated system, which keta
applies to the bars of the chain in the local axes of each. In a bar, $\mathbf{F}(x)$ denotes the
force that the tendon cut at $x$ exerts on the downstream part, under the small-slope
assumption:

$$ \mathbf{F}(x) = \bigl(P,\ P\,e_y',\ P\,e_z'\bigr) $$ (8.14)

At a start anchorage, the tendon pushes the concrete with $\mathbf{F}$, applied at the point
$(e_y, e_z)$: a force and the moment $(G,\ P e_z,\ -P e_y)$ about the centroid, with
$G = e_y F_z - e_z F_y$. At an end anchorage, it exerts the opposite. Along the bar, the change
in $\mathbf{F}$ is taken by the concrete: the load density is
$\mathrm{d}\mathbf{F}/\mathrm{d}x$, that is

$$ n(x) = P',\qquad p_y(x) = (P\,e_y')',\qquad p_z(x) = (P\,e_z')' $$ (8.15)

The axial component is the friction drag; the transverse components contain the radial thrust
$P\,e''$ and the friction term $P'\,e'$. The drag $P'$ acts at the level of the tendon
and not at the centroid: it is accompanied by a distributed couple of density $P'\,e$, and not by
a shear force. Finally, a tendon with a lateral eccentricity that deviates vertically twists the bar:
the distributed torque is $\mathrm{d}G/\mathrm{d}x$, since $e_y' F_z - e_z' F_y = 0$.

At a kink in the profile, the deviation is concentrated: the bar receives the point force
$\mathbf{F}(x^+) - \mathbf{F}(x^-)$, which includes the rotation of the tangent and the force drop
by friction, together with the couple of the force jump at the eccentricity. A parabola of sag
$f$ over a span $L$, without friction, thus produces the uniform radial thrust

$$ p = P\,e'' = \frac{8\,P\,f}{L^2} $$ (8.16)

**Figure 8.3** — Equivalent loads of a tendon

### 8.5.2 Discretisation of the distributed loads

The part of each bar travelled by the tendon is divided into eight pieces, plus the kinks of the
profile. On each piece $[x_a, x_b]$ of length $h$, keta replaces each density by a linear
load $w(x) = w_a + (w_b - w_a)(x - x_a)/h$ that has the same resultant and the same moment as the
actual load:

$$ \int_{x_a}^{x_b} w\,\mathrm{d}x = F(x_b) - F(x_a),\qquad
\int_{x_a}^{x_b} (x - x_a)\,w\,\mathrm{d}x = h\,F(x_b) - \int_{x_a}^{x_b} F\,\mathrm{d}x $$ (8.17)

the second equality following from an integration by parts; the integral of $F$ is evaluated
by the composite Simpson rule on eight sub-intervals. This gives $w_b = 6M_1/h^2 - 2R/h$ and
$w_a = 2R/h - w_b$, $R$ and $M_1$ denoting the resultant and the moment. The distributed
couple $P'e$ and the torque are treated in the same way. The resultants telescope from one piece
to the next and from one bar to the next: the load system is self-equilibrated to within round-off
errors, whatever the number of kinks in the profile.

Without friction, on a polynomial segment, the density $P\,e''$ is at most linear and the fit
reproduces it without error; with friction, the force profile is that of the grid of section 8.3.
The internal forces are then obtained by the ordinary solution of chapter 4.

### 8.5.3 Tendon inclined relative to the bar

As an option, the bar receives only the component of the force along its axis, and the
corresponding transverse component:

$$ N = P\cos\alpha,\qquad \cos\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + e_y'^2 + e_z'^2}},\qquad \mathbf{F} = P\cos\alpha\,\bigl(1,\ e_y',\ e_z'\bigr) $$ (8.18)

The difference from the small-slope assumption is 2.5 % for a slope of 0.23. This option is used
mainly for steeply inclined external tendons.

## 8.6 Primary and secondary effects

Let the structure be cut at a section through which the tendon passes. The cut tendon exerts on the
section the force $P$ at the point $(e_y, e_z)$: this is the primary (isostatic) effect of
prestressing, independent of the restraints. With the sign convention of chapter 2,

$$ N^\text{iso} = -P c,\quad M_y^\text{iso} = -P c\,e_z,\quad M_z^\text{iso} = P c\,e_y,\quad
V_z^\text{iso} = -P c\,e_z',\quad V_y^\text{iso} = -P c\,e_y' $$ (8.19)

where $c = \cos\alpha$ for a tendon computed with the exact angle, $c = 1$ otherwise, and
$P$ is the effective force (losses deducted, including the local loss field if it is kept). Under
friction, $\mathrm{d}M_y^\text{iso}/\mathrm{d}x$ is not $V_z^\text{iso}$: the difference is the
distributed couple $P'e$ met above.

On a statically determinate structure, the internal forces obtained with the equivalent loads are
those of (8.19). On a statically indeterminate structure, the redundant restraints oppose
the deformations imposed by the tendon and develop reactions: the secondary (hyperstatic) effect
is

$$ M^\text{hyp}(x) = M(x) - M^\text{iso}(x) $$ (8.20)

Since it is produced only by support reactions, it is linear between two supports
(EN 1992-1-1 §5.10.7). For two equal spans of length $L$, with a parabolic tendon of sag $f$
in each, centred on the three supports and without friction, the secondary moment is $P f$ at
the central support, in absolute value, and puts the bottom fibre in tension; the total moment at
midspan reduces to $P f/2$. keta recovers both values to within $10^{-9}$ with bars
without shear deformation (with it, the relative stiffness of the spans changes slightly and the
difference reaches 0.2 % for a rectangular section 1.5 m deep over a 30 m span).

**Figure 8.4** — Primary, secondary and total moments of a prestressed continuous beam

In staged construction, keta keeps the primary effect of the tendons up to date at each stage and
derives the secondary effect from it (chapter 10).

## 8.7 Immediate losses

### 8.7.1 Elastic shortening

A bonded tendon, already anchored, follows the concrete at its level: any strain increment
$\Delta\varepsilon_c$ of the concrete at that location changes its force by

$$ \Delta P = E_p\,A_p\,\Delta\varepsilon_c,\qquad
\Delta\varepsilon_c = \frac{1}{E}\left(\frac{N}{A} + \frac{M_y\,e_z}{I_y} - \frac{M_z\,e_y}{I_z}\right) $$ (8.21)

(a compression shortens the tendon: $\Delta P < 0$ is a loss). This is the so-called
“$K = 1$” rule: each computation increment of a staged analysis (load, stressing of another
tendon, creep, shrinkage, deactivation) makes the already anchored tendons lose or gain what the
strain of their concrete imposes on them. By default, the strain is the length-weighted mean, over the
active part of the tendon between its anchorages, of the value at the middle of each bar, and the
loss is a uniform fraction of the whole force profile. Two options refine this computation: the mean
over all the stations of the anchored length, or a loss evaluated point by point and kept as a field
along the tendon, which a pretensioned strand requires, since its transmission zones do not lose in
the same way as the plateau.

The loss itself loads the structure, which deforms and makes the tendons lose again: keta iterates
until the correction becomes negligible ($10^{-9}\,P_0$), at most two hundred times. For a
concentric tendon in a bar of rigidity $EA$, stressed after a first identical tendon, the loss of
the first one is thus

$$ \Delta P_1 = \frac{\rho}{1 + \rho}\,P_2,\qquad \rho = \frac{E_p A_p}{E A}\left(1 + \frac{A\,e_z^2}{I_y} + \frac{A\,e_y^2}{I_z}\right) $$ (8.22)

instead of $\rho\,P_2$ with a single pass (option). For $E = 35$ GPa, $A = 0.5$ m²,
$A_p = 3\,000$ mm² and $P_2 = 4$ MN, keta gives 129.389 kN, and the formula 129.389 kN.

The tendons stressed in a single operation (one group of a stage) are simultaneous: the jack
compensates for their mutual shortening and they cause no loss to one another ($K = 0$). The
successive groups of a stage, on the other hand, cause losses to one another in order.

### 8.7.2 Units stressed one after another

A tendon made of $n$ identical units stressed in succession loses on average the fraction
$(n-1)/(2n)$ of its own elastic shortening (EN 1992-1-1, expression (5.44)). keta applies this rule
with a single pass; with iterated losses, it simulates the sequence: unit $j$ is stressed while
the first $j - 1$, anchored, follow the concrete with the fraction $(j-1)/n$ of the area. The
total loss is

$$ \Delta P = \sum_{j=2}^{n} \frac{j-1}{n}\,\frac{\rho\,P/n}{1 + \rho\,(j-1)/n}
\;\xrightarrow[\rho \to 0]{}\; \frac{n-1}{2n}\,\rho\,P $$ (8.23)

For $n = 2$ and the previous data, keta gives 32.879 kN against 33.429 kN for rule (5.44), in
agreement with (8.23).

## 8.8 Time-dependent losses

Shrinkage and creep shorten the concrete at the level of the tendon, and the steel relaxes. keta
computes these losses in two ways during a staged analysis, or estimates them by the lump-sum rules
of the former codes.

### 8.8.1 Losses computed through the structure

This is the default mode of a staged analysis. Between two dates, the creep and shrinkage of each
bar are imposed on the structure (chapter 10). Each bonded tendon loses $E_pA_p$ times the free
creep and shrinkage strain of the concrete at its level,

$$ \Delta P = E_p\,A_p\,\bigl(\Delta\varepsilon_{cc} + \Delta\varepsilon_{cs}\bigr) $$ (8.24)

averaged over the active part of the tendon as in (8.21); this loss loads the structure,
whose response makes all the tendons lose again, iteratively as for (8.21). Since the loss
itself creeps in the next time step, the result follows the hereditary integral of chapter 9. The
relaxation of each tendon is computed on its current stress by the equivalent-time method
(chapter 9). On a concentric bar, with a non-ageing creep law of final coefficient 2, the loss
computed by keta after 10 000 days (243.054 kN for $P_0 = 4$ MN and $\rho = 0.033$)
coincides with the solution of the Volterra integral equation of the problem to within
$2\cdot 10^{-8}$.

### 8.8.2 EN 1992-1-1 formula

As an option, each time interval $[t_1, t_2]$ (or each sub-step of the interval) applies
expression (5.46) of EN 1992-1-1 in incremental form:

$$ \Delta\sigma_p = \frac{-E_p\,(\Delta\varepsilon_{cc} + \Delta\varepsilon_{cs}) + c_r\,\Delta\sigma_{pr}}
{1 + \dfrac{E_p A_p}{E A_c}\left(1 + \dfrac{A_c\,z_{cp}^2}{I_c}\right)\bigl(1 + 0.8\,\Delta\varphi\bigr)} $$ (8.25)

where $\Delta\varepsilon_{cc}$ is the creep strain of the concrete at the level of the tendon
that the creep engine computes for the interval (the same one that loads the structure),
$\Delta\varepsilon_{cs}$ the free shrinkage of the interval, $\Delta\varphi = \varphi(t_2, t_1)$
the creep coefficient of the interval and $\Delta\sigma_{pr}$ the relaxation of the interval. The
term $A_c z_{cp}^2/I_c$ is extended to both bending planes, $A_c(e_z^2/I_y + e_y^2/I_z)$. All
the section quantities are length-weighted means over the active part of the tendon. The loss is
applied to the tendon before the elastic redistribution of the creep increment; it receives no
$K = 1$ pass of its own, the denominator taking its place. With a single step for the interval,
keta reproduces the value of (5.46) (246.044 kN in the previous example, against 243.054 kN by the
computation through the structure).

At the level of an isolated section, the same compatibility is written for several tendons and for
the passive reinforcement, which restrains creep and shrinkage (chapter 21).

### 8.8.3 Relaxation in the losses

The pure relaxation $\Delta\sigma_{pr}$ is given by the laws of chapter 9. It enters
(8.25) with a coefficient $c_r$ that depends on how it is computed:

$$ c_r = 0.8 \;\text{ if }\; \Delta\sigma_{pr} = \sigma_{pi}\bigl[\rho(t_2 - t_\text{t}) - \rho(t_1 - t_\text{t})\bigr],\qquad
c_r = 1 \;\text{ if }\; \Delta\sigma_{pr} \text{ is computed by equivalent time} $$ (8.26)

In the first case, the relaxation is read on the curve of the initial stress $\sigma_{pi}$, from
the stressing date $t_\text{t}$, and the factor 0.8 of expression (5.46) accounts for the drop in
stress due to the other losses. In the second (BPEL law, or EN 1992-1-1 law with the losses computed
through the structure), the relaxation is read on the current stress: the reduction is already
included. Heat curing adds the equivalent time $t_{eb}$ to the relaxation clock
(EN 1992-1-1 §10.3.2).

### 8.8.4 Lump-sum code losses

For preliminary design, keta provides the lump-sum losses of the Instruction provisoire n° 2 and of
the BPEL, from a final concrete stress at the level of the tendon $\sigma_b$ (compression
positive) given by the engineer. With $n = 6$, the modular ratio imposed by these texts:

$$ \Delta\sigma_\text{el} = \frac{n}{2}\,\sigma_b = 3\,\sigma_b,\qquad
\Delta\sigma_r = \varepsilon_r\,E_p,\qquad
\Delta\sigma_\text{fl} = \begin{cases} 2\,n\,\sigma_b & \text{(IP2)} \\ 2.5\,n\,\sigma_b & \text{(BPEL)} \end{cases} $$ (8.27)

The elastic loss covers the non-simultaneity of the stressing operations. The BPEL adds five sixths
of the final relaxation, computed by

$$ \Delta\sigma_\rho = \frac{6}{100}\,\rho_{1000}\left(\frac{\sigma_{pi}}{R_g} - \mu_0\right)\sigma_{pi} \;\ge 0,\qquad
\Delta\sigma_\text{diff} = \Delta\sigma_r + \Delta\sigma_\text{fl} + \frac{5}{6}\,\Delta\sigma_\rho $$ (8.28)

with $\mu_0 = 0.43$ for $\rho_{1000} \le 2.5$ %, 0.35 up to 8 % and 0.30 beyond. The IP2
takes the given pure final relaxation $\Delta\sigma_\rho$, reduced by the interaction:

$$ \Delta\sigma_\text{diff} = \Delta\sigma_r + \Delta\sigma_\text{fl} +
\Delta\sigma_\rho\left(1 - \frac{\Delta\sigma_r + \Delta\sigma_\text{fl}}{\sigma_{pi} - 0.55\,R_g}\right) $$ (8.29)

as long as $\Delta\sigma_r + \Delta\sigma_\text{fl} < \sigma_{pi} - 0.55\,R_g$; beyond that, the
stress drop absorbs the relaxation and $\Delta\sigma_\text{diff} = \Delta\sigma_r + \Delta\sigma_\text{fl}$.
The lump-sum shrinkage is $\varepsilon_r = 4\cdot 10^{-4}$ (IP2) or $3\cdot 10^{-4}$ (BPEL) in a
dry atmosphere (relative humidity below 65 %), and $3\cdot 10^{-4}$ or $2\cdot 10^{-4}$
above. Some printed editions associate the higher value with the more humid atmosphere, which
contradicts the shrinkage law of the same text; keta adopts the physical reading, and the value of
$\varepsilon_r$ can be imposed to reproduce a computation made with the other. Example:
$\sigma_b = 10$ MPa, $\sigma_{pi} = 1\,395$ MPa, $R_g = 1\,860$ MPa,
$\rho_{1000} = 2.5$ %, humidity 70 %; the BPEL gives 30 MPa of elastic loss, 39 + 150 MPa of
shrinkage and creep and 67 MPa of relaxation, that is 274.8 MPa in total.

These rules give an order of magnitude. The losses of a structure built in stages are computed by
the two previous methods.

## 8.9 Pretensioning

### 8.9.1 Bed, release and shortening

A pretensioned strand is first stressed on a bed: it carries $P_0$ but does not act on the
structure. While it remains on the bed, it relaxes (the loss is taken by the bed), and the surrounding
concrete, which slides on the bed and is restrained by the strand only in the ratio
$E_pA_p/(E_cA_c)$, shrinks freely, without creeping since it is not loaded. At release, the
strand first undergoes the thermal loss of steam curing (EN 1992-1-1 §10.5.2), then transfers its
force to the concrete by bond. Once bonded, it undergoes its own elastic shortening:

$$ \Delta P = \Delta\sigma_\theta\,A_p + \frac{\rho}{1 + \rho}\,\bigl(P_0 - \Delta\sigma_\theta\,A_p\bigr) $$ (8.30)

with $\rho$ defined in (8.22). For a strand with an eccentricity of 0.3 m in a
bar of 0.5 m² and 0.05 m⁴, a thermal loss of 20 MPa and $P_0 = 4$ MN, keta gives 295.301 kN, and
the formula 295.301 kN.

### 8.9.2 Transmission laws

Near each bonded end, the force rises from zero to $P_0$ over the transmission length. After an
unbonded length $g$ (debonding sleeve), the fraction of force at the distance $d$ from the
start of bond follows one of the following laws:

$$ \frac{P}{P_0} = \min\!\left(1, \frac{d}{l_1}\right),\qquad
\frac{P}{P_0} = 1 - \left(1 - \min\!\left(1, \frac{d}{l_1}\right)\right)^{2},\qquad
\frac{P}{P_0} = \begin{cases} \alpha\,d/l_1 & d < l_1 \\ \alpha + (1-\alpha)\dfrac{d - l_1}{l_2 - l_1} & l_1 \le d < l_2 \\ 1 & d \ge l_2 \end{cases} $$ (8.31)

respectively linear, parabolic and bilinear; without a law, the force jumps to $P_0$ right at
the bonded end. The force at a point is the smaller of the two values counted from each end. The
parabola is represented by 256 chords, which bounds the error on the force to
$2^{-17}\,P_0$. A tendon that represents $n$ identical strands carries $n$ times the
force and the area of one strand.

**Note.**

These three laws and the debonding sleeves are built when a data file is read. The Python
module does not offer them under this name: it takes the force profile of the strand point by point,
which can be derived from (8.31).

**Figure 8.5** — Bond transmission laws of a pretensioned strand

Over the transmission length, the change in force $P'$ is taken by bond at the level of the
strand: this is the axial drag of (8.15), accompanied by the distributed couple
$P'e$. It produces no shear force, as the $V_z$ diagram of a beam prestressed by straight
strands confirms.

## 8.10 Results provided

| Quantity | Where | Convention |
|---|---|---|
| Jacking force, cumulative loss, effective force | per tendon and per stage | N, loss positive |
| Local loss field | tendon stations (option) | N |
| Force after friction and anchorage draw-in | computation grid | N, tension positive |
| Primary and secondary effects | bar stations, per stage | chapter 2 |

For each tendon and each stage, keta provides the force applied by the jack, the cumulative loss
(elastic and time-dependent) and the effective force; with local losses, the loss field along the
tendon. The force profile after friction and anchorage draw-in is available on the computation grid.
The equivalent loads of a tendon, at a given fraction of its force, can be placed in an ordinary load
case and combined with the other actions. The internal forces in the bars include the effect of
prestressing; the primary and secondary effects are available separately in a staged analysis
(chapter 10).

## 8.11 Scope

- The equivalent loads are those of small slopes ($N = P$), unless the exact-angle option is
used; they are computed on the initial geometry.

- The force is interpolated linearly between the points of a grid of twenty intervals per metre;
the kinks of the profile are double points of it.

- Anchorage draw-in and the losses due to the deformation of the concrete require the area
$A_p$ of the tendon; a force tendon undergoes none of them.

- The parabola through three points accepts only the abscissae $0$, $S/2$ and $S$;
construction by successive connected parabolas is not offered (the $C^2$ spline takes its
place).

- In a staged analysis, time-dependent losses follow EN 1992-1-1 (expression (5.46)) or the
computation through the structure; the BPEL combination with five sixths of the relaxation alone
exists only in lump-sum form.

- The lump-sum losses require the final concrete stress at the level of the tendon, which keta does
not predict.

# Chapter 9 Time-dependent behaviour of concrete

Loaded concrete keeps deforming for years: it creeps. It also shortens without load, as it dries and
as the cement hydrates: it shrinks. These two phenomena make deflections evolve, redistribute the
internal forces of a structure whose static system changed during construction, and make
prestressing tendons lose tension, while their steel also relaxes. This chapter describes the
modulus, shrinkage, creep and relaxation laws that keta contains, the way it accumulates the effects
of a varying stress history, and the numerical methods that follow from it. The application to
staged construction is the subject of chapter 10, and prestress losses that of chapter 8.

## 9.1 Assumptions

- creep is linear in stress (ageing linear viscoelasticity): the responses to stress increments
applied at different ages add up (Boltzmann's principle); a nonlinear correction is available for high
compressive stresses;

- in a bar, the law applies separately to the three generalised stress components $N/A$,
$M_y/I_y$ and $M_z/I_z$: the section remains plane and creep does not depend on the position
of the fibre, except in the options that work fibre by fibre;

- shrinkage is an imposed strain, independent of stress and uniform over the section;

- the temperature is constant, apart from the fictitious ages specific to certain laws and the age
shift of heat curing;

- ages and durations are in days, from casting; an age below half a day is raised to 0.5 day;

- prestressing steel relaxes according to a pure relaxation law (constant strain), extended to a
variable strain by the equivalent-time method.

## 9.2 Creep function

Under a stress $\sigma_0$ applied at age $t_0$ and sustained, the strain at age $t$
is

$$ \varepsilon(t) = \sigma_0\,J(t, t_0) + \varepsilon_{cs}(t),\qquad
J(t, t_0) = \frac{1}{E(t_0)} + \frac{\varphi(t, t_0)}{E_\text{ref}(t_0)} $$ (9.1)

$J$ is the creep function, $\varphi$ the creep coefficient, $E_\text{ref}$ the modulus
to which each code relates this coefficient, and $\varepsilon_{cs}$ the shrinkage, negative when
the concrete shortens. The reference modulus differs from one text to another, so that the
coefficients $\varphi$ of two laws cannot be compared directly; the functions $J$ can.

| Law | $E_\text{ref}$ | Range |
|---|---|---|
| EN 1992-1-1, Annex B | $E_c = 1.05\,E_{cm}$ | — |
| EN 1992-2, Annex B (high-strength) | $1.05\,E_{cm}$ | $40 \le f_{ck} \le 90$ MPa |
| CEB-FIP Model Code 1990 | $E_{ci}$ at 28 days | — |
| fib Model Code 2010 | $E_{ci}$ at 28 days | — |
| BPEL 91 (and lightweight concrete of BPEL 99) | $E_{i28}$ | $f_{c28} \le 60$ MPa |
| BHP (1995 recommendations) | $E_{i28}$ | $40 \le f_{c28} \le 80$ MPa |
| B3 (Bažant and Baweja) | $1/(q_1 + \Delta_{0,01})$ | bounded mix composition |
| IP2, Model Code 1978 | $E_{28}$ | — |
| Courbon | constant modulus | — |

In a structural analysis, the stiffness of the bars uses the modulus of the material, constant, or
the modulus at the age of the concrete at each date if the engineer asks for it (chapter 10). The
creep function that keta integrates is then $J(t, t_0) = 1/E + \varphi(t, t_0)/E_\text{ref}(t_0)$,
so that the instantaneous term is that of the stiffness. A material described only by the data of
EN 1992-1-1 (strength, humidity, notional size, cement), without choosing a law, relates its creep
coefficient to the modulus of the material itself.

## 9.3 EN 1992-1-1 laws

### 9.3.1 Strength and modulus

The mean strength is $f_{cm} = f_{ck} + 8$ MPa. The secant modulus and its development follow
§3.1:

$$ E_{cm} = 22\,000\left(\frac{f_{cm}}{10}\right)^{0.3}\ \text{MPa},\qquad
E_{cm}(t) = \beta_{cc}(t)^{0.3}\,E_{cm},\qquad \beta_{cc}(t) = e^{\,s\left(1 - \sqrt{28/t}\right)} $$ (9.2)

with $s = 0.20$, 0.25 or 0.38 for cements of class R, N or S.

### 9.3.2 Creep

The creep coefficient is that of Annex B:

$$ \varphi(t, t_0) = \varphi_{RH}\;\beta(f_{cm})\;\beta(t_0)\;\left(\frac{t - t_0}{\beta_H + t - t_0}\right)^{0.3} $$ (9.3)

$$ \varphi_{RH} = \left[1 + \frac{1 - RH/100}{0.1\,\sqrt[3]{h_0}}\,\alpha_1\right]\alpha_2,\qquad
\beta(f_{cm}) = \frac{16.8}{\sqrt{f_{cm}}},\qquad \beta(t_0) = \frac{1}{0.1 + t_{0}^{\,0.20}} $$ (9.4)

$$ \beta_H = 1.5\left[1 + (0.012\,RH)^{18}\right]h_0 + 250\,\alpha_3 \;\le\; 1\,500\,\alpha_3 $$ (9.5)

where $h_0 = 2A_c/u$ is the notional size in millimetres and
$\alpha_{1,2,3} = (35/f_{cm})^{0.7;\,0.2;\,0.5}$ if $f_{cm} > 35$ MPa, 1 otherwise. The age
at loading is adjusted according to the cement class,

$$ t_{0} \leftarrow \max\!\left(0.5,\ t_0\left(\frac{9}{2 + t_0^{1.2}} + 1\right)^{\alpha}\right),\qquad \alpha = -1,\ 0,\ 1 \text{ for S, N, R} $$ (9.6)

and the coefficient is related to $E_c = 1.05\,E_{cm}$ (expression (3.6)). The following figure
shows the development of $\varphi$ and the effect of the age at loading: young concrete creeps
more.

**Figure 9.1** — Creep coefficient for three ages at loading

### 9.3.3 Shrinkage

Total shrinkage is the sum of drying shrinkage, counted from the age $t_s$ at the end of
curing, and autogenous shrinkage, counted from casting (§3.1.4 and Annex B):

$$ \varepsilon_{cs}(t) = -\left[\beta_{ds}(t, t_s)\,k_h\,\varepsilon_{cd,0} + \beta_{as}(t)\,\varepsilon_{ca}(\infty)\right] $$ (9.7)

$$ \varepsilon_{cd,0} = 0.85\left[(220 + 110\,\alpha_{ds1})\,e^{-\alpha_{ds2}\,f_{cm}/10}\right]10^{-6}\;1.55\left[1 - \left(\frac{RH}{100}\right)^3\right],\qquad
\beta_{ds} = \frac{t - t_s}{t - t_s + 0.04\sqrt{h_0^3}} $$ (9.8)

$$ \varepsilon_{ca}(\infty) = 2.5\,(f_{ck} - 10)\,10^{-6},\qquad \beta_{as}(t) = 1 - e^{-0.2\sqrt{t}} $$ (9.9)

with $(\alpha_{ds1}, \alpha_{ds2}) = (3,\ 0.13)$, $(4,\ 0.12)$, $(6,\ 0.11)$ for cements S,
N, R, and $k_h$ interpolated linearly between 1.0 ($h_0 \le 100$ mm), 0.85 (200), 0.75 (300)
and 0.70 ($h_0 \ge 500$ mm). Steam-cured concrete has no autogenous shrinkage.

### 9.3.4 High-strength concrete

Annex B of EN 1992-2 separates basic creep and drying creep:

$$ \varphi(t, t_0) = \frac{1}{1 + n\rho_s}\left[\varphi_{b0}\,\frac{\sqrt{t - t_0}}{\sqrt{t - t_0} + \beta_{bc}}
+ \varphi_{d0}\,\bigl(\varepsilon_{cd}(t) - \varepsilon_{cd}(t_0)\bigr)\right] $$ (9.10)

with, without silica fume, $\varphi_{b0} = 1.4$, $\beta_{bc} = 0.40\,e^{3.1 f_{cm}(t_0)/f_{ck}}$,
$\varphi_{d0} = 3\,200$, and with silica fume $\varphi_{b0} = 3.6/f_{cm}(t_0)^{0.37}$,
$\beta_{bc} = 0.37\,e^{2.8 f_{cm}(t_0)/f_{ck}}$, $\varphi_{d0} = 1\,000$. Drying shrinkage there
takes the development $(t - t_s)/(t - t_s + \beta_{cd} h_0^2)$, $\beta_{cd} = 0.021$ or 0.007.
The divisor $1 + n\rho_s$, where $\rho_s$ is the percentage of bonded reinforcement and
$n = E_s/E_{28}$, expresses the restraint provided by the steel; it also applies to
shrinkage.

## 9.4 BPEL laws

BPEL 91 (Annex 1) gives the early-age strength as

$$ f_{cj} = \frac{j}{4.76 + 0.83\,j}\,f_{c28}\ \ (f_{c28} \le 40\ \text{MPa}),\qquad
f_{cj} = \frac{j}{1.40 + 0.95\,j}\,f_{c28}\ \ \text{above} $$ (9.11)

without capping at $f_{c28}$ after 28 days, and the instantaneous and long-term moduli as

$$ E_{ij} = 11\,000\,f_{cj}^{1/3},\qquad E_{vj} = 3\,700\,f_{cj}^{1/3}\quad[\text{MPa}] $$ (9.12)

Shrinkage and creep are written with the mean radius $r_m = A_c/u$ in centimetres, the humidity
$\rho_h$ in per cent and the reinforcement coefficient $k_s = 1/(1 + 20\,\rho_s)$:

$$ \varepsilon_{cs}(t) = -k_s\,\varepsilon_0\bigl[r(t) - r(t_s)\bigr],\qquad
\varepsilon_0 = (100 - \rho_h)\left(6 + \frac{80}{10 + 3 r_m}\right)10^{-6},\qquad r(t) = \frac{t}{t + 9\,r_m} $$ (9.13)

$$ \varphi(t, t_0) = k_s\left[0.4 + k_c\,\frac{100}{100 + t_0}\right]\frac{\sqrt{t - t_0}}{\sqrt{t - t_0} + 5\sqrt{r_m}},\qquad
k_c = \frac{120 - \rho_h}{30} + \frac{2}{3}\,\frac{100 - \rho_h}{20 + r_m} $$ (9.14)

related to $E_{i28}$. BPEL 99 (Annex 5) adapts these laws to lightweight concrete, with a modulus
$1\,650\,\rho_{bs}^2 f_{cj}^{1/3}$ (oven-dry density $\rho_{bs}$ in t/m³, a constant
reconstructed from a poorly legible printed text: at $\rho_{bs} = 2.4$ it gives 86 % of the value
for normal-weight concrete), and the 1995 BHP recommendations adapt them to concretes of 40 to 80 MPa,
in a form close to (9.10).

## 9.5 CEB-FIP Model Code 1990

The tangent modulus and its development are
$E_{ci}(t) = 21\,500\,(f_{cm}/10)^{1/3}\sqrt{\beta_{cc}(t)}$ MPa, with $s = 0.38$ (SL), 0.25 (N
and R) or 0.20 (RS). Creep (expressions 2.1-61 to 2.1-71) reads, with $h$ in millimetres:

$$ \varphi(t, t_0) = \left[1 + \frac{1 - RH/100}{0.46\,(h/100)^{1/3}}\right]\frac{5.3}{\sqrt{f_{cm}/10}}\;
\frac{1}{0.1 + t_0^{0.2}}\left(\frac{t - t_0}{\beta_H + t - t_0}\right)^{0.3} $$ (9.15)

with $\beta_H = 150\,[1 + (1.2\,RH/100)^{18}]\,h/100 + 250 \le 1\,500$ and the age at loading
adjusted as in (9.6). Drying shrinkage (2.1-74 to 2.1-79) is

$$ \varepsilon_{cs}(t) = \bigl[160 + 10\,\beta_{sc}\,(9 - f_{cm}/10)\bigr]10^{-6}\;\beta_{RH}\;
\sqrt{\frac{t - t_s}{350\,(h/100)^2 + t - t_s}} $$ (9.16)

with $\beta_{RH} = -1.55\,[1 - (RH/100)^3]$ below 99 % and $+0.25$ above (swelling in a
saturated atmosphere), and $\beta_{sc} = 4$, 5 or 8 according to the cement.

## 9.6 fib Model Code 2010

Creep is the sum of basic creep and drying creep (5.1-63 to 5.1-73):

$$ \varphi = \frac{1}{1 + n\rho_s}\left[\frac{1.8}{f_{cm}^{0.7}}\ln\!\left(\Bigl(\frac{30}{t_0} + 0.035\Bigr)^2 (t - t_0) + 1\right)
+ \frac{412}{f_{cm}^{1.4}}\;\frac{1 - RH/100}{\sqrt[3]{0.1\,h/100}}\;\frac{1}{0.1 + t_0^{0.2}}\left(\frac{t - t_0}{\beta_h + t - t_0}\right)^{\gamma(t_0)}\right] $$ (9.17)

with $\beta_h = 1.5\,h + 250\,\alpha_{fcm} \le 1\,500\,\alpha_{fcm}$,
$\alpha_{fcm} = \sqrt{35/f_{cm}}$, $\gamma(t_0) = 1/(2.3 + 3.5/\sqrt{t_0})$, the age $t_0$
being adjusted according to the cement. Shrinkage is the sum of autogenous shrinkage and drying
shrinkage:

$$ \varepsilon_{cas} = -\alpha_{as}\left(\frac{f_{cm}/10}{6 + f_{cm}/10}\right)^{2.5}10^{-6}\bigl(1 - e^{-0.2\sqrt{t}}\bigr),\qquad
\varepsilon_{cds} = (220 + 110\,\alpha_{ds1})\,e^{-\alpha_{ds2} f_{cm}/10}\,10^{-6}\,\beta_{RH}\sqrt{\frac{t - t_s}{t - t_s + 0.035\,h^2}} $$ (9.18)

with $\alpha_{as} = 800$, 700, 600 for cements S, N, R. The modulus is tangent,
$E_{ci}(t) = 21\,500\,(f_{cm}/10)^{1/3}\sqrt{\beta_{cc}(t)}$; the secant reduction
$\alpha_i$ is available as an option. The cement class has no effect on $\beta_{cc}$ beyond
$f_{cm} = 60$ MPa ($s = 0.20$).

## 9.7 Other laws

The B3 model of Bažant and Baweja, in the form of ACI 209.2R, gives the compliance
$J = q_1 + C_0(t, t_0) + C_d(t, t_0, t_c)$ directly from the concrete mix (water, cement,
aggregate, cement type), the shape factor and the curing method. keta derives from it

$$ \varphi(t, t_0) = \frac{C_0 + C_d}{(q_1 + \Delta_{0,01})(1 + n\rho_s)},\qquad n = 15 $$ (9.19)

The drying-creep parameter $q_5$ reads the final shrinkage in microstrain; the B3 model has no
autogenous shrinkage in this form. Basic creep grows as the logarithm of the duration and does not
tend to a limit.

The older French laws are available: the Instruction provisoire n° 2 of 1973
($E_{28} = 76\,650\sqrt{\sigma_{28}}$ in t/m², modulus capped at 28 days), the 1978 CEB-FIP Model
Code and Courbon's non-ageing law,

$$ \varphi(t, t_0) = 2\left(1 - e^{-0.006\,(t - t_0)}\right) $$ (9.20)

with constant modulus and no shrinkage. The IP2 and the Model Code 1978 work on the fictitious age
$t' = t\,(\theta + 10)/30$, where $\theta$ is the ambient temperature. For the Model Code 1978,
the coefficient $\varphi_{f2}(h_0)$ is read on a chart that keta does not tabulate: it must be
given. The law of Annex B of the 2023 EN 1992-1-1 is also available.

The next two figures compare the creep functions and the shrinkage of five laws for the same
concrete.

**Figure 9.2** — Creep function of five laws for the same concrete

**Figure 9.3** — Shrinkage of five laws for the same concrete

## 9.8 Affinity coefficients and composite laws

To calibrate a law on tests, each term may be multiplied by an affinity coefficient: modulus,
autogenous shrinkage, drying shrinkage, basic creep, drying creep and, for some laws, the time
development. For a law that distinguishes the two components,

$$ \varepsilon_{cs} = k_{re}\,\varepsilon_{ca} + k_{rd}\,\varepsilon_{cd},\qquad
\varphi = k_{fe}\,\varphi_b + k_{fd}\,\varphi_d $$ (9.21)

and the single coefficient of a law that does not distinguish them (BPEL, Model Code 1990) applies to
the whole. The time-development coefficients divide the age in the time function of their term. The
creep of a material may also come from one law and its shrinkage from another; the reference modulus
follows the creep law.

## 9.9 Nonlinear creep and creep in tension

Under a compressive stress above $0.45\,f_{cm}(t_0)$, EN 1992-1-1 §3.1.4(4) increases the creep
coefficient:

$$ \varphi_\text{nl}(t, t_0) = \varphi(t, t_0)\;e^{\,1.5\,(k_\sigma - 0.45)},\qquad
k_\sigma = \max\!\left(0.45,\ \frac{|\sigma_c|}{f_{cm}(t_0)}\right) $$ (9.22)

keta applies this factor, on request, to each load increment, with the stress of the most compressed
fibre of the section at the time of the increment. For a stress of $0.6\,f_{cm}$, the factor is
1.252.

Some laws make no provision for creep in tension. On request, a fibre in tension then receives no
creep increment: keta recomputes the increment of the section (axial strain and two curvatures) by
least squares over the fibres of the section, the target value being zero at the fibres in tension
and unchanged at the fibres in compression.

## 9.10 Maturity and heat curing

Steam-cured concrete hardens faster. For the relaxation of pretensioned strands, the equivalent time
of EN 1992-1-1, expression (10.2), is added to the relaxation clock:

$$ t_{eb} = t_{pa}\;1.14^{\,\theta_\text{max} - 20},\qquad
t_{pa} = \frac{\sum_i (\theta_i - 20)\,\Delta t_i}{\theta_\text{max} - 20} $$ (9.23)

where the $\theta_i$ are the temperatures of the curing cycle, in degrees Celsius, held during
$\Delta t_i$. For the laws of the BPEL family, shrinkage and the age term of creep are evaluated
on the age shifted by $t_{pa}\,1.08^{\,\theta_\text{max} - 20}$, the duration under load being
unchanged; for EN 1992-1-1, autogenous shrinkage is suppressed and drying shrinkage counts from the end
of curing. The Arrhenius equivalent age, which integrates an arbitrary temperature history, is not
offered.

## 9.11 Relaxation of steel

### 9.11.1 EN 1992-1-1

The pure relaxation loss at time $t$ (in hours) of a tendon stressed to $\sigma_{pi}$
follows expressions (3.28) to (3.30):

$$ \frac{\Delta\sigma_{pr}}{\sigma_{pi}} = k_1\,\rho_{1000}\,e^{k_3\mu}\left(\frac{t}{1\,000}\right)^{0.75(1-\mu)}10^{-5},\qquad
\mu = \frac{\sigma_{pi}}{f_{pk}} \le 1 $$ (9.24)

with $(k_1, k_3) = (5.39,\ 6.7)$ for class 1 (ordinary wires and strands),
$(0.66,\ 9.1)$ for class 2 (low relaxation) and $(1.98,\ 8.0)$ for class 3 (bars),
$\rho_{1000}$ in per cent. The time may be capped, for example at the 500 000 hours of
§3.3.2(8).

### 9.11.2 BPEL

The law of BPEL 91 (Annex 2), with $t$ in days:

$$ \Delta\sigma_\rho(t) = k_1\,\rho_{1000}\left(\frac{24\,t}{1\,000}\right)^{\frac34(1-\mu)}e^{(10\mu - 7.5)/k_2}\;\sigma,\qquad \mu = \frac{\sigma}{f_{prg}} $$ (9.25)

with $k_1 = 6\cdot 10^{-3}$ if $\rho_{1000} \le 2.5$ %, $8\cdot 10^{-3}$ otherwise, and
$k_2 = 1.10$ if $\rho_{1000} < 2.5$ %, 1.25 up to 8 %, 1.50 beyond. Finally, the IP2 gives
$p(h) = p\,(h/10^5)^{0.19}\,(\sigma_{pi} - 0.55R_g)/(0.25R_g)\,\sigma_{pi}$, zero below
$0.55\,R_g$, with $p = \max(2.4\,\rho_{1000},\ \rho_{3000} + 2.5)/100$.

**Figure 9.4** — Pure relaxation of a strand

### 9.11.3 Equivalent-time method

These laws assume a constant strain. In a structure, the stress in the steel also decreases through
creep and shrinkage of the concrete. The equivalent-time method (BPEL 91 Annex 2 §4, EN 1992-1-1
Annex D) assumes that the steel, which has already lost $\Delta\sigma_\text{cum}$ and now carries
$\sigma$, continues along the relaxation curve of the stress $\sigma + \Delta\sigma_\text{cum}$
from the time $t^*$ at which this curve reaches the loss already incurred:

$$ \rho(t^*;\ \sigma + \Delta\sigma_\text{cum}) = \Delta\sigma_\text{cum},\qquad
\Delta\sigma_{pr} = \rho(t^* + \Delta t;\ \sigma + \Delta\sigma_\text{cum}) - \Delta\sigma_\text{cum} $$ (9.26)

Since the loss is a power of time, $t^*$ is obtained in closed form,
$t^* = t_\text{ref}\,(\Delta\sigma_\text{cum}/\rho(t_\text{ref}))^{1/p}$, $p = \frac34(1 - \mu)$; a
bisection takes over as $\mu$ tends to 1. Under constant strain, the method telescopes: one hundred
steps of 100 hours reproduce the relaxation at 10 000 hours to within round-off. A stress drop of
100 MPa after 1 000 hours reduces the loss at 10 000 hours from 32.6 to 24.1 MPa for a class 2 strand
stressed to $0.75\,f_{pk}$.

## 9.12 Superposition principle

Under an arbitrary stress history, Boltzmann's superposition principle adds up the responses to the
stress increments, each with the creep function of its age of application:

$$ \varepsilon(t) = \int_{t_0}^{t} J(t, \tau)\,\mathrm{d}\sigma(\tau) + \varepsilon_{cs}(t) $$ (9.27)

This is a Volterra integral equation. Solved for the stress under an imposed strain, it gives the
relaxation function $R(t, t_0)$, the stress under a unit strain imposed at $t_0$ and
sustained. keta provides a direct integration of it by the trapezoidal rule on a given time grid
(preferably logarithmic),

$$ \varepsilon_i = J(t_i, t_0)\,\sigma_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{i} \frac{J(t_i, t_{j-1}) + J(t_i, t_j)}{2}\,(\sigma_j - \sigma_{j-1}) $$ (9.28)

solved for the stress by forward substitution (Bažant's step-by-step algorithm). It keeps the whole
history and costs $O(n^2)$; it serves as the reference for the methods that follow.

## 9.13 Time integration methods

In a structural analysis, the stress in each section changes at each construction event and under
the effect of creep itself. keta offers four methods to compute the creep strain over an interval
$[t_1, t_2]$. All of them work on the ages of the concrete $a = t - t_\text{cast}$, bounded
below by 0.5 day. The shrinkage of the interval, counted from the age of 0.5 day, is

$$ \Delta\varepsilon_{cs} = \varepsilon_{cs}(a_2) - \varepsilon_{cs}(a_1),\qquad a_i = \max\bigl(0.5,\ t_i - t_\text{cast}\bigr) $$ (9.29)

### 9.13.1 Superposition of increments

This is the default method. Each section keeps the list of its loading events: the increment of
generalised stress $\Delta\sigma_j$ that appeared at the start of a step, at age $t_j$. Over
the step $[a_1, a_2]$, the creep strain is

$$ \Delta\varepsilon_{cc} = \sum_j \lambda_j\,\Delta\sigma_j\,\frac{\varphi(a_2, t_j) - \varphi(a_1, t_j)}{E_\text{ref}(t_j)} $$ (9.30)

where $\lambda_j$ is the nonlinear factor (9.22) of the event (1 by default). The
stress is constant over the step, at its value at the start; the redistribution of the step appears
as a new event at the next step. For this explicit integration to converge to the solution of
(9.27), keta divides each interval into logarithmic sub-steps, starting 0.1 day after
the beginning of the interval, at a rate of four per decade by default. The number of sub-steps per
decade is adjustable; zero gives one step per interval. The coefficients
$\varphi(a_2, t_j) - \varphi(a_1, t_j)$ are shared by the sections of the same material, and
$\varphi$ is cached.

### 9.13.2 Kelvin chains

The previous method keeps the whole history. The Kelvin chain method replaces it by a small number
of internal variables. The creep function at an age at loading $t_0$ is approximated by a sum of
exponentials,

$$ J(t_0 + \Delta t, t_0) \approx a_0 + \sum_{\mu=1}^{m} a_\mu\left(1 - e^{-\Delta t/\tau_\mu}\right),\qquad a_\mu \ge 0 $$ (9.31)

which is the compliance of a spring $E_0 = 1/a_0$ in series with $m$ Kelvin units (a spring
$E_\mu = 1/a_\mu$ in parallel with a dashpot, retardation time $\tau_\mu = \eta_\mu/E_\mu$).
The term $a_0 = J(t_0, t_0)$ is imposed. The retardation times are fixed, evenly spaced on a
logarithmic scale from $10^{-2}$ to $10^{5}$ days; the compliances $a_\mu$ are fitted by
non-negative least squares (the NNLS algorithm of Lawson and Hanson) on 120 logarithmically spaced
durations from $10^{-2}$ to $10^{5}$ days, each equation being divided by $J$ so that the
relative error is uniform. Non-negativity is not a convenience: a negative compliance would give a
unit of negative stiffness and a non-monotonic creep.

**Figure 9.5** — Kelvin chain

With eight units (one per decade, the default value), the maximum relative error on the creep
function of EN 1992-1-1 is 0.6 to 1.7 % depending on the concrete and the age at loading; with sixteen
units, it falls below 0.1 % for durations longer than one day, the error remaining of the order of
1 % in the very first hours. A law made of a single exponential, such as Courbon's, is less well
represented by this fixed spectrum (8 % with eight units).

A unit is integrated exactly from one step to the next if the stress varies linearly over the step
(the exponential algorithm of Bažant and Wu). With $y = \Delta t/\tau_\mu$ and
$\lambda = (1 - e^{-y})/y$, the internal strain $\gamma_\mu$ of the unit becomes

$$ \gamma_\mu^{n+1} = e^{-y}\,\gamma_\mu^{n} + a_\mu\,\sigma_n\,(1 - e^{-y}) + a_\mu\,\Delta\sigma\,(1 - \lambda) $$ (9.32)

and the time-dependent strain of the step is the sum of the $\gamma_\mu^{n+1} - \gamma_\mu^{n}$.
Under a constant stress, the step telescopes: subdividing an interval changes nothing.

A chain fitted at one age represents the creep function (to within the fitting error) for a stress
applied at that age, but not for a stress applied later, on older concrete. keta therefore follows
the superposition principle: each loading event receives its own chain, fitted at the age of the
event. A change of stress smaller than $10^{-8}$ times the stress does not open an event: it is
added to the last chain. The fits are shared between the bars of the same material loaded at the same
age, the age being rounded on a logarithmic grid of 4 096 steps per decade (0.056 %). Forcing a whole
history through a single chain, fitted at the first loading, would make an error of the order of 13 %
on a two-step history.

### 9.13.3 Single step of the age-adjusted effective modulus

The cheapest method handles each interval in one step: the stress at the start of the interval
produces the strain

$$ \Delta\varepsilon_{cc} = \lambda\,\varphi(a_2, a_1)\,\frac{\sigma(a_1)}{E_\text{ref}(a_1)} $$ (9.33)

It ignores the age of earlier loadings and does not accumulate: the sum of the
$\varphi(a_{k+1}, a_k)$ over a subdivision is not $\varphi(a_n, a_0)$, because each term
restarts from the beginning of the creep curve, where it is steepest. Subdividing an interval
therefore overestimates creep. The method is meaningful only with one interval per stage. The
age-adjusted effective modulus $E/(1 + \chi\,\Delta\varphi)$, $\chi = 0.8$, appears in the
denominator of the losses (chapter 8).

### 9.13.4 Incremental fibre method

The last method follows creep in a few fibres of the section: two in a plane, four in space, placed
at the radii of gyration, which reproduce the axial force and the moments of the section. The creep
coefficient is put in the form $\varphi(t, t_0) = A(t_0)\,f(t - t_0)$, $A$ being its final
value and $f$ the time function. Each fibre keeps the amplitude
$S = \sum_j \Delta\sigma_j\,A(t_j)/E_\text{ref}(t_j)$ of its stress steps and its creep strain
$e$. Under loading, $e = S\,f(t_e)$, the equivalent duration $t_e$ being chosen so that
$e$ is continuous at the change of step:

$$ f(t_e) = \frac{e}{S},\qquad e(t + \Delta t) = S\,f(t_e + \Delta t) $$ (9.34)

In recovery (unloading, or reversal of sign), the fibre restarts from its strain $e_1$ towards
the new amplitude, $e = e_1 + (S - e_1)\,f(t_r)$. With four fibres, the part of their strains
that a plane section cannot follow is prevented by a self-equilibrated stress. This method, which has
no memory of the age of each stress step, creeps more slowly than superposition just after a change
of stress.

### 9.13.5 Comparison

An EN 1992-1-1 concrete column ($f_{ck} = 35$ MPa, humidity 60 %, $h_0 = 300$ mm), cast on
day 0, receives 2 MN on day 28 and a further 1 MN on day 100. The reference is
(9.27) in the form $u = (L/A)\,[N_1 J(t, 28) + N_2 J(t, 100)]$, plus shrinkage.
The errors on the shortening at day 1 000 are as follows.

| Method | Dates given | Error |
|---|---|---|
| Superposition of increments, 4 sub-steps per decade | 28, 100, 1 000 | −0.2 % |
| Kelvin chains, 8 units | 28, 100, 1 000 | −1.0 % |
| Single step | 28, 100, 1 000 | +12 % |
| Single step | 25 dates, 8 per decade | +255 % |
| Incremental fibre method | 28, 100, 1 000 | −0.4 % |

The column is statically determinate: its stress changes only at the loading dates. When creep
redistributes the internal forces, the stress also varies between the dates, and the choice of dates
matters more (chapter 10).

## 9.14 Choice of dates

The dates of an analysis are those of the stages. Between two dates, the stress is piecewise
constant, at its value at the start of each step: the redistributions due to creep are explicit. The
superposition of increments subdivides itself into logarithmic sub-steps, which is enough in practice;
the other methods have no subdivision of their own and require closely spaced dates where the internal
forces change quickly, that is just after each change of the static system or of the loads. A
logarithmic spacing from the event (a few dates per decade) is the right choice for Kelvin chains; it
must be avoided for the single step, which must keep one interval per stage.

$$ t_k = t_1 + 0.1\cdot 10^{\,k/m}\ \text{days},\qquad k = 0, 1, \dots,\quad t_k < t_2 \quad (m = 4 \text{ by default}) $$ (9.35)

are the ends of the sub-steps that the superposition of increments inserts in each interval
$[t_1, t_2]$ between two stage dates.

## 9.15 Scope

- The laws are those of the texts cited, within their ranges of validity; keta rejects a strength
outside the range (BPEL above 60 MPa, BHP outside 40 to 80 MPa, EN 1992-2 outside 40 to 90 MPa) and a
B3 mix composition outside its bounds.

- Temperature enters only through the fictitious ages and heat curing; the Arrhenius equivalent age
is not available.

- Creep is uniaxial in each generalised stress component; shear and torsional creep are not
represented.

- For the BPEL relaxation law, keta takes $k_2 = 1.25$ at $\rho_{1000} = 2.5$ %, a bound
that the text leaves ambiguous, whereas $k_1$ is $6\cdot 10^{-3}$ there.

# Chapter 10 Staged construction

A concrete bridge is never loaded in its final state all at once. Its spans are cast or erected one
after another, on falsework or props that are later removed, its tendons are stressed while the
structure is still statically determinate, its balanced cantilevers are closed, and all the while the
concrete creeps and shrinks. The final internal forces depend on this history: a load applied to a
cantilever does not redistribute as if the span had been continuous from the outset, and creep slowly
takes back part of the difference. This chapter describes how keta follows staged construction: the
way it accumulates the increments of each stage, the operations a stage may contain, the treatment of
creep, prestressing and cables from stage to stage, the tools specific to certain construction
methods (form traveller, incremental launching) and the factored states it derives. The
time-dependent laws are those of chapter 9, and the prestress losses those of chapter 8.

**Figure 10.1** — A structure that changes from one stage to the next

## 10.1 Assumptions

- each increment is computed linearly, under small displacements, on the substructure active at
that moment (active bars, supports and links), except in second-order stages and for catenary
cables;

- an activated element is born stress-free in the position then occupied by its nodes;

- states are superposed: the state at a stage is the sum of the increments since the origin;

- time enters only through creep, shrinkage and relaxation, between the dates of the stages; the
operations of a given stage are simultaneous as far as time is concerned;

- time-dependent effects are decided by the materials (a concrete given a law creeps and shrinks)
and by the tendons (a tendon given relaxation data relaxes), never by a flag in the staging
plan;

- shells are active from the first stage, cast at date zero; only bars are activated stage by
stage.

## 10.2 Incremental superposition

A staged analysis is a sequence of dated stages. Each operation of a stage produces a load increment
