$\Delta\mathbf{F}_k$ that is solved on the stiffness $\mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{A}_k}$ of the
substructure $\mathcal{A}_k$ active at that moment, then added component by component to the
cumulative state:

$$ \mathbf{K}_{\mathcal{A}_k}\,\Delta\mathbf{u}_k = \Delta\mathbf{F}_k,\qquad
\mathbf{S}_n = \sum_{k \le n} \Delta\mathbf{S}_k $$ (10.1)

where $\mathbf{S}$ stands equally for the displacements, the reactions, and the internal forces
at the ends and at the stations of the bars. There is no global solution: the forces “locked in” a
structure whose static system has changed come from the fact that each increment saw only the
structure of its own moment. Inactive bars carry zero internal forces. keta keeps one factorisation
of the stiffness per distinct active substructure, so that a plan returning to a configuration
already seen does not refactorise it; the key is only a hint, the assembled stiffness being compared
before any reuse.

Within each stage, the operations are carried out in the following order, which is that of a
construction site:

| Step | Operations |
|---|---|
| 1 | relaxation of the strands still on their bed during the elapsed interval |
| 2 | activations: added supports, bars, links |
| 3 | creep and shrinkage over the elapsed interval, time-dependent losses of the tendons |
| 4 | casting of parts of composite sections |
| 5 | deactivations of bars and links, removal of supports |
| 6 | changes of section, insertion of hinges, closures |
| 7 | catenary cables: installation, adjustments, rupture |
| 8 | grouting of ungrouted tendons |
| 9 | support modifications, then jacking |
| 10 | load cases of the stage |
| 11 | stressing and destressing, group after group |

After each increment, the bonded tendons already anchored undergo the corresponding elastic loss
(chapter 8, rule $K = 1$), which is itself an increment.

## 10.3 Activation and deactivation

### 10.3.1 Activated bars

An activated bar enters the stiffness of the subsequent increments without initial stress. Its
internal forces are those of the increments it receives from its activation onwards:

$$ \mathbf{S}_{\text{bar}}(t) = \sum_{k \,:\, t_k \ge t_\text{activation}} \Delta\mathbf{S}_{\text{bar},k} $$ (10.2)

A bar that no activation list names is active from the start, cast at date zero. By default, the
displacements at the stations of an activated bar count only the subsequent increments. Two options
change this starting point without creating any internal force:

- the bar is born straight on the displaced positions of its nodes: its stations start from the
chord of the end translations, and the displacements printed are then totals, continuous with those
of the nodes;

- the bar extends the deformed structure: if only one of its nodes already belongs to the structure,
the other takes the rigid-body motion of that node,
$\mathbf{u}_j = \mathbf{u}_i + \boldsymbol{\theta}_i \times (\mathbf{x}_j - \mathbf{x}_i)$,
$\boldsymbol{\theta}_j = \boldsymbol{\theta}_i$. This is the case of a segment placed at the tip of
a cantilever that has already rotated.

### 10.3.2 Concrete age and modulus

The age $a$ of a bar at the time of its activation may be given: the bar is then deemed to have
been cast $a$ days earlier. A negative age describes deferred casting: the bar is in place but
neither creeps nor shrinks before it is cast. This age governs creep, shrinkage and, on request, the
modulus: the stiffness of the increments of stage $k$, of date $t_k$, may use the modulus of
the concrete law at the age reached,

$$ t_\text{cast} = t_\text{activation} - a,\qquad E_k = E\bigl(t_k - t_\text{cast}\bigr) $$ (10.3)

evaluated once per stage and per bar. By default, the modulus is that of the material.

### 10.3.3 Deactivation

A deactivated bar exerted on its nodes the forces $-\mathbf{f}$, opposite to its cumulative end
forces $\mathbf{f}$. Its removal therefore applies to the remaining structure the increment

$$ \Delta\mathbf{F} = +\mathbf{f}_\text{bar} $$ (10.4)

(release of the locked-in forces). Its internal forces and its creep memory are erased: if it is
reactivated later, it is born again stress-free. The deactivation of a bar on elastic soil is
rejected. An elastic link is deactivated in the same way; a rigid link cannot be. Links activated
during the staged analysis are also born free of force.

## 10.4 Supports

### 10.4.1 Addition, removal and modification

An added support restrains the displacements from the position reached: it carries a reaction only
for the subsequent increments. A removed support releases its cumulative reaction
$\mathbf{R}$:

$$ \Delta\mathbf{F} = -\mathbf{R}_\text{support} $$ (10.5)

In a beam of two 6 m spans under 25 kN/m, the reaction $5qL/4 = 187.5$ kN of the central
support, removed afterwards, is thus transferred to the 12 m span and the end supports. A modified
support takes on new conditions: a released component releases its reaction, and a newly restrained
component is placed on the deformed structure, without reaction.

### 10.4.2 Jacking

Jacking brings the total displacement of the restrained components of a support back to zero: the
increment is an imposed displacement

$$ \Delta\mathbf{u}_\text{support} = -\mathbf{u}_\text{support}^\text{cumulative} $$ (10.6)

on each non-zero restrained component. An arbitrary relative support displacement is applied by an
imposed-displacement load case. Jacking an inclined support is rejected.

## 10.5 Hinges, closures and sections

A stage hinge releases, for the subsequent increments, local components at one end of a bar. It is
allowed only where the cumulative force on these components is zero
($|f| \le 10^{-9}\max(1, \|\mathbf{f}\|_\infty)$): releasing a loaded component would shift the
equilibrium, which is a matter for deactivation. Closure restores continuity: the relative rotation
$\Delta\theta_\text{open}$ acquired while the hinge was open remains frozen, at zero force, and
only the subsequent increments see the continuity. Closure may in addition force a relative jump
$\boldsymbol{\delta}$ (axial gap, twist, rotations about the two section axes) in the closed
joint, applied as a concentrated dislocation at the end:

$$ \Delta\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{d}^*(\boldsymbol{\delta}) $$ (10.7)

free on a statically determinate structure, it creates a self-equilibrated stress state on a
statically indeterminate one; this is the tool for adjustment by jacking at closure.

The section of an active bar may be changed: the internal forces acquired remain, and the
subsequent increments see the new stiffness. The change is rejected for a concrete that creeps (the
locked-in stress of the old section would creep like that of the new one), for a bar of variable
inertia and for a composite bar. Concrete added to an existing section is cast as one part of a
composite section: each part is born stress-free, has its own age and its own internal forces, and
creeps with an implicit step of modulus

$$ E_\text{eff} = \left(\frac{1}{E} + \frac{\varphi(a_2, a_1)}{E_\text{ref}(a_1)}\right)^{-1} $$ (10.8)

over the interval $[a_1, a_2]$, the earlier history of the part producing an imposed strain. The
implicit step remains stable when a part almost entirely restrained by the others creeps strongly,
which an explicit step does not.

## 10.6 Loads

A load case named in a stage is applied once, to the active substructure of that stage, and then
remains in the cumulative state. A span load on an inactive bar is not applied (the chronology check
reports it). A form traveller is placed, moved forward and removed by load cases (next section); the
weight of a segment is the load of the stage in which it is activated.

## 10.7 Form traveller

A form traveller (or a launching girder) is a rigid body of weight $W$, with its centre of
gravity at $(x_G, y_G)$ in the plane normal to gravity, resting on the deck at $N \ge 3$
points. Its reactions are those of a rigid body. With three non-aligned points, statics gives
them:

$$ \sum_i F_i = W,\qquad \sum_i F_i\,x_i = W\,x_G,\qquad \sum_i F_i\,y_i = W\,y_G $$ (10.9)

With more than three points, keta assumes identical elastic supports: the rigid body moves along a
plane, the reactions are linear in the plane, $F_i = a + b\,x_i + c\,y_i$, and
(10.9) determines $(a, b, c)$. This is the minimum-norm distribution. For example,
600 kN centred 1 m from the front line of a traveller on four supports 5 m apart give 240 kN on each
front support and 60 kN on each rear support. A support whose reaction would be negative signals
overturning, unless it is an anchorage, which can pull. The loads on the deck are the forces
$-F_i$ along gravity; a move of the traveller is a single load case: removal at the old position
and placing at the new one. Supports of different stiffnesses or a flexible traveller require the
traveller to be modelled in the structure.

## 10.8 Creep during the stages

### 10.8.1 Imposed strains

Between the date of the previous stage and that of the current stage, each active concrete bar
(except those cast in the stage) receives its creep and shrinkage strain as an imposed strain, which
the active structure, if statically indeterminate, redistributes. The methods for computing the creep
strain are those of chapter 9. For a bar, the three generalised stress components $N/A$,
$M_y/I_y$ and $M_z/I_z$ give the creep axial strain and the two creep curvatures:

$$ \Delta\varepsilon_0 = \mathcal{C}\!\left[\frac{N}{A}\right],\qquad
\Delta\kappa_y = \mathcal{C}\!\left[\frac{M_y}{I_y}\right],\qquad \Delta\kappa_z = \mathcal{C}\!\left[\frac{M_z}{I_z}\right] $$ (10.10)

where $\mathcal{C}$ denotes the creep operator of the chosen method (for example
$\sum_j \Delta\sigma_j\,[\varphi(a_2, t_j) - \varphi(a_1, t_j)]/E_\text{ref}(t_j)$ for the
superposition of increments). The imposed curvatures have the sign that adds creep to the elastic
deflection. The shrinkage of the interval is added to the axial strain. By default, the stress of the
bar is taken at its central station and the imposed strain is uniform over the bar; as an option, it
is computed at each station and applied as the piecewise linear field that it is, by two concentrated
dislocations at the Gauss points of each interval between stations, which reproduce without error,
for this field, the nodal forces and the displacements at the stations. This option is needed as soon
as a bar is long compared with the variation of the stress: a span whose moment changes sign along its
length.

### 10.8.2 Redistribution

The textbook case is that of two simply supported loaded spans, then made continuous over their
common support. With a non-ageing law $\varphi(t - t_0) = \varphi_\infty(1 - e^{-\alpha(t - t_0)})$
at constant modulus, the Volterra integral equation of continuity over the support is solved by
Laplace transform:

$$ M_B(t) = M_\text{cont}\;\frac{\varphi_\infty}{1 + \varphi_\infty}\left(1 - e^{-\alpha\,(1 + \varphi_\infty)(t - t_0)}\right) $$ (10.11)

where $M_\text{cont}$ is the support moment of the beam cast continuous. For two 20 m spans under
50 kN/m, Courbon's law ($\varphi_\infty = 2$, $\alpha = 0.006$ d−1) and creep
computed along the bars, the superposition of increments gives, at 100, 1 000 and 10 000 days,
errors of +7.8 %, −0.23 % and −0.11 % with four sub-steps per decade, and of +0.4 %, −0.06 % and
−0.06 % with forty. Kelvin chains, with dates given at eight per decade, differ by +3.5 %, −1.9 % and
+0.15 %; with only the three reading dates, their explicit integration oscillates (errors of +80 %,
−84 % and +183 %). The single step, with eight dates per decade, tends towards the moment of the
continuous beam: it overestimates the redistribution by 50 %. With the mid-bar scheme and four bars
per span, the asymptote is overestimated by 4 %.

**Figure 10.2** — Creep redistribution of the support moment after closure

### 10.8.3 Order and consistency

The creep of the interval is computed on the cumulative state at the start of the stage and applied
after the activations of the stage: a bar cast in the stage does not creep over the interval, but it
is part of the structure that redistributes the creep of the others. The time-dependent losses of the
tendons over the interval are computed with the creep strains of the same engine (chapter 8), before
the elastic redistribution of the creep increment. A bar carrying a strand still held by its bed
shrinks freely, without creeping.

## 10.9 Prestressing in stages

### 10.9.1 Stressing and destressing

A stressing operation brings a tendon to a target fraction of its force $P_0$; the increment is
the difference from the fraction already applied, and its equivalent loads are those of chapter 8,
all the bars of the tendon having to be active. The tendons of a given group are stressed
simultaneously ($K = 0$ between them); the successive groups, and the later increments, cause
losses in the tendons already anchored ($K = 1$). A target below the applied fraction is a
destressing: the jack releases the corresponding share of the current effective force,

$$ \Delta P = -\,\frac{f_\text{applied} - f_\text{target}}{f_\text{applied}}\;P_\text{eff} $$ (10.12)

and the structure receives the opposite of the equivalent loads of this share, together with, if
losses are kept locally, the same share of the loss field. A cycle of stressing followed by full
destressing of a single tendon, without creep, leaves no internal force. Partial destressing restarts
the relaxation clock on the new stress; full destressing takes the tendon out of service, and it may
be restressed later.

### 10.9.2 Ungrouted tendons and grouting

An ungrouted tendon slides in its duct: the variations of concrete strain along the tendon do not
make it lose point by point. When losses are kept locally, keta first computes the force field that
bond would give, $T_i$, then projects it onto the profiles admissible under Coulomb friction: on
each interval of the tendon grid, with friction exponent
$a_j = \mu(\Delta\theta_j + k\,h_j) + \varphi\,h_j$,

$$ \min_{N}\ \sum_i w_i\,(N_i - T_i)^2 \quad\text{subject to}\quad e^{-a_j}\,N_j \le N_{j+1} \le e^{a_j}\,N_j $$ (10.13)

Without friction, the solution is the weighted mean over the free length; otherwise, the intervals
where a constraint is active slip and the others stick. Grouting makes the tendon bonded from that
stage onwards. Partial grouting, over an interval of the chain, makes the tendon bonded over that
interval; each neighbouring free run, anchored by the grouted zone, then slides between its own
anchorages.

### 10.9.3 Pretensioning on a bed

A strand stressed on its bed does not act on the structure; it relaxes during the intervals in which
it remains there, the loss being taken by the bed. At release, it undergoes the thermal loss of
curing, transfers its force by bond according to its force profile (transmission laws, chapter 8),
then undergoes its own elastic shortening as a loss. Local losses distinguish the loss of the
plateau from that of the transmission zones.

### 10.9.4 Shell tendons

Tendons carried by shells are stressed by fractions of their force profile. They are bonded: each
increment strains them by the mean strain of the concrete along their profile, and the loss, which
reduces the whole profile uniformly, is iterated as for bar tendons. Between dates, they lose through
creep and shrinkage through the structure and through EN 1992-1-1 relaxation in equivalent time.
Their losses are not coupled with those of the bar tendons of a mixed model.

## 10.10 Catenary cables in stages

A catenary cable (chapter 7) enters the staged analysis when an activation list names it; its two
anchorages must then belong to the active structure. Its unstressed length $L_0$ is determined
from its data (unstressed length, end tension or horizontal tension) at the positions of its
anchorages at that moment. From then on, each increment is coupled:

$$ \mathbf{K}\,\Delta\mathbf{u} = \Delta\mathbf{F} + \sum_c \bigl[\mathbf{q}_c(\mathbf{x} + \Delta\mathbf{u};\ L_0') - \mathbf{q}_c(\mathbf{x};\ L_0)\bigr] $$ (10.14)

where $\mathbf{q}_c$ is the force of the elastic catenary of cable $c$ on its nodes,
evaluated at the true positions $\mathbf{x}$ of its anchorages (cumulative displacements
included). keta solves it by the modified Newton method on $\mathbf{K} + \mathbf{K}_t$,
$\mathbf{K}_t$ being the tangent stiffness of the cables at the start of the increment, factorised
once, until the true residual is at the level of round-off errors. The change in the cable forces then
becomes a nodal load of the increment, and the rest of the computation is linear. On an installed
cable, a stage may impose a new unstressed length, a horizontal tension or an end tension (reached at
the equilibrium of the increment, the anchorages moving with the adjustment, by a secant on
$L_0$), a thermal expansion $L_0' = L_0(1 + \alpha\Delta T)$, or rupture: the force of the
cable is released statically, and a dynamic factor $\phi \ge 1$ gives in addition the peak
$(\phi - 1)$ times this release, to be added to the cumulative state for the accidental
situation. Catenary cables are rejected with pseudo-plastic soil, unilateral supports or rigid links;
the frame remains under small displacements.

## 10.11 Analysis regimes

### 10.11.1 Second order

A stage may be declared second-order. Each increment then solves the equilibrium of the total state
with the geometric stiffness of the total axial force:

$$ \bigl[\mathbf{K} + \mathbf{K}_g(N_1)\bigr]\,\Delta\mathbf{u} = \Delta\mathbf{F} - \sum_e \bigl[\mathbf{k}_{g,e}(N_1) - \mathbf{k}_{g,e}(N_0)\bigr]\,\mathbf{d}_e $$ (10.15)

where $N_0$ is the cumulative axial force of each bar, $N_1 = N_0 + N(\Delta\mathbf{u})$ is
obtained by fixed-point iteration, and $\mathbf{d}_e$ is the displacement of the bar since its
stress-free activation, increased by the geometric imperfection introduced in the stage. A later axial
load thus amplifies an earlier deflection. On a 5 m cantilever column loaded laterally in a linear
stage, then by $0.4\,P_\text{cr}$ in a second-order stage, keta amplifies the deflection by
1.657 619, against 1.657 619 for the analytical solution $\delta = H(\tan kL - kL)/(Pk)$. Stages
that are all second-order give the result of a single second-order analysis. The analysis is rejected
beyond the critical load (detected by the inertia of the factorisation), and with imposed
displacements, installed catenary cables, nonlinear soil, unilateral supports, rigid links or shells.
The creep and shrinkage increments of a second-order stage go through the same increment.

### 10.11.2 Large displacements

A separate driver chains steps under large displacements (corotational formulation of
chapter 17): each step activates bars and cables, adds its loads and may redefine unstressed lengths
of cables, then is brought to equilibrium from the previous state. A bar placed between a node in
place and a new node is placed stress-free in the deformed geometry; a bar placed between two nodes
already in place (a closure) is placed with its own geometry, so that the gap strains it:

$$ \mathbf{r}(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{F}_\text{int}(\mathbf{u}) - \sum_{k \le n} \mathbf{F}_k = \mathbf{0} $$ (10.16)

This driver handles neither creep nor prestressing, and rejects rigid links, constraints and skew
supports.

## 10.12 Incremental launching

A girder can be pushed along its axis only if this axis is a curve of constant curvature and
torsion: a straight line (possibly on a gradient), a circle in plan or a helix. Launching is then a
screw motion that preserves the curve and the direction of gravity, and each position is congruent
to the girder in its reference position, the supports having moved along it. keta therefore keeps the
mesh fixed and moves the supports: a pier at ground abscissa $P$ carries, for an advance
$a$, the point of the girder at abscissa

$$ \sigma = P - a + L_g $$ (10.17)

measured from the rear end ($a = 0$ puts the front of the girder, of length $L_g$, at
ground abscissa 0). The contact is placed at its true abscissa: a prismatic bar is split at that
point in the model of the position (at the same fraction of the chord as of the alignment interval);
within $10^{-7}$ of the bar length from a node, the contact is carried by the node. Splitting a
bar of variable section, with rigid arms or carrying a tendon is rejected. Each engaged pier holds the
girder vertically and laterally in the alignment axes at the contact; the first engaged pier in the
list also holds the longitudinal direction and the torsion (the launching jacks). A position in which
fewer than two piers carry the girder is declared unstable and is not computed.

For each position, under self-weight, keta gives the vertical reaction and the guiding force at
each pier, the moment in the girder at the contact, the uplifted piers (negative reaction) and the
front overhang (the launching nose, modelled by the leading bars) and rear overhang; it also gives the
envelope of the moments at the stations. For a 40 m girder on three piers 20 m apart, it recovers,
with the span $L = 20$ m, the reactions $3/8$, $10/8$ and $3/8$ of $qL$ and
the moment $qL^2/8$ over the central pier; for a 15 m rear overhang, the moment
$q\cdot 15^2/2$ at the contact.

**Figure 10.3** — Pier reactions during incremental launching

## 10.13 States and factoring

### 10.13.1 Registers by origin

On request, keta keeps the cumulative state in three registers according to the origin of each
increment, whose sum is the cumulative state:

$$ \mathbf{S} = S(G) + S(P_0) + S(\Delta P) $$ (10.18)

$S(G)$ receives the loads, the creep and shrinkage of the structure (redistribution is
classified with the permanent actions, as is customary) and the releases of locked-in forces;
$S(P_0)$ the stressing and destressing operations and the immediate losses they cause;
$S(\Delta P)$ the time-dependent losses (creep, shrinkage, relaxation) and the elastic losses
they bring about, with their sign: a loss is a negative prestressing effect. A deactivation, a removal
or modification of a support, or jacking mix the origins in the same increment: the attribution is
no longer unambiguous after them, keta records this and then rejects factored states.

### 10.13.2 Factored states

A factored state multiplies each register by its coefficient:

$$ \mathbf{S}_\text{factored} = \mathbf{S} + (k_G - 1)\,S(G) + (k_{P_0} - 1)\,S(P_0) + (k_{\Delta P} - 1)\,S(\Delta P) $$ (10.19)

BPEL 91 (art. 4.1.2) defines the characteristic values $P_1 = 1.02\,P_0 - 0.80\,\Delta P$ and
$P_2 = 0.98\,P_0 - 1.20\,\Delta P$, that is the coefficients $(1,\ 1.02,\ 0.80)$ and
$(1,\ 0.98,\ 1.20)$. EN 1992-1-1 §5.10.9 applies a single coefficient to the total prestress,
$r_\text{inf}$ or $r_\text{sup}$, on $S(P_0) + S(\Delta P)$, the values being supplied by
the engineer. The envelope of the factored states retains, component by component and independently
for each origin, the favourable or unfavourable coefficient of each pair (eight coefficients:
favourable and unfavourable $k_G$, $k_{P_0}$ and $k_{\Delta P}$, or $k_P$ for the
total prestress). These states cover displacements, reactions, and internal forces in bars and links,
not shells.

### 10.13.3 Primary and secondary effects

At each recorded stage, keta computes the primary effect of the tendons acting on the structure, at
the stations, by (8.19) with the effective force, and derives from it the secondary
effect

$$ \mathbf{S}^\text{hyp} = S(P_0) + S(\Delta P) - \mathbf{S}^\text{iso} $$ (10.20)

zero on a statically determinate structure, and linear between the supports of a continuous beam
(EN 1992-1-1 §5.10.7). The primary effect is computed only for the internal forces at the stations
($N$, $V_y$, $V_z$, $M_y$, $M_z$): not for torsion, end forces or
displacements.

## 10.14 Chronology check

Before the analysis, keta can run through the plan dry, in the order of the engine, on a simulated
state (bars, supports, links, cast parts, tendons, date), and report all the problems at once. An
error is a condition that the analysis would reject or an operation that makes no sense; a warning,
an operation that is legitimate but has no effect:

| Severity | Examples |
|---|---|
| Error | date going backwards, unknown bar or node, bar already active, deactivation of an inactive bar or of a bar on soil, live tendon on a removed bar, removal of an inactive support, jacking of an inclined support, change of section of a concrete that creeps, hinge already inserted, closure without a hinge, catenary cable anchored outside the structure, second-order stage with elements that are not allowed |
| Warning | span load on an inactive bar, age given to a bar that the stage does not cast, extension without a node in place, grouting of an ungrouted tendon that was never stressed |

An empty report proves that the references resolve and that the order is consistent; it proves
neither the convergence of the analysis nor that a hinge is inserted where no force is locked in,
which depends on the computed state.

## 10.15 Resuming a staged analysis

The state of a staged analysis between two stages can be resumed to continue with another plan,
without recomputing the common prefix: variants of the end of construction, study of several closure
dates. The resumed state comprises the cumulative state, the active substructure, the accumulated
forces of each bar and each support, the state of the tendons (fractions, losses, local fields,
relaxation clocks), the creep memories of each station and the casting dates. The model of the
continuation must contain the footprint of the prefix: same nodes, same bars, same supports, same
tendons already stressed; it may add bars, tendons and cases. Since each increment was solved on the
active substructure alone, the continuation is then identical, bit for bit, to the analysis of the
whole chain on the new model:

$$ \mathbf{S}_n^{\text{resumed}} = \mathbf{S}_n^{\text{full chain}} $$ (10.21)

A model that does not contain the footprint, or an option on which the increments depend, is
rejected with the reason. The identity of the constitutive laws, which are functions, is the
responsibility of the engineer.

## 10.16 Results provided

For each stage: the cumulative state and the increment of the stage (nodal displacements,
reactions, internal forces at the ends and at the stations of the bars, link forces), the applied
force, the cumulative loss and the effective force of each tendon, the state of the catenary cables
(unstressed length, horizontal tension, end tensions), the internal forces of each part of the
composite sections and, on request, the registers by origin, the primary effect and the active
substructure, whose tangent stiffness serves for subsequent analyses (eigenmodes, stability) about
the state of the stage.

## 10.17 Scope

- The increments are linear, except for second-order stages and catenary cables; the
large-displacement driver is separate and has neither creep nor prestressing.

- Shells are not activated in stages.

- Jacking resets the displacement of a support to zero; resetting its reaction to zero, imposing an
absolute displacement and jacking by a factor are not offered.

- A hinge cannot be replaced directly by another: it must be closed and a new one inserted.

- Launching knows only the self-weight of the girder, on a straight, circular or helical
alignment.

- In the incremental fibre method, the arrangement of the fibres (two in a plane, four in space)
must match the bending plane studied: two fibres arranged along the local $y$ axis do not see
bending about that axis.

# Chapter 11 Influence lines and surfaces

Under moving loads, the question is no longer “what is the effect of this load?” but “where must
the loads be placed for the effect at a section to be the most adverse?”. The influence line answers
it: for a given response (the moment over a pier, the reaction of an abutment, the deflection at
mid-span), it gives the value of that response when a unit load stands at any point of the running
path. On a deck modelled as a grillage or with shells, the position of the load has two coordinates
and the line becomes a surface. This chapter describes how keta computes these lines and surfaces,
how it interpolates and integrates them, and how it derives from them the extreme effects of a
distributed load, a vehicle or a set of wheels. The code load models built on these tools
(EN 1991-2, *fascicule 61 titre II*, railway loads) are described in chapters 12 and 13; fatigue
under traffic, in chapter 14.

## 11.1 Assumptions

- the structure is linear: its stiffness is that of the initial model, in small displacements, and
the response is proportional to the load;

- the moving load is a unit force of given direction (vertical downwards by default,
$(0, 0, -1)$); unit moments are not swept;

- the load travels along a continuous chain of bars (influence line) or over a set of deck nodes
(influence surface);

- the response studied is a linear function of the displacements and of the load: displacement of a
node, support reaction, internal force or displacement at a bar section;

- the effect of a set of loads is the sum of the effects of each (superposition); dynamic effects
are covered by the factors of the load models, not here.

## 11.2 Principle

The response $R$ studied is an affine function of the free nodal displacements:

$$ R = \mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{u} + h $$ (11.1)

where $\mathbf{g}$ is the gradient of the response and $h$ a local term that depends only on
the load (it is non-zero only when the load stands at the node of the reaction studied or on the bar
that carries the section studied). A unit load placed at $s$ produces the equivalent nodal forces
$\mathbf{r}(s)$, and $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{r}(s)$. Since the stiffness matrix
is symmetric,

$$ \eta(s) = \mathbf{g}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{r}(s) + h(s) = \mathbf{w}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{r}(s) + h(s),\qquad \mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{g} $$ (11.2)

A single solution, that of the adjoint problem $\mathbf{K}\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{g}$, therefore
replaces one solution per load position; each ordinate then costs a dot product over the twelve
components at most of $\mathbf{r}(s)$. This is the Maxwell-Betti reciprocal theorem. The vector
$\mathbf{w}$ is the deflected shape of the structure under the “load” $\mathbf{g}$: for a
moment at a section, two opposite unit couples on either side of the section, which impose a unit
relative rotation; for a reaction, a unit force at the support. This is the Müller-Breslau
principle: the influence line of an internal force is the deflected shape produced by a unit
discontinuity of the conjugate displacement at the section.

keta builds $\mathbf{g}$ without approximation, by evaluating the response for a unit
displacement on each of the few degrees of freedom it reads. The matrix is factorised once per line;
the factorisation can be kept and reused for other responses and other paths of the same model, only
the adjoint solution being repeated. The ordinates are mathematically identical to those of a direct
solution per position: on a grillage, the influence surface of the deflection of a node coincides
with the deflected shape under a unit load applied at that node, and the sum of the ordinates of the
reactions of all the supports equals 1 to within $4\times 10^{-14}$.

## 11.3 Influence line

### 11.3.1 Running path

The path is a chain of contiguous bars; keta determines the direction of travel along each bar
from its neighbours, and rejects a broken chain. The curvilinear abscissa $s$ accumulates along
the chain. Each bar receives $n$ equally spaced stations, ends included (eleven by default), a
node shared by two bars carrying a single station:

$$ s_{b,k} = s_b + \frac{k}{n-1}\,L_b,\qquad k = 0, \dots, n-1 $$ (11.3)

At each station, the unit load is a point force on the bar, and $\mathbf{r}(s)$ are its
equivalent nodal forces (chapter 3). The line is zero outside the path.

### 11.3.2 Responses

The available responses are:

- the displacement of a node, one of its six global components;

- the reaction of a support, one of its six components: it is the sum of the forces that the bars,
the shells and the elastic links meeting at the node exert on it, less the load applied at the node,
so that a support spring does give $-k\,u$;

- an internal force ($N, V_y, V_z, T, M_y, M_z$) at a section of abscissa $x$ of a
bar;

- a displacement or a rotation, in global components, at a section of a bar, read by the same
recovery as the static results (chapter 4).

For a bar internal force, the local term $h(s)$ accounts for the presence of the unit load on
the bar studied. The internal force is recovered from the equilibrium of the segment $[0, x]$
under the end forces and the load, if it lies there; for the moment, with the unit load $P$
placed at abscissa $a$ of the bar,

$$ M(x) = M(0) + V(0)\,x - \mathbb{1}_{a \le x}\;P\,(x - a) $$ (11.4)

The line of a shear force therefore has a unit jump at the section studied, that of a moment a
kink.

### 11.3.3 Interpolation between stations

Between two stations of a prismatic bar, the line is the deflected shape of the adjoint problem: a
cubic. keta interpolates it by the Hermite cubic that passes through the two ordinates with the
slopes $\eta'_k$ to the right of the first station and $\eta'_{k+1}$ to the left of the
second:

$$ \eta(s) = (2t^3 - 3t^2 + 1)\,\eta_k + (t^3 - 2t^2 + t)\,h\,\eta'_k + (-2t^3 + 3t^2)\,\eta_{k+1} + (t^3 - t^2)\,h\,\eta'_{k+1},\qquad t = \frac{s - s_k}{h} $$ (11.5)

The slopes are estimated by second-order differences on two additional ordinates taken inside the
interval, at $10^{-3}h$ and $2\times 10^{-3}h$ from each end, computed by the same dot
product. The kinks at the nodes and the jump at the section studied thus stay at the stations. The
ordinates at the stations are those of the model; the interpolation between them carries a small
error that decreases as the square of the spacing. For the moment at mid-span of the central span of
a 25 + 30 + 25 m continuous beam, the integral of the negative zone departs from the effect of a
distributed load computed directly by:

| Stations per bar | 3 | 11 | 21 | 41 | 6 (section off a station) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| relative difference | $5.6 \times 10^{-4}$ | $2.3 \times 10^{-5}$ | $5.6 \times 10^{-6}$ | $1.4 \times 10^{-6}$ | 2.3 % |

The last column shows the only condition to be met: the section studied must coincide with a
station of the path (a bar end, or an abscissa of the station grid). Otherwise the jump or the kink
falls inside an interval, and the interpolation is wrong there; keta does not detect it. The simplest
course is to place a node at the section studied.

**Figure 11.1** — Influence lines of the moment of a 25 + 30 + 25 m continuous beam: over pier 1 and at mid-span of the central span

## 11.4 Extreme effects

### 11.4.1 Concentrated loads and vehicles

A vehicle is a set of axles $P_k$ placed at distances $a_k$ from a reference point,
possibly supplemented by uniformly loaded segments (start $b_j$, length $\ell_j$, total load
$Q_j$). Placed at the reference $r$, it produces the effect

$$ E(r) = \sum_k P_k\,\eta(r + a_k) + \sum_j \frac{Q_j}{\ell_j}\int_{r + b_j}^{r + b_j + \ell_j} \eta(s)\,\mathrm{d}s $$ (11.6)

keta slides the reference from the entry of the vehicle onto the path to its exit, on a regular
grid of positions (501 positions by default); an axle off the path does not count. It retains the
maximum, the minimum and the corresponding positions. Travel in the opposite direction is obtained
with the reversed vehicle. For a single load, the extremes are those of the line, including at the
interior extrema of each cubic. For a vehicle of two 300 kN axles 1.2 m apart on the previous beam,
the maximum effect on the moment at mid-span of the central span, recomputed by a static analysis
with the axles at the position found, differs by $2\times 10^{-5}$ in relative terms.

### 11.4.2 Distributed load on the sign zones

A distributed load of intensity $q$, free to occupy any part of the path, produces the maximum
effect when it loads the zones where the line is positive, and those alone:

$$ E^{+} = q\int \max(\eta, 0)\,\mathrm{d}s,\qquad E^{-} = q\int \min(\eta, 0)\,\mathrm{d}s $$ (11.7)

keta splits each interval at the zeros of the line: for a cubic, the intervals of monotonicity are
bounded by the roots of the derivative, and each zero is isolated by bisection; for a piecewise
linear line, the zero is computed directly. The two-point Gauss rule integrates each piece of cubic
without error. keta also returns the list of the zones of each sign, with their bounds and their
area.

**Figure 11.2** — Sign zones of the influence line of the moment at mid-span of the central span

When the intensity depends on the loaded length $L$ (system A of the *fascicule 61*, laws
in $a\sqrt{L}$, $b/L^p$, tabulated), loading all the adverse zones is not necessarily the
worst case: lengthening the loaded length reduces the intensity. The extreme effect is then sought
over the subsets $S$ of the zones of the same sign, of lengths $L_z$ and areas
$A_z$:

$$ E^{*} = \max_{S}\ v\!\left(\sum_{z \in S} L_z\right)\,\sum_{z \in S} A_z $$ (11.8)

keta enumerates the subsets in Gray-code order, where a single zone enters or leaves at each step:
length and area are updated in constant time, and the optimum retained is the best of the
$2^n$ subsets. Beyond 24 zones, the calculation is refused.

### 11.4.3 Prefix integrals

Sliding a vehicle requires the integral of the line over a window at each position. keta builds
once the table of the cumulative integrals at the stations,

$$ C_k = \int_{s_0}^{s_k} \eta\,\mathrm{d}s,\qquad \int_a^b \eta\,\mathrm{d}s = \left(C_{k_b} + \int_{s_{k_b}}^{b}\eta\right) - \left(C_{k_a} + \int_{s_{k_a}}^{a}\eta\right) $$ (11.9)

where $k_a$ and $k_b$ are the stations that precede $a$ and $b$, found by
bisection. Each window integral costs a time proportional to the logarithm of the number of stations
instead of a pass over the line. The line may have duplicated abscissae (a jump): an interval of zero
length adds nothing to the table.

## 11.5 Influence surfaces

### 11.5.1 Grid of nodes

On a deck modelled as a grillage or with shells, the unit load is placed in turn on each node of a
grid of $n_x \times n_y$ existing nodes of the model, and the ordinates are obtained by the same
adjoint solution (11.2). The grid must be rectangular in plan (global $X$ and
$Y$ axes, strictly increasing grid lines, tolerance of $10^{-9}$ times the extent); the
levels of the nodes may vary. Between the nodes, the surface is bilinear over each cell:

$$ \eta(x, y) = (1-\xi)(1-\zeta)\,\eta_{00} + \xi(1-\zeta)\,\eta_{10} + (1-\xi)\zeta\,\eta_{01} + \xi\zeta\,\eta_{11} $$ (11.10)

with $\xi, \zeta$ the reduced coordinates in the cell; it is zero outside the grid. Unlike
the line, the surface is not enriched between the nodes: its accuracy depends on the grid spacing,
and a local effect (the moment of a slab under a wheel) calls for a fine grid around the section
studied.

**Figure 11.3** — Influence surface of the moment of a grillage girder (24 × 12 m, 13 × 7 nodes), supported on its two transverse edges

### 11.5.2 Integrals over the surface

The effect of a uniformly loaded rectangle (the contact area of a wheel, a tandem) is the integral
of the surface over the rectangle, cut at the edges of the grid. It is computed without error for
the bilinear interpolant, as the product of the integrals of the shape functions in each
direction:

$$ \iint_{[x_0, x_1]\times[y_0, y_1]} \eta\,\mathrm{d}x\,\mathrm{d}y = \sum_{\text{nodes}} \eta_{ij}\left(\int_{x_0}^{x_1} N_i\,\mathrm{d}x\right)\left(\int_{y_0}^{y_1} N_j\,\mathrm{d}y\right) $$ (11.11)

The contact area is applied in full, favourable parts included. For a distributed load free to
load the adverse zones, the positive part of the surface must be integrated. The zero contour of a
bilinear function is a hyperbola; keta therefore splits each cell into two triangles, along each of
the two diagonals, and takes the mean. On a triangle, the interpolant is linear, its zero contour is
straight, and the split by sign involves no approximation. On a cell of constant sign, the mean gives
back the bilinear integral:

$$ \tfrac{1}{2}\left[\frac{2a + b + c + 2d}{6} + \frac{a + 2b + 2c + d}{6}\right] = \frac{a + b + c + d}{4} $$ (11.12)

($a, b, c, d$ the corner ordinates, per unit cell area). On the cells crossed by the zero
contour, the error is of order $h^2$.

### 11.5.3 Wheels and contact areas

A set of wheels is a set of loads $P_k$ placed at $(\Delta x_k, \Delta y_k)$ from a
reference point; its effect is

$$ E(x_r, y_r) = \sum_k P_k\,\eta(x_r + \Delta x_k,\ y_r + \Delta y_k) $$ (11.13)

a wheel off the grid not counting. keta sweeps the reference over a grid of $61 \times 61$
positions by default and retains the extremes; a loaded rectangle is swept in the same way, its
reference being its centre. The placement of the EN 1991-2 load models on a surface (lanes, tandems,
distributed loads, groups) is described in chapter 12.

### 11.5.4 Scattered nodes

A skew deck, a splayed slip road or an irregular grillage has no rectangular grid. keta then
triangulates the plan positions of the chosen nodes (Delaunay triangulation of the point set, with
the convex hull as boundary, no node added) and interpolates linearly within each triangle:

$$ \eta(x, y) = \lambda_1\,\eta_1 + \lambda_2\,\eta_2 + \lambda_3\,\eta_3 $$ (11.14)

with $\lambda_i$ the barycentric coordinates. The surface takes the computed ordinates at the
nodes and is zero outside the convex hull; its integrals by sign are computed without approximation,
each triangle being split along its zero contour. A point is located through a grid of bins, in
constant time on average.

## 11.6 Scope

Influence lines and surfaces are computed on the linear stiffness of the initial model: a staged
or non-linear state is not taken as the reference state. A model that contains links with a
non-linear law is refused; a unilateral support is treated there as bilateral; a Winkler foundation
is represented there by the consistent matrix (chapter 6). The reaction of a node is read on the bars
and the shells that meet at it: the reaction of a master node of a rigid link is refused, as is a
reaction in a model with continuum elements, and cables do not contribute to it. The elastic links
meeting at the node do contribute: the reaction of a fixed node connected to the deck by an elastic
link (a bearing modelled in this way) is the one the link transmits. The load swept is a force; a
unit moment is not. The section studied by a line must coincide with a station of the path. The
surface on a grid is not enriched between the nodes.

# Chapter 12 Road traffic loads

Road traffic loads are variable, moving loads: a vehicle can stand anywhere on the carriageway,
the lanes may or may not be loaded, and distributed loads apply only to the parts of the structure
where they are adverse. The problem set by this chapter is therefore a search problem: for each
effect studied (moment or shear force at a section, support reaction, displacement), find the
arrangement of loads allowed by the code that makes it maximum, then the one that makes it minimum.
Since the structure remains linear, the effect of any arrangement is obtained by superposition from
the influence line or surface of the effect, computed once and for all (chapter 11); the search then
bears on positions and no longer on structural analyses.

The chapter describes in turn the elementary operations on an influence line (distributed loads,
sliding vehicles), the load models of EN 1991-2 and of the *fascicule 61 titre II* as keta
defines them, the search for the most adverse arrangement across the width of the deck, transverse
distribution, and finally the placing of wheels on an influence surface. Railway loads are the
subject of chapter 13 and fatigue load models of chapter 14; the dynamic response of a structure to
a passing vehicle belongs to chapter 15.

## 12.1 Assumptions

- The structure is linear elastic, in small displacements: the effect of an arrangement of loads
is the sum of the effects of its loads, and the influence line does not depend on the loads applied.
Cables, which make the problem non-linear (chapter 7), are excluded from the calculation of
reactions by influence lines.

- The loads are static. The characteristic values of EN 1991-2 already include dynamic
amplification; for the *fascicule 61*, the dynamic amplification factor is computed separately
and applied by the user as a multiplying factor.

- Vertical loads have a fixed direction (gravity); they travel along a path formed by a continuous
sequence of deck bars, or over a grid of nodes for an influence surface. Braking forces act along
the axis of the bars of the path.

- A distributed load applies only where it is adverse; an axle, a wheel or track contact area
applies in full, even if part of its contact area is favourable.

- The loads in tonnes of the French code are converted into newtons by
1 t = 1000 g = 9806.65 N, unless otherwise requested.

- The transverse direction is handled, as chosen, by a distribution factor per lane (reading the
weighted longitudinal effect alone), by the eccentricity of the lanes on a grillage or space-frame
model (influence lines for bending and torsion), or by an influence surface.

## 12.2 Effect of an arrangement of loads on an influence line

Let $s$ denote the curvilinear abscissa along the running path and $\eta(s)$ the
ordinate of the influence line, that is, the value of the effect studied under a unit force placed at
$s$. A vehicle is defined by a reference point and, relative to it, point axles of load
$P_j$ at distance $a_j$, and uniform loads of resultant $P_k$ spread over a length
$\ell_k$ from $b_k$. When the reference is at $r$, the effect is

$$ E(r) = \sum_j P_j\,\eta(r + a_j) + \sum_k \frac{P_k}{\ell_k}\int_{r+b_k}^{r+b_k+\ell_k}\eta(s)\,ds $$ (12.1)

A load off the path does not count: $\eta$ is taken as zero beyond the ends. The integrals are
computed from cumulative sums of the line, so that any window costs a time proportional to the
logarithm of the number of points. A uniform load of intensity $q$ free to cover any part of the
path gives

$$ E^{+} = q\int_{\eta > 0}\eta\,ds,\qquad E^{-} = q\int_{\eta < 0}\eta\,ds $$ (12.2)

The zeros of the line are computed directly: by linear interpolation between two points of a
sampled line, as roots of the Hermite cubic when the line is known with its slopes. For a prismatic
bar, the influence line is indeed a third-degree polynomial on each bar segment (the deflected shape
of the dual problem), and keta uses it in that form whenever the layout allows; a bar of variable
section, a bar on an elastic foundation, a truss or a cable fall back on a line sampled at the chosen
spacing (0.5 m by default).

**Figure 12.1** — Placing of the distributed load and of the LM1 tandem on the influence line of the mid-span moment of a two-span 30 m beam

### 12.2.1 Sign zones and threshold

The traffic load engine splits the line into sign zones with a relative threshold $\sigma$
(1 % by default). With $\eta_{\max} = \max_s |\eta(s)|$, a point belongs to a positive or a
negative zone according to

$$ \eta(s) > \sigma\,\eta_{\max}\quad\text{(positive zone)},\qquad \eta(s) < -\sigma\,\eta_{\max}\quad\text{(negative zone)} $$ (12.3)

A zone is a maximal sequence of such points, bounded by the crossings of the threshold, computed
on each interval like the zeros. The threshold avoids loading, over a great length, negligible
ordinates that would increase the loaded length (and hence decrease the intensity of system A, see
below) without adding any effect. A dip below the threshold separates two zones of the same sign,
which may be loaded separately; a point of zero ordinate (a support, the jump of a shear force at
its section) belongs to no zone. With a zero threshold, the bounds of the zones are the zeros of the
line. At the section studied and at the junctions of bars, the path carries two points (the left
and right limits) so that the jump in the line of a shear force is not smoothed over one step.

### 12.2.2 Sliding vehicle

The vehicle is moved along the line from the position where its last element enters the path to
the one where its first element leaves it. For a piecewise affine line and point axles,
$E(r)$ is affine between the positions where an axle passes over a point of the line: its
extremes are reached at these positions. keta therefore takes as candidate positions the union of a
grid of spacing $\Delta$ (0.5 m by default) and of the breakpoints

$$ \mathcal{R} = \{\,r_0 + k\,\Delta\,\} \;\cup\; \{\,s_i - a_j\,\} \;\cup\; \{\,s_i - b_k,\; s_i - b_k - \ell_k\,\} $$ (12.4)

so that, for point axles, the extreme is among the candidates. On a cubic line, the effect of an
axle is cubic between two breakpoints and that of a distributed load of degree four; keta then adds
the stationary points of these polynomials, on those intervals alone where an upper bound of the
effect can still beat the best placing known. Both directions of travel are studied (vehicle
reversed within its overall length); one of them alone may also be retained. An option restricts
the search to the grid alone, without breakpoints: the extreme found is then smaller than or equal,
in absolute value, to that of the search with breakpoints.

**Note.**

The elementary vehicle functions on an influence line, used outside the traffic load engine,
sweep the line on a uniform grid (500 steps by default) in the direction of definition of the
vehicle only: the result is approximate to within one step, and the opposite direction is obtained by
reversing the vehicle.

### 12.2.3 Several lorries in a line

System Bc admits two lorries per line of traffic, military loads up to ten vehicles. Each lorry is
placed independently of the others, on the sole condition that their overall lengths do not
overlap: two successive references are at least $d$ apart, the overall length of the vehicle
(10.50 m for Bc). A lorry that would reduce the effect is never added. This selection problem is solved without approximation by dynamic programming over the sorted
candidate positions $r_1 < r_2 < \dots$, of effects $v_i = E(r_i)$:

$$ F_k(i) = \max\Big(F_k(i-1),\; v_i + F_{k-1}\big(p(i)\big)\Big),\qquad p(i) = \max\{\,j : r_j \le r_i - d\,\} $$ (12.5)

$F_k(i)$ is the best effect of at most $k$ lorries placed among the first $i$
positions; the placing retained is read by tracing back the choices. The optimum “at most $n$
lorries” excludes the useless lorries by itself. On a cubic line, the stationary points of a line of
lorries in contact (at exactly the distance $d$) are added to the candidates.

### 12.2.4 Different vehicles and removal of the distributed load

To place several different vehicles simultaneously on the same line, together with a distributed
load $q$, each vehicle $v$ occupies around its reference $r_v$ an occupancy interval,
which must not overlap that of another, and a removal interval (contained in the former) where the
distributed load is suppressed. The total effect

$$ J = q\,A_\text{sign} + \sum_v\Big[E_v(r_v) - q\,A_\text{sign}\big(\text{removal of } v \text{ at } r_v\big)\Big] $$ (12.6)

where $A_\text{sign}$ is the area of the parts of the line of the same sign, is separable by
vehicle. keta seeks its optimum on a grid of positions (200 steps by default) by dynamic programming
over the pair (set of vehicles already placed, occupied right-hand end), for at most twelve vehicles,
in a time proportional to $P\,k\,2^k$ for $k$ vehicles and $P$ positions. Every
vehicle must be placed: a deck too short to receive them all raises an error.

## 12.3 Intensity depending on the loaded length

The intensity of system A of the *fascicule 61* decreases with the loaded length. Loading all
the adverse zones is then no longer necessarily the most adverse case: a zone of small area but
great length lowers the intensity applied to all the others. For a set $S$ of zones of the
same sign, of lengths $\ell_z$ and areas $A_z$, the effect is

$$ E(S) = v\big(L(S)\big)\,A(S),\qquad L(S) = \sum_{z\in S}\ell_z,\qquad A(S) = \sum_{z\in S}A_z $$ (12.7)

keta enumerates the subsets and retains the most adverse. The traffic load engine enumerates up to
$2^{12}$ subsets; beyond twelve adverse zones, it loads the zones in decreasing order of effect
per metre and retains the best of the prefixes, which is then no more than a heuristic. The general
intensity-law function runs through the subsets in Gray-code order (one zone enters or leaves at
each step, $L$ and $A$ are updated in constant time) up to 24 zones, and refuses beyond.

Example: three-span continuous beam of 30 m spans, moment at mid-span of the first. The adverse
zones are the first span (area 82.5 m², that is $0.0917\,L^2$) and the third (7.5 m², that is
$L^2/120$). With $A(l) = 0.23 + 36/(l+12)$, loading the first span alone gives
$A(30) \times 82.5 = 89.7$ t·m per metre of width; loading both,
$A(60) \times 90 = 65.7$ t·m/m. The first arrangement is more adverse by 37 %.

The intensity laws available outside the codes are: constant, tabulated (linear interpolation,
extended by plateaus), $a\sqrt{L}$, $b\,L^{-p}$, $b + c\ln L$ or a user function; the
length may be bounded (or imposed) before the law is applied, and the total load $v(L)\,L$
capped.

## 12.4 Division of the carriageway into lanes

### 12.4.1 Notional lanes of EN 1991-2

The carriageway of width $w$ is divided according to EN 1991-2 §4.2.3:

| Width w | Number of lanes | Width of a lane | Remaining area |
|---|---|---|---|
| w < 5.4 m | 1 | 3 m | w − 3 m |
| 5.4 ≤ w < 6 m | 2 | w/2 | 0 |
| 6 m ≤ w | Int(w/3) | 3 m | w − 3 × Int(w/3) |

A 10.5 m carriageway thus has three lanes and a remaining area of 1.5 m. In the traffic load
engine, the deck is described by juxtaposed transverse zones, from left to right, centred on the
axis of the bars; each zone is divided by this rule (or receives an imposed number of lanes), the
lanes are laid from its left edge and the remaining area occupies the rest on the right. The
numbering of the lanes is not geometric: lane number 1 is the most adverse for the effect studied
(see below).

### 12.4.2 Lanes of the fascicule 61 titre II

The *fascicule 61* counts the lanes of a loadable width $w$ according to

$$ n = \begin{cases} 1 & w < 5\ \text{m} \\ 2 & 5 \le w \le 6\ \text{m} \\ \mathrm{Int}(w/3) & w > 6\ \text{m}\end{cases}\qquad v = \frac{w}{n} $$ (12.8)

The lanes share the zone: $v$ is their actual width. The class of the bridge (1, 2 or 3) is
an input; keta does not deduce it from the trafficked width. It fixes the reference lane width
$v_0$ = 3.50 m, 3.00 m or 2.75 m, and the reduction factors of systems A and B.

## 12.5 Load models of EN 1991-2

**Figure 12.2** — LM1 tandem, Bt tandem and Bc lorry: geometry adopted by keta

### 12.5.1 Load Model 1

Each lane of rank $i$ carries a tandem of two axles of load $\alpha_{Qi}Q_{ik}$ spaced
1.20 m apart, and a uniform load $\alpha_{qi}q_{ik}$ over its width $w_i$; the remaining
area carries $\alpha_{qr}q_{rk}$ (EN 1991-2 §4.3.2, table 4.2):

| Location | Qik (per axle) | qik |
|---|---|---|
| lane 1 | 300 kN | 9 kN/m² |
| lane 2 | 200 kN | 2.5 kN/m² |
| lane 3 | 100 kN | 2.5 kN/m² |
| other lanes | 0 | 2.5 kN/m² |
| remaining area | 0 | 2.5 kN/m² |

On an influence line, the effect of a lane is

$$ E_i = \alpha_{Qi}Q_{ik}\,\big[\eta(r) + \eta(r + 1.2)\big] + \alpha_{qi}\,q_{ik}\,w_i \int_{Z}\eta\,ds $$ (12.9)

the tandem being placed at its most adverse position and the uniform load on the zones $Z$ of
the same sign. The traffic load engine accumulates the lanes with their transverse distribution
factors $k_i$: a single tandem of axle load $\sum_i \alpha_{Qi}Q_{ik}k_i$ and a load per
unit length $\sum_i \alpha_{qi}q_{ik}w_ik_i$ (remaining area included, with its own factor).
Since the lines of the lanes are proportional, the most adverse position is the same for all the
tandems and this accumulation loses nothing. A lane whose factor has the opposite sign to the effect
sought is not loaded with a tandem; its uniform load is placed on the zones of opposite sign of the
line, where it is adverse. Frequent values are obtained with $\psi_1$ = 0.75 for the tandem and
0.40 for the uniform load.

The adjustment factors depend on the traffic class. The elementary functions offer the values
recommended by EN 1991-2 (all the $\alpha$ equal to 1) and the 2nd class of the French National
Annex; the traffic load engine has six classes, the 2nd being adopted when none is given:

| Class | αQ1 | αQi (i ≥ 2) | αq1 | αqi (i ≥ 2) | αqr | βQ (LM2) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1.2 | 1.2 | 0.8 |
| 2 | 0.9 | 0.8 | 0.7 | 1 | 1 | 0.8 |
| 3 | 0.8 | 0.5 | 0.5 | 1 | 1 | 0.8 |
| 4 | 0.32 | 0.48 | 0.58 | 2.09 | 2.09 | 0.56 |
| 5 | 0.20 | 0.30 | 0.36 | 1.30 | 1.30 | 0.36 |
| 6 | 0.06 | 0.09 | 0.21 | 0.76 | 0.76 | 0.15 |

Classes 1 and 2 are those of the French National Annex; classes 3 to 6 do not come from it, and
classes 4 to 6 express weight restrictions.

Across the width, the traffic load engine leaves the lanes at their geometric location and ranks
them by decreasing distribution factor: lane number 1 is the most effective for the effect studied
(EN 1991-2 §4.2.4). The factor of a lane is read at its axis (tandem centred) or, as an option, taken
at its most adverse value over the width of the lane (tandem free within its lane). The placing of
the lanes themselves across the width, at a step of a few centimetres, is done only on an influence
surface (last section).

### 12.5.2 Load Model 2

LM2 is a single axle of $\beta_Q \times 400$ kN (EN 1991-2 §4.3.3), that is 320 kN with
$\beta_Q$ = 0.8. On a line, it is placed freely along the deck and, in the traffic load engine,
at the most adverse point of the transverse distribution over the whole width $B$ of the
deck:

$$ E = \psi\,\beta_Q\,Q_{ak}\;\underset{|y|\le B/2}{\mathrm{ext}}\,k(y)\;\underset{r}{\mathrm{ext}}\,\eta(r),\qquad Q_{ak} = 400\ \text{kN} $$ (12.10)

with $\psi$ = 1 (characteristic value) or 0.75 (frequent value). On a surface, it is
represented by two point wheels of $\beta_Q \times 200$ kN 2.00 m apart; the 0.35 × 0.60 m
contact areas are not modelled.

### 12.5.3 Load Model 3: special vehicles

The special vehicles of annex A of EN 1991-2 are lines of axles of 150, 200 or 240 kN spaced
1.50 m apart, from 600/150 to 3600/240/240; the vehicles with two trailers have 12 m between their
two groups, and those whose total load is not a multiple of the axle load end with a make-up line
(100 kN for the 1500/200, 120 kN for the 3000/240). The arrangement of the wheels within a line of
axles is given by the user, as a list of transverse positions and fractions of the load: keta does
not contain it.

On an influence surface, group gr5 combines the special vehicle with LM1 taken at its frequent
values ($\psi_1$ = 0.75 and 0.40, EN 1990 annex A2), excluded from a box surrounding the
vehicle: the transverse strip of the vehicle and, longitudinally, a clearance distance beyond its
outer axles, set by the National Annex. The search is by branch and bound: the positions of the
vehicle are examined in decreasing order of their own effect, each completed by the optimal LM1
outside its box, and the search stops when the effect of the vehicle plus that of LM1 without
exclusion can no longer beat the best total.

On a line, the traffic load engine places a single special vehicle and the accompanying LM1
(absent, frequent, characteristic, or at adjustable accompanying values, 0.5 for the tandem and 0.3
for the uniform load by default). The vehicle occupies two lanes if its width exceeds
3 m, one otherwise; in those lanes, LM1 is removed over the window
$[r - L_\text{ex},\ r + L_v + L_\text{ex}]$, where $L_v$ is the length of the vehicle and
$L_\text{ex}$ the exclusion length (10 m by default). For each position $r$ of the
vehicle,

$$ E(r) = E_\text{SV}(r) + \sum_{z}\Big[\,\int_{z\setminus W} q\,\eta\,ds + \int_{z\cap W} q_W\,\eta\,ds\Big] + E_\text{TS} $$ (12.11)

where $W$ is the exclusion window, $q$ the intensity of all the lanes, $q_W$ that of
the lanes not occupied by the vehicle alone; a zone is retained only if its contribution is adverse.
The tandems of the lanes of the vehicle are placed outside the window, those of the other lanes
anywhere, each at its most adverse position. The arrangement without vehicle (LM1 alone) is also
among the candidates, for the case where the vehicle and its window are longer than the structure.
The vehicle is defined there by its total load and its axle load, with
$n = \mathrm{round}(\text{total}/\text{axle})$ lines of axles 1.50 m apart, a width of 3 m and
two lines of wheels at ± 1.00 m.

**Important.**

On an influence line, the make-up line of annex A is not reproduced: a 1500/200 counts there
eight lines of 200 kN (1600 kN) and a 3000/240 thirteen lines of 240 kN (3120 kN). Vehicles with two
trailers are not available there; they are on an influence surface.

### 12.5.4 Crowd and footways

LM4 is a crowd load of 5 kN/m², placed on the adverse zones of the carriageway and the footways.
The traffic load engine also offers the footbridge intensity of EN 1991-2 §5.3.2.1,

$$ q_{fk} = 2 + \frac{120}{L + 30}\ \text{kN/m}^2,\qquad 2.5 \le q_{fk} \le 5.0\ \text{kN/m}^2 $$ (12.12)

whose length $L$ is the loaded length, coupled with the choice of zones as for system A.
Footways receive 5 kN/m² alone or 3 kN/m² together with LM1 (combination value of group gr1a,
EN 1991-2 table 4.4a). On an influence surface, group gr1a combines the characteristic LM1 and the
footways at 3 kN/m² on their adverse parts; group gr4 applies the 5 kN/m² crowd load to the adverse
parts of the carriageway and the footways. The service vehicle of footbridges (§5.6.3) is not
provided.

## 12.6 Fascicule 61 titre II

### 12.6.1 System A

System A is a uniform load of intensity

$$ A(l) = 0.23 + \frac{36}{l + 12}\ \text{t/m}^2 $$ (12.13)

where $l$ is the loaded length in metres, multiplied by the reduction factor $a_1$
(a function of the class and of the number of loaded lanes) and by $a_2 = v_0/v$. A lane of
actual width $v$ therefore carries the load per unit length

$$ q = a_1\,a_2\,A(l)\,v = a_1\,v_0\,A(l) $$ (12.14)

independent of the actual width. keta adopts for $a_1$:

| Class | 1 lane | 2 lanes | 3 lanes | 4 lanes | 5 lanes or more | v0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | 1 | 1 | 0.9 | 0.75 | 0.70 | 3.50 m |
| 2nd | 1 | 0.9 | — | — | — | 3.00 m |
| 3rd | 0.9 | 0.8 | — | — | — | 2.75 m |

A dash marks a combination that the *fascicule* does not admit; it is skipped by the search
over the number of loaded lanes. The coupling of the intensity with the loaded length is solved by
(12.7). The floor $(0.4 - 0.0002\,l)$ t/m² governs, with $a_1$ = 1, only
between 344 and 495 m of loaded length, and by very little; with $a_1$ = 0.75, it governs from
121 m. In the traffic load engine, it is a separate load, weighted by $a_2$ only: the code value
$\max(a_1A(l),\ 0.4 - 0.0002\,l)$ is obtained by studying both loads. The elementary function
for the intensity per lane takes this maximum itself, but always with the factor $a_1$ of a
single loaded lane.

**Figure 12.3** — Intensity A(l) of system A and its floor (t/m²)

Footways carry 0.150 t/m², and the footbridge load has the intensity
$0.2 + 15/(50 + l)$ t/m².

### 12.6.2 System B

System Bc consists of 30 t lorries (6 t front axle, two 12 t rear axles) with 4.50 m between the
front axle and the first rear axle and 1.50 m between the rear axles; at most two lorries per line of
traffic, at least 4.50 m apart (overall length of 10.50 m per lorry), wheels 2.00 m apart, overall
width of 2.50 m. The wheel contact areas are 0.20 × 0.20 m at the front and 0.25 × 0.25 m at the
rear. System Bt is a tandem of two 16 t axles spaced 1.35 m apart, with contact areas of 0.25 m
longitudinally by 0.60 m transversely, at most two tandems across the width. The loads are
multiplied by a factor that depends on the class and on the number of lines of traffic:

| Factor | Class | 1 line | 2 lines | 3 lines | 4 lines | 5 lines or more |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| bc | 1st | 1.20 | 1.10 | 0.95 | 0.80 | 0.70 |
| bc | 2nd | 1.00 | 1.00 | — | — | — |
| bc | 3rd | 1.00 | 0.80 | — | — | — |
| bt | 1st | 1.00 | 1.00 | — |  |  |
| bt | 2nd | 0.90 | 0.90 | — |  |  |

System Bt is not defined for 3rd-class bridges: keta refuses the calculation. The 10 t single
wheel Br is not provided. Outside the traffic load engine, the elementary functions give a line of
two Bc lorries and a Bt tandem as point axles, without factor.

The dynamic amplification factor of the *fascicule 61 titre II*, article 5.5,

$$ \delta = 1 + \frac{0.4}{1 + 0.2\,L} + \frac{0.6}{1 + 4\,G/S} $$ (12.15)

($L$ the length of the element in metres, $G$ its self-weight, $S$ the maximum
B load that can be placed on it) is provided separately; it is not applied automatically to the
vehicles. The cap on $\delta$ specific to 3rd-class bridges is not programmed. For
$L$ = 20 m, $G$ = 1000 kN and $S$ = 600 kN, $\delta = 1.158$.

### 12.6.3 Braking

The braking of system A is a horizontal force distributed along the axis of the bars of the path,
of intensity $A(l)/(20 + 0.0035\,S)$, where $S$ is the loaded area in m², weighted like
$A(l)$ by $a_1$ and $v_0$. Its resultant is

$$ F = \frac{a_1\,A(l)\,S}{20 + 0.0035\,S} $$ (12.16)

The loaded area $S$ is the loaded length multiplied by the width of the lanes retained: it is
coupled with the choice of zones like the intensity of system A. The floor has its own braking, of
the same form, without the factor $a_1$. The braking of system Bc is a single 30 t lorry applied
as forces along the axis of the bars, without the factor $b_c$. Any vehicle defined by the user
may also be applied along this axis, with a signed multiplying factor. The braking force of LM1 of
EN 1991-2 §4.4.1, $Q_{lk} = 0.6\,\alpha_{Q1}(2Q_{1k}) + 0.10\,\alpha_{q1}q_{1k}w_1L$ with its
bounds, is not computed by keta.

### 12.6.4 Dispersal of wheel loads

The wheel loads may be dispersed: a contact area of length $a$ carrying the load $P$
becomes a uniform load

$$ q = \frac{P}{a + 2\,\ell_\text{dif}}\quad\text{over the length}\quad a + 2\,\ell_\text{dif} $$ (12.17)

where $\ell_\text{dif}$ is the dispersal length given for the deck; across the width, the
distribution factor is averaged over the dispersed contact area. Dispersal never applies to
distributed loads. Without dispersal and without contact area, an axle is a point force.

### 12.6.5 Military loads and exceptional convoys

Military loads and exceptional convoys are vehicles of the catalogue, travelling alone, without
reduction factor:

| Vehicle | Load | Geometry adopted |
|---|---|---|
| Mc80 | 72 t | two 4.90 × 0.85 m tracks 2.80 m apart centre to centre; up to 10 tanks per line, 30.50 m clear between two tanks |
| Mc120 | 110 t | two 6.10 × 1.00 m tracks 3.30 m apart centre to centre; up to 10 tanks, pitch of 36.60 m |
| Me80 | 2 × 22 t | two axles 1.50 m apart, contact area 0.12 × 3.50 m |
| Me120 | 2 × 33 t | two axles 1.80 m apart, contact area 0.15 × 4.00 m |
| convoy D | 280 t | two 140 t blocks over 11 m, 8 m between them, width 3.30 m |
| convoy E | 400 t | two 200 t blocks over 15 m, 18 m between them, width 3.30 m |
| C1, C2 | 94 t, 120 t | tractor (three axles) and trailer spread over 7.75 m |
| D2F1, D3F1 | 245 t, 250 t | uniform block of 21.70 m (width 3.20 m) or 17.05 m (5.15 m) |
| D3F2 | 250 t | two 125 t blocks over 9.30 m, 14.70 m between them, width 5.15 m |
| E2F1, E3F1 | 350 t, 400 t | uniform block of 31.00 m (3.20 m) or 26.35 m (5.15 m) |
| E3F2 | 376 t | two 188 t blocks over 12.40 m, 11.60 m between them, width 5.15 m |

Convoys D and E are those of the *fascicule 61*; convoys C1 to E3F2 are the standard
exceptional transport convoys (circular R/EG.3 of 1983). The latter travel on the axis of their
zone, to within ± 0.30 m, instead of being set against an edge. The tracks and the blocks are
uniform loads over their length. On an influence line alone, without a description of the deck,
Mc120 is a uniform block of 110 t over 6.10 m.

The catalogue also contains the vehicles of the Cerema guide *Transports exceptionnels*
(2022): vehicles with 12 t axles at a pitch of 1.35 m of 72, 94 and 120 t for new structures,
semi-trailers of 72, 94 and 120 t for existing structures, mobile cranes of 48, 72, 94 and 108 t
(contact areas of 0.40 × 0.40 m), as well as the 3rd- and 4th-class lorries of the 1946
regulations.

## 12.7 Arrangement across the width of the deck

### 12.7.1 Transverse factor

The traffic load engine studies each line of traffic or lane independently and accumulates their
effects with the reduction prescribed by the code. With a transverse distribution described by
factors $k(y)$ (next section), the loadable lanes are sorted by decreasing factor
($k_{(1)} \ge k_{(2)} \ge \dots$), and the transverse factor of a vehicle is

$$ T = \max_{1 \le n \le n_{\max}}\ b(n)\sum_{i=1}^{n}k_{(i)} $$ (12.18)

where $b(n)$ is $b_c(n)$, $b_t(n)$, a factor given by the user or 1, and
$n_{\max}$ is the number of lanes limited by the number of lines admitted for the vehicle. Since
the factors reduce with the number of lines, loading every lane does not always give the maximum:
the number of lanes is swept from 1 to $n_{\max}$. The lines of lorries have the overall width of
the vehicle and are set side by side from one edge of their zone; keta tries both edges and retains
the more adverse. For system A, the factor is $\max_n a_1(n)\,v_0\sum_{i\le n}k_{(i)}$, from
(12.14); for footways and crowd loading, it is the integral of $k$ over the
loaded width. Since the factors may change sign across the width, the maximum of an effect may be
reached with the minimum factor: both sorting directions are tried and the more adverse is
retained.

Without a transverse description of the deck, a single line is placed longitudinally, without
weighting, and distributed loads are applied over a width of one metre.

### 12.7.2 Eccentricity of the lanes on a grillage or space-frame model

When the deck is a single beam of a space-frame model, the eccentricity of the lanes produces
torsion. keta then computes two influence lines along the path: that of a unit force,
$\eta_F$, and that of a unit torque about the axis of the path, $\eta_T$. A lane, a line of
traffic or a zone of axis $y$ (positive to the left of the direction of travel) has the
line

$$ \eta_y(s) = \eta_F(s) + y\,\eta_T(s) $$ (12.19)

Each element is placed independently on its own line, then the elements are accumulated, the most
adverse first, with the code factor for the number of loaded elements ($a_1$, $b_c$,
$b_t$ or the user's); the footway zones accumulate without factor. When the load case is
reconstructed (below), the eccentricity of a point load gives a point couple; that of a distributed
load is lumped into ten couples per segment. A load direction with a moment component is not
admitted, and the study of “$n$ lorries abreast” merged into a single vehicle for torsion is not
carried out: the accumulation is over lines studied separately.

The loaded transverse zones are chosen by the user, or all of them by default; the number of lanes
of each zone follows the division rule or an imposed value. The number of loaded lanes is then swept
as above. A non-loadable central reserve must be described as an unloaded zone; a dual carriageway
is not treated as such (two independent lane numberings). The exhaustive search over the positions
and the ranks of the lanes exists only for LM1 on an influence surface.

## 12.8 Transverse distribution

### 12.8.1 Courbon's method

For a deck with girders under the carriageway connected by infinitely rigid cross-girders, the
girders having no torsional stiffness and the same span, Courbon's method distributes a unit load
placed at the transverse abscissa $y$ like the rigid-body motion (translation and rotation) of
the deck on elastic supports of relative stiffnesses $w_i$ (bending stiffnesses of the
girders):

$$ K_i(y) = w_i\left[\frac{1}{W} + \frac{(y - y_c)(y_i - y_c)}{J}\right],\qquad W = \sum_j w_j,\quad y_c = \frac{\sum_j w_jy_j}{W},\quad J = \sum_j w_j\,(y_j - y_c)^2 $$ (12.20)

For equal girders, this reduces to the usual form $K_i = 1/n + e\,x_i/\sum_j x_j^2$,
$e$ and $x_i$ being measured from the axis. For four equal girders at
$y_i$ = −3, −1, 1 and 3 m and a load at $y$ = 2 m, one obtains
$K$ = −0.05, 0.15, 0.35 and 0.55. Since $K_i$ is linear in $y$, its mean over a lane
is its value at the centre of the lane.

**Figure 12.4** — Courbon factor of the edge girder of a deck with four girders spaced 3 m apart

### 12.8.2 Tabulated factors

The distribution may also be given by a table of factors, attached to the loaded bars of the
deck: a factor constant over the whole width, two factors at the two edges interpolated linearly, or
$n$ factors at regular intervals, interpolated piecewise linearly. The bars not listed have a
factor of 1. The factor of a load of contact width $2h$ centred at $y$ is the mean

$$ \bar k(y) = \frac{1}{2h}\int_{y-h}^{y+h}k(t)\,dt $$ (12.21)

computed in closed form on the polyline. $\bar k$ is piecewise quadratic in $y$: its
extreme over an interval (a lane, a traffic strip) is reached at a bound, at a node of the table
shifted by $\pm h$, or at the vertex of a piece, and keta obtains it by examining these points.
When all the deck bars carry the same profile, it applies to any response studied (arch, hangers,
reactions); otherwise the profile of the bar studied is applied over the whole path, which is an
approximation.

Outside the traffic load engine, an influence line and a table of factors form a separable
surface $\eta(x, y) = \eta(x)\,K(y)$, built without approximation on the grid formed by the
points of the line and the abscissae of the table; all the placings on a surface (wheels, contact
areas, distributed-load zones) apply to it.

## 12.9 Wheels on an influence surface

On an influence surface sampled on a grid that is rectangular in plan, the ordinate is bilinear
within each cell (chapter 11). A vehicle is a set of wheels $(\Delta x_i, \Delta y_i, P_i)$
around its reference point; its effect at $(x, y)$ is

$$ f(x, y) = \sum_i P_i\,\eta(x + \Delta x_i,\ y + \Delta y_i) $$ (12.22)

Between the positions where a wheel crosses a grid line, each wheel stays within one cell and
$f$ is bilinear: its extreme is reached at a corner. keta evaluates all the corners of the
rectangles formed by the abscissae $x_g - \Delta x_i$, the ordinates $y_g - \Delta y_i$ and
the bounds of the traffic strip: the extreme is one of these corners. The vehicle may be
constrained to a transverse strip (all its wheels within $[y_0, y_1]$), in both directions of
travel or one only; a fixed transverse position is obtained with a strip of the width of the vehicle.
A wheel off the grid does not count. The mode “overhanging, inner wheels within the lane” does not
exist.

LM1 on an influence surface follows the rules of EN 1991-2 §4.2.4 and §4.3.2: $n$ notional
lanes (division of EN 1991-2 §4.2.3, or given number and width) laid anywhere on the carriageway
without overlapping; the lane of rank $r \le 3$ carries a tandem of two axles 1.20 m apart,
each of two point wheels 2.00 m apart, centred in the lane; the uniform load of the lane and that of
the remaining area load only the adverse parts, longitudinally as well as transversely. A tandem that
is favourable everywhere in its lane is omitted. The positions of the lanes are searched at a step
of 5 cm and at each position where a wheel or a lane edge meets a grid line; the best
non-overlapping lanes and their ranks are found by enumeration. The integral of the adverse parts
splits each cell along its two diagonals into triangles where the interpolation is linear and the
zero contour straight, and takes the mean of the two splits:

$$ \frac12\left[\frac{2a + b + c + 2d}{6} + \frac{a + 2b + 2c + d}{6}\right] = \frac{a + b + c + d}{4} $$ (12.23)

(reduced integral of a cell of constant sign, $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ being its four
ordinates). The result is that of the bilinear surface on the cells of constant sign; on a cell
crossed by the zero, the departure from the bilinear surface is $O(h^2)$. The 2.40 m wheel
spacing for local effects and the 0.40 × 0.40 m contact areas are not modelled. A rectangular
contact area (track, wide wheel) is slid over the grid and integrated in full, favourable parts
included, by the integral of the bilinear surface over the rectangle. Influence surfaces may also be
built on an arbitrary set of scattered nodes (skew or splayed deck): the set is triangulated, the
interpolation is linear on each triangle and zero outside the convex hull.

With a 9 m carriageway and a surface constant across the width and equal to the line of a 30 m
simply supported span (mid-span moment), LM1 gives
$(300 + 200 + 100) \times (7.5 + 6.9) + (27 + 7.5 + 7.5) \times 112.5 = 13\,365$ kN·m: three
tandems at mid-span and the three uniform loads over the whole span.

## 12.10 Concurrent effects

For a component studied (called the leading component), the traffic load engine seeks its two
extremes, then rebuilds, for each, the actual load case: point forces and distributed loads on the
deck bars, eccentricity couples included, and solves it statically:

$$ \mathcal{P}^\star = \arg\max_{\mathcal{P}}\,E(\mathcal{P}),\qquad \mathbf{K}\,\mathbf{u}^\star = \mathbf{F}(\mathcal{P}^\star) $$ (12.24)

where $\mathcal{P}$ denotes an admissible arrangement of the loads and
$\mathbf{F}(\mathcal{P})$ its equivalent nodal forces. The concurrent state (internal forces,
displacements, reactions and stresses at all sections) is therefore that of an actual arrangement of
loads, never a mixture of extremes. Without a leading component, each component of each section has
its own influence line and its two independent extremes. A fibre normal stress, a linear combination
$\sigma = \sum_j c_j S_j$ of the internal forces $S_j$ of the section, has the influence
line $\eta_\sigma = \sum_j c_j\,\eta_j$ and its own extremes, which are not those that the
bounded internal forces would give. On an influence surface, the concurrent value of another
response is computed with the same arrangement: same vehicle, same lanes, same tandems, distributed
loads on the zones where the leading response is adverse.

**Note.**

The displacement envelope covers the displacements of the nodes or of the study sections;
the traffic results are superposed on the other cases through the combinations (chapter 5), each
extreme being a load case in its own right.

# Chapter 13 Railway loads and track-bridge interaction

A railway bridge is loaded by trains whose vertical loads are heavy and concentrated, whose speed
can excite the structure into resonance, and whose horizontal forces (braking, traction) pass from
the rail to the deck through the ballast. The continuous welded rail, for its part, is restrained by
the ballast along its whole length: it interacts with the deck, which expands and deflects beneath
it. This chapter describes what keta computes for these three questions: the load models of
EN 1991-2 section 6 and their factors, the dynamic response of a deck to the passage of a train at a
given speed, and the track-bridge interaction analysis of UIC leaflet 774-3. The search for the most
adverse placing on an influence line or surface is that of chapter 12; the time integration of the
equations of motion is set out in chapter 15, and the service trains for fatigue in chapter 14.

## 13.1 Assumptions
