isotropic hardenings on a single effective plastic strain, is integrated by implicit Euler over each
step.

### 18.6.3 Cyclic concrete

Cyclic concrete follows the parabola-rectangle envelope, without tension and zero beyond
$\varepsilon_{cu2}$. Unloaded from a point $\varepsilon_m$ on the envelope, it returns
linearly to a residual strain $\varepsilon_p$ on the axis, and reloads along the same straight
line. The residual strain is the regression of Karsan and Jirsa (*Behavior of concrete under
compressive loadings*, 1969), in units of $\varepsilon_{c2}$, with
$\eta = |\varepsilon_m|/\varepsilon_{c2}$:

$$ \frac{\varepsilon_p}{\varepsilon_{c2}} = 0.145\,\eta^2 + 0.127\,\eta\quad (\eta \le 2),\qquad
\frac{\varepsilon_p}{\varepsilon_{c2}} = 0.707\,(\eta - 2) + 0.834\quad (\eta > 2) $$ (18.18)

The linear extension is of class $C^1$ at $\eta = 2$ and keeps $\varepsilon_p <
|\varepsilon_m|$. There is no stiffness degradation in the inner loops.

### 18.6.4 Damage

Two damage laws are formulated in nominal stress. That of Simo and Ju gives

$$ \sigma = (1 - d)\,E\,\varepsilon,\qquad d = 1 - \frac{r_0\,(1 - A)}{r} - A\,e^{B(r_0 - r)},\qquad
r = \max_\text{history}\sqrt{\sigma^2/E} \ \ge r_0 $$ (18.19)

That of Oliver combines a damage $d = 1 - (r_0/r)\,e^{A(1 - r/r_0)}$, with a different threshold
in tension and in compression (factor $1/n$), with isotropic plasticity of the nominal stress.
Their strain, a strictly increasing function of the stress, is inverted by a safeguarded Newton method,
down to rounding.

### 18.6.5 Creep and shrinkage of the fibres

A law may carry a Kelvin chain (at most six units $(a_i, \tau_i)$) and a table of shrinkage as
a function of age. The creep strain enters the law as an imposed strain, and each unit,
$\dot e_i = (a_i\,s(\sigma) - e_i)/\tau_i$, is integrated exactly over a step of duration
$\Delta t$ for a driving stress $s$ linear within the step (exponential algorithm):

$$ e_i^{n+1} = e_i^n\,E_i + a_i s_n\,(1 - E_i) + a_i\,(s_{n+1} - s_n)\Bigl(1 - \frac{1 - E_i}{x_i}\Bigr),
\qquad E_i = e^{-x_i},\quad x_i = \Delta t/\tau_i $$ (18.20)

The nonlinear creep of EN 1992-1-1 §3.1.4(4) multiplies the driving stress by
$\exp(1.5\,(|\sigma|/f_{ck} - 0.45))$ beyond $0.45\,f_{ck}$. This subject is developed in
chapter 9.

## 18.7 Force-based bar element

A displacement-based element interpolates the transverse displacement by cubics: its curvature is
linear and cannot follow the localisation of curvature in a plastic zone without a fine mesh. A
force-based element, on the contrary, interpolates the internal forces. For a prismatic bar without
span load, the internal forces are known exactly by equilibrium from the end forces: one element per
bar carries the exact moment diagram, at any level of yielding, and only the integration of the
deformations along the bar requires accuracy (Spacone, Ciampi and Filippou, 1996; Neuenhofer and
Filippou, 1997).

### 18.7.1 Basic system

The element is described in its basic system, the simply supported beam, with six modes:

$$ \mathbf{v} = (\Delta L,\ \vartheta_{y,i},\ \vartheta_{y,j},\ \vartheta_{z,i},\ \vartheta_{z,j},\ \phi),\qquad
\mathbf{q} = (N,\ M_{y,i},\ M_{y,j},\ M_{z,i},\ M_{z,j},\ T) $$ (18.21)

where the basic rotations are the nodal rotations minus the rotation of the chord
($\vartheta_y = \theta_y + (w_j - w_i)/L$, $\vartheta_z = \theta_z - (v_j - v_i)/L$) and
$\phi = \theta_{x,j} - \theta_{x,i}$. The forces in the section at abscissa $x$ are

$$ N(x) = q_0,\qquad M_y(x) = \Bigl(1 - \frac{x}{L}\Bigr)q_1 - \frac{x}{L}\,q_2,\qquad
M_z(x) = \Bigl(1 - \frac{x}{L}\Bigr)q_3 - \frac{x}{L}\,q_4 $$ (18.22)

written $\mathbf{s}(x) = \mathbf{b}(x)\,\mathbf{q}$. Torsion is elastic and uncoupled:
$T = (GJ/L)\,\phi$. For elastic fibres, the element reproduces keta's Euler-Bernoulli beam
matrix.

**Figure 18.5** — Force-based element: basic system, exact moment diagram and Gauss-Lobatto points

### 18.7.2 Element state determination

The global analysis gives the basic deformations $\mathbf{v}$; the forces $\mathbf{q}$
must be deduced from them. keta iterates on $\mathbf{q}$:

$$ \mathbf{d}_k = \mathbf{s}^{-1}\bigl(\mathbf{b}(x_k)\,\mathbf{q}\bigr),\qquad
\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{v} - \sum_k w_k\,\mathbf{b}_k^\mathsf{T}\,\mathbf{d}_k,\qquad
\mathbf{f}_b = \sum_k w_k\,\mathbf{b}_k^\mathsf{T}\,\mathbf{f}_{s,k}\,\mathbf{b}_k,\qquad
\mathbf{q} \leftarrow \mathbf{q} + \mathbf{f}_b^{-1}\,\mathbf{r} $$ (18.23)

where $x_k$ and $w_k$ are the Gauss-Lobatto points and weights (from 3 to 6 points, 5 by
default) and $\mathbf{s}^{-1}$ the state determination of the section under imposed
$(N, M_y, M_z)$, from the committed states of its fibres. The Lobatto rule places a point at each
end, where the hinges of a frame form; with $n$ points it integrates polynomials of degree
$2n - 3$ exactly. Since the section is solved to convergence at each iteration, the section
residuals of the original algorithm disappear and only the compatibility residual of the element
remains. The section flexibility $\mathbf{f}_s$ is the inverse of the regularised tangent
$\mathbf{k}_s + 10^{-6}\,\mathbf{k}_{s,0}$: this regularisation affects only the tangent, never the
forces, which always come from the laws. The stiffness of the element is $\mathbf{f}_b^{-1}$,
transferred to the nodes by the compatibility matrix of the basic system.

The two iterations, of the element and of the section, converge on a relative residual
($10^{-11}$ for the element in energy norm, $10^{-12}$ for the section). A heavily yielded
section has an almost flat response: the last decimals of the force-deformation inversion stagnate at
a precision floor. When the residual stops decreasing (six passes without progress for the element,
ten for the section), the best state is accepted if it is already a thousand times below the tolerance
of the element, or within $10^{-5}$ for the section; otherwise, the step is declared without
equilibrium. Global equilibrium is judged separately, in forces.

A fibre element whose law has a flat plateau cannot invert the section once the latter is
saturated: the curvature is no longer a function of the moment. Load control nevertheless reaches the
limit load, reported as a lack of equilibrium; to follow the descending branch, a slight hardening is
needed ($b$ from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2}$), much smaller than the geometric softening.

The accuracy depends on the localisation of plasticity. For a rectangular steel cantilever under a
tip load, the elastic deflection is exact with one element (up to the fibres); at 90 % of the plastic
collapse load $M_p/L$, the difference from the exact integral of the curvature is 0.17 % with one
element and $3\cdot 10^{-5}$ with four; at 97 %, 4 % and 0.1 %.

### 18.7.3 Corotational option

With the geometric option, the basic deformations are measured in the chord frame of the element,
as in chapter 17: elongation of the chord, deformational rotations through the logarithmic map, total
nodal rotations. The nodal forces and the tangent are

$$ \mathbf{f} = \mathbf{B}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{q},\qquad
\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{B}^\mathsf{T}\,\mathbf{k}_b\,\mathbf{B} + \sum_a q_a\,\frac{\partial^2 v_a}{\partial\mathbf{u}^2},\qquad
\mathbf{B} = \frac{\partial\mathbf{v}}{\partial\mathbf{u}} $$ (18.24)

where $\mathbf{k}_b = \mathbf{f}_b^{-1}$ is the basic stiffness of the element. The derivatives
of the kinematics are obtained by fourth-order central finite differences: the rounding they leave on
the equilibrium residual is of the order of $10^{-11}$ in relative terms, and the error on the
tangent affects only the rate of convergence. The P-δ effect within an element is not in the
interpolation of the forces, which remains linear in the chord frame: compressed bars must be divided
into two to four elements.

## 18.8 Nonlinear analysis of the structure

The equilibrium of the framework, fibre bars and elastic bars together, reads
$\mathbf{r}(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{F}_0 + \lambda\mathbf{F} - \mathbf{f}_\text{int}(\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{0}$.
It is solved by Newton's method on the assembled tangent, factorised densely (the analysis is
intended for small frameworks). Each step is followed by a line search by halving (at most twelve
times), which restores the element forces at each trial. Equilibrium is reached when

$$ \|\mathbf{r}\|_2 \le 10^{-9}\,\max\bigl(\|\mathbf{F}_0 + \lambda\mathbf{F}\|_2,\ \|\mathbf{f}_\text{int}\|_2\bigr) $$ (18.25)

in at most 40 iterations; the internal force enters the scale so that a step driven by imposed
strains alone (restrained shrinkage) has a measure. The states of the fibres are committed once per
accepted step. Three control modes are available:

- load control: equal increments up to $\lambda = 1$ (10 by default); a limit point shows up as
a lack of equilibrium, which brackets the limit load between two increments;

- displacement control: one component of a node follows a piecewise linear history, possibly
cyclic, and $\lambda$ becomes an unknown. Each correction combines
$\delta\mathbf{u} = \delta\mathbf{u}_r + \delta\lambda\,\delta\mathbf{u}_F$, where
$\delta\lambda$ is chosen so that the controlled component takes its value; the limit points of
the load are passed and the descending branch is followed;

- arc length, in the same way as in chapter 17 (cylindrical form, choice of root, reduction and
adaptation of the radius).

The analysis may also chain construction stages: each stage activates bars and adds loads from the
committed states of the previous stages (a fibre that has yielded remains so), with creep and
shrinkage between the stages (chapters 9 and 10). Fibre bars refuse span loads, releases, offsets,
Winkler foundations, variable sections, coupled elastic supports and imposed support displacements; in
corotational mode, only nodal forces are accepted.

The shell plasticity analysis (chapter 24) accepts nonlinear bars in the same model: force-based
fibre bars, which there also accept span loads (through the exact particular solution of the basic
system), releases, rigid arms, variable sections and a coupled Winkler foundation, and bilinear or N-M
hinges, whose forces are obtained by an implicit return onto the polygon. This analysis is under load
control, in small or large displacements.

## 18.9 Statically determinate reinforced concrete beam

For a statically determinate beam, the moment is known from statics whatever the stiffness:
$M(x) = M_g(x) + P\,m_P(x)$ under a fixed uniform permanent load and a controlled point load
$P$. There is nothing to iterate on the structure. The curvature of each section is the inverse
of the moment-curvature law of the section, and the deflection under the load is the virtual work
integral

$$ \delta(P) = \int_0^L \kappa\bigl(M(x)\bigr)\,\bar m(x)\,\mathrm{d}x $$ (18.26)

where $\bar m$ is the moment due to a unit force at the point of the deflection. keta integrates
it by adaptive Gauss-Legendre quadrature, on the sub-intervals separated by the abscissae where
$M(x)$ crosses a kink of $\kappa(M)$ (a fibre reaching a break of slope in its law), down to
rounding: the solution depends on no mesh. The section is a rectangle of Sargin concrete (integrated in
closed form, by polynomial division and logarithm) with discrete reinforcing bars, under zero axial
force; second order therefore plays no part. The law of the reinforcement may be a polygonal table, or
one interpolated by natural cubic splines, or the “mean strain” steel law of DAfStb Heft 525, which
represents tension stiffening between the cracks:

$$ \sigma_{sr} = f_{ct,\text{eff}}\Bigl(\frac{1}{\rho_\text{eff}} + \alpha_e - 1\Bigr),\qquad
\varepsilon_{sm} = \varepsilon_{s2} - \beta_t\,(\varepsilon_{sr2} - \varepsilon_{sr1})\quad
(1.3\,\sigma_{sr} \le \sigma \le f_y) $$ (18.27)

with $\varepsilon_{sr1} = f_{ct,\text{eff}}/E_c$, $\varepsilon_{sr2} = \sigma_{sr}/E_s$ and
$\varepsilon_{s2}$ the strain of the bare steel; the uncracked, crack-formation and yielding stages
have their own expressions, linear in $\sigma$. The limit load under load control is reached when
the section under the load arrives at the peak of its moment-curvature curve.

## 18.10 Scope

The hinges are exact for the model as stated, but this model (position, law, polygon) is the user's
responsibility; no analysis itself checks a rotation capacity or a code ductility. The table
summarises the other limits.

| computation | covered | not covered or refused |
|---|---|---|
| hinges, event to event | moment, N-M polygon, kinematic hardening, span loads, permanent case, second order | imposed displacements and strains, hinge on a cable, on a variable bar or on a release |
| fibre sections | laws of EN 1992-1-1 and NF P18-710, hardening steel, bonded or unbonded tendons | mesh other than rectangular in the core; accuracy in $1/n^2$ in elasticity, slower at the ultimate point |
| fibre element | biaxial bending, axial force, hereditary laws, corotational option, staged construction | shear, nonlinear torsion, span loads (outside the shell analysis), fibre hinges |
| analysis of the structure | load, displacement and arc-length control | dense solution: small frameworks |
| reinforced concrete beam | statically determinate, Sargin rectangle, tabulated steels or with tension stiffening | axial force, statically indeterminate structures |

# Chapter 19 Torsion and warping

A twisted beam rotates about its axis; its cross-section, in general, does not remain plane: it
warps. If nothing prevents this warping, the torsion is uniform and the torque is carried by the
Saint-Venant shear stresses alone. If warping is restrained, by a fixed end, by a neighbouring section
that warps less or by the variation of the torque along the bar, normal stresses appear, the torsional
stiffness increases and part of the torque is carried by bending of the walls. For a box girder or a
solid section, this effect is small and localised. For an open thin-walled section (I section,
channel, twin-web girder), it is of first order: it governs the rotation of a twisted cantilever and
the critical lateral-torsional buckling load. This chapter describes the Saint-Venant torsion of the
standard bar element, then Vlasov non-uniform torsion, carried by an element with seven degrees of
freedom per node, in first order, in second order, in buckling and in large displacements. The
computation of the section constants ($J$, $I_w$, shear centre) is the subject of
chapter 20; lateral-torsional buckling is stated in chapter 17.

## 19.1 Assumptions

- the material is linearly elastic and isotropic, with moduli $E$ and $G$;

- the cross-section does not deform in its plane: neither distortion nor local buckling of the
walls;

- non-uniform torsion follows Vlasov's theory of open thin-walled sections: warping is proportional
to the rate of twist $\theta'$, and the shear strain of the middle surface of the walls is
neglected;

- the section is doubly symmetric: its shear centre is its centroid, and there is no Wagner
asymmetry term;

- the bars are straight; at a node where warping is free, the bars that meet are collinear;

- in first and second order, the displacements are small; the large-displacement analysis accepts
large rotations with small strains.

## 19.2 Saint-Venant torsion

In uniform torsion, the rotation $\theta(x)$ varies linearly and the torque is proportional to
the rate of twist:

$$ T = G J\,\theta' $$ (19.1)

$J$ is the Saint-Venant torsion constant of the section. keta's bar element with six degrees of
freedom per node (chapter 3) knows only this torsion: its torsion matrix is
$(GJ/L)\,[1, -1 ; -1, 1]$ on the rotations $\theta_x$ of its ends, and warping has no degree
of freedom in it. The orders of magnitude differ greatly with the shape of the section:

| section | torsion constant |
|---|---|
| open thin-walled (walls $b_k \times t_k$) | $J = \sum_k b_k t_k^3/3$ |
| single-cell box (area $A_m$ enclosed by the midline) | $J = 4A_m^2 \big/ \oint \mathrm{d}s/t$ (Bredt) |
| arbitrary section | Saint-Venant warping function, by finite elements (chapter 20) |

For an IPE 300, $J = 20.1\ \mathrm{cm^4}$, four hundred times less than the bending second
moment of area $I_y$: the uniform torsion of an open section is very flexible, and restrained
warping accounts for a large part of the stiffness.

## 19.3 Non-uniform torsion

### 19.3.1 Warping and bimoment

In Vlasov's theory, a point on the midline of a wall, located by its sectorial coordinate
$\omega(s)$ referred to the shear centre, moves out of the plane of the section by
$u = -\omega\,\theta'$. If $\theta'$ varies along the bar, this displacement creates an axial
strain and hence a normal stress, whose resultant is a force of a new kind, the bimoment:

$$ \sigma_w = -E\,\omega\,\theta'' = \frac{B\,\omega}{I_w},\qquad
B = \int_A \sigma_w\,\omega\,\mathrm{d}A = -E I_w\,\theta'',\qquad I_w = \int_A \omega^2\,\mathrm{d}A $$ (19.2)

$I_w$ is the warping constant. The stresses $\sigma_w$ are self-equilibrating: they give
neither axial force nor bending moment. For an I section, they are easily read: the rotation
$\theta$ moves the two flanges laterally in opposite directions, by $\pm h_s\theta/2$, where
$h_s = h - t_f$ is the distance between their mid-planes; each flange bends in its plane under a
moment $M_f$, equal and opposite to that of the other, and the bimoment is the product
$B = M_f\,h_s$. The warping constant is then the one keta computes for an I section,

$$ I_w = \frac{t_f\,b^3\,(h - t_f)^2}{24} $$ (19.3)

that is, $125.9\cdot 10^3\ \mathrm{cm^6}$ ($1.259\cdot 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m^6}$) for an
IPE 300.

**Figure 19.1** — Restrained warping of an I section: opposite bending of the flanges and bimoment B = Mf hs

### 19.3.2 Vlasov equation

The torque is then shared between a Saint-Venant part, carried by the shear of the walls, and a
warping part, carried by the shear forces that bending of the flanges induces in their plane:

$$ T = T_\text{sv} + T_w,\qquad T_\text{sv} = G J\,\theta',\qquad T_w = -E I_w\,\theta''' = B' $$ (19.4)

and the equilibrium of a segment under a distributed torque $m_x$ gives the Vlasov
equation:

$$ E I_w\,\theta'''' - G J\,\theta'' = m_x $$ (19.5)

The end conditions apply to $\theta$ (rotation restrained or torque imposed) and to
$\theta'$ (warping restrained, $\theta' = 0$, or free, $B = 0$). The fork support of
bridges and building beams restrains the torsional rotation and leaves warping free.

The homogeneous solution contains $\cosh kx$ and $\sinh kx$, with

$$ k = \sqrt{\frac{G J}{E I_w}} $$ (19.6)

The length $1/k$ measures the distance over which a restrained warping is felt; beyond it, the
torsion becomes uniform again. For an IPE 300, $1/k = 1.28\ \mathrm{m}$. For a cantilever of
length $L$, fixed (rotation and warping restrained) and loaded at its tip by a torque $T$,
the equation gives

$$ \theta(L) = \frac{T}{GJ}\left(L - \frac{\tanh kL}{k}\right),\qquad
T_\text{sv}(x) = T\left(1 - \frac{\cosh k(L - x)}{\cosh kL}\right),\qquad
B(x) = -\frac{T}{k}\,\frac{\sinh k(L - x)}{\cosh kL} $$ (19.7)

At the fixed end, all the torque is carried by warping ($T_\text{sv} = 0$) and the bimoment is
$-T\tanh(kL)/k$; at the tip, the torque is almost entirely Saint-Venant torque. keta's
computation reproduces these three expressions to machine precision, at every node of a cantilever
divided into elements, and with a single element for the tip rotation.

**Figure 19.2** — 4 m IPE 300 cantilever twisted at its tip, warping restrained at the fixed end: sharing of the torque and bimoment computed by keta

## 19.4 Seven-degree-of-freedom element

### 19.4.1 Warping degree of freedom

keta adds a seventh degree of freedom at each node, the warping:

$$ \mathbf{u}_\text{node} = \bigl(u_x, u_y, u_z, \theta_x, \theta_y, \theta_z, \psi\bigr),\qquad \psi = \theta_x' $$ (19.8)

This analysis is distinct from the standard linear analysis: it takes the bar model as it is, with
its supports and loads, and solves it with seven degrees of freedom per node. A node may have its
warping restrained; otherwise, $\psi$ is free. Since $\psi$ is a scalar, independent of the
direction of the bar, it expresses the continuity of warping between two collinear bars; between two
bars at an angle, this continuity has no meaning, and keta requires the warping of the node to be
restrained. A node reached by no bar with a constant $I_w > 0$ has no warping degree of
freedom: its bars work in Saint-Venant torsion. The warping constant of each bar is that of its
section, or a value given for the analysis.

### 19.4.2 Exact torsion block

The torsion block of the element, on $(\theta_i, \psi_i, \theta_j, \psi_j)$, is built from the
exact solution of (19.5). keta writes the homogeneous solution in the basis
$\{1, x, F_2(x), F_3(x)\}$ of the transfer functions of the beam (hyperbolic functions, or
trigonometric ones when the effective torsional stiffness becomes negative in second order, series
expansions when it is close to zero). If $\mathbf{H}$ relates the coefficients in this basis to
the end values $(\theta, \theta')$ and $\mathbf{D}$ to the end forces $(T, B)$, the
stiffness matrix is

$$ \mathbf{k}_t = \mathbf{D}\,\mathbf{H}^{-1} $$ (19.9)

(symmetrised). A single element per bar is therefore exact in pure torsion. The fixed-end forces of
linearly varying distributed torques and of point torques are computed in the same basis, from a
particular solution of (19.5): they too are exact. A transverse load applied at the
distance $(e_y, e_z)$ from the shear centre also creates the distributed torque
$e_y q_z - e_z q_y$. The axial and bending blocks are those of keta's element (Timoshenko in first
order). When $|G_t|\,L^2/(E I_w) > 400$, that is $kL > 20$, the hyperbolic functions
lose their precision through cancellation: keta requires the bar to be subdivided.

### 19.4.3 Results and refusals

The analysis returns, for each node, seven displacements (including $\psi$, in rad/m); for
each bar, the twelve end forces and the two bimoments, with the convention $B = -EI_w\theta''$;
and, at each end, the sharing of the torque:

$$ M_{T1} = G J\,\psi,\qquad M_{T3} = N r_0^2\,\psi,\qquad M_{T2} = M_T - M_{T1} - M_{T3} $$ (19.10)

where $M_{T1}$ is the Saint-Venant torque, $M_{T3}$ the Wagner torque (second order only,
see below) and $M_{T2}$ the warping torque. The warping normal stresses at a point of the section
follow from them through (19.2), with the sectorial coordinate of chapter 20. The
analysis does not give the distribution of the secondary shear stresses in the walls, nor the forces
at intermediate sections of a bar: the bar must be subdivided to read the sharing of the torque along
it.

The analysis refuses bars with released ends, with rigid arms, on a Winkler foundation or of
variable section, truss bars and cables, imposed support displacements, coupled elastic supports and
unilateral supports, shells and continuum elements, and monosymmetric sections (Wagner coefficient
$\beta_x \ne 0$).

## 19.5 Second order and buckling

### 19.5.1 Second-order energy

Under axial force and bending moments, the thin-walled bar couples bending and torsion. The
second-order energy of the doubly symmetric bar (Trahair, *Flexural-Torsional Buckling of
Structures*, 1993, chapter 3) is

$$ U_2 = \int_0^L \Bigl[\frac{N}{2}\bigl(v'^2 + w'^2 + r_0^2\,\theta'^2\bigr) + M_y\,\theta\,v'' + M_z\,\theta\,w''\Bigr]\mathrm{d}x
+ \frac{1}{2}\sum (\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{e})\,\theta^2,\qquad r_0^2 = \frac{I_y + I_z}{A} $$ (19.11)

The first term is the geometric stiffness of the axial force, Wagner term included; the second, the
coupling by which a bending moment twists a beam that moves laterally; the last, the effect of the
height at which the loads are applied: a downward load applied above the shear centre
($\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{e} < 0$) is destabilising, a load applied below it is stabilising. The
signs of the moments are keta's ($M_y > 0$ puts the $+z$ fibre in tension).

In the second-order analysis, the axial force enters the uncoupled blocks without approximation:
bending takes the stiffness of the beam-column (stability functions, chapter 17, Euler-Bernoulli), and
torsion the effective stiffness

$$ G_t = G J + N\,r_0^2 $$ (19.12)

in the exact solution of $E I_w\theta'''' - G_t\theta'' = m_x$. Tension stiffens torsion,
compression softens it. The coupling terms due to the moments and to the load heights are integrated
with the cubic Hermite shape functions of $v$, $w$ and $\theta$, by a five-point Gauss
rule (exact for the parabolic moment of a uniform load). This coupling is a discretisation, which
converges as $h^2$ to $h^4$; the uncoupled blocks are exact. The analysis starts from the
first-order state, rebuilds the blocks with the forces of the previous iteration and stops when the
relative change in the displacements is below $10^{-10}$, or at the rounding floor of the
solution ($64\,\varepsilon$ times the ratio of the extreme pivots, capped at $10^{-6}$), in
at most 50 iterations. An indefinite tangent means that the load exceeds the critical state: the
analysis stops. For a twisted cantilever under axial force, the tip angle follows
(19.7) with $GJ$ replaced by $G_t$, to machine precision.

### 19.5.2 Flexural-torsional buckling

Linear flexural-torsional buckling starts from the first-order state of the case and solves

$$ \bigl(\mathbf{K} + \lambda\,\mathbf{K}_g\bigr)\,\boldsymbol{\varphi} = \mathbf{0} $$ (19.13)

where $\mathbf{K}_g$ is the matrix of (19.11) built on $N$, $M_y$,
$M_z$ and the load heights of this state. The modes have seven components per node. The same
analysis gives the lateral-torsional buckling of a beam in bending and the torsional buckling of a
column. For a column on fork supports, the torsional critical load is

$$ N_{cr,T} = \frac{1}{r_0^2}\left(G J + \frac{\pi^2 E I_w}{L^2}\right) $$ (19.14)

which keta recovers to within $2\cdot 10^{-7}$ with 32 elements, alongside the flexural modes.
For a beam on fork supports under uniform moment, the critical moment tends to the closed form of
chapter 17 (difference of $2\cdot 10^{-7}$ with 16 elements for a 6 m IPE 300). Under uniform
load, the result accounts for the height of application; for the same IPE 300, it is within 0.5 % of
the approximate formula with factors $C_1 = 1.127$ and $C_2 = 0.454$, whether the load is at
the shear centre, on the top flange or on the bottom flange (the factors $C_1$, $C_2$ are
themselves rounded).

**Figure 19.3** — Critical lateral-torsional buckling moment of an IPE 300 under uniform moment, fork supports: keta's warping elements and closed form

Flexural-torsional buckling is distinct from the linear buckling of chapter 17: the latter uses the
six-degree-of-freedom element, which carries the Wagner term in Saint-Venant torsion but ignores
warping and the coupling through the bending moments. For an open section, it therefore
underestimates the torsional stiffness (no $EI_w$), which lowers the torsional critical load of a
column, and it ignores the lateral-torsional buckling of a beam in bending.

## 19.6 Large displacements with warping

The large-displacement analysis with warping gives the corotational bar of chapter 17 the seventh
degree of freedom. The energy of the element is

$$ W = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{d}^\mathsf{T}\bar{\mathbf{K}}\,\mathbf{d} + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{t}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{K}_{tw}\,\mathbf{t},\qquad
\mathbf{t} = (\bar\theta_{x,i}, \psi_i, \bar\theta_{x,j}, \psi_j),\qquad
\mathbf{K}_{tw} = E I_w\!\int_0^L \mathbf{N}''^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{N}''\,\mathrm{d}x + G J\!\int_0^L \mathbf{N}'^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{N}'\,\mathrm{d}x $$ (19.15)

where the first term is the corotational energy of the axial force and of bending, and the second
the Vlasov energy, written on the deformational torsional rotations $\bar\theta_x$ (with the
rigid-body rotation of the frame removed) and on the warpings, with the cubic Hermite interpolation
$\mathbf{N}$ of the torsional rotation. This block is polynomial, and not exact as in small
displacements: it converges with subdivision. The forces and the tangent are the exact gradient and
Hessian of $W$, by automatic differentiation; the load is applied in increments, with Newton's
method in each increment. The bending-torsion coupling comes from the rotation of the frame and
converges with refinement; there is no Wagner term, which restricts the analysis to bars without
large axial force.

The analysis accepts bars with rigid arms (a load height is represented there by an arm) and nodal
forces, which keep their direction. It refuses nodal moments, span loads, imposed displacements,
releases, Winkler foundations, variable sections, cables, elastic supports, shells, links and
monosymmetric sections. Warping is restrained at the designated nodes and at the nodes reached by no
bar with a constant $I_w > 0$.

## 19.7 Scope

The table summarises what keta covers in torsion.

| covered | not covered |
|---|---|
| Saint-Venant torsion in all the bar analyses | warping in the standard six-degree-of-freedom bar element |
| Vlasov non-uniform torsion, doubly symmetric sections, straight bars | monosymmetric or asymmetric sections (eccentric shear centre, coefficient $\beta_x$): refused |
| exact solution of the element in pure torsion, distributed and point torques | box girders: Benscoter reduction of the warping of closed sections, absent |
| second order, Wagner term, load height | distortion of the section and buckling of the walls |
| lateral-torsional and torsional buckling | distribution of the secondary shear stresses in the walls |
| large displacements with warping under nodal forces | continuity of warping between non-collinear bars (the node must be restrained) |
| computation of $J$, $I_w$ and the shear centre of a section (chapter 20) | nonlinear torsion of the material (fibres remain in elastic Saint-Venant torsion, chapter 18) |

For a bridge box girder, Saint-Venant torsion is dominant and restrained warping is a local effect,
which Vlasov's theory of open sections would overestimate. keta has no specific treatment of closed
sections and does not recognise them: the non-uniform torsion analysis assumes an open section, and it
is up to the user not to use it for a box girder, or not to give it a constant $I_w$.

# Chapter 20 Section properties

The beam element (chapter 3) sees only a few numbers of the cross-section: the area $A$, the
second moments of area $I_y$ and $I_z$, the torsion constant $J$, the shear areas
$A_{vy}$ and $A_{vz}$, and, for non-uniform torsion (chapter 19), the warping constant
$I_w$ referred to the shear centre. This chapter explains how keta obtains these numbers and how
it goes back from the bar to the section to give the stresses at a point. Three levels of computation
coexist: closed forms for parametric sections and rolled sections, which are instantaneous; a
thin-walled theory, without a mesh, for open sections and multi-cell boxes; and the finite element
solution of the Saint-Venant problem on an arbitrary polygonal section, which serves as the reference
for the other two. The chapter also covers the share of the shear force carried by the inclined chords
of a beam of variable depth. Reinforced and prestressed concrete sections, whose behaviour is not
linear, are the subject of chapter 21.

## 20.1 Assumptions

- the section is plane, in the local $(y, z)$ axes of the bar; $x$ is the axis of the bar.
The properties are computed at the elastic centroid;

- the material is linearly elastic and isotropic; a section made of several materials is
transformed by the ratio of the Young's moduli;

- the theory is that of Saint-Venant: the section deforms freely out of its plane (warping) and
keeps its shape in its plane; it does not distort;

- the normal stresses follow the Navier-Bernoulli assumption; the shear stresses are those of
Saint-Venant uniform torsion and simple bending;

- curved edges are represented by polygons; the section is in one piece (several disjoint regions
are refused by the warping computation);

- in thin-walled theory, each wall is a straight strip of constant or linearly varying thickness,
the thickness being small compared with the length; shear lag is not represented.

## 20.2 Section library

### 20.2.1 Parametric shapes

Six shapes are described by their dimensions: the rectangle, the solid circle, the circular tube,
the doubly symmetric I section (with or without root fillets), the rectangular box of uniform
thickness per wall and the tee with a top flange. Their properties are closed forms. A seventh,
generic shape receives its properties as they are, without geometry; it allows neither the
computation of stresses at a point nor that of the shear areas.

**Figure 20.1** — Parametric shapes and their dimensions (local axes of the section)

For the rectangle of sides $a \ge c$, the torsion constant is the Saint-Venant series
(Timoshenko and Goodier, *Theory of Elasticity*, chap. 10), summed until the current term
becomes negligible:

$$ J = \frac{a\,c^3}{3}\left[1 - \frac{192}{\pi^5}\,\frac{c}{a}\sum_{n\ \text{odd}} \frac{1}{n^5}\tanh\frac{n\pi a}{2c}\right] $$ (20.1)

The circle and the tube have $J = I_y + I_z = 2I$, the exact value for a section of
revolution. The box follows Bredt's formula on its midlines, $b_m = b - t_w$ and
$h_m = h - t_f$:

$$ J = \frac{4A_m^2}{\displaystyle\oint\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{t}} = \frac{4\,(b_m h_m)^2}{2\,b_m/t_f + 2\,h_m/t_w} $$ (20.2)

The I section and the tee have the open-wall constant, $J = \sum b\,t^3/3$ over their flanges
and web. The table below summarises what each shape provides.

| Shape | $J$ | $W_{pl}$ | $I_w$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| rectangle | Saint-Venant series (20.1) | $bh^2/4$, $hb^2/4$ | — |
| solid circle | $\pi d^4/32$ | $d^3/6$ | — |
| tube | $\pi(r_e^4 - r_i^4)/2$ | $d_m^2\,t$ (thin wall) | — |
| doubly symmetric I | $\sum b t^3/3$; with fillets, El Darwish and Johnston | closed form, fillets included | $t_f b^3 (h - t_f)^2/24$ |
| box | Bredt (20.2) | closed form | — |
| tee | $\sum b t^3/3$ | not computed | — |

The elastic section moduli are $W_{el} = I/v$, $v$ being the distance from the extreme
fibre to the centroid. The shear areas of these formulae ($5A/6$ for the rectangle, $0.9A$
for the circle, $A/2$ for the tube, the web $h_w t_w$ for the I and the tee, the two webs
$2h_i t_w$ for the box) serve only as provisional values: as soon as a bar receives the section,
keta replaces them by the energy-based areas for the material of that bar (see below). Finally, each
shape carries a few named stress points (corners, extreme fibres, mid-web), used when the finite
element stress computation is not available.

### 20.2.2 Rolled sections

The catalogue contains the European sections IPE 80 to 600 and HEA, HEB, HEM 100 to 1000, with the
nominal dimensions of EN 10365: $h$, $b$, $t_w$, $t_f$ and the root radius
$r$. The four fillets are circular spandrels, an $r\times r$ square minus a quarter disc,
counted exactly in $A$, $I_y$, $I_z$, $W_{el}$ and $W_{pl}$. A spandrel has
as area, distance from its centroid to the two faces of the corner, and second moment of area about
its own axis

$$ A_s = \left(1 - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) r^2,\qquad
d = \frac{5/6 - \pi/4}{1 - \pi/4}\,r,\qquad
I_s = \left(1 - \frac{5\pi}{16}\right) r^4 - A_s d^2 $$ (20.3)

and it is placed at the lever arm $h/2 - t_f - d$ for major-axis bending, $t_w/2 + d$ for
the minor axis. The torsion constant with fillets follows El Darwish and Johnston (1965), the rule
from which the European tables derive:

$$ J = \frac{2}{3}\,b\,t_f^3 + \frac{(h - 2t_f)\,t_w^3}{3} + 2\alpha D^4 - 0.420\,t_f^4,\qquad
D = \frac{(t_f + r)^2 + t_w\,(r + t_w/4)}{2r + t_f} $$ (20.4)

where $\alpha$ is a polynomial in $t_w/t_f$ and $r/t_f$. The fallback web shear area
is that of EN 1993-1-1 § 6.2.6(3)a, $A_{vz} = A - 2bt_f + (t_w + 2r)\,t_f \ge h_w t_w$. For an
IPE 300, keta obtains $A = 53.81\ \text{cm}^2$, $I_y = 8356\ \text{cm}^4$,
$I_z = 603.8\ \text{cm}^4$ and $I_w = 125.9\cdot 10^3\ \text{cm}^6$, the tabulated values;
$J = 19.92\ \text{cm}^4$, within 1 % of the table (20.12). Without the fillets, the area would be
3 to 4 % too low and $J$ 10 to 30 % too low.

Equal-leg angles (EN 10056-1), INP beams with tapered flanges (DIN 1025-1) and UPE parallel-flange
channels (DIN 1026-2) are described by their outline, root and toe fillets included, drawn as arcs
tangent to the adjacent faces and divided into 256 chords per fillet; the area deficit of an arc so
divided is $r^2(\theta - \sin\theta)/2$ per chord, about $5 \cdot 10^{-6}\,r^2$ per fillet, that is less than $10^{-6}$ of the area
of a usual section.
Their properties are those of a polygon, product of inertia and principal axes included.

### 20.2.3 Polygons and imported outlines

Any other section is described as an outer polygon pierced by voids: bridge boxes and tees, bulb
beams, built-up sections. The orientation of the outlines is normalised by the computation. An outline
may be read from a DXF file in text format (LWPOLYLINE, POLYLINE, LINE and ARC entities): isolated
segments and arcs are chained into closed loops, the largest loop becomes the outline, the others
voids. Arcs and polyline bulges are divided into chords under a sagitta tolerance; the angular step
$\Delta\varphi$ satisfies

$$ R\left(1 - \cos\frac{\Delta\varphi}{2}\right) \le \varepsilon_f,\qquad \varepsilon_f = 10^{-3}\,R\ \text{by default} $$ (20.5)

that is, about 71 chords per turn, and an area error of the order of $1.3\cdot 10^{-3}$ of each
sector, smaller than the error of the subsequent mesh. Splines, blocks and the binary format are
refused rather than silently straightened.

## 20.3 Geometric properties

For a polygon, the area, the first moments and the second moments of area are surface integrals
that Green's theorem reduces to a sum over the sides. For a side going from $(y_0, z_0)$ to
$(y_1, z_1)$, with $c = y_0 z_1 - y_1 z_0$:

$$ \begin{aligned}
A &= \sum \frac{c}{2}, & S_y = \int z\,\mathrm{d}A &= \sum \frac{c\,(z_0 + z_1)}{6},\\
\int z^2\,\mathrm{d}A &= \sum \frac{c\,(z_0^2 + z_0 z_1 + z_1^2)}{12}, &
\int yz\,\mathrm{d}A &= \sum \frac{c\,(y_0 z_1 + 2y_0 z_0 + 2y_1 z_1 + y_1 z_0)}{24}
\end{aligned} $$ (20.6)

the voids being traversed in the opposite direction to the outer outline. These sums are exact for
the polygon. The moments are then referred to the centroid, $I_y = \int z^2\,\mathrm{d}A - A z_G^2$,
and the principal axes follow:

$$ I_{1,2} = \frac{I_y + I_z}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{I_y - I_z}{2}\right)^2 + I_{yz}^2} $$ (20.7)

The beam element assumes that $y$ and $z$ are principal. keta does not rotate the section
by itself: a polygon whose product of inertia exceeds 5 % of the larger second moment of area is
refused, with a message asking for it to be entered in its principal axes. The computation of the
properties alone (without a bar), on the other hand, gives $I_{yz}$, $I_1$, $I_2$ and
the principal angle for any section: on a 100 × 10 mm angle with sharp corners,
$I_y = 180.0\ \text{cm}^4$, $I_{yz} = -106.6\ \text{cm}^4$ and
$I_1 = 286.6\ \text{cm}^4$, the values of the decomposition into two rectangles.

The elastic section modulus of a polygon is computed on the vertices of the outer outline furthest
from the centroid. Without solving for warping, the torsion constant of a polygon is estimated by
Saint-Venant's approximation for solid sections, $J \approx \min\bigl(I_p,\ A^4/(40\,I_p)\bigr)$
with $I_p = I_y + I_z$ (the exact factor of the formula is $4\pi^2 \approx 39.5$). This
estimate is crude for a hollow or thin section; a polygonal section entered in a model therefore
receives by default the finite element solution of the next section.

## 20.4 Plastic properties

The plastic section modulus is the first moment of the two halves of the section on either side of
the plastic neutral axis, which divides the area into two equal parts. For a doubly symmetric
section, this axis is the axis of symmetry, and the closed forms are, for the I and the box,

$$ W_{pl,y}^{\,I} = b\,t_f\,(h - t_f) + \frac{t_w h_w^2}{4},\qquad
W_{pl,y}^{\,\text{box}} = b\,t_f\,(h - t_f) + \frac{t_w h_i^2}{2} $$ (20.8)

increased, for the rolled I, by $4A_s(h/2 - t_f - d)$ for the fillets. The tube uses the
thin-wall approximation $d_m^2 t$, which differs from the exact value $(d^3 - d_i^3)/6$ by
less than 0.1 % for $t/d = 1/25$. keta does not compute the plastic modulus of a tee, of an
arbitrary polygon or of a composite section: it remains zero, which means “unknown” for the checks that
read it.

## 20.5 Saint-Venant problem

For an arbitrary polygon, torsion and shear have no closed form. keta then solves by finite elements
the three Laplace problems of Saint-Venant's theory, which give $J$, the shear areas, the shear
centre, $I_w$ and the shear stress fields. The formulation is that of Pilkey (*Analysis and
Design of Elastic Beams*, 2002, chap. 5) and of Gruttmann and Wagner (“Shear correction factors in
Timoshenko's beam theory for arbitrary shaped cross-sections”, *Computational Mechanics* 27,
2001). All the integrals are taken at the elastic centroid.

### 20.5.1 Torsion and warping function

In uniform torsion, the section rotates by $\theta' x$ about the axis and warps by
$u_x = \theta'\,\omega(y, z)$. Equilibrium with no stress on the lateral surface gives a Neumann
problem for the warping function:

$$ \Delta\omega = 0\ \text{in } A,\qquad
\frac{\partial\omega}{\partial n} = z\,n_y - y\,n_z\ \text{on the boundary} $$ (20.9)

In weak form, for any test function $w$,
$\int_A \nabla w\cdot\nabla\omega\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_A \nabla w\cdot(z, -y)\,\mathrm{d}A$.
$\omega$ is defined only up to a constant; keta fixes one node, which has no effect on the results
since the right-hand side sums to zero. The torsion constant is obtained from the strain energy:

$$ J = \int_A \left(y^2 + z^2 + y\,\frac{\partial\omega}{\partial z} - z\,\frac{\partial\omega}{\partial y}\right)\mathrm{d}A
= I_y + I_z - \boldsymbol{\omega}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{f}_t $$ (20.10)

where $\mathbf{f}_t$ is the discrete right-hand side. The torsional shear stress is
$\boldsymbol{\tau} = (T/J)\,\bigl(\nabla\omega + (-z, y)\bigr)$.

### 20.5.2 Bending and shear

Under a shear force, Saint-Venant writes the shear field from two potentials $\psi_y$ and
$\psi_z$, solutions of problems with the same operator as (20.9):

$$ \int_A \nabla w\cdot\nabla\psi_y\,\mathrm{d}A =
\int_A \left[\frac{\nu}{2}\,\nabla w\cdot\mathbf{d} + 2(1 + \nu)\,w\,(I_y\,y - I_{yz}\,z)\right]\mathrm{d}A $$ (20.11)

with $\mathbf{d} = \bigl(I_y r - I_{yz} q,\ I_{yz} r + I_y q\bigr)$, $r = y^2 - z^2$,
$q = 2yz$, and the analogous equation for $\psi_z$, with source $I_z z - I_{yz} y$ and
compatibility term $\mathbf{h} = \bigl(-I_{yz} r + I_z q,\ -I_z r - I_{yz} q\bigr)$. The shear
stress is

$$ \boldsymbol{\tau} = \frac{V_y}{\Delta}\Bigl(\nabla\psi_y - \frac{\nu}{2}\,\mathbf{d}\Bigr)
+ \frac{V_z}{\Delta}\Bigl(\nabla\psi_z - \frac{\nu}{2}\,\mathbf{h}\Bigr),\qquad
\Delta = 2(1 + \nu)\,(I_y I_z - I_{yz}^2) $$ (20.12)

It depends on Poisson's ratio, because bending deforms the section in its plane (anticlastic
effect); it satisfies the free-edge condition exactly, which the Jourawski formula
$\tau = VS/(Ib)$ does not. The shear areas of the Timoshenko beam are those that reproduce the
energy of this field:

$$ A_{vy} = \frac{\Delta^2}{\kappa_y},\qquad
\kappa_y = \int_A \Bigl|\nabla\psi_y - \frac{\nu}{2}\,\mathbf{d}\Bigr|^2\mathrm{d}A $$ (20.13)

and likewise for $A_{vz}$; a section without symmetry also has a coupling area
$A_{vyz}$. For $\nu = 0$, the rectangle gives $A_v = 5A/6$; for $\nu = 0.3$, a
0.30 × 0.60 m rectangle gives $A_{vz} = 0.833\,A$ for a force parallel to the long side and
$A_{vy} = 0.784\,A$ for the other direction. The solid circle and the tube have a closed form,
derived from the Saint-Venant flexure energy:

$$ A_v^{\text{circle}} = \frac{6\,(1 + \nu)^2}{7 + 14\nu + 8\nu^2}\,A,\qquad
A_v^{\text{tube}} = \frac{6\,(1+\nu)^2 (1 + m^2)^2\,A}{(7 + 14\nu + 8\nu^2)(1 + m^2)^2 + 4\,(5 + 10\nu + 4\nu^2)\,m^2},\quad m = \frac{r_i}{r_e} $$ (20.14)

### 20.5.3 Shear centre and warping constant

The shear centre is the point through which the shear force must pass so as not to twist the
section. keta gives two definitions. The centre of elasticity, the one it uses, makes the shear field
(20.12) free of torque; it is read from the coupling of the shear potentials with the
torsion right-hand side:

$$ y_C = \frac{\frac{\nu}{2}\int_A (I_z y + I_{yz} z)(y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A - \mathbf{f}_t^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\psi}_z}{\Delta},\qquad
z_C = \frac{\frac{\nu}{2}\int_A (I_y z + I_{yz} y)(y^2 + z^2)\,\mathrm{d}A + \mathbf{f}_t^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\psi}_y}{\Delta} $$ (20.15)

Trefftz's geometric centre cancels the sectorial products of the warping function,
$y_T = (I_{yz} I_{\omega z} - I_z I_{\omega y})/(I_y I_z - I_{yz}^2)$, with
$I_{\omega y} = \int y\,\omega\,\mathrm{d}A$. The two definitions differ only by the effect of
Poisson's ratio. The warping constant is referred to the shear centre:

$$ I_w = \int_A \omega^2\,\mathrm{d}A - \frac{1}{A}\left(\int_A \omega\,\mathrm{d}A\right)^2 - z_C\,I_{\omega y} + y_C\,I_{\omega z} $$ (20.16)

keta also provides Vlasov's sectorial coordinate referred to the shear centre, with zero mean, at
each node; it is this coordinate that gives the warping stress $\sigma_w = B\,\omega_C/I_w$ under
a bimoment $B$.

**Figure 20.2** — 312 × 104 mm channel (8 mm web, 12 mm flanges): centroid G, shear centre C and sectorial coordinate ω referred to C, computed by finite elements

On the channel of the figure, the finite element solution places the shear centre 37.2 mm from the
midline of the web, on the side away from the flanges; the thin-walled theory described below gives
37.5 mm, that is, the classical formula $e = 3b^2 t_f/(6bt_f + ht_w)$. The warping constants
differ by 0.7 % (79.3 and 78.8 · 10³ cm⁶) and the torsion constants by 2 % (16.3 and 16.6 cm⁴): the
difference comes from the junctions and the free ends of the walls, which thin-walled theory
idealises.

### 20.5.4 Discretisation

The section is meshed with straight-sided six-node triangles. The shape functions are the
second-degree polynomials in barycentric coordinates $(\eta, \xi, \zeta = 1 - \eta - \xi)$:

$$ N_1 = \eta(2\eta - 1),\ N_2 = \xi(2\xi - 1),\ N_3 = \zeta(2\zeta - 1),\quad
N_4 = 4\eta\xi,\ N_5 = 4\xi\zeta,\ N_6 = 4\eta\zeta $$ (20.17)

The Jacobian is constant over the element. The integrals are computed by the symmetric four-point
Gauss rule, exact for polynomials of the third degree: the centroid, with weight $-27/48$ (a
negative weight is correct for this rule), and the three points $(0.6; 0.2; 0.2)$ with weight
$25/48$. The assembled matrix, symmetric and positive definite once one node is fixed, is
factorised once by a sparse $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{D}\mathbf{L}^{\mathsf T}$ decomposition; the three
right-hand sides (torsion, $V_y$, $V_z$) are solved on this factorisation.

**Figure 20.3** — Six-node triangle: node numbering and Gauss points

The mesher is a Delaunay triangulation (Bowyer-Watson algorithm) of the boundary points, sampled
at the target spacing $h$, and of an interior triangular lattice at the same spacing, kept at
least $0.65\,h$ from any boundary. Under this condition, each boundary sub-edge is a Gabriel edge
and belongs to the triangulation; the mesher checks this, as well as the equality of the meshed area
and the Green area to within $10^{-9}$. If the check fails, because the spacing does not resolve
the thinnest wall, it halves the spacing, at most three times, then stops with a message asking for a
finer spacing. The interior nodes then undergo a pass of Laplacian smoothing, which moves a node only
if the quality of the neighbouring triangles is improved. The default spacing is one twentieth of the
largest dimension of the section; for the shear areas of the parametric shapes, keta takes
$\min(L/40,\ t_\text{min}/4)$. The computation is deterministic: the same section always gives
the same mesh and the same properties, bit for bit.

Quadratic triangles converge quickly. On the 0.30 × 0.60 m rectangle, the difference of $J$
from the series (20.1) is $3.7\cdot 10^{-5}$, $2.8\cdot 10^{-6}$ and
$2.0\cdot 10^{-7}$ for spacings of 30, 15 and 7.5 mm, a convergence close to $h^4$.

## 20.6 Transformed sections

A section made of several materials (concrete and steel, two concretes) is described by regions:
each mesh element whose centroid falls within the outline of a region takes its material, the last
region listed prevailing; the other elements take the reference material, of index 0. The mesher
respects the outline of the regions, which must therefore be drawn inside the section. All the
integrals are weighted by $n_e = E_e/E_\text{ref}$:

$$ A^* = \sum_e n_e A_e,\qquad y_G = \frac{1}{A^*}\int n\,y\,\mathrm{d}A,\qquad
I_y^* = \int n\,(z - z_G)^2\,\mathrm{d}A $$ (20.18)

and the warping problems likewise. The normal stress of an element is that of the transformed
section multiplied by its $n_e$. In the shear potentials, the compatibility term $\nu_e/2$
takes the ratio of each material, whereas the equilibrium term keeps the $2(1 + \bar\nu)$ of
$\Delta$, $\bar\nu$ being the mean of the ratios weighted by $n$: the right-hand side
thus still sums to zero and the result does not depend on the fixed node. The shear areas and
$J$ are values referred to $E_\text{ref}$; they are the true rigidities divided by
$G_\text{ref}$ when all the materials have the same Poisson's ratio. On a square of side 1 whose
upper half has a double modulus, keta finds $A^* = 1.5$, $z_G = 1/12$ and
$I_y^* = 0.11458$, the hand values.

## 20.7 Stress field

### 20.7.1 Stress at a point

The internal forces of the bar are $(N, V_y, V_z, T, M_y, M_z)$ and, in non-uniform torsion, the
bimoment $B$. The normal stress, positive in tension and in coordinates referred to the centroid,
is written without assuming principal axes:

$$ \sigma_{xx} = \frac{N}{A} + \frac{M_y\,(I_z z - I_{yz} y) - M_z\,(I_y y - I_{yz} z)}{I_y I_z - I_{yz}^2}
+ \frac{B\,\omega_C}{I_w} $$ (20.19)

A positive $M_y$ puts the fibres of positive $z$ in tension, a positive $M_z$
compresses those of positive $y$ (chapter 2). The shear stress is the sum of the torsional shear
and the field (20.12); the von Mises stress is
$\sigma_{vm} = \sqrt{\sigma^2 + 3(\tau_y^2 + \tau_z^2)}$. The fields of the straight-sided
triangles are polynomials evaluated directly at the requested point, without extrapolation. Since the
normal stress is affine in $(y, z)$, its extremes lie on the boundary, at a vertex of the outline:
reading them at the boundary nodes, which include all the vertices, gives them exactly. The von Mises
maximum, on the other hand, is taken at the mesh nodes; it is an approximate value. Principal stresses
are not provided.

### 20.7.2 Stresses at the output sections of the bars

After a structural analysis, keta returns at each output section of each bar the extremes of
$\sigma$, the maximum of $|\tau|$ and that of von Mises. Since the field is linear in the six
internal forces, the warping problem is solved only once per section geometry and Poisson's ratio,
and six unit nodal fields are stored; the field of an output section is their combination:

$$ \boldsymbol{s}(\text{node}) = \sum_{k=1}^{6} a_k\,\boldsymbol{s}_k(\text{node}),\qquad
(a_k) = (N, V_y, V_z, M_y, M_z, T) $$ (20.20)

The nodal value is the average of the elements that meet at that node, the shear being
discontinuous from one element to the next. The extremes are sought over a set of candidate nodes: all
the boundary nodes, which make the extremes of $\sigma$ exact, and the nodes that govern each unit
action and each pair of unit actions of either sign. The maxima of $\tau$ and of von Mises of a
combined field may lie elsewhere: they are maxima over this set, not bounds. The parametric shapes are
then drawn as polygons (circle with 48 sides, fillets of rolled sections with 8 chords per quarter
circle, so that the section used for stresses has the same stiffness as that of the analysis). The
mesh, a constrained Delaunay triangulation refined by Ruppert's method (minimum angle of 30°), aims at
1200, 3000 or 9000 elements per section depending on the chosen fineness; the mesher of the previous
section serves as a fallback. A section without geometry, or whose solution has failed, falls back on
the named stress points of its shape (normal stress only), and keta reports it with the reason.

## 20.8 Thin walls

Open sections and bridge boxes lend themselves to thin-walled theory, faster than finite elements
and without a mesh. The section is a plane graph: the nodes are points of the midline, the edges are
straight walls.

### 20.8.1 Model and properties

A wall of length $L$, thickness $t$, unit direction $\mathbf{e} = (e_y, e_z)$ and
midpoint $(y_m, z_m)$ is a rectangle centred on its midline; its area and second moments of area
are exact:

$$ A_s = tL,\qquad
I_{y,s} = A_s\left(z_m^2 + \frac{L^2 e_z^2 + t^2 e_y^2}{12}\right),\qquad
I_{yz,s} = A_s\left(y_m z_m + \frac{(L^2 - t^2)\,e_y e_z}{12}\right) $$ (20.21)

The material that overlaps at the junctions is counted twice: this is the classical idealisation, an
effect of order $t/L$, and the reason why the $J$ of a rolled section computed in this way is
lower than that of the finite elements (neither fillet nor junction stiffening). The elastic section
moduli are taken at the ends of the midline.

### 20.8.2 Wall of linearly varying thickness

A wall may have a thickness that varies linearly from $t_a$ at node $a$ to $t_b$ at
node $b$, symmetrically on either side of the midline (thickened box web, haunch). All the formulae
remain valid with $t = t(s)$ under the integrals: the second moments of area are polynomial, the
strip term becomes $\int t^3\,\mathrm{d}s/12$, and

$$ \int_0^L \frac{\mathrm{d}s}{t} = L\,\frac{\ln(t_b/t_a)}{t_b - t_a},\qquad
\frac{1}{3}\int_0^L t^3\,\mathrm{d}s = \frac{L\,(t_a + t_b)(t_a^2 + t_b^2)}{12} $$ (20.22)

The rational and logarithmic integrals (flow energy, no-twist conditions, sectorial moments) are
computed by an 8-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature on segments of the wall whose thickness ratio remains
below 1.5: the result is exact to within rounding.

### 20.8.3 Multi-cell Bredt torsion

The independent cells are the fundamental cycles of a spanning tree of the graph: with $V$
nodes and $E$ walls of a connected graph, there are $n = E - V + 1$ of them. Working in this
basis of the cycle space is equivalent to working on the faces of the drawing, without needing to know
the drawing. For a unit rotation $G\theta' = 1$, the circulating flows $x_k$ of the cells are
solutions of the compatibility system

$$ \mathbf{M}\,\mathbf{x} = 2\,\mathbf{A},\qquad
M_{kl} = \sum_{s} c_k(s)\,c_l(s)\,\frac{L_s}{t_s},\qquad
J = 2\sum_k x_k A_k + \sum_{\text{open}} \frac{b\,t^3}{3} $$ (20.23)

where $c_k(s) = \pm 1$ states whether wall $s$ belongs to cycle $k$ and in which
direction, and $A_k$ is the area of the cell. For a single cell, (20.2) is
recovered. The walls that belong to no cycle (cantilevers of a box, flanges of an open section) carry
the open Saint-Venant term; those of a cell carry the closed term alone. Under a torque $T$, keta
gives the flow of each cell, the flow and the stress $q/t$ of each closed wall, and the
Saint-Venant stress $G\theta' t$ of the open walls. A box with midlines of 0.60 × 1.00 m (flanges
of 0.60 m and 30 mm, webs of 1.00 m and 20 mm) has $J = 1.0286\cdot 10^{-2}\ \text{m}^4$, the value
of (20.2); an added central web leaves $J$ unchanged: the two symmetric cells have
the same flow and the central web carries none.

### 20.8.4 Shear flow

The longitudinal equilibrium of a wall element gives the variation of the flow $q = \tau t$
along the midline:

$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}s} = -(K_z z + K_y y)\,t,\qquad
K_z = \frac{V_z I_z - V_y I_{yz}}{I_y I_z - I_{yz}^2},\quad
K_y = \frac{V_y I_y - V_z I_{yz}}{I_y I_z - I_{yz}^2} $$ (20.24)

that is, the familiar formula $q = V S(s)/I$ in principal axes. keta takes as unknowns the flows
at the start of the $E$ walls. The $V - 1$ independent nodal equilibria and the $n$
no-twist conditions of the cells (a force applied at the shear centre twists nothing) form a square
system, which reduces to the classical accumulation from the free end to the root for an open section,
and to the “cut the cells, then restore compatibility” method for a closed section. The shear areas
come from the energy of the flow:

$$ A_v = \frac{V^2}{\displaystyle\oint \frac{q^2}{t}\,\mathrm{d}s} $$ (20.25)

**Figure 20.4** — 2.40 × 1.20 m box (0.30 m webs, 0.20 and 0.18 m slabs) under a vertical shear force of 1 MN: shear stress along the walls, computed by finite elements

### 20.8.5 Sectorial coordinate and shear centre

The sectorial coordinate referred to a pole $P$ is integrated along the walls:

$$ \mathrm{d}\omega = (y - y_P)\,\mathrm{d}z - (z - z_P)\,\mathrm{d}y - \frac{q_1}{t}\,\mathrm{d}s $$ (20.26)

where $q_1$ is the unit torsional flow of (20.23). The corrective term is zero
for an open section; for a closed section, it makes $\omega$ single-valued around each cell, since
its integral over a cycle is $2A_k - \oint q_1/t\,\mathrm{d}s = 0$. The shear centre $S$
cancels the sectorial products:

$$ \begin{bmatrix} I_{yz} & -I_z \\ I_y & -I_{yz} \end{bmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} y_P - y_S \\ z_P - z_S \end{pmatrix} = -\begin{pmatrix} I_{\omega y} \\ I_{\omega z} \end{pmatrix} $$ (20.27)

and, once $\omega$ is referred to this pole and brought to zero mean,
$I_w = \int \omega_S^2\,\mathrm{d}A$ and $\sigma_w = B\,\omega_S/I_w$. In a wall of constant
thickness of an open section, $\omega$ is linear; in a cell with a wall of linearly varying
thickness, it follows $\int \mathrm{d}s/t$ and becomes logarithmic. For the channel of the
previous figure, the thin-walled computation gives $I_w = 78.75\cdot 10^3\ \text{cm}^6$, the closed
formula $t_f b^3 h^2 (3bt_f + 2ht_w)/\bigl(12\,(6bt_f + ht_w)\bigr)$ to within
$6\cdot 10^{-7}$.

### 20.8.6 Midline derived from the outline

The midline of an outline cannot be found without help: pairing the two faces of a wall is
ambiguous at the junctions. The user states how the points of the outline group into walls, in one of
two ways. By quadrilaterals: each wall is given by four points $p, q, r, s$ taken in order,
$p \to q$ and $s \to r$ being its two faces and $ps$, $qr$ its ends. The midline
joins the midpoints of the ends, and the thickness at an end is that end projected onto the normal
$\mathbf{n}$ to the midline,

$$ t_a = \bigl|(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s})\cdot\mathbf{n}\bigr|,\qquad t_b = \bigl|(\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{r})\cdot\mathbf{n}\bigr| $$ (20.28)

which gives the true thickness of a mitred corner, not its diagonal. End midpoints closer than a
tolerance (by default $10^{-6}$ of the extent of the outline) are merged into a single node. By
nodes and branches: a node is the list of outline points gathered at a junction, a branch connects two
nodes. The centre of the points of each node gives the axis of each branch; the spread of the points
of a node across this axis gives the thickness of the branch at that end and the point of its midline;
finally, each node is moved to the least-squares intersection of the midlines of its branches, the
mitre point of a corner. When the thicknesses of the two ends differ, the wall has a linearly varying
thickness. A wall without a determinate midline is refused: zero length or thickness, or faces of a
quadrilateral whose lengths differ by more than half of the longer one.

**Figure 20.5** — Wall described by four points of the outline: midline and end thicknesses

## 20.9 Inclined chords: the Résal effect

In a beam of variable depth, the inclined chord (soffit of a haunched span, slab of a box of
variable depth) carries its axial force along its own line. The shear force of the section, the
resultant of the stresses on the facet, therefore includes the transverse component of this force, and
the web carries only the remainder: this is the Résal effect (BPEL 91 art. 7.1.2; EN 1992-1-1
§ 6.2.1(1), terms $V_{ccd}$ and $V_{td}$). A chord of area $A_f$, with centroid
$(y_f, z_f)$ referred to that of the section, whose line has the slopes
$\mathrm{d}y_f/\mathrm{d}x$ and $\mathrm{d}z_f/\mathrm{d}x$, carries the force
$N_f = \sigma_f A_f$, where $\sigma_f$ is the linear stress of the section at that point:

$$ \sigma_f = \frac{N}{A} + \frac{M_y z_f}{I_y} - \frac{M_z y_f}{I_z},\qquad
V_{z,\text{web}} = V_z - \sum_f N_f\,\frac{\mathrm{d}z_f}{\mathrm{d}x},\qquad
V_{y,\text{web}} = V_y - \sum_f N_f\,\frac{\mathrm{d}y_f}{\mathrm{d}x} $$ (20.29)

The share carried by the chords is linear in the forces of the section, with factors that depend
only on the section:

$$ V_z - V_{z,\text{web}} = \mathbf{k}_z\cdot(N, M_y, M_z),\qquad
\mathbf{k}_z = \sum_f A_f\,\frac{\mathrm{d}z_f}{\mathrm{d}x}\left(\frac{1}{A},\ \frac{z_f}{I_y},\ -\frac{y_f}{I_z}\right) $$ (20.30)

**Figure 20.6** — Résal effect: the inclined chord carries part of the shear force

For two equal chords a distance $h$ apart, without a web, the bottom chord inclined at
$\alpha$, under a moment $M$ alone that puts the top chord in tension, the bottom chord
carries $N_f = -M/h$; if it rises by $\alpha$ as $x$ increases, (20.29)
leaves the web $V + (M/h)\tan\alpha$. keta recovers this value (588.16 kN for
$V_z = 500$ kN, $M_y = 1$ MN·m, $h = 2$ m and $\alpha$ = 10°). keta returns raw, signed values: it is up
to the user to read whether the effect relieves the web (a haunch that deepens towards the larger
moment) or loads it.

## 20.10 Transfer of the properties to the bar

A bar reads $A$, $I_y$, $I_z$, $J$, $A_{vy}$, $A_{vz}$ and, in
non-uniform torsion, $I_w$. The shear areas depend on Poisson's ratio, which belongs to the
material and not to the section. When a bar receives a parametric section whose areas are still the
provisional values of its shape, keta computes the energy-based areas (20.13) for the
$\nu$ of the material of the bar: closed forms (20.14) for the circle and the tube,
Saint-Venant solution of the rectangle in closed form, finite element solution on the actual outline
(fillets included) for the other shapes. A section used with two materials of different ratios is
duplicated, each copy carrying the areas of its $\nu$:

$$ \frac{1}{GA_v} \ \text{in the flexibility of the element},\qquad G = \frac{E}{2(1 + \nu)},\qquad A_v = A_v(\nu) $$ (20.31)

Areas entered by hand are kept; a zero area means a bar without shear deformation
(Euler-Bernoulli). A global option reverts to the classical factors $5/6$ and $0.9$ of the
shape formulae.

When the Saint-Venant problem has been solved for a section (systematically for a polygon entered in
a model), the result is attached to the section and shared by all the bars that use it: it replaces
$J$, $A_{vy}$ and $A_{vz}$. The area and the bending second moments of area remain those
of the closed forms or of the Green integrals, which are already exact. The warping constant of a
parametric I section is the closed form of the table; for another section, it is given to the bar by
the non-uniform torsion analysis (chapter 19). Composite bars made of several parts cast at different
dates (steel girder and slab, box cast in several pours) are sections transformed part by part,
$A^* = \sum n_i A_i$, $I_y^* = \sum n_i\bigl(I_{y,i} + A_i (z_i - z_G)^2\bigr)$,
$J^* = \sum (G_i/G_\text{ref})\,J_i$, carried by an element on rigid arms up to their centroid;
their treatment is that of staged construction (chapter 10).

## 20.11 Scope

- the section is in one piece; several disjoint regions are refused by the warping computation,
which has no meaning component by component about a common centre;

- curved edges are polygons: the $J$ of a circle divided into $n$ sides carries the
geometric error of the inscribed polygon, of the order of $2\pi^2/(3n^2)$ on the area;

- a bar polygon must be given in its principal axes (product of inertia below 5 % of the larger
second moment of area); keta does not rotate the section;

- the plastic section modulus is computed only for the rectangle, the circle, the tube, the I and the
box;

- a composite section is weighted by the Young's moduli alone: $J$ and the shear areas are the
true rigidities only if the Poisson's ratios are equal;

- thin-walled theory knows only one material per graph and neglects effects of order $t/L$,
fillets and shear lag;

- the non-uniform torsion of the bar handles only doubly symmetric sections (chapter 19), even though
the shear centre and $I_w$ are computed for any section; the monosymmetry coefficients are not
computed.

# Chapter 21 Reinforced and prestressed concrete sections

A concrete section does not respond linearly: concrete in tension cracks, concrete in compression
becomes plastic, steel yields, and prestress imposes on its tendons an elongation that the concrete
does not share. The elastic properties of chapter 20 are therefore no longer sufficient; for each
action effect $(N, M_y, M_z)$, the strain plane of the section that balances it with the laws of
the materials must be found. This is the problem dealt with in this chapter, at serviceability
(stresses, cracking, curvature) and at the ultimate limit state (resisting moment, interaction
diagrams, required reinforcement), according to EN 1992-1-1 and, where the code provides them,
EN 1992-2 and the German national annex. It also covers prestress losses at section level, the shear,
torsion and punching shear formulae, slab reinforcement by Wood-Armer, and the checks of composite
beams (EN 1994-1-1) and steel members (EN 1993-1-1 and 1-5) that keta provides. Prestress at the scale
of the structure (profile, friction, equivalent loads) is in chapter 8, creep and shrinkage in
chapter 9, the material nonlinearity of the bars of a framework in chapter 18, fire resistance in
chapter 23.

keta computes values here: neutral axes, stresses, crack widths, resisting moments, steel areas. It
pronounces no verdict: it does not itself compare a utilisation ratio with 1, and it applies no
partial factors other than those the user gives it.

## 21.1 Assumptions

- plane sections remain plane (Navier-Bernoulli): the strain is a plane
$\varepsilon(y, z) = \varepsilon_0 + \kappa_y z - \kappa_z y$, positive in tension;

- bonded reinforcing bars and bonded tendons have the strain of the concrete at their level,
increased by their initial strain; an unbonded tendon keeps the force of its initial elongation;

- concrete is described by a uniaxial law (parabola-rectangle, bilinear relation, Sargin law,
straight line), without tensile strength unless a softening law is explicitly given; steels by a
symmetric uniaxial law;

- the laws are read as they are given: design values for the ultimate limit state, mean or
characteristic values without partial factor for serviceability;

- the section is a set of polygonal outlines with voids; steels are points; the concrete they
displace is deducted on request;

- shear force and torsion take no part in the equilibrium of the section: they are handled by the
separate formulae of EN 1992-1-1 § 6.2 to 6.4;

- creep enters the serviceability states through the effective modulus $E_{cm}/(1 + \varphi)$,
and the losses through the age-adjusted effective modulus method; the ultimate law is not stretched by
creep.

## 21.2 Design laws of the materials

### 21.2.1 Concrete: parabola-rectangle and simplified relations

The basic law is the parabola-rectangle of EN 1992-1-1 § 3.1.7(1), expression (3.17), written in
shortening $\varepsilon_c > 0$:

$$ \sigma_c = f_{cd}\left[1 - \left(1 - \frac{\varepsilon_c}{\varepsilon_{c2}}\right)^{n}\right]\ \ (0 \le \varepsilon_c \le \varepsilon_{c2}),\qquad
\sigma_c = f_{cd}\ \ (\varepsilon_{c2} \le \varepsilon_c \le \varepsilon_{cu2}) $$ (21.1)

The parameters are those of table 3.1: $n = 2$, $\varepsilon_{c2} = 2\ ‰$ and
$\varepsilon_{cu2} = 3.5\ ‰$ up to C50/60, and beyond

$$ n = 1.4 + 23.4\left(\frac{90 - f_{ck}}{100}\right)^4,\quad
\varepsilon_{c2} = 2.0 + 0.085\,(f_{ck} - 50)^{0.53}\ ‰,\quad
\varepsilon_{cu2} = 2.6 + 35\left(\frac{90 - f_{ck}}{100}\right)^4\ ‰ $$ (21.2)

($f_{ck}$ in MPa). The exponent and the two strains may also be given freely. The exponent 1
gives the bilinear relation of § 3.1.7(2), a straight line up to $f_{cd}$ at
$\varepsilon_{c3}$ then a plateau up to $\varepsilon_{cu3}$; keta derives
$\varepsilon_{c3} = 1.75\ ‰$ (beyond C50/60, $1.75 + 0.55\,(f_{ck} - 50)/40\ ‰$) and
$\varepsilon_{cu3} = \varepsilon_{cu2}$. For rectangular or T sections treated in closed form, the
rectangular stress block of § 3.1.7(3) is available: a stress $\eta f_{cd}$ over the depth
$\lambda x$, with

$$ \lambda = 0.8 - \frac{f_{ck} - 50}{400},\qquad \eta = 1 - \frac{f_{ck} - 50}{200}\qquad (f_{ck} > 50\ \text{MPa};\ 0.8 \text{ and } 1 \text{ below}) $$ (21.3)

At serviceability, cracked concrete follows a straight line of slope $E_{cm}$ (or the effective
modulus) in compression and carries nothing in tension.

**Figure 21.1** — Concrete laws plotted by keta: parabola-rectangle of C30/37 and of C70/85, bilinear relation of C30/37, Sargin law of C30/37 (mean values)

### 21.2.2 Concrete: Sargin law and tension softening

For nonlinear analysis, keta offers the law of EN 1992-1-1 § 3.1.5, expression (3.14), in
compression only up to $\varepsilon_{cu1}$:

$$ \frac{\sigma_c}{f_{cm}} = \frac{k\,\eta - \eta^2}{1 + (k - 2)\,\eta},\qquad
\eta = \frac{\varepsilon_c}{\varepsilon_{c1}},\qquad k = 1.05\,\frac{E_{cm}\,\varepsilon_{c1}}{f_{cm}} $$ (21.4)

Its parameters come from table 3.1 when only $f_{ck}$ is given: $f_{cm} = f_{ck} + 8$ MPa,
$E_{cm} = 22\,(f_{cm}/10)^{0.3}$ GPa, $\varepsilon_{c1} = 0.7\,f_{cm}^{0.31} \le 2.8\ ‰$,
$\varepsilon_{cu1} = 3.5\ ‰$ up to C50/60 and
$2.8 + 27\,\bigl((98 - f_{cm})/100\bigr)^4\ ‰$ beyond. For C30/37, keta finds
$E_{cm} = 32.84$ GPa, $\varepsilon_{c1} = 2.16\ ‰$ and $k = 1.96$, and its stresses
reproduce (21.4) to within rounding. When used for a resistance, this law must be given
with design values, as § 5.8.6(3) requires. A variant of the parabola-rectangle carries a softening
tension branch: a straight line up to $f_t$ at $\varepsilon_{cr} = f_t/E_t$, then a linear
decrease to zero at

$$ \varepsilon_{tu} = \varepsilon_{cr} + \frac{2\,G_f}{f_t\,l_c} $$ (21.5)

so that the energy dissipated per unit crack area is the fracture energy $G_f$, whatever the
band width $l_c$ (crack band method). A conventional law for class T3 ultra-high performance
fibre-reinforced concretes (NF P18-710) is also available for fibre sections.

### 21.2.3 Reinforcing steel and structural steel

Reinforcing steel follows the design diagram of figure 3.8 of EN 1992-1-1, symmetric in compression:
a straight line of slope $E_s$ up to $\varepsilon_{yd} = f_{yd}/E_s$, then an inclined branch
up to the limit strain $\varepsilon_{ud}$,

$$ \sigma_s = f_{yd} + (f_{td} - f_{yd})\,\frac{\varepsilon_s - \varepsilon_{yd}}{\varepsilon_{ud} - \varepsilon_{yd}}\qquad (\varepsilon_{yd} \le \varepsilon_s \le \varepsilon_{ud}) $$ (21.6)

The resistance engine describes it by $(f_{yd}, E_s, f_{td}, \varepsilon_{ud})$, by default
B500 with $f_{td} = 525/1.15$ MPa at $\varepsilon_{ud} = 25\ ‰$; it may be extended by a
plateau at $f_{td}$ up to a higher limit strain. A horizontal branch is obtained with
$f_{td} = f_{yd}$. In fibre sections, the same figure is described by the class of the steel,
$k = (f_t/f_y)_k$ and $\varepsilon_{uk}$: the branch passes through
$(\varepsilon_{uk}, k f_{yd})$ and stops at $\varepsilon_{ud} \le \varepsilon_{uk}$.
Structural steel follows a symmetric bilinear law with a plateau at $f_y$, with an optional limit
strain.

**Figure 21.2** — Design laws of the steels plotted by keta: B500B (figure 3.8, k = 1.08, εuk = 5 %, εud = 4.5 %) and Y1860S7 strand (figure 3.10, εuk = 3.5 %, εud = 3.15 %)

### 21.2.4 Prestressing steel

Prestressing steel follows the design diagram of figure 3.10 (§ 3.3.6(7)): a straight line of slope
$E_p$ (195 GPa for strands, 205 GPa for bars) up to $f_{pd} = f_{p0,1k}/\gamma_s$, then either
an inclined branch towards $(\varepsilon_{uk}, f_{pk}/\gamma_s)$ bounded at
$\varepsilon_{ud}$, or a horizontal plateau without limit:

$$ \sigma_p = f_{pd} + \left(\frac{f_{pk}}{\gamma_s} - f_{pd}\right)\frac{\varepsilon_p - f_{pd}/E_p}{\varepsilon_{uk} - f_{pd}/E_p}\qquad (\varepsilon_p \le \varepsilon_{ud}) $$ (21.7)

The default law is that of the Y1860S7 strand: $f_{p0,1k} = 1640$ MPa, $f_{pk} = 1860$ MPa,
$\varepsilon_{uk} = 3.5\ \%$, $\varepsilon_{ud} = 0.9\,\varepsilon_{uk}$. A tendon enters the
section through its position, its area and its initial elongation $\Delta\varepsilon_p(0)$
(§ 6.1(6), figure 6.1): its strain when the concrete at its level is unstrained. keta computes this
elongation from the stress $\sigma_{pm}$ of the tendon and the stress $\sigma_{cp}$ of the
concrete at its level, by inverting the law on its rising branch:

$$ \Delta\varepsilon_p(0) = \sigma_p^{-1}(\sigma_{pm}) - \frac{\sigma_{cp}}{E_{cm}} $$ (21.8)

A bonded tendon then carries $\sigma_p\bigl(\Delta\varepsilon_p(0) + \varepsilon(y_p, z_p)\bigr)$.
An unbonded tendon keeps the stress of its initial elongation; at the ultimate limit state, this stress
is increased by a fixed $\Delta\sigma_{p,ULS}$ (100 MPa recommended, § 5.10.8(2)), without
exceeding the top of the law.

## 21.3 Equilibrium of a section

### 21.3.1 Strain plane and stress resultants

Everything that follows rests on the same computation: the resultants of a strain plane. With
$\varepsilon(y, z) = \varepsilon_0 + \kappa_y z - \kappa_z y$, the forces are, at the origin of the
axes of the section,

$$ \begin{pmatrix} N \\ M_y \\ M_z \end{pmatrix} = \int_{A_c} \sigma_c(\varepsilon)\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ z \\ -y \end{pmatrix}\mathrm{d}A
+ \sum_i A_i\,\sigma_i\bigl(\varepsilon_{0,i} + \varepsilon(y_i, z_i)\bigr)\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ z_i \\ -y_i \end{pmatrix} $$ (21.9)

where the sum is over the bars and the bonded tendons, each with its initial strain
$\varepsilon_{0,i}$ (zero for a bar cast in an unloaded section; negative for a bar that has
restrained creep and shrinkage). A positive $M_y$ puts the top fibre in tension (chapter 2). The
tangent stiffness $\partial(N, M_y, M_z)/\partial(\varepsilon_0, \kappa_y, \kappa_z)$ is obtained by
the same integrals with the tangent modulus of the laws.

### 21.3.2 Boundary integrals

Under a plane, the stress in the concrete depends only on the coordinate $s$ taken along the
strain gradient. With $t$ the transverse coordinate, Green's theorem reduces each surface integral
to an integral over the outlines, traversed anticlockwise (the voids clockwise):

$$ \int_{A_c} f(s)\,t^k\,\mathrm{d}A = -\oint f(s)\,\frac{t^{k+1}}{k+1}\,\mathrm{d}s $$ (21.10)

less the same integral around each disc of concrete displaced by a steel. Along an edge, the strain
is linear; the edge is cut at the kinks of the law (zero strain, start of the plateau, yield limits of a
steel), and each piece is integrated by a 16-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature after the change of
variable $\xi \mapsto \xi^2(3 - 2\xi)$, whose derivative vanishes at both ends. The result is
exact for polynomial laws (parabola of exponent 2, bilinear relation, straight line), exact to within
rounding for a fractional exponent or for the Sargin law, and the change of variable absorbs the
fractional power of a parabola at the start of its plateau. There is neither a mesh nor a subdivision
of the compression zone. On a 0.30 × 0.60 m rectangle reinforced with 3 HA 20 at 5 cm from the edge, in
C30/37 at $f_{cd} = 17$ MPa, at pivot B with a steel having an inclined branch, keta finds a
resisting moment of 213.972 kN·m, the value of the closed form of the parabola-rectangle diagram
($\alpha = 17/21$, $k_a = 99/238$) to within $10^{-15}$.

The fibre section engine, used for moment-curvature curves and nonlinear bars (chapter 18), instead
divides a rectangle into fibres of area $A_j$, to which the bars and tendons are added, and
replaces the integral by the sum $\sum_j \sigma(\varepsilon_j) A_j$.

### 21.3.3 Search for the equilibrium state

For a given action effect $\mathbf{S} = (N, M_y, M_z)$, the state of the section is the plane
$\mathbf{e} = (\varepsilon_0, \kappa_y, \kappa_z)$ that solves $\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{e}) = \mathbf{S}$.
keta seeks it by the damped Newton method:

$$ \bigl(\mathbf{K}_t(\mathbf{e}_k) + \mu\,\mathbf{K}_0\bigr)\,\Delta\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{S} - \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{e}_k),\qquad
\mathbf{e}_{k+1} = \mathbf{e}_k + 2^{-j}\Delta\mathbf{e} $$ (21.11)

The starting point is the plane of the section on its initial moduli: with concrete without tension,
the tangent at the zero plane is that of the steels alone, and the first step would be wrong. The step
is halved (at most 40 times) as long as the norm of the residual does not decrease. When the tangent
allows no progress (nothing in compression and nothing bonded responds to the residual), it is
supplemented by a share $\mu$ of the initial stiffness, multiplied by 10 at each failure and
reduced after each success; beyond $\mu = 10^3$, the action effect is declared beyond the reach of
the section. The moments are compared with the forces through the size of the section. The computation
stops when the relative residual falls below $10^{-13}$, or below $10^{-10}$ if it can no
longer decrease, in at most 200 iterations. A state in which a vertex of the concrete, a bonded tendon
or a bar exceeds the limit strain of its law is refused: it is a resistance, not a state. The cracked
state derives from a convex potential and its plane is unique; with a softening law (Sargin beyond
$\varepsilon_{c1}$, tension softening), the plane found is an equilibrium whose uniqueness is not
proven.

The fibre engine uses the same method, with the full $3\times 3$ tangent matrix, a gradient
descent on the maximum secant stiffness when the tangent is singular (plastic plateau), a line search
that stays within the strain limits of the laws, a tolerance of $10^{-8}$ relative to each
component of the target, and at most 100 iterations.

### 21.3.4 Composite section without a mesh

A section made of several materials (steel girder under a slab, concrete cast in two strengths,
encased section) is described by its parts, each with its outlines and its law: concrete
(parabola-rectangle, Sargin, tension softening), straight line, bilinear steel with a plateau or with
hardening. All share the strain plane, as do the bonded point reinforcements:

$$ \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{e}) = \sum_{\text{parts } p} \int_{A_p} \sigma_p(\varepsilon)\,(1, z, -y)\,\mathrm{d}A + \sum_i A_i\,\sigma_i(\varepsilon_{0,i} + \varepsilon_i)\,(1, z_i, -y_i) $$ (21.12)

Each integral is the boundary integral (21.10) of the law of its part; a part lodged
within another is drawn as a void of the latter. The state under an action effect comes from the same
damped iteration, and keta gives what each part carries and the stress in each steel. The resisting
moment of a composite section is not computed by this engine.

## 21.4 Stresses at serviceability

### 21.4.1 Rectangular or T section

For a rectangular section, or a T section with its flange in compression, reinforced with two
layers (tension $A_s$ at the effective depth $d$, compression $A_{s2}$ at $d_2$), in
uniaxial bending with an axial force applied at the gross centroid, keta gives the two states of
EN 1992-1-1 § 7.1(2). The modular ratio accounts for creep through the effective modulus (expression
7.20):

$$ \alpha_e = \frac{E_s}{E_{c,\text{eff}}} = \frac{E_s\,(1 + \varphi)}{E_{cm}} $$ (21.13)

In the uncracked state, the whole section participates, the steels being counted with
$\alpha_e - 1$ (the steel replaces the concrete). In the cracked state, the concrete in tension is
neglected, the tension steels are counted with $\alpha_e$ and the compression steels with
