$\alpha_e - 1$. The neutral axis $x$ is the depth at which the resultant of the linear stress
block passes through the point of application of the action; in simple bending, it is the root of the
equation of first moments:

$$ \frac{b\,x^2}{2} + (\alpha_e - 1)\,A_{s2}\,(x - d_2) = \alpha_e\,A_s\,(d - x),\qquad
\sigma_c = -\frac{M\,x}{I_{II}},\quad \sigma_s = \alpha_e\,\frac{M\,(d - x)}{I_{II}} $$ (21.14)

keta finds it by bisection on an interval, scanned between 0 and $4h$, where the function
changes sign; a section that cannot balance the action in the cracked state (tension over the whole
depth) is refused. For the 0.30 × 0.60 m rectangle reinforced with 3 HA 20 ($d = 0.55$ m) under
150 kN·m, without creep ($\varphi = 0$, $E_{cm} = 32.84$ GPa, $\alpha_e = 6.09$), keta
finds $x = 0.1272$ m, $\sigma_s = 313.5$ MPa and $\sigma_c = -15.49$ MPa, the values of
the hand solution of (21.14). The cracking moment is the moment that brings the bottom fibre
of the uncracked state to $f_{ct,\text{eff}}$ (by default $f_{ctm}$ of table 3.1,
$0.30\,f_{ck}^{2/3}$ up to C50/60 and $2.12\ln(1 + f_{cm}/10)$ beyond).

### 21.4.2 Uncracked and prestressed polygonal section

For an arbitrary polygonal section, as long as the concrete is uncracked, the state is linear:
concrete of the outlines with modulus $E_{cm}$, tendons with modulus $E_p$, bars with modulus
$E_s$. A bonded tendon follows the concrete at its level from its initial elongation, an unbonded
tendon keeps its force, a bar follows the concrete from a stress-free state:

$$ \sigma_{p,i} = E_p\,\Delta\varepsilon_{p,i}(0) + \frac{E_p}{E_{cm}}\,\sigma_c(y_i, z_i)\ \ \text{(bonded)},\qquad
\sigma_{p,i} = E_p\,\Delta\varepsilon_{p,i}(0)\ \ \text{(unbonded)},\qquad
\sigma_{s,j} = E_s\,\varepsilon_{0,j} + \frac{E_s}{E_{cm}}\,\sigma_c(y_j, z_j) $$ (21.15)

The concrete carries the action effect less the forces in the steels, and its stress is a plane:

$$ \sigma_c(y, z) = \frac{N_c}{A_c} + \text{bending due to } (M_{y,c}, M_{z,c}),\qquad
(N_c, M_{y,c}, M_{z,c}) = (N, M_y, M_z) - \sum_i A_i\,\sigma_i\,(1,\ z_i,\ -y_i) $$ (21.16)

These relations form a linear system. With bonded tendons, its solution is $N/A + Mz/I$ of the
transformed section $A_c + (E_p/E_{cm})A_p$ under the action effect and the decompression forces
$A_p E_p \Delta\varepsilon_p(0)$ applied in compression at the tendons. The concrete is that of the
outlines less the concrete displaced by the steels: one disc per tendon (the area of the duct while it
is empty, the area of the tendon once grouted or for a pretensioned wire), centred if necessary beside
the tendon, which bears on the wall of its duct, and counted for its area, its first moments and its
own second moment of area $a^2/(4\pi)$; on request, one disc per bar. A disc that extends outside
the concrete or overlaps another is refused. A plane reaches its extremes over polygons at vertices:
the extreme fibres are the vertex in greatest tension and the vertex in greatest compression of the
outlines. keta gives the stress in each tendon and each bar, that of the concrete at their level and
at any requested point (a point outside the concrete is refused), the extreme fibres and the strain
plane.

### 21.4.3 Cracked state and nonlinear state

When the concrete no longer follows a straight line, the state is the plane that balances the
action effect in the sense of (21.9). In the cracked state, the concrete is elastic in
compression and carries nothing in tension, the steels remaining elastic:

$$ \sigma_c(\varepsilon) = E_c\,\min(\varepsilon, 0),\qquad
\sigma_s = E_s\,(\varepsilon_{0,s} + \varepsilon),\qquad E_c = E_{cm}\ \text{or}\ \frac{E_{cm}}{1 + \varphi} $$ (21.17)

the effective modulus being given for a long-term action. In the nonlinear state, each material
follows its law: the concrete the parabola-rectangle, the Sargin law, the parabola-rectangle with
tension softening or a straight line; bonded tendons the law of prestressing steel from
$\Delta\varepsilon_p(0)$; bars the bilinear curve of figure 3.8. The force of a tendon at
decompression acts as an external compression at the tendon: for a rectangular or T section, the
equilibrium equation reduces to the classical cubic equation of the neutral axis. A section that the
action leaves in compression everywhere is in its uncracked state. On the previous rectangle, the
cracked state of the polygonal section reproduces the neutral axis and the steel stress of the closed
form.

### 21.4.4 Choice of state

EN 1992-1-1 § 7.1(2) allows the stresses to be computed on the uncracked section as long as the
flexural tensile stress does not exceed $f_{ct,\text{eff}}$. keta computes the uncracked state,
reads its largest concrete stress and switches to the cracked state beyond:

$$ \max_{\text{vertices}} \sigma_c^{I} \le f_{ct,\text{eff}} \ \Rightarrow\ \text{uncracked state};\quad \text{otherwise cracked state} $$ (21.18)

The choice is based on the given action effect alone. A section cracked by an earlier, larger action
effect remains cracked: keta does not know this, and it is then up to the user to request the cracked
state directly.

## 21.5 Moment-curvature and deflections

### 21.5.1 Moment-curvature curve

For a fibre section (rectangle, bars, bonded or unbonded tendons), keta plots the curve
$M(\kappa)$ at constant axial force: for each curvature, the strain at the centre
$\varepsilon_0$ is sought by bisection on the equation $N(\varepsilon_0, \kappa) = N_\text{Ed}$,
and the moment is read. The curve stops at the ultimate point, the largest curvature whose axial
equilibrium keeps all the fibres and all the bonded tendons within the limits of their law:

$$ \kappa_u = \max\bigl\{\kappa\ :\ \exists\,\varepsilon_0,\ N(\varepsilon_0, \kappa) = N_\text{Ed},\
\varepsilon_{\min,j} \le \varepsilon_{0,j} + \varepsilon_0 + \kappa\,z_j \le \varepsilon_{\max,j}\ \forall j\bigr\} $$ (21.19)

A limit strain may be imposed on steels with a plateau, which have none of their own. The curve is
plotted in bending about $y$; the ultimate point may be sought in any direction of bending.

**Figure 21.3** — Moment-curvature of a 0.30 × 0.60 m rectangle reinforced with 3 HA 20, computed by keta with fibres: concrete without tension and concrete with tension softening (fcm = 38 MPa, ft = 2.9 MPa, Gf = 140 N/m, lc = 0.10 m), B500B steel at fy = 500 MPa without partial factor

### 21.5.2 Mean curvature and deflection

For the rectangular or T section, the mean curvature of a cracked member interpolates the
curvatures of the two states according to EN 1992-1-1 § 7.4.3, expressions (7.18) and (7.19):

$$ \kappa = \zeta\,\kappa_{II} + (1 - \zeta)\,\kappa_I,\qquad
\zeta = 1 - \beta\left(\frac{\sigma_{sr}}{\sigma_s}\right)^2 = 1 - \beta\left(\frac{M_{cr}}{M}\right)^2 $$ (21.20)

with $\beta = 1$ for a single short-term loading and 0.5 for sustained or repeated loading;
$\zeta = 0$ below the cracking moment. The mid-span deflection of a simply supported beam under a
given moment diagram is the unit-load integral $\delta = \int_0^L \kappa(x)\,\bar m(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$,
$\bar m = x/2$ or $(L - x)/2$, computed by Simpson's rule on each half-span. Shrinkage adds the
curvature of expression (7.21),

$$ \frac{1}{r_{cs}} = \varepsilon_{cs}\,\alpha_e\,\frac{S}{I} $$ (21.21)

where $S$ is the first moment of the reinforcement about the centroid of the transformed
section (state I) or about the neutral axis (state II) and $I$ the corresponding second moment of
area. The deflection with shrinkage interpolates the total curvature with the same $\zeta$; it is
integrated by an adaptive 5-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature to $10^{-12}$ in relative terms, on
the pieces lying between the cracking points $|M| = M_{cr}$, located over 256 intervals and then
refined by bisection.

## 21.6 Ultimate resistance to combined bending and axial force

### 21.6.1 Ultimate strain planes: pivots A, B and C

At the ultimate limit state (EN 1992-1-1 § 6.1(5), figure 6.1), the strain plane of a section at
failure passes through one of three pivots. For a direction $\alpha$ of the neutral axis, keta
measures $s$ along $\mathbf{u} = (\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$, compression being on the side of
$\mathbf{u}$, and writes the plane $\varepsilon(s) = \varepsilon_\text{top} + g\,(s - s_\text{max})$,
$h = s_\text{max} - s_\text{min}$ being the depth of concrete in this direction. A parameter
$\tau \in [0, 3]$ runs through the planes from the most tensioned to the most compressed:

$$ \begin{aligned}
&\text{A } (0 \le \tau \le 1): & \varepsilon_\text{top} &= \varepsilon_a - \tau(\varepsilon_a + \varepsilon_{cu}), &
g &= \max_i \frac{\varepsilon_\text{top} - \varepsilon_{\lim,i}}{s_\text{max} - s_i}\\
&\text{B } (1 \le \tau \le 2): & \varepsilon_\text{top} &= -\varepsilon_{cu}, &
\varepsilon(s_\text{min}) &= (2 - \tau)\,\varepsilon^{A}_\text{bot}\\
&\text{C } (2 \le \tau \le 3): & \varepsilon_\text{top} &= -\varepsilon_{cu} + (\tau - 2)(\varepsilon_{cu} - \varepsilon_{c}), &
\varepsilon\bigl(s_\text{max} - (1 - \tfrac{\varepsilon_c}{\varepsilon_{cu}})\,h\bigr) &= -\varepsilon_c
\end{aligned} $$ (21.22)

At pivot A, the first steel to reach its limit $\varepsilon_{\lim,i}$ sets the slope: a bar at
$\varepsilon_{ud} - \varepsilon_{0,i}$, a bonded tendon limited to
$\varepsilon_{ud} - \Delta\varepsilon_p(0)$; $\varepsilon_a$ is the smallest of these limits,
and $\tau = 0$ is the uniform tension $\varepsilon_a$. Without steel, the furthest concrete
fibre serves as the pivot. At pivot B, the most compressed fibre is at crushing
$-\varepsilon_{cu}$ and the opposite fibre goes from its value at the end of pivot A to zero. At
pivot C, the plane rotates about the point located at $(1 - \varepsilon_c/\varepsilon_{cu})\,h$
from the most compressed fibre, up to the uniform compression $-\varepsilon_c$. For the
parabola-rectangle, $\varepsilon_{cu} = \varepsilon_{cu2}$ and $\varepsilon_c = \varepsilon_{c2}$;
for another law, they are its compressive limit strain and the strain at which it reaches its largest
compression ($\varepsilon_{cu1}$ and $\varepsilon_{c1}$ for the Sargin law). A law that
carries tension is refused: its tensile limit would be one more pivot. The axial force decreases as
$\tau$ increases.

**Figure 21.4** — Ultimate strain planes: rotation about pivots A, B and C

### 21.6.2 Resisting moment in a given direction

The resisting moment at the axial force $N_\text{Ed}$, in the direction $\theta$ of
$(M_y, M_z)$, is sought in two loops. For a direction $\alpha$ of the neutral axis, the axial
force decreases with $\tau$: bisection gives the plane that carries $N_\text{Ed}$, to within
$10^{-15}$ on $\tau$; if $N_\text{Ed}$ lies outside the interval
$[N(\tau = 3), N(\tau = 0)]$, it is beyond the axial capacity. Then $\alpha$ is swept over
144 values around the circle; the component of the resisting moment perpendicular to the requested
direction changes sign where that moment is parallel to it (and in the same sense), and a second
bisection refines $\alpha$. A sample at which this component is already zero, to within
$10^{-12}$ of the moment, is retained as it is: this is the case of a doubly symmetric section
loaded along a principal axis ($\theta = 0$ or $\pi/2$), where the component vanishes
without changing sign. On the 0.40 × 0.60 m rectangle reinforced with 6 HA 20 of figure 21.5, under
$N = -1$ MN, keta thus finds 431.1 kN·m for $\theta = 0$ and 247.9 kN·m for
$\theta = \pi/2$. The direction is defined by

$$ \mathbf{M}_R(\alpha) \times \mathbf{d}_\theta = 0,\quad \mathbf{M}_R\cdot\mathbf{d}_\theta > 0,\qquad
\mathbf{d}_\theta = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta),\qquad M_{Rd} = |\mathbf{M}_R| $$ (21.23)

The concrete is integrated by the boundary integrals of its law, by default the parabola-rectangle
of table 3.1 for $f_{ck}$ at $f_{cd}$; the bars follow (21.6) from their
initial strain. The steels are points: by default, the concrete they displace is not deducted, as in
design charts; on request, the disc of each tendon and each bar is removed.

### 21.6.3 Interaction diagrams

The $N$-$M$ interaction diagram of a direction $\alpha$ is the sequence of the
resultants of the ultimate planes for $\tau$ distributed over $[0, 3]$ (61 points by
default), in a single pass and without root finding. The $M_y$-$M_z$ diagram at constant
axial force is obtained by rotating $\theta$; keta also gives, for a fibre section, the curve of
the ultimate points of several bending directions at constant $N$, the steel with a plateau then
being limited (1 % by default).

**Figure 21.5** — 0.40 × 0.60 m rectangle reinforced with 6 HA 20, C30/37 (fcd = 17 MPa), B500: N-My diagram and My-Mz diagram under N = −1 MN, computed by keta

The ends of the diagram can be checked by hand. In uniform tension $\varepsilon_{ud}$, the six
bars carry $6\,A_s\,f_{td} = 0.860$ MN. In uniform compression
$-\varepsilon_{c2} = -2\ ‰$, the concrete carries $bhf_{cd} = 4.080$ MN and the bars, still
elastic since $2\ ‰ < \varepsilon_{yd} = 2.17\ ‰$, $6 A_s E_s \varepsilon_{c2} = 0.754$ MN:
keta finds 4.834 MN, and not $bhf_{cd} + A_s f_{yd} = 4.900$ MN. The capacity is sought at fixed
axial force, in the direction of the moment; the capacity along a ray of the space
$(N, M_y, M_z)$, at constant eccentricity, is not computed.

### 21.6.4 Prestressed sections

In the resistance engine, a bonded tendon follows the plane from its initial elongation,
$\sigma_p\bigl(\Delta\varepsilon_p(0) + \varepsilon\bigr)$, and its limit enters pivot A; an
unbonded tendon carries $\min\bigl(\sigma_p(\Delta\varepsilon_p(0)) + \Delta\sigma_{p,ULS},\ \sigma_{p,\max}\bigr)$
whatever the plane. A section without bars or without tendons is accepted. To connect the section to a
structural analysis, keta gives the primary action of the prestress, opposite to the resultant of the
tendon forces at their initial elongation,

$$ (N, M_y, M_z)_\text{iso} = \sum_i \bigl(-P_i,\ -P_i z_i,\ P_i y_i\bigr),\qquad P_i = A_{p,i}\,\sigma_p\bigl(\Delta\varepsilon_{p,i}(0)\bigr) $$ (21.24)

and splits a total effect of the prestress, read on the framework, into this primary part and a
secondary (hyperstatic) part, the difference of the two. The tendons are assumed normal to the
section: their inclination is not taken into account in the section.

### 21.6.5 Rectangular section with the rectangular stress block

For the rectangular or T section, keta also computes the resisting moment with the rectangular stress
block (21.3), the top fibre at $\varepsilon_{cu3}$ and the steels elastic-perfectly
plastic (without strain limit): the neutral axis $x$ is the root, found by bisection, of the force
equilibrium, and the moment is taken at the gross centroid,

$$ -\eta f_{cd}\,A_c(\lambda x) + A_s\,\sigma_s + A_{s2}\,\sigma_{s2} = N,\qquad
M_{Rd} = F_c\,z_c + A_s\sigma_s\,d + A_{s2}\sigma_{s2}\,d_2 - N\,z_G $$ (21.25)

with $f_{cd} = \alpha_{cc}f_{ck}/\gamma_c$. For the 0.30 × 0.60 m rectangle with 3 HA 20 and
$\alpha_{cc} = 1$, keta finds $x = 85.4$ mm and $M_{Rd} = 211.38$ kN·m, the value of
$A_s f_{yd}(d - \lambda x/2)$.

## 21.7 Shear, torsion and punching shear

These checks are the formulae of EN 1992-1-1, given one by one with their clause, and those of the
German national annex where it modifies them; they return values, which the user combines.

### 21.7.1 Shear

The resistance without shear reinforcement is expression (6.2):

$$ V_{Rd,c} = \max\Bigl(C_{Rd,c}\,k\,(100\,\rho_l f_{ck})^{1/3} + k_1\sigma_{cp},\ v_{\min} + k_1\sigma_{cp}\Bigr)\,b_w d,\qquad
k = 1 + \sqrt{200/d} \le 2 $$ (21.26)

with $\rho_l \le 0.02$, $\sigma_{cp} = N_\text{Ed}/A_c < 0.2 f_{cd}$, and, in the EN,
$C_{Rd,c} = 0.18/\gamma_c$, $k_1 = 0.15$, $v_{\min} = 0.035\,k^{3/2} f_{ck}^{1/2}$
(6.3N); in the German annex $C_{Rd,c} = 0.15/\gamma_c$, $k_1 = 0.12$ and
$v_{\min} = (0.0525/\gamma_c)\,k^{3/2} f_{ck}^{1/2}$ for $d \le 600$ mm. For a slab with
$d = 0.25$ m, $\rho_l = 0.8\ \%$ and C30/37, keta gives 163.93 kN/m. With vertical
reinforcement (§ 6.2.3), the lever arm is $z = 0.9d$ (limited in the German annex by
$\max(d - c_{v,l} - 30\ \text{mm},\ d - 2c_{v,l})$), and

$$ \frac{A_{sw}}{s} = \frac{V_\text{Ed}}{z\,f_{ywd}\cot\theta}\quad (6.8),\qquad
V_{Rd,\max} = \frac{\alpha_{cw}\,b_w z\,\nu_1 f_{cd}}{\cot\theta + \tan\theta}\quad (6.9),\qquad
\nu = 0.6\left(1 - \frac{f_{ck}}{250}\right) $$ (21.27)

The German annex gives $\nu_1 = 0.75\,\min(1;\ 1.1 - f_{ck}/500)$, the concrete contribution
$V_{Rd,cc} = 0.5 \cdot 0.48 f_{ck}^{1/3}(1 - 1.2\sigma_{cd}/f_{cd})\,b_w z$ and the inclination
$\cot\theta = (1.2 + 1.4\sigma_{cd}/f_{cd})/(1 - V_{Rd,cc}/V_\text{Ed})$ limited to
$[1; 3]$ (1.75 for bridges). The minimum ratio is
$\rho_{w,\min} = 0.08\sqrt{f_{ck}}/f_{yk}$ (9.5N). The shear force is not reduced for
$\Delta F_{td}$ (6.18), and the resistance of regions uncracked in bending, governed by the
principal tensile stress (6.4), is not computed.

### 21.7.2 Torsion, web-flange shear and construction joints

Torsion follows the equivalent box of § 6.3.2: for a given thickness $t_\text{ef}$ (in the
German annex, twice the distance from the face to the axis of the longitudinal reinforcement),
$A_k = (b - t_\text{ef})(h - t_\text{ef})$ and $u_k = 2(b + h - 2t_\text{ef})$, and

$$ \tau_t t_\text{ef} = \frac{T_\text{Ed}}{2A_k}\ (6.26),\quad
\frac{A_{sw}}{s} = \frac{T_\text{Ed}\tan\theta}{2A_k f_{yd}},\quad
A_{sl} = \frac{T_\text{Ed}\,u_k\cot\theta}{2A_k f_{yd}}\ (6.28),\quad
T_{Rd,\max} = 2\nu\alpha_{cw} f_{cd} A_k t_\text{ef}\sin\theta\cos\theta\ (6.30) $$ (21.28)

The transverse reinforcement of a flange follows expression (6.21),
$A_{sf}/s_f = v_\text{Ed} h_f/(\cot\theta_f\,f_{yd})$. The shear along a construction joint
follows expression (6.25), $v_{Rdi} = c f_{ctd} + \mu\sigma_n + \rho f_{yd}(\mu\sin\alpha + \cos\alpha)$
($1.2\mu$ in the steel term for the German annex), from which keta derives the required
reinforcement ratio and the limit $0.5\nu f_{cd}$.

### 21.7.3 Punching shear

For a rectangular internal column $a\times b$, the basic control perimeter at $2d$ is
$u_1 = 2(a + b) + 4\pi d$ (§ 6.4.2), the design shear stress
$v_\text{Ed} = \beta V_\text{Ed}/(u_1 d)$ (6.38) and the resistance

$$ v_{Rd,c} = C_{Rd,c}\,k\,(100\,\rho_l f_{ck})^{1/3} + 0.1\,\sigma_{cp} \ge v_{\min} + 0.1\,\sigma_{cp},\qquad
\rho_l = \sqrt{\rho_{ly}\rho_{lz}} \le 0.02\quad (6.47) $$ (21.29)

The German annex reduces $C_{Rd,c}$ to $0.18/\gamma_c\,(0.1\,u_0/d + 0.6)$ when
$u_0/d < 4$, limits $\rho_l$ by $0.5 f_{cd}/f_{yd}$, sets $\beta$ according to the
position of the column (1.10 internal, 1.40 edge, 1.50 corner, 1.35 and 1.20 at the end and at the
corner of a wall) and $v_{Rd,\max} = 1.4\,v_{Rd,c}$. The method of the Swiss standard SIA 262
(§ 4.3.6) is also available: $\tau_{cd} = 0.3\eta_t\sqrt{f_{ck}}/\gamma_c$, slab rotation at level
of approximation III $\psi = 1.2\,(r_s/d)(f_{sd}/E_s)(m_{sd}/m_{Rd})^{1.5}$,
$k_r = 1/(0.45 + 0.18\,\psi d k_g)$ and $V_{Rd,c} = k_r\tau_{cd}\,d\,u_\text{red}$.

## 21.8 Serviceability limit states

### 21.8.1 Stress limits

Clause 7.2 of EN 1992-1-1 names five stress limits:

$$ \sigma_c \le k_1 f_{ck},\quad \sigma_c \le k_2 f_{ck},\quad \sigma_s \le k_3 f_{yk},\quad
\sigma_s \le k_4 f_{yk},\quad \sigma_p \le k_5 f_{pk} $$ (21.30)

the compression of the concrete under the characteristic combination in exposure classes XD, XF and
XS, the compression under quasi-permanent loads below which creep is linear, the tension of the
reinforcement under the characteristic combination and under an imposed deformation, and the mean
stress of the tendons. The recommended values are 0.6, 0.45, 0.8, 1 and 0.75; a national annex may give
others. The tendon limit refers to $f_{pk}$, as in the 2004 text and its French version; the
consolidated British reprints give $f_{yk}$, a misprint that no corrigendum has corrected. For a
serviceability state (uncracked, cracked or nonlinear), keta gives the ratio of each stress to its
limit: the compression at the most compressed vertex, the largest tension in the bars and that in the
tendons. It is up to the user to know which combination each ratio belongs to.

### 21.8.2 Crack width

Crack width follows § 7.3.4 of EN 1992-1-1, the 2010 corrigendum included:

$$ w_k = s_{r,\max}\,(\varepsilon_{sm} - \varepsilon_{cm}),\qquad
\varepsilon_{sm} - \varepsilon_{cm} = \frac{\sigma_s - k_t\,\dfrac{f_{ct,\text{eff}}}{\rho_{p,\text{eff}}}\,(1 + \alpha_e\,\rho_{p,\text{eff}})}{E_s} \ \ge\ 0.6\,\frac{\sigma_s}{E_s} $$ (21.31)

$$ s_{r,\max} = k_3\,c + k_1 k_2 k_4\,\frac{\phi}{\rho_{p,\text{eff}}},\qquad
\rho_{p,\text{eff}} = \frac{A_s + \xi_1 A_p'}{A_{c,\text{eff}}},\qquad \xi_1 = \sqrt{\xi\,\frac{\phi_s}{\phi_p}} $$ (21.32)

($\sqrt{\xi}$ with tendons alone), and $s_{r,\max} = 1.3\,(h - x)$ (7.14) when the bars are
spaced more than $5(c + \phi/2)$ apart or when no bonded steel lies within the effective area. The
default coefficients are $k_1 = 0.8$ (high bond), $k_2 = 0.5$ (bending), $k_3 = 3.4$,
$k_4 = 0.425$ and $k_t = 0.6$ (short term). On a polygonal section, the geometric quantities
are read along the strain gradient of the cracked state: $h$ is the depth of the section in this
direction, $x$ the compression depth, $d$ the depth of the centroid of the tension bars (of
the bonded tendons in tension if there is no bar). The effective area is the concrete lying within

$$ h_{c,\text{ef}} = \min\bigl(2.5\,(h - d),\ (h - x)/3\bigr) $$ (21.33)

of the fibre in greatest tension, obtained by cutting each outline with a straight line: it is exact
for a polygon with voids and an oblique neutral axis. The $h/2$ term of the standard is never
governing when a zone is in compression, since $(h - x)/3 < h/3$. The bars and bonded tendons
whose centre lies within this band enter $\rho_{p,\text{eff}}$; $\sigma_s$ is the change in
stress of the bar in greatest tension from the zero strain of the concrete at its level, $E_s$
times the strain of the plane, or failing a bar that of the bonded tendon in greatest tension.
Expression (7.10) carries $\xi_1$ since the 2010 corrigendum; the earlier text carried
$\xi_1^2$, a form that the German version keeps and that keta offers as an option. A section
without a compression zone (tie, figure 7.1 c) is refused by this computation: the chain (7.8) to
(7.14) remains available on its own, the user giving the effective area.

**Figure 21.6** — Crack width of an arbitrary section: depths read along the strain gradient of the cracked state and effective area Ac,eff

For the 0.30 × 0.60 m rectangle with 3 HA 20 under 150 kN·m, the cover and diameter of expression (7.11) being left at their default values (30 mm and 16 mm,
not those of the bars of the section), keta finds $h_{c,\text{ef}} = 125$ mm, $\rho_{p,\text{eff}} = 2.51\ \%$,
$s_{r,\max} = 210$ mm and $w_k = 0.246$ mm, by hand as on the polygonal section. The variant
of the German annex computes $s_{r,\max} = \phi/(3.6\,\rho_\text{eff}) \le \sigma_s\phi/(3.6 f_{ct,\text{eff}})$
without prestress.

### 21.8.3 Simplified control and minimum reinforcement

The minimum area of crack-control reinforcement follows expressions (7.1) and (7.2) for rectangles
and webs:

$$ A_{s,\min}\,\sigma_s = k_c\,k\,f_{ct,\text{eff}}\,A_{ct},\qquad
k_c = 0.4\left[1 - \frac{\sigma_c}{k_1\,(h/h^*)\,f_{ct,\text{eff}}}\right] \in [0, 1] $$ (21.34)

with $h^* = \min(h, 1\ \text{m})$, $k_1 = 1.5$ in compression and $2h^*/(3h)$ in
tension. The coefficient $k$ for self-equilibrating stresses is that of the German annex, 0.8 for
$h \le 300$ mm and 0.5 for $h \ge 800$ mm, linear in between; the EN value (1.0 to 0.65) and
the $k_c$ of T sections and boxes are not coded. Control without direct calculation follows table
7.2DE of the German annex, written as a formula, $\sigma_s = \sqrt{3.48\cdot 10^6\,w_k/\phi_s^*}$
(MPa, $w_k$ and $\phi_s^*$ in mm), with the diameter conversion
$\phi_s = \phi_s^* f_{ct,\text{eff}}/2.9$ MPa for minimum reinforcement; tables 7.2N and 7.3N of the
EN are not coded.

### 21.8.4 Brittle failure

The uncracked state is linear: under the sustained action effect increased by a moment $M$ of
direction $\theta$, the stress at a vertex $j$ is
$\sigma_j = \sigma_{cp,j} + M/W_j(\theta)$, where $\sigma_{cp,j}$ is its stress under the
prestress and the sustained action effect and $W_j$ the section modulus of the transformed section
at that point. The cracking moment is the smallest moment that brings a vertex to $f_{ct}$:

$$ M_{cr} = \min_j\,\bigl(f_{ct} - \sigma_{cp,j}\bigr)\,W_j(\theta) $$ (21.35)

The prestress therefore shifts the cracking moment by $-\sigma_{cp}W$. Computed on the section
with the tendons released (zero initial elongations), it is the moment $M_\text{rep}$ of
EN 1992-2 § 6.1(109) b), from which the minimum reinforcement that prevents brittle failure is
derived:

$$ A_{s,\min} = \frac{M_\text{rep}}{z_s\,f_{yk}}\quad (6.101\text{a}),\qquad
A_{s,\min}\,f_{yk} + A_p\,\Delta\sigma_p \ge \frac{M_\text{rep}}{z}\quad (6.101\text{b}),\quad
\Delta\sigma_p = \min(0.4\,f_{ptk};\ 500\ \text{MPa}) $$ (21.36)

$z_s$ is the lever arm of the reinforcing bars at the ultimate limit state, read on the
ultimate plane that balances the axial force: the distance between the point of application of the
resultant of the compressed concrete and that of the resultant of the tension bars. On the
0.30 × 0.60 m rectangle with no reinforcement counted, $M_{cr} = f_{ctm} bh^2/6 = 52.14$ kN·m.
Method a) of § 6.1(109), by reduction of the prestressing area, is not coded.

### 21.8.5 Fatigue

keta gives the quantities of the simplified method of § 6.8: the design fatigue strength of concrete
(6.76), the reference stress range of straight and bent bars at $N^* = 10^6$ cycles (table 6.3N:
162.5 MPa; 175 MPa in the German annex), and the damage-equivalent stress range:

$$ f_{cd,fat} = k_1\,\beta_{cc}(t_0)\,f_{cd}\left(1 - \frac{f_{ck}}{250}\right),\qquad
\Delta\sigma_{s,equ}(N^*) = \lambda_s\,(\sigma_{s,\max} - \sigma_{s,\min}) $$ (21.37)

with $k_1 = 0.85$ (EN) or 1.0 (German annex). The stresses come from the serviceability states
described above; the damage computation of the structure under traffic is in chapter 14.

## 21.9 Prestress losses at section level

The losses are computed on the transformed serviceability section: concrete of the outlines less the
voids and the displaced concrete, modulus $E_{cm}$; bonded tendons at their initial elongation,
unbonded tendons at a frozen force. The elastic shortening of a tendon under the prestress alone is
$(E_p/E_{cm})\,|\sigma_c|$, $\sigma_c$ being the stress of the concrete at its level
(§ 5.10.5.1): this is the whole loss of a pretensioned wire, and for $n$ post-tensioned tendons
stressed one after another, the mean share $j = (n - 1)/(2n)$ (expression 5.44). Between
$t_0$ and $t$, each steel follows the concrete at its level, which shortens by shrinkage, by
creep under the quasi-permanent stress present at $t_0$, and by the deformation, on the adjusted
modulus $E_{cm}/(1 + \chi\varphi)$, due to the change of stress that the losses themselves cause.
Written for each steel $i$ (tendon or bar) of modulus $E_i$, compatibility gives the linear
system

$$ \Delta\sigma_i + \frac{E_i}{E_{cm}}\,(1 + \chi\varphi)\sum_j f_{ij}\,A_j\,\Delta\sigma_j
= -\varepsilon_{cs}\,E_i + \rho\,\Delta\sigma_{pr,i} - \frac{E_i}{E_{cm}}\,\varphi\,\sigma_{c,QP,i},\qquad
f_{ij} = \frac{1}{A_c} + \mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{I}_c^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{e}_j $$ (21.38)

where $\Delta\sigma_i$ is the tension lost (positive), $f_{ij}$ the stress of the concrete
at the level of steel $i$ per unit force at steel $j$ (eccentricities $\mathbf{e}$ in
biaxial bending), $\chi$ the ageing coefficient and $\rho$ the retained share of the pure
relaxation, both 0.8 in EN 1992-1-1 and adjustable; relaxation is zero for a bar,
$\varepsilon_{cs} < 0$ is a shortening and $\sigma_c < 0$ a compression. With a single
tendon and no bar, this is expression (5.46); on a 0.50 × 1.00 m rectangle with a tendon of
1500 mm² at an eccentricity of 0.35 m, at $\varphi = 2$, $\varepsilon_{cs} = -300\cdot 10^{-6}$
and 40 MPa of pure relaxation, keta finds 169.60 MPa, the value of (5.46). With several tendons, the
same compatibility couples them: tendons at the same point lose as a single tendon of their total area,
and the loss of one tendon relieves the concrete at the others. Bars restrain creep and shrinkage: they
go into compression, unload the concrete, and the loss of the tendons is reduced. keta gives the loss
of each steel by cause (creep, shrinkage, relaxation) and the plane of the change of stress in the
concrete.

After the losses, each steel keeps the initial strain

$$ \varepsilon_{0,i} = \frac{\sigma_i - \Delta\sigma_i}{E_i} - \frac{\sigma_{c,i}^{\,\text{after}}}{E_{cm}} $$ (21.39)

its strain when the concrete at its level, at the stress that the losses have left there, is
unloaded. Carried into the section, for tendons as for bars, it makes the uncracked state under the
same action effect the state after losses, from which subsequent actions start: imposed load,
cracking, resisting moment. A sequence of ages can be computed with the laws of EN 1992-1-1: creep and
shrinkage of annex B, shrinkage counted from tensioning, relaxation of expressions (3.28) to (3.30) at
time $t - t_0$, without the 500 000 h cap of § 3.3.2(8). Each value is the cumulative loss since
$t_0$ on the section as it is at $t_0$.

## 21.10 Design of reinforcement

### 21.10.1 Arbitrary section

For a polygonal section under $(N_\text{Ed}, M_{y,\text{Ed}}, M_{z,\text{Ed}})$, the user lays
out the bars and gives them relative weights $w_i$; keta seeks the smallest factor
$\omega$ such that the section with areas $A_i = \omega w_i$ carries the action effect:

$$ \omega^* = \min\bigl\{\omega \in [0, \omega_{\max}]\ :\ M_{Rd}(\omega;\ N_\text{Ed}, \theta_\text{Ed}) \ge |M_\text{Ed}|\bigr\},\qquad \theta_\text{Ed} = \operatorname{atan2}(M_{z,\text{Ed}}, M_{y,\text{Ed}}) $$ (21.40)

by bisection to within $10^{-15}\,\omega_{\max}$, assuming that the resistance increases with
$\omega$. The total area is $\omega^*\sum w_i$. The distribution between the bars is
therefore the one the user sets: there is neither optimisation by independent zones, nor several
simultaneous action effects, nor prestress in this design, nor automatic choice of the diameters.

### 21.10.2 Rectangular section

For a rectangle in combined bending and axial force, keta computes the steel areas in closed form from
the reduced moment, with the parabola-rectangle diagram and the steel of figure 3.8:

$$ \mu = \frac{M_{Eds}}{b d^2 f_{cd}},\qquad \mu = \alpha_R\,\xi\,(1 - k_a\xi),\qquad
A_{s1} = \frac{1}{\sigma_{s1}}\left(\frac{M_{Eds}}{\zeta d} + N_\text{Ed}\right) $$ (21.41)

where $M_{Eds}$ is the moment referred to the tension steel, $\alpha_R$ and $k_a$ the
exact coefficients of the parabola-rectangle block for the concrete strain, and
$\zeta = 1 - k_a\xi$. The plane is at pivot A (steel at its limit, concrete strain sought by
bisection) or at pivot B ($\varepsilon_{cu2}$, $\xi$ the root of a quadratic equation). Beyond
$\xi_{\lim}$ (0.45 up to C50/60 for a linear elastic analysis, German annex 5.4), the compression
zone is frozen and the remainder $\Delta M = M_{Eds} - M_{\lim}$ is carried by a couple of steels:
$A_{s1} = (M_{\lim}/(\zeta d) + \Delta M/(d - d_2) + N_\text{Ed})/\sigma_{s1}$ and
$A_{s2} = \Delta M/\bigl((d - d_2)\,|\sigma_{s2}|\bigr)$.

## 21.11 Slabs and shells

### 21.11.1 Wood-Armer moments

A slab reinforced with two layers, along $x$ and along a direction $y'$ at the angle
$\alpha$ to $x$, must resist the moment tensor
$\mathbf{S} = \begin{bmatrix} m_x & m_{xy} \\ m_{xy} & m_y \end{bmatrix}$ on every yield
line. A layer of capacity $X$ per unit width resists, on a line of normal $\mathbf{n}$,
$X(\mathbf{e}_1\cdot\mathbf{n})^2$ (Johansen's criterion); the condition is that
$X\mathbf{e}_1\mathbf{e}_1^{\mathsf T} + Y\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\mathsf T} - \mathbf{S}$ be positive
semi-definite, $\mathbf{a} = (\cos\alpha, \sin\alpha)$. It reduces to the orthogonal case on
Armer's transformed tensor:

$$ s'_{11} = m_x - 2m_{xy}\cot\alpha + m_y\cot^2\alpha,\qquad
s'_{12} = \frac{m_{xy} - m_y\cot\alpha}{\sin\alpha},\qquad s'_{22} = \frac{m_y}{\sin^2\alpha} $$ (21.42)

and the minimum of $X + Y$ is in closed form (Wood's rules, 1968):

$$ X = s'_{11} + |s'_{12}|,\quad Y = s'_{22} + |s'_{12}|;\qquad
\text{if } X < 0:\ X = 0,\ Y = s'_{22} + \frac{s'^2_{12}}{|s'_{11}|}\quad (\text{and symmetrically}) $$ (21.43)

and no steel is required when both remain negative. The top steel resists $\mathbf{S}$, the
bottom steel $-\mathbf{S}$ (a positive moment puts the $+z$ face of the facet in tension,
chapter 24); the design moments are returned signed, positive on the top face and negative on the bottom
face. Since the method is not linear, the moments must be combined before design; the envelope over
several combinations then takes the maximum of the top values and the minimum of the bottom values.
For $(m_x, m_y, m_{xy}) = (10, -8, 3)$ kN·m/m, keta gives
$m_{x,\text{top}} = 10 + 9/8 = 11.125$ and $m_{y,\text{bot}} = -(8 + 9/10) = -8.9$.

### 21.11.2 Assessment of given capacities

Given the capacities of the four layers, the utilisation of a face is the smallest
$\lambda \ge 0$ such that $\lambda\mathbf{C} - \mathbf{S}$ is positive semi-definite,
$\mathbf{C} = X\mathbf{e}_1\mathbf{e}_1^{\mathsf T} + Y\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^{\mathsf T}$: it is the
largest ratio of action effect to capacity over all yield-line directions (Denton and Burgoyne, 1996).
The search over the angle is done exactly: the admissible set of $\lambda$ is a half-line whose
origin is 0 or a root of one of the three polynomial conditions for a positive semi-definite
$2\times 2$ matrix,

$$ \lambda C_{11} - S_{11} \ge 0,\quad \lambda C_{22} - S_{22} \ge 0,\quad
(\lambda C_{11} - S_{11})(\lambda C_{22} - S_{22}) - (\lambda C_{12} - S_{12})^2 \ge 0 $$ (21.44)

and these candidates are tried in increasing order. The utilisation is infinite when a direction in
tension has no capacity; keta also returns the normal of the critical line.

### 21.11.3 Sandwich model for shells

For a shell element subjected to the six stress resultants, the forces are carried by two layers at
the levels of the steels $z_\text{top} > 0$ and $z_\text{bot} < 0$ from the mid-surface:

$$ \mathbf{n}_\text{top} = \frac{\mathbf{m} - \mathbf{n}\,z_\text{bot}}{z_\text{top} - z_\text{bot}},\qquad
\mathbf{n}_\text{bot} = \frac{\mathbf{n}\,z_\text{top} - \mathbf{m}}{z_\text{top} - z_\text{bot}} $$ (21.45)

component by component, each layer being designed by the same kernel on its membrane tensor
(Clark-Nielsen method); keta gives the steel forces and the remaining principal concrete force. A
second formulation, that of Baumann (EN 1992-1-1 annex F) with the strut at 45°, distributes
$n/2 \pm m/z$ between the layers ($z = 0.9d$ by default), gives the orthogonal steels of each
layer, $Z_x = N_x + |N_{xy}|$ and $Z_y = N_y + |N_{xy}|$, or $Z_x = 0$ and
$Z_y = N_y + N_{xy}^2/|N_x|$ when $N_x < -|N_{xy}|$, and treats the transverse shear force
$v_0 = \sqrt{q_x^2 + q_y^2}$ by (21.26) then (21.27).

## 21.12 Composite beams and steel members

### 21.12.1 Steel-concrete composite beams

For composite beams, keta gives the formulae of EN 1994-1-1 with their intermediate quantities:
resistance of headed studs (§ 6.6.3.1) and reduction for profiled sheeting with transverse ribs
(§ 6.6.4.2), effective width (§ 5.4.1.2), plastic resisting moment in sagging, plastic neutral axis in
the slab, the flange or the web, and partial shear connection by the linear interpolation (6.1),
plastic resisting moment in hogging with the class of the compressed plates, uncracked and cracked
elastic section, long-term modular ratios (5.6), deflection of a simply supported span with its
construction stage, minimum degree of shear connection (6.12 to 6.17), cracked lengths for global
analysis (15 % of the span), stiffness of the inverted U-frame and table 6.1 for lateral-torsional
buckling, composite columns (§ 6.7: $N_{pl,Rd}$, plastic $N$-$M$ interaction, effective
flexural stiffness, simplified method) and beams with large web openings according to the SCI P355
guide (Lawson and Hicks, 2011). For example:

$$ P_{Rd} = \frac{\min\bigl(0.8 f_u\,\pi d^2/4,\ 0.29\,\alpha d^2\sqrt{f_{ck}E_{cm}}\bigr)}{\gamma_v},\qquad
M_{Rd} = M_{pl,a,Rd} + (M_{pl,Rd} - M_{pl,a,Rd})\,\eta,\qquad n_L = n_0\,(1 + \psi_L\varphi_t) $$ (21.46)

The steel section enters through its actual dimensions and its tabulated $A$ and
$W_{pl}$, fillets included.

### 21.12.2 Steel members

Likewise, keta gives the check formulae of EN 1993-1-1 and EN 1993-1-5: class of the plates
(table 5.2), buckling factors $k_\sigma$ and reduction of slender plates,

$$ \bar\lambda_p = \frac{b/t}{28.4\,\varepsilon\sqrt{k_\sigma}},\quad
\rho = \frac{\bar\lambda_p - 0.055\,(3 + \psi)}{\bar\lambda_p^2} \le 1,\qquad
\chi = \frac{1}{\Phi + \sqrt{\Phi^2 - \bar\lambda^2}},\quad \Phi = \frac{1}{2}\bigl[1 + \alpha(\bar\lambda - 0.2) + \bar\lambda^2\bigr] $$ (21.47)

effective section under uniform compression, stiffeners on an elastic foundation (annex A.2),
cross-section resistances (shear, interaction with moment and axial force), flexural and
lateral-torsional buckling curves (tables 6.1 to 6.5), interaction factors of annexes A and B. For
$\bar\lambda = 1$ on curve b, keta finds $\chi = 0.5970$. The quantities that the standard
leaves to “an appropriate method” ($M_{cr}$, $N_{cr,T}$, deflections) come from the structural
analyses, in particular from non-uniform torsion (chapter 19).

## 21.13 Scope

- the serviceability states and the resistance apply to polygonal sections with voids and point
steels; the rectangular or T section in closed form is limited to uniaxial bending and two layers, the
flange being assumed in compression;

- the resistance engine accepts for the concrete only the parabola-rectangle (free exponent and
strains) and the Sargin law; laws carrying tension, the piecewise cubic law and structural steel as an
outline material do not enter it; the composite section without a mesh has no resisting moment;

- confined concrete, aged strength and modulus in the section laws, and the stretching of the ultimate
law by creep are not treated;

- the capacity is computed at fixed axial force in the direction of the moment, not along a ray of
the space $(N, M_y, M_z)$;

- the tendons are normal to the section; their inclination enters only the structural analysis
(chapter 8);

- the choice of the cracked state is based on the present action effect alone; the cracking history
is the user's responsibility;

- the principal tensile stress in the webs, the classification of the fibres inside and outside the
cover zone and the strain at the centroid on the ultimate plane are not provided;

- the design keeps the distribution of the bars given by the user; it chooses neither diameters, nor
layers, nor spacings.

# Chapter 22 Wind

This chapter deals with the action of wind on a framed structure: deck, pylon or pier. As in
EN 1991-1-4, the wind is split into a ten-minute mean velocity, which increases with height, and a
zero-mean turbulence. The mean velocity gives static loads; the turbulence gives random forces that
the structure filters through its natural modes. When the structure moves, the flow around it
changes: the resulting forces, called aeroelastic, modify the apparent damping and stiffness and can
lead to an instability, flutter. keta computes in turn the wind profile and the static load cases,
the response to turbulent wind in the frequency domain and then in the time domain, the critical
flutter velocity, the equivalent static loads and the concomitant internal forces.

The natural modes used are those of chapter 15, possibly computed about a loaded state
(chapter 17). Vortex shedding is the subject of a short section at the end of the chapter.

## 22.1 Assumptions

- the wind blows horizontally, in a given direction $\mathbf{d}$; the vertical component of
the direction supplied is ignored. $\mathbf{z}$ denotes the upward vertical and
$\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{z}\times\mathbf{d}$ the pitch axis, horizontal and perpendicular to the
wind;

- the mean velocity follows the logarithmic profile of EN 1991-1-4, with a constant orography
factor;

- the turbulence is a stationary Gaussian process; its three components $u$
(along-wind), $v$ (lateral) and $w$ (vertical) are mutually uncorrelated;

- the aerodynamic forces are computed by strips: each bar is a strip of length $L$,
represented by its midpoint, where the flow is two-dimensional. Cables receive no wind;

- a single aerodynamic section (reference width $B$, coefficients $C_D$,
$C_L$, $C_M$) applies to the whole model;

- the turbulence forces are quasi-steady (Davenport and Scanlan theory), possibly corrected by
an admittance; they are linear in $u$ and $w$;

- the structure responds linearly about its mean state, on a finite number of modes normalised
to unit mass;

- flutter is treated with the self-excited forces of the Theodorsen flat plate or with Scanlan
flutter derivatives given as a table.

## 22.2 Mean wind

### 22.2.1 EN 1991-1-4 profile

The terrain is characterised by its roughness length $z_0$ and the minimum height
$z_\text{min}$ of its category. The terrain factor, the roughness factor and the mean velocity
at height $z$ are those of EN 1991-1-4 §4.3.2, expressions (4.3) to (4.5):

$$ k_r = 0.19\left(\frac{z_0}{0.05}\right)^{0.07},\qquad
v_m(z) = k_r \ln\!\left(\frac{z_e}{z_0}\right) c_0\, v_b,\qquad z_e = \max(z, z_\text{min}) $$ (22.1)

where $v_b$ is the basic wind velocity and $c_0$ the orography factor. The turbulence
intensity and the peak velocity pressure are those of expressions (4.7) and (4.8):

$$ I_v(z) = \frac{k_I}{c_0 \ln(z_e/z_0)},\qquad
q_p(z) = \bigl[1 + 7\,I_v(z)\bigr]\,\tfrac12\,\rho\, v_m(z)^2 $$ (22.2)

with by default $k_I = 1$, $\rho = 1.225$ kg/m³, $v_b = 26$ m/s and
$z_0 = 0.05$ m (category II). Below $z_\text{min}$, the profile is held at its value at
$z_\text{min}$. The upper bound $z_\text{max} = 200$ m of the standard is not enforced.
The figure below shows $q_p(z)$ computed by keta for the terrain categories of the
standard.

**Figure 22.1** — Peak velocity pressure qp(z) of EN 1991-1-4 (vb = 26 m/s, c0 = 1) for terrain categories 0 to IV

### 22.2.2 Static load cases

The mean wind on a strip of width $B$ produces, per unit length, a drag along
$\mathbf{d}$, a lift along $\mathbf{z}$ and a pitching moment about
$\mathbf{a}$:

$$ D = q\,B\,C_D,\qquad L = q\,B\,C_L,\qquad M = q\,B^2\,C_M $$ (22.3)

The moment is positive nose-up: it raises the windward edge. keta builds two load cases of this
form, which differ by the pressure $q$:

- the peak wind case takes $q = q_p(z)$ from (22.2). It applies to each bar a
linearly varying load between the pressures at its two ends, evaluated at their heights, and
multiplies it by the yaw factor $\sin^2\beta = 1 - (\mathbf{e}_x\cdot\mathbf{d})^2$, where
$\mathbf{e}_x$ is the bar axis: only the component of the flow perpendicular to the bar loads
it (independence principle). A bar parallel to the wind receives nothing;

- the mean wind case of the turbulence model takes the mean pressure
$q = \tfrac12\rho\, v_m(z)^2$, with neither gust factor nor yaw factor, and with the
coefficients read from the incidence table at the mean incidence $\alpha_0$. It is the mean
state about which the following sections compute the fluctuations.

In both cases, the distributed moment, varying linearly between $m_1$ and $m_2$ at the
ends of a bar of length $L$, is replaced by two nodal moments
$L(m_1/3 + m_2/6)$ and $L(m_1/6 + m_2/3)$, which are its consistent nodal forces for a
linear interpolation.

### 22.2.3 Coefficients as functions of incidence

The coefficients depend on the incidence $\alpha$ of the wind on the deck. They are given by
a table $(\alpha_k, C_{D,k}, C_{L,k}, C_{M,k})$, with strictly increasing incidences,
interpolated linearly. The slope used by the turbulence and aeroelastic terms is that of the segment
containing $\alpha$:

$$ C'(\alpha) = \frac{C_{k+1} - C_k}{\alpha_{k+1} - \alpha_k},\qquad \alpha_k \le \alpha < \alpha_{k+1} $$ (22.4)

At a point of the table, the slope is the mean of the two adjacent segments. Outside the table,
the coefficients are held constant and their slopes are zero: a mean incidence outside the measured
range does not create a slope by extrapolation. A section described only by its coefficients and two
slopes $C_L'$, $C_M'$ is converted into a linear table over $[-1, 1]$ rad; its drag
has no slope.

## 22.3 Atmospheric turbulence

### 22.3.1 Spectra of the three components

At a point at height $z$, the mean velocity $U = v_m(z)$ and the standard deviation
$\sigma_u = I_v(z)\,U$ come from the profile. The transverse standard deviations are taken in
proportion, $\sigma_v = r_v\sigma_u$ and $\sigma_w = r_w\sigma_u$, with by default
$r_v = 0.75$ and $r_w = 0.5$. The along-wind integral length scale follows EN 1991-1-4,
expression (B.1),

$$ L_u(z) = 300\left(\frac{z_e}{200}\right)^{\alpha},\qquad \alpha = 0.67 + 0.05\ln z_0 $$ (22.5)

and the scales of the other components in proportion: $L_v = L_u/4$ and
$L_w = L_u/12$ by default. The standard gives only the $u$ component; the ratios for
$v$ and $w$ are user parameters, whose default values are usual orders of magnitude.

The one-sided spectrum $S_a(n)$ of component $a$, in (m/s)²/Hz, is written in reduced
form as a function of the reduced frequency $f = n\,L_a/U$. keta offers the form of
EN 1991-1-4, expression (B.2), applied to each component on its own length scale, and the von Kármán
forms:

$$ \frac{n\,S_a(n)}{\sigma_a^2} =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{6.8\,f}{(1 + 10.2\,f)^{5/3}} & \text{EN 1991-1-4, } a = u, v, w\\[2ex]
\dfrac{4\,f}{(1 + 70.8\,f^2)^{5/6}} & \text{von Kármán, } a = u\\[2ex]
\dfrac{4\,f\,(1 + 755.2\,f^2)}{(1 + 283.2\,f^2)^{11/6}} & \text{von Kármán, } a = v, w
\end{cases} $$ (22.6)

These forms are normalised: the integral of $S_a$ over all frequencies equals
$\sigma_a^2$. This is what permits their use with the standard deviation taken from the
profile; the Kaimal forms written with the friction velocity ($200 f/(1 + 50 f)^{5/3}$ and
similar) carry between 6 and 18 times the variance when used with $\sigma_u^2$, and keta does
not use them. Numerical integration of the three forms returns $\sigma_a^2$ to within
$4\cdot10^{-5}$ for the form of the standard and to within $2\cdot10^{-4}$ for the von
Kármán forms, whose published constant 70.8 is rounded.

**Figure 22.2** — Reduced turbulence spectra: EN 1991-1-4 (solid line) and von Kármán (u dashed, v and w dotted)

### 22.3.2 Spatial coherence

Two points $j$ and $k$ separated by $\Delta y$ laterally (along $\mathbf{a}$)
and by $\Delta z$ vertically see fluctuations that are less correlated the higher the
frequency. keta takes the Davenport coherence, real, per component:

$$ \mathrm{coh}_a(n) = \exp\!\left(-\,\frac{2\,n\,\sqrt{(C_{ay}\Delta y)^2 + (C_{az}\Delta z)^2}}{U_j + U_k}\right) $$ (22.7)

The reference velocity is the mean of the velocities at the two points. The default decay
coefficients are $C_{uy} = C_{uz} = 10$, $C_{vy} = C_{vz} = 6.5$ and
$C_{wy} = C_{wz} = 3$. The longitudinal separation (along the wind) does not enter the
coherence. The cross-spectral density of the velocities at points $j$ and $k$ is then

$$ S_{a,jk}(n) = \sqrt{S_{a,j}(n)\,S_{a,k}(n)}\;\mathrm{coh}_a(n), $$ (22.8)

and the three components form a symmetric $3N\times 3N$ cross-spectral matrix, with
uncoupled blocks, for $N$ points.

### 22.3.3 Aerodynamic admittance

A gust shorter than the width of the deck does not load all of it: the actual force is lower than
the quasi-steady force. This is accounted for by an admittance $\chi^2(K)$, a function of the
reduced frequency on the half-width $K = \omega B/(2U) = \pi n B/U$. keta offers four choices:
the quasi-steady admittance $\chi^2 = 1$; the exact Sears function for a flat plate traversed
by a vertical gust,

$$ S(K) = \bigl[J_0(K) - i J_1(K)\bigr]\,C(K) + i J_1(K),\qquad \chi^2 = |S(K)|^2, $$ (22.9)

where $C(K)$ is the Theodorsen function (22.18); the Liepmann approximation
$\chi^2 = 1/(1 + 2\pi K)$; a table $(K, \chi^2)$ interpolated linearly and held constant
outside its bounds. The admittance may differ for each of the three forces (drag, lift, moment). It
applies in amplitude, $\chi_r$ on force $r$, so that the cross terms of two forces carry
$\chi_r\chi_s$.

## 22.4 Response to turbulent wind

### 22.4.1 Buffeting forces

On a strip subjected to the fluctuations $u$ and $w$, the relative velocity and the
incidence change; to first order, the forces per unit length fluctuate by

$$ \begin{bmatrix} D \\ L \\ M \end{bmatrix}
= \frac{q B}{U}
\begin{bmatrix} 2C_D & C_D' - C_L \\ 2C_L & C_L' + C_D \\ 2B\,C_M & B\,C_M' \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} u \\ w \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{A}\begin{bmatrix} u \\ w \end{bmatrix},
\qquad q = \tfrac12\rho U^2 $$ (22.10)

with the coefficients and their slopes at the mean incidence $\alpha_0$. The drag follows
the wind, the lift is vertical and the moment acts about $\mathbf{a}$. The lateral component
$v$ (yaw) is not taken into account. Each strip has its own mean velocity, standard deviations
and length scales, evaluated at the height of its midpoint.

### 22.4.2 Modal forces

For mode $i$, $\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{i,s}$ denotes the vector (translation along
$\mathbf{d}$, vertical translation, rotation about $\mathbf{a}$) at the midpoint of strip
$s$, the mean of the modal values at its two nodes. The modal force is
$Q_i = \sum_s L_s\,\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{i,s}\cdot\mathbf{A}_s (u_s, w_s)$. Since $u$ and
$w$ are uncorrelated, the matrix of cross-spectral densities of the modal forces is

$$ \mathbf{S}_Q(n) = \mathbf{G}_u\,\mathbf{S}_u(n)\,\mathbf{G}_u^{\mathsf T} + \mathbf{G}_w\,\mathbf{S}_w(n)\,\mathbf{G}_w^{\mathsf T},
\qquad G_{c,is} = L_s\,\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{i,s}\cdot\mathbf{A}_{s,c}\,\chi_s(n) $$ (22.11)

where $\mathbf{S}_u$ and $\mathbf{S}_w$ are the cross-spectral matrices
(22.8) of the strip midpoints and $\mathbf{A}_{s,c}$ the column of
$\mathbf{A}$ associated with component $c$, each row being multiplied by the admittance
of its force. The cost of one frequency is $O(mN^2)$ for $m$ modes and $N$
strips.

### 22.4.3 Modal response

The modal coordinates $\mathbf{q}$, with unit masses, satisfy

$$ \ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \bigl(2\boldsymbol{\zeta}\boldsymbol{\Omega} + \mathbf{C}_\text{ae}\bigr)\dot{\mathbf{q}}
+ \bigl(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^2 + \mathbf{K}_\text{ae}\bigr)\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{Q}(t) $$ (22.12)

where $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ and $\boldsymbol{\zeta}$ are the natural circular
frequencies and the structural damping ratios, and $\mathbf{C}_\text{ae}$,
$\mathbf{K}_\text{ae}$ the aeroelastic matrices of the next section (zero if they are not
requested). With the transfer function $\mathbf{H}(\omega) = [\boldsymbol{\Omega}^2 + \mathbf{K}_\text{ae} - \omega^2\mathbf{I}
+ i\omega(2\boldsymbol{\zeta}\boldsymbol{\Omega} + \mathbf{C}_\text{ae})]^{-1}$, the spectral
density of a response $r = \boldsymbol{\psi}\cdot\mathbf{q}$ (a nodal displacement,
$\boldsymbol{\psi}$ being the row of the modes at that degree of freedom) and its variance
are

$$ S_r(n) = \boldsymbol{\psi}^{\mathsf T}\,\mathbf{H}(2\pi n)\,\mathbf{S}_Q(n)\,\mathbf{H}(2\pi n)^{*}\,\boldsymbol{\psi},
\qquad \sigma_r^2 = \int_0^\infty S_r(n)\,\mathrm{d}n $$ (22.13)

The cross terms between modes come directly out of this matrix product: there is no modal
combination rule, and two close modes whose forces are coherent add up as the physics requires. The
integral is computed by the trapezoidal rule on a logarithmic frequency grid of 300 intervals between
$0.02\,n_1$ and $5\,n_m$, supplemented by 120 points distributed over
$n_i(1 \pm 25\,\zeta_i)$ around each natural frequency: the resonance peak, of width
$\zeta_i n_i$, is thus described by several tens of points whatever the damping. The full modal
covariance $\mathbf{C}_q = \int \mathbf{H}\mathbf{S}_Q\mathbf{H}^{*}\,\mathrm{d}n$ is also
supplied; it is used for the equivalent loads.

### 22.4.4 Background and resonant parts, peak value

The background (quasi-static) part is the response obtained by replacing
$\mathbf{H}(\omega)$ by $\mathbf{H}(0) = (\boldsymbol{\Omega}^2 + \mathbf{K}_\text{ae})^{-1}$;
the resonant part is the remainder:

$$ \sigma_B^2 = \int_0^\infty \boldsymbol{\psi}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{H}(0)\,\mathbf{S}_Q\,\mathbf{H}(0)^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\psi}\,\mathrm{d}n,
\qquad \sigma_R^2 = \sigma_r^2 - \sigma_B^2 $$ (22.14)

For a lightly damped oscillator, $\sigma_R^2$ tends to the Davenport formula
$\pi n_0 S_Q(n_0)/(4\zeta\omega_0^4)$, from which it differs by a term in $O(\zeta)$. The
peak value over the duration $T$ (600 s by default) is $g\,\sigma_r$, with the Davenport
up-crossing rate and peak factor:

$$ \nu = \sqrt{\frac{\int n^2 S_r\,\mathrm{d}n}{\int S_r\,\mathrm{d}n}},\qquad
g = \sqrt{2\ln(\nu T)} + \frac{0.5772}{\sqrt{2\ln(\nu T)}} $$ (22.15)

The peak factor is set to zero when $\nu T \le 1$. The quantities supplied for each
requested response are $\sigma_r$, $\sigma_B$, $\sigma_R$, $\nu$ and $g$;
the extreme value is $\bar r \pm g\sigma_r$, where the mean response $\bar r$ comes from
the static analysis of the mean wind case. The up-crossing rate and the peak factor are those of the
total response: keta does not compute a separate peak factor for each part.

### 22.4.5 Aeroelastic terms

When the strip moves with velocity $(\dot x_D, \dot x_L)$ and rotates by $\theta$, the
relative wind becomes $u - \dot x_D$, $w - \dot x_L$ and the incidence
$\alpha_0 + \theta$. The corresponding quasi-steady forces, moved to the left-hand side of
(22.12), give the modal matrices

$$ C_{\text{ae},ij} = \sum_s L_s\,\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{i,s}^{\mathsf T}\bigl[\mathbf{A}_s \;\; \mathbf{0}\bigr]\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{j,s},
\qquad
K_{\text{ae},ij} = -\sum_s L_s\,q_s B\,\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{i,s}^{\mathsf T}
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & C_D' \\ 0 & 0 & C_L' \\ 0 & 0 & B\,C_M' \end{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\varphi}_{j,s} $$ (22.16)

The first is an aerodynamic damping coupled between modes, which includes the drag damping
$\rho U B C_D$; the second an aerodynamic stiffness due to the change in incidence. For a deck in
pure heave with mass per unit length $m$, the classical aerodynamic damping ratio
$\zeta_a = \rho U B (C_L' + C_D)/(4 m\omega)$ is recovered. Before any calculation, keta checks
that all the eigenvalues of the state-space system
$\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{0} & \mathbf{I}\\ -(\boldsymbol{\Omega}^2 + \mathbf{K}_\text{ae}) &
-(2\boldsymbol{\zeta}\boldsymbol{\Omega} + \mathbf{C}_\text{ae})\end{bmatrix}$ have a strictly
negative real part. Otherwise the calculation is refused: a negative total damping (galloping), a
divergence or a quasi-steady flutter has no stationary spectral response.

**Note.**

A second, simpler calculation takes only the drag under the $u$ component alone, with a
single spectrum, a single coherence coefficient and the square-root-of-sum-of-squares combination of
the modes. It ignores the cross terms between modes and is suitable only for well-separated
modes.

## 22.5 Flutter

### 22.5.1 Theodorsen flat plate

Flutter is a dynamic instability: beyond a critical velocity, the self-excited forces supply more
energy than the damping dissipates, and a coupled bending and torsional oscillation grows. For a flat
plate of half-chord $b$, whose elastic axis lies $a\,b$ behind mid-chord, in heave
$h$ (positive downwards) and pitch $\alpha$ (positive nose-up), Theodorsen's theory gives
the lift $L$ (upwards) and the moment $M$ about the elastic axis:

$$ \begin{aligned}
L &= \pi\rho b^2\bigl(\ddot h + U\dot\alpha - b a\,\ddot\alpha\bigr) + 2\pi\rho U b\, C(k)\,\Bigl[\dot h + U\alpha + b\bigl(\tfrac12 - a\bigr)\dot\alpha\Bigr]\\
M &= \pi\rho b^2\Bigl[b a\,\ddot h - U b\bigl(\tfrac12 - a\bigr)\dot\alpha - b^2\bigl(\tfrac18 + a^2\bigr)\ddot\alpha\Bigr]
+ 2\pi\rho U b^2\bigl(a + \tfrac12\bigr) C(k)\,\Bigl[\dot h + U\alpha + b\bigl(\tfrac12 - a\bigr)\dot\alpha\Bigr]
\end{aligned} $$ (22.17)

Theodorsen's circulation function, of the reduced frequency $k = \omega b/U$, is written with
the Hankel functions of the second kind:

$$ C(k) = F(k) + i\,G(k) = \frac{H_1^{(2)}(k)}{H_1^{(2)}(k) + i\,H_0^{(2)}(k)}
\;\approx\; 1 - \frac{0.165}{1 - 0.0455\,i/k} - \frac{0.335}{1 - 0.3\,i/k} $$ (22.18)

keta evaluates the exact form through Bessel functions ($C(0.1) = 0.8319 - 0.1723\,i$ and
$C(1) = 0.5394 - 0.1003\,i$, values from the tables of Bisplinghoff, Ashley and Halfman) for
the Sears admittance, and R. T. Jones's approximation, on the right, in the flutter calculations.
The difference between the two stays below 0.015 in modulus for $k$ from 0.01 to 10; it is
largest near $k = 0.4$.

**Figure 22.3** — Theodorsen function C(k) = F + iG, Bessel-function form, and Sears and Liepmann admittances, computed by keta

The two-degree-of-freedom section has mass per unit length $m$, pitch inertia $I$
about the elastic axis, static unbalance $S$, uncoupled circular frequencies
$\omega_h$, $\omega_\alpha$ and damping ratios $\zeta_h$, $\zeta_\alpha$. Its
equation of motion is
$\begin{bmatrix} m & S\\ S & I\end{bmatrix}\ddot{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{C}_s\dot{\mathbf{x}}
+ \mathbf{K}_s\mathbf{x} = (-L, M)$, where the forces (22.17) are moved to the
left-hand side as aerodynamic mass, damping and stiffness matrices that depend on $k$.

### 22.5.2 p-k method

At a given velocity $U$, each branch (the heave branch starts from $\omega_h$, the
pitch branch from $\omega_\alpha$) is tracked by the p-k method: the aerodynamic forces are
frozen at the current circular frequency $\omega$, the eigenvalues $p$ of the quadratic
problem

$$ \det\bigl[p^2\,\mathbf{M}(\omega) + p\,\mathbf{C}(\omega) + \mathbf{K}(\omega)\bigr] = 0 $$ (22.19)

are computed through its state-space form of double order, the eigenvalue with positive imaginary
part closest to $\omega$ is retained, and the process is repeated with
$\omega = \operatorname{Im} p$ until $\operatorname{Im} p$ no longer changes (relative
difference $10^{-9}$, at most 60 iterations). The damping ratio of the branch is
$\zeta = -\operatorname{Re} p/|p|$. The velocity is swept in regular steps over the requested
interval; the flutter velocity is the first at which the damping of the least damped branch changes
from positive to negative, refined by 60 bisections. The flutter frequency is that of the branch
that loses its damping.

### 22.5.3 Scanlan derivatives

A real deck is not a flat plate. Its self-excited forces in harmonic motion are measured in a wind
tunnel and given by the Scanlan flutter derivatives, functions of the reduced frequency
$K = B\omega/U$ on the full width. With $L$ and $h$ positive downwards, $M$
and $\alpha$ nose-up:

$$ \begin{aligned}
L &= qB\Bigl[K H_1^*\frac{\dot h}{U} + K H_2^*\frac{B\dot\alpha}{U} + K^2 H_3^*\,\alpha + K^2 H_4^*\frac{h}{B}\Bigr]\\
M &= qB^2\Bigl[K A_1^*\frac{\dot h}{U} + K A_2^*\frac{B\dot\alpha}{U} + K^2 A_3^*\,\alpha + K^2 A_4^*\frac{h}{B}\Bigr]
\end{aligned} $$ (22.20)

which amounts, in harmonic motion, to adding to the left-hand side the impedance

$$ \mathbf{Z} = -qK^2\begin{bmatrix} H_4^* + i H_1^* & B\,(H_3^* + i H_2^*)\\ B\,(A_4^* + i A_1^*) & B^2 (A_3^* + i A_2^*)\end{bmatrix}, $$ (22.21)

whose real part is a stiffness and whose imaginary part divided by $\omega$ is a damping. The
eight derivatives are given as a table as functions of $K$, interpolated linearly and held
constant outside the table. The drag derivatives $P_i^*$ are not taken into account. keta can
also derive the flat-plate derivatives from (22.17), and recovers the closed forms of
Simiu and Scanlan, for example $H_1^* = -2\pi F/K$ and
$A_2^* = -\pi(K/4 - G - KF/4)/(2K^2)$, to within $3\cdot10^{-14}$.

### 22.5.4 Multimodal analysis

On a model, each bar is a strip of length $L_s$ that moves as
$\mathbf{x}_s = (h_s, \alpha_s) = \mathbf{T}_s\mathbf{q}$: $h_s$ is minus the vertical
translation of its midpoint and $\alpha_s$ its rotation about $\mathbf{a}$, for each
retained mode. Drag is ignored. The modal impedance is the sum of the projected strip
impedances:

$$ \mathbf{Z}_q(U, \omega) = \sum_s L_s\,\mathbf{T}_s^{\mathsf T}\,\mathbf{Z}_s(U, \omega)\,\mathbf{T}_s $$ (22.22)

and the p-k problem becomes
$\det[p^2(\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{M}_a) + p(2\boldsymbol{\zeta}\boldsymbol{\Omega} + \mathbf{C}_a)
+ \boldsymbol{\Omega}^2 + \mathbf{K}_a] = 0$, each branch starting from a natural circular
frequency (tolerance $10^{-10}$, at most 100 iterations). The strips carry either the
Theodorsen matrices (22.17) or the Scanlan derivatives. Two modes of a section model
return the velocity of the two-degree-of-freedom calculation; a simply supported deck, whose bending
and torsional modes are sines, reduces exactly to a section with masses
$1/\sum_s L_s\varphi_s^2$.

**Important.**

The critical velocity is detected by the sweep. A range of negative damping that opens and
closes between two velocities of the sweep is not seen: the step must be reduced if several branches
cross in the interval. Nor does the calculation say whether the flutter is pure torsional or
coupled: reading the branches shows it.

## 22.6 Time-domain response

### 22.6.1 Wind field synthesis

A step-by-step analysis needs velocity histories at the $N$ strip midpoints that respect the
spectra and the coherences. keta uses the spectral representation of Shinozuka and Deodatis with
double-indexed frequencies. For one component ($u$ or $w$), let $\mathbf{H}(n)$ be
the Cholesky factor of the $N\times N$ cross-spectral matrix,
$\mathbf{S}(n) = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{H}^{*}$; the velocity at point $j$ is

$$ v_j(t) = \sum_{m=1}^{j}\sum_{l=1}^{n_f}\sqrt{2\,\Delta n}\,\bigl|H_{jm}(n_{ml})\bigr|\cos\bigl(2\pi n_{ml}t + \phi_{ml}\bigr),
\qquad n_{ml} = (l-1)\,\Delta n + \frac{m}{N}\Delta n $$ (22.23)

with $\Delta n = n_\text{max}/n_f$ and phases $\phi_{ml}$ uniform on
$[0, 2\pi[$, drawn by a generator with a fixed seed, independent of the platform (the Davenport
coherence being real, the phase angles of the terms of $\mathbf{H}$ are zero). The sum is
evaluated by one fast Fourier transform per point, over the period $T = N/\Delta n$ divided
into a power-of-2 number of steps, at least four times the number of frequencies. All the
frequencies being distinct, the cosines are orthogonal over one period: the time variance and
covariances of the series are exactly $\sum_{ml}\Delta n\,H_{jm}H_{km}$, that is the
discretised target spectrum, and not a statistical estimate. The variance carried differs from the
integral of the continuous spectrum by the discretisation in $\Delta n$ and by the truncation:
the part of the spectrum beyond $n_\text{max}$ is lost.

### 22.6.2 Step-by-step integration

The modal forces are formed at each step with the quasi-steady matrix (22.10),
without admittance (the admittance is a frequency filter that has no direct equivalent in time).
The modal system (22.12), with its aeroelastic terms if requested, is integrated by
the average-acceleration Newmark method, unconditionally stable and second-order accurate:

$$ \Bigl[\boldsymbol{\Omega}^2 + \mathbf{K}_\text{ae} + \frac{2}{\Delta t}(2\boldsymbol{\zeta}\boldsymbol{\Omega} + \mathbf{C}_\text{ae}) + \frac{4}{\Delta t^2}\mathbf{I}\Bigr]\mathbf{q}_{k+1} = \mathbf{Q}_{k+1} + \dots $$ (22.24)

The force history of one period is repeated (two periods by default); the first is discarded as
the transient. For each requested displacement, keta supplies the retained series, its standard
deviation about its mean, its maximum and its minimum. On a 200 m deck in twenty strips, without
admittance, with three modes and 1024 frequencies up to 2 Hz, the mean of the standard deviations of
four realisations recovers the standard deviation of the spectral calculation of the mid-span
deflection to within 0.1 %.

## 22.7 Equivalent static loads

A spectral calculation gives standard deviations of responses, not a load distribution that could
be entered in a static analysis to obtain the concomitant internal forces. keta builds this
distribution by Kasperski's load-response correlation method. For loads $\mathbf{F}$ with
covariance $\mathbf{C}_F$ and a target response $r = \mathbf{I}\cdot\mathbf{F}$, the
load

$$ \mathbf{F}_e = g\,\frac{\mathbf{C}_F\,\mathbf{I}}{\sqrt{\mathbf{I}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{C}_F\,\mathbf{I}}} $$ (22.25)

gives exactly $r(\mathbf{F}_e) = g\,\sigma_r$, since
$\mathbf{I}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{C}_F\mathbf{I} = \sigma_r^2$, and it is the most probable load
distribution among those that produce this value. In modal space, with the covariance
$\mathbf{C}_q$ of the modal coordinates and $r = \boldsymbol{\psi}\cdot\mathbf{q}$, one
forms $\mathbf{q}_e = g\,\mathbf{C}_q\boldsymbol{\psi}/\sqrt{\boldsymbol{\psi}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{C}_q\boldsymbol{\psi}}$,
then the inertia forces

$$ \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{M}\,\boldsymbol{\Phi}\,\boldsymbol{\Omega}^2\,\mathbf{q}_e $$ (22.26)

which reproduce these modal amplitudes in a static analysis, since
$\mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\varphi}_i\omega_i^2 = \boldsymbol{\varphi}_i$. The
background and resonant parts and the cross terms between modes are included together. A linear
static analysis of this case returns the target peak value $g\sigma_r$ to rounding, and
supplies at the same time all the concomitant internal forces. For a single mode, the load reduces
to $g\,\sigma_{q_i}\omega_i^2\mathbf{M}\boldsymbol{\varphi}_i$. The total design load is the sum
of the mean wind case and this peak load.

## 22.8 Nonlinear loop

On a structure in high tension or high compression (cable-stayed deck, arch, pylon), the axial
force modifies the natural frequencies, and the wind itself modifies the axial force. keta iterates
the following chain, to second order (chapter 17):

- second-order static analysis under the permanent loads, the mean wind and, from the second
iteration on, the equivalent peak load; the axial force of each bar is taken from it;

- natural modes about this axial force (geometric stiffness);

- spectral response of the target response on these modes, then peak load
(22.26) by the modal load-response correlation;

- second-order static analysis under permanent loads, mean wind and peak: extreme value of the
target response and new axial force.

The iteration stops when the standard deviation and the extreme of the target response change by
less than $10^{-6}$ in relative value (at most 20 iterations, 6 modes by default). Without axial
force, it returns the ordinary spectral calculation in two iterations. On a simply supported beam of
span $L$ tensioned by a force $T$, the frequency of the first bending mode becomes

$$ f_1 = f_0\,\sqrt{1 + \frac{T L^2}{\pi^2 EI}} $$ (22.27)

and the response decreases accordingly. The loop relies on the geometric stiffness of the axial
force: it does not take the tangent state of a large-displacement analysis with cables.

## 22.9 Concomitant internal forces

The design of a section requires triplets of concomitant internal forces, for example
$(N, M_y, M_z)$, and not three extremes taken separately. For $k$ Gaussian effects with
mean $\mathbf{m}$ and covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$, the equiprobability ellipsoid
$(\mathbf{E} - \mathbf{m})^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{E} - \mathbf{m}) = g^2$
contains the peak states. Following Capra and Davidovici (*Calcul dynamique des structures en zone
sismique*, 1980), keta replaces it by the vertices of a circumscribed polygon or polyhedron. For
two effects with standard deviations $\sigma_a$, $\sigma_b$ and correlation $\rho$,
the eight sides are the tangents

$$ \frac{x}{\sigma_a} \pm \frac{y}{\sigma_b} = \pm\, g\sqrt{2(1 \pm \rho)},\qquad |x| \le g\sigma_a,\quad |y| \le g\sigma_b $$ (22.28)

($x$, $y$ deviations from the mean), cut by the rectangle of peak values; each side
touches the ellipse at a point inside the side. For three effects, this octagon is built in each of
the three coordinate planes (24 vertices), and the third coordinate of each vertex is its
conditional mean
$E_c = m_c + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{c,ab}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab}^{-1}(E_a - m_a, E_b - m_b)$. A
rank-deficient covariance is treated in its principal axes: an octagon in the plane at rank 2,
$\mathbf{m}\pm g\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ at rank 1, the mean alone at rank 0.

**Figure 22.4** — Capra and Davidovici octagon circumscribed to the equiprobability ellipse (σa = 2, σb = 1, ρ = 0.6), computed by keta

The polyhedron takes a given covariance. keta supplies the covariance of the displacements
through the modal covariance; that of the internal forces of a section is not computed
directly.

## 22.10 Vortex shedding

A bluff section in a steady wind sheds alternating vortices at the frequency
$n = St\,U/b$. Resonance with a mode of frequency $n_1$ occurs at the critical velocity, and
its sensitivity is measured by the Scruton number (EN 1991-1-4 §E.1.3):

$$ v_\text{crit} = \frac{n_1\, b}{St},\qquad Sc = \frac{4\pi\, m\,\zeta}{\rho\, b^2},\qquad
\frac{y_\text{max}}{b} = \frac{K\,K_w\,c_\text{lat}}{St^2\,Sc} $$ (22.29)

The third expression is the amplitude of Annex E of EN 1991-1-4 (approach 1), with by default
$St = 0.18$, $K = 0.13$, $K_w = 0.6$ and $c_\text{lat} = 0.7$. These
coefficients are input data: keta does not iterate the dependence of $c_\text{lat}$ and
$K_w$ on the amplitude and the mode shape, which the standard requires to be established. This
estimate is only an order of magnitude.

## 22.11 Scope

The scope and its limits are as follows:

- one aerodynamic section and one mean incidence for the whole model; no incidence specific to each
bar and no wind frame attached to the bar;

- no lateral component $v$ in the buffeting forces, no drag derivatives $P_i^*$ in
flutter, no admittance in the time-domain calculation;

- strips at the bar midpoints: the accuracy of the calculation depends on the division of the deck
into bars, like that of a one-point-per-bar integration;

- linear response on a finite number of modes: the modal truncation must be checked by the user,
in particular for the background part;

- the flutter velocity is that of the first crossing detected by the sweep;

- the nonlinear loop is limited to second order.

# Chapter 23 Fire

This chapter deals with the fire resistance of a reinforced concrete or steel frame. The problem
is posed in two stages, as in the advanced calculation methods of EN 1992-1-2 and EN 1993-1-2. First a
thermal problem: under a nominal fire curve, heat enters the section through its exposed faces, and
the temperature field in the section is sought at each instant. Then a mechanical problem: at the
temperature of each fibre, concrete and steel lose strength and stiffness and expand; the equilibrium
state of the frame is sought, loaded by the actions concomitant with the fire, with its hot bars. The
absence of equilibrium signals failure.

keta also treats the heating of steel members by the simplified method of EN 1993-1-2, with a
uniform temperature over the section. The fibre laws at ambient temperature and the integration of
sections are those of chapters 18 and 21; heat conduction in continuum elements is described in
chapter 25.

## 23.1 Assumptions

- conduction is two-dimensional: the section is prismatic and heat does not travel along the bar
(the framework of Annex B of EN 1992-1-2);

- the thermal problem is uncoupled from the mechanical problem: cracking and deformations do not
modify the conduction;

- the water in the concrete enters only through the peak in specific heat of EN 1992-1-2 §3.3.2;
there is neither moisture transport nor a spalling model. The spalled thickness is removed by hand
from the geometry of the section;

- the thermal and mechanical properties are those of EN 1992-1-2 (concrete, reinforcement) and of
EN 1993-1-2 (structural steel);

- each fibre of the section is thermo-elastic with a secant modulus taken on its law at its
temperature; transient creep is present only through the law of EN 1992-1-2, which includes it
implicitly;

- the frame is in small displacements; each exposed bar receives a single strain plane, obtained
from its mean internal forces: an exposed span must be divided into several bars;

- prestressing steel is not treated in fire;

- all lengths of the thermal analysis are in metres.

## 23.2 Fire exposure

### 23.2.1 Temperature-time curves

The fire is described by the gas temperature $\theta_g(t)$, in °C, as a function of time
$t$ in minutes. keta offers the nominal curves of EN 1991-1-2 §3.2, the increased hydrocarbon
curve, a constant temperature and a curve given point by point:

$$ \begin{aligned}
\text{ISO 834:}\quad &\theta_g = 20 + 345\log_{10}(8t + 1)\\
\text{external:}\quad &\theta_g = 20 + 660\bigl(1 - 0.687\,e^{-0.32t} - 0.313\,e^{-3.8t}\bigr)\\
\text{hydrocarbon:}\quad &\theta_g = 20 + 1080\bigl(1 - 0.325\,e^{-0.167t} - 0.675\,e^{-2.5t}\bigr)\\
\text{increased hydrocarbon:}\quad &\theta_g = 20 + 1280\bigl(1 - 0.325\,e^{-0.167t} - 0.675\,e^{-2.5t}\bigr)
\end{aligned} $$ (23.1)

A curve given as a table $(t, \theta_g)$ is interpolated linearly and held constant beyond
its bounds. For conduction in sections, the possible exposures are the ISO 834 curve, the two
hydrocarbon curves, a constant gas temperature, a table of gas temperature, a table of surface
temperature (imposed directly) and the adiabatic face; an unexposed face is adiabatic. The external
curve is used only for the heating of steel members.

**Figure 23.1** — Nominal fire curves computed by keta

### 23.2.2 Heat flux received by a surface

The net heat flux received by a surface at temperature $\theta_m$ is the sum of a convective
exchange and a radiative exchange (EN 1991-1-2 §3.1):

$$ \dot h_\text{net} = \alpha_c\,(\theta_g - \theta_m) + \varepsilon_m\,\sigma\,\bigl[(\theta_g + 273)^4 - (\theta_m + 273)^4\bigr] $$ (23.2)

with $\sigma = 5.67\cdot10^{-8}$ W/m²K⁴ and the emissivity $\varepsilon_m = 0.7$ by
default. The coefficient of heat transfer by convection is 25 W/m²K for the ISO 834 curve and the
external curve, 50 W/m²K for the hydrocarbon curves (EN 1991-1-2 §3.2) and, in sections, for curves
given as tables (25 W/m²K by default for a table applied to a steel member). For a constant gas
temperature, it is 4 W/m²K as long as the surface remains below 50 °C (unexposed face), 25 W/m²K
above. It can also be imposed, constant or as a function of the surface temperature.

## 23.3 Heating of a steel member

A steel member has a high conductivity and a small thickness: its temperature is taken as uniform
over the section. EN 1993-1-2 §4.2.5 gives the temperature increase during a step $\Delta t$.
For an unprotected member with section factor $A_m/V$ and shadow factor
$k_\text{sh}$:

$$ \Delta\theta_a = k_\text{sh}\,\frac{A_m/V}{c_a(\theta_a)\,\rho_a}\,\dot h_\text{net}\,\Delta t $$ (23.3)

For a member protected by a material of thickness $d_p$, conductivity $\lambda_p$,
density $\rho_p$ and specific heat $c_p$:

$$ \Delta\theta_a = \frac{\lambda_p\,A_p/V}{d_p\,c_a\,\rho_a}\,\frac{\theta_g - \theta_a}{1 + \phi/3}\,\Delta t
- \bigl(e^{\phi/10} - 1\bigr)\,\Delta\theta_g,\qquad \phi = \frac{c_p\,\rho_p}{c_a\,\rho_a}\,d_p\,A_p/V $$ (23.4)

and the increase is taken as zero if it is negative while the gases are hotter than the steel, as
the standard requires. The specific heat of steel $c_a(\theta)$ is that of EN 1993-1-2
§3.4.1.2, with its peak at 735 °C, and $\rho_a = 7850$ kg/m³. The gas temperature is taken at
the end of the step; the default step is 5 s. After 30 minutes of ISO 834 fire, an unprotected member
with section factor $A_m/V = 200$ m⁻¹ reaches 828.8 °C, a value returned by a separate
step-by-step integration of the same formulas.

The critical temperature of a member whose degree of utilisation in fire is $\mu_0$ is that
of EN 1993-1-2 §4.2.4, expression (4.22), valid for $0.013 \le \mu_0 \le 1$:

$$ \theta_{a,\text{cr}} = 39.19\,\ln\!\left[\frac{1}{0.9674\,\mu_0^{3.833}} - 1\right] + 482 $$ (23.5)

## 23.4 Conduction in the section

### 23.4.1 Heat equation

In a concrete section, the temperature $\theta(y, z, t)$ satisfies the nonlinear Fourier
equation

$$ \rho(\theta)\,c(\theta)\,\frac{\partial\theta}{\partial t} = \nabla\cdot\bigl(\lambda(\theta)\,\nabla\theta\bigr) $$ (23.6)

with, on an exposed face, the flux (23.2) and, on an adiabatic face, zero flux. The
initial temperature is uniform (20 °C by default) or given point by point.

### 23.4.2 Thermal properties of concrete

The properties are those of EN 1992-1-2 §3.3, for $20 \le \theta \le 1200$ °C. The thermal
conductivity lies between an upper limit and a lower limit; keta takes a combination of the two,
$\lambda = a\,\lambda_\text{inf} + (1 - a)\,\lambda_\text{sup}$, with $a = 1$ (lower limit,
recommended by the French National Annex for normal concretes) by default and $a = 0$ for
high-strength concretes:

$$ \lambda_\text{sup} = 2 - 0.2451\,\frac{\theta}{100} + 0.0107\left(\frac{\theta}{100}\right)^2,\qquad
\lambda_\text{inf} = 1.36 - 0.136\,\frac{\theta}{100} + 0.0057\left(\frac{\theta}{100}\right)^2 $$ (23.7)

The specific heat of dry concrete is 900 J/kgK up to 100 °C, increases linearly to 1000 J/kgK at
200 °C and then 1100 J/kgK at 400 °C, and remains constant beyond. The evaporation of water adds a
plateau between 100 and 115 °C, of value $c_\text{peak}$ = 900, 1470 or 2020 J/kgK for a moisture
content of 0, 1.5 or 3 % by weight (interpolated between these values), which decreases linearly to
the dry curve at 200 °C. The density decreases through the loss of water:

$$ \frac{\rho(\theta)}{\rho(20)} =
\begin{cases}
1 & \theta \le 115\\
1 - 0.02\,(\theta - 115)/85 & 115 < \theta \le 200\\
0.98 - 0.03\,(\theta - 200)/200 & 200 < \theta \le 400\\
0.95 - 0.07\,(\theta - 400)/800 & 400 < \theta \le 1200
\end{cases} $$ (23.8)

The conductivity, the specific heat and the density can also be given as constants, or as tables
as functions of temperature. Finally, the volumetric enthalpy $H(\theta)$ can replace the
product $\rho c$: it represents without approximation a latent heat concentrated over a narrow
temperature interval.

### 23.4.3 Mesh

The section is divided into square cells of side $h$ (1 cm by default), on a Cartesian grid.
Three geometries are possible:

- a slab, treated in one dimension through its thickness: a single column of cells, adiabatic
lateral faces; only its top and bottom faces can be exposed;

- a rectangle, in two dimensions, with four faces that can be exposed separately;

- an arbitrary polygonal outline, traversed in either direction, rasterised: a cell belongs to the
section if its centre lies inside the polygon. Each cell boundary face takes the exposure of the side
of the polygon closest to its midpoint. An outline not parallel to the axes is therefore represented
as a staircase.

For the slab and the rectangle, the step is adjusted so that a whole number of cells covers each
dimension exactly; for a dimension $b$ and a requested mesh size $h$,

$$ n_b = \max\bigl(1,\ \operatorname{round}(b/h)\bigr),\qquad h_b = \frac{b}{n_b} $$ (23.9)

and, for an outline, the grid covers the bounding rectangle with $\lceil b/h\rceil$ cells of
side $h$. keta refuses a mesh coarser than one third of the smallest dimension of the section
(the width of the bounding rectangle for an outline), a mesh size of more than 1 m and dimensions of
more than 100 m, which almost always reveal an input in millimetres.

### 23.4.4 Finite volumes and boundary conditions

Equation (23.6) is discretised by cell-centred finite volumes; in the interior,
the scheme is that of the five-point Laplacian. The flux between two neighbouring cells $a$ and
$b$ crosses two half-cells in series, hence the conductance per unit length of bar

$$ K_{ab} = \frac{2\,\lambda_a\lambda_b}{d\,(\lambda_a + \lambda_b)}\,\ell $$ (23.10)

where $d$ is the distance between the centres and $\ell$ the length of the common face.
