On an exposed face, heat crosses in series the air film, the protection if any (resistance
$R_p$ in m²K/W) and the half-cell. Radiation is written exactly as a linear exchange
coefficient,

$$ h_\text{rad} = \varepsilon\,\sigma\,(T_g^2 + T_s^2)(T_g + T_s),\qquad
U = \left[\frac{1}{\alpha_c + h_\text{rad}} + R_p + \frac{h/2}{\lambda}\right]^{-1} $$ (23.11)

($T_g$, $T_s$ absolute temperatures of the gas and of the surface, with 273.15 K), so
that the flux towards the centre of the boundary cell is $U(\theta_g - \theta_i)$. The surface
temperature $\theta_s$ that enters $h_\text{rad}$ is the root of the equation obtained by
equating the surface flux and the flux through the protection and the half-cell; it is obtained by
fixed-point iteration (at most 25 iterations, tolerance $10^{-8}$ °C) before the step is
solved. An imposed surface temperature acts through the resistance of the protection and the
half-cell alone.

**Figure 23.2** — Exchange at an exposed face: resistances in series of the film, the protection and the half-cell

### 23.4.5 Time integration

The time scheme is the implicit Euler scheme, unconditionally stable. The properties
$\lambda$, $\rho$ and $c$ are taken at the temperature of the previous step: each step
is then a symmetric positive definite linear system,

$$ \Bigl(\frac{\rho c\,A}{\Delta t} + \mathbf{K}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_n)\Bigr)\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n+1}
= \frac{\rho c\,A}{\Delta t}\,\boldsymbol{\theta}_n + \mathbf{f}(t_{n+1}) $$ (23.12)

whose sparsity pattern is the same throughout the fire; the symbolic factorisation is done once.
The scheme is first-order in time; the step is a choice of accuracy, not of stability, and is 30 s
by default. When the enthalpy is given, each step solves
$A\,[H(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n+1}) - H(\boldsymbol{\theta}_n)]/\Delta t + \mathbf{K}\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n+1} = \mathbf{f}$
by Newton's method with the tangent capacity $\mathrm{d}H/\mathrm{d}\theta$ and an exact line
search: this residual is the gradient of a convex functional, the iteration converges whatever the
latent heat, and the energy balance of the step is satisfied to within the iteration tolerance
(relative correction $10^{-10}$).

The results are the temperature fields at the requested instants and at the end of the fire,
with the mean temperature and the maximum temperature of the section.

**Figure 23.3** — Cell temperature, at distance x from the exposed face, in 20 cm of concrete heated on one face by the ISO 834 curve (siliceous aggregates, lower limit of conductivity, dry concrete, 1 cm mesh), computed by keta

## 23.5 Mechanical properties at elevated temperature

### 23.5.1 Concrete

The stress-strain law of concrete at temperature $\theta$ is that of EN 1992-1-2 §3.2.2.1. In
absolute value (compression is negative in keta):

$$ \sigma(\varepsilon) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{3\,\varepsilon\,f_{c,\theta}}{\varepsilon_{c1,\theta}\Bigl[2 + \bigl(\varepsilon/\varepsilon_{c1,\theta}\bigr)^3\Bigr]} & \varepsilon \le \varepsilon_{c1,\theta}\\[3ex]
f_{c,\theta}\,\dfrac{\varepsilon_{cu1,\theta} - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon_{cu1,\theta} - \varepsilon_{c1,\theta}} & \varepsilon_{c1,\theta} < \varepsilon < \varepsilon_{cu1,\theta}
\end{cases}
\qquad f_{c,\theta} = k_c(\theta)\,f_{ck} $$ (23.13)

The descending branch is the linear branch permitted by the standard. Beyond
$\varepsilon_{cu1,\theta}$ the stress is zero. The factor $k_c(\theta)$ and the strains
$\varepsilon_{c1,\theta}$, $\varepsilon_{cu1,\theta}$ are interpolated linearly in
Table 3.1 of EN 1992-1-2, in the column for siliceous or calcareous aggregates. The initial modulus is
$3f_{c,\theta}/(2\varepsilon_{c1,\theta})$. Concrete has no tensile strength (cracked
analysis). On request, the initial modulus is kept in tension, without a strength limit.

**Figure 23.4** — EN 1992-1-2 law of siliceous concrete at elevated temperature (factors kc, εc1, εcu1 of keta)

### 23.5.2 Steels

For structural steel (EN 1993-1-2 §3.2, Table 3.1) and for reinforcing steel (EN 1992-1-2 §3.2.3,
Tables 3.2a for class N, hot rolled or cold worked, and 3.2b for class X), three factors reduce the
effective yield strength, the proportional limit and the modulus:
$f_{y,\theta} = k_y f_y$, $f_{p,\theta} = k_p f_y$, $E_\theta = k_E E$. The law is
linear up to $\varepsilon_{p,\theta} = f_{p,\theta}/E_\theta$, elliptical up to
$\varepsilon_{y,\theta} = 0.02$, then constant:

$$ \sigma = f_{p,\theta} - c + \frac{b}{a}\sqrt{a^2 - (\varepsilon_{y,\theta} - \varepsilon)^2},\qquad
\begin{aligned}
a^2 &= (\varepsilon_{y,\theta} - \varepsilon_{p,\theta})(\varepsilon_{y,\theta} - \varepsilon_{p,\theta} + c/E_\theta)\\
b^2 &= c\,(\varepsilon_{y,\theta} - \varepsilon_{p,\theta})E_\theta + c^2\\
c &= \frac{(f_{y,\theta} - f_{p,\theta})^2}{(\varepsilon_{y,\theta} - \varepsilon_{p,\theta})E_\theta - 2(f_{y,\theta} - f_{p,\theta})}
\end{aligned} $$ (23.14)

The plateau is not limited: the descending branch of the standard beyond 15 % is not represented.
At 20 °C, $k_p = k_y = 1$ and the law reduces to the bilinear law.

**Figure 23.5** — Reduction factors at elevated temperature in keta: concrete strength (kc, siliceous and calcareous aggregates), yield strength of class N cold-worked reinforcement (ks) and of structural steel (ky)

### 23.5.3 Thermal expansion

The free thermal strain is that of EN 1992-1-2 §3.3.1, as a function of $\theta$ in °C:

$$ \begin{aligned}
\text{siliceous concrete:}\quad &\varepsilon_{th} = -1.8\cdot10^{-4} + 9\cdot10^{-6}\,\theta + 2.3\cdot10^{-11}\,\theta^3 \quad(\theta \le 700),\qquad 14\cdot10^{-3}\ \text{beyond}\\
\text{calcareous concrete:}\quad &\varepsilon_{th} = -1.2\cdot10^{-4} + 6\cdot10^{-6}\,\theta + 1.4\cdot10^{-11}\,\theta^3 \quad(\theta \le 805),\qquad 12\cdot10^{-3}\ \text{beyond}\\
\text{reinforcement:}\quad &\varepsilon_{th} = -2.416\cdot10^{-4} + 1.2\cdot10^{-5}\,\theta + 0.4\cdot10^{-8}\,\theta^2 \quad(\theta \le 750),\\
&\qquad 11\cdot10^{-3}\ (750 < \theta \le 860),\qquad -6.2\cdot10^{-3} + 2\cdot10^{-5}\,\theta\ (\theta > 860)
\end{aligned} $$ (23.15)

## 23.6 Hot section

At a given instant of the fire, the section becomes a set of fibres: each cell of the thermal mesh
is a concrete fibre, at its temperature; each reinforcing bar is a steel fibre. A bar takes the
temperature of the hottest cell covered by its disc of diameter $\phi$ (a cell is covered if its
point nearest to the centre of the bar is closer than $\phi/2$). This choice is on the safe
side: with the 1 cm mesh, a 16 mm bar whose axis is 15 mm from the face takes the temperature of the
surface cell.

For a strain plane $\varepsilon(y, z) = \varepsilon_0 + \kappa_y(z - z_r) - \kappa_z(y - y_r)$,
the mechanical strain of fibre $i$ is
$\varepsilon_{e,i} = \varepsilon_i - \varepsilon_{th,i}$, its stress
$\sigma_i = f_i(\varepsilon_{e,i})$ by its law at its temperature, and its secant modulus
$E_i = \sigma_i/\varepsilon_{e,i}$. A negative (descending branch) or undefined modulus is
replaced by zero: the fibre stops carrying load and the load is transferred to the others. The
stiffnesses of the hot section and its thermal resultants are taken about the centre of stiffness
$(y_c, z_c) = (\sum E_i A_i y_i, \sum E_i A_i z_i)/EA$, which the heating moves away from the
cold centroid:

$$ \begin{aligned}
EA &= \sum_i E_i A_i, & EI_y &= \sum_i E_i A_i (z_i - z_c)^2, & EI_z &= \sum_i E_i A_i (y_i - y_c)^2\\
N_{th} &= \sum_i E_i A_i\,\varepsilon_{th,i}, & M_{th,y} &= \sum_i E_i A_i\,\varepsilon_{th,i}(z_i - z_c), & M_{th,z} &= -\sum_i E_i A_i\,\varepsilon_{th,i}(y_i - y_c)
\end{aligned} $$ (23.16)

The equivalent expansion $\varepsilon_0 = N_{th}/EA$ and the thermal curvatures
$\kappa_{th} = M_{th}/EI$ are those that a free bar would take; a restrained bar develops the
force $-EA\,\varepsilon_0$, the classical restrained-expansion force. The centre of stiffness can
also be held at its cold position. If $EA$ or one of the bending stiffnesses becomes zero, the
section has lost all stiffness and the calculation stops on this finding of failure. For a slab,
meshed as a single column, the transverse bending stiffness comes only from the reinforcement
distributed over the width.

## 23.7 Equilibrium of the hot frame

### 23.7.1 Secant iteration

The mechanical calculation seeks the equilibrium of the frame under the load case concomitant
with the fire, at a given instant (the fire duration), with its exposed bars in their hot state. The
thermal problem is first solved once for each exposed bar. Then, at each iteration:

- each exposed bar receives an equivalent section: $A = EA/E$, $I_y = EI_y/E$,
$I_z = EI_z/E$, where $E$ is the modulus of its material; the shear areas and the torsion
constant are reduced in the ratio $EA_\text{hot}/EA_\text{cold}$, for want of an integration
of shear over the hot section; the density is corrected so that the self-weight remains that of the
cold section;

- the load case is supplemented, for each exposed bar, by the imposed strain
$(\varepsilon_0, \kappa_{th,y}, \kappa_{th,z})$ (chapter 3);

- the frame is analysed by linear statics; for each bar its mean internal forces
$(N, M_y, M_z)$ over its length (trapezoidal mean over 11 sections) are taken, transferred to the
centre of stiffness, and a new strain plane is deduced

$$ \varepsilon_0 = \frac{N + N_{th}}{EA},\qquad \kappa_y = \frac{M_y + M_{th,y}}{EI_y},\qquad \kappa_z = \frac{M_z + M_{th,z}}{EI_z} $$ (23.17)

which gives new secant moduli. The process is repeated until the relative change in the nodal
displacements, in the infinity norm, is below $10^{-3}$ (adjustable tolerance), within a limit of
500 iterations. The fixed point sought is that of the secant method: at convergence, the fibre
stresses, taken with the secant moduli of the strain plane, have as resultants the internal forces of
each bar, and the frame is in equilibrium under its loads, to within the tolerance.

The shift of the centre of stiffness creates an eccentricity of the axial force with respect to
the line of the nodes. keta accounts for it by an additional imposed curvature
$(-z_c N/EI_y,\; y_c N/EI_z)$, with the axial force of the previous iteration; it can also
carry this shift over into the offset of the bar.

### 23.7.2 Tangent corrections and relaxation

Between two analyses of the frame, the strain plane of each section is refined, with the internal
forces frozen, by a few Newton iterations (four by default) on the section, with the $3\times 3$
tangent matrix

$$ \mathbf{k}_t = \sum_i E_{t,i}A_i
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & z_i - z_r & -(y_i - y_r)\\ \cdot & (z_i - z_r)^2 & -(z_i - z_r)(y_i - y_r)\\ \text{sym.} & \cdot & (y_i - y_r)^2\end{bmatrix} $$ (23.18)

and a line search (the step is halved, at most twelve times, as long as the residual does not
decrease): the laws have plateaus, and a full Newton step often overshoots the solution. These
corrections accelerate convergence without changing the secant fixed point.

On a section that cracks, the secant iteration can oscillate between two states. When the residual
no longer decreases (it stays above 0.99 times its value two iterations earlier), the update of the
strain plane is under-relaxed by a factor $\omega$, halved at each new stagnation down to
$1/16$; the convergence criterion then applies to the change divided by $\omega$. If the
stagnation persists twenty-five times at the minimum factor, the tangent corrections are abandoned and
the iteration resumes as pure secant. A calculation that converges without stagnating is never
relaxed.

**Important.**

Lack of convergence is not a numerical defect to be worked around: it means that the frame has
no equilibrium state under these loads at this fire duration. keta then stops with a failure message
and supplies no approximate state.

As an option, the materials are degraded without the thermal strains being applied: this gives
the effect of the loss of stiffness and strength alone. The results are the displacements, the
reactions and the internal forces of the hot frame and, for each exposed bar, its section state
(stiffnesses, centre of stiffness, thermal resultants, maximum and mean concrete temperatures, maximum
reinforcement temperature).

## 23.8 Capacity of a hot section

For a steel section at uniform temperature $\theta$, keta gives the ratio
$M_{fi}/M_{20}$ of the resistant moments hot and cold. The fibres of the section whose law is
bilinear or elastic receive the elliptical law (23.14) of structural steel at
$\theta$; the other fibres keep their law. The two moments are read from the moment-curvature
curve at zero axial force (chapter 18) at the curvature

$$ \kappa = \frac{0.2}{z_\text{max}} $$ (23.19)

($z_\text{max}$ distance of the furthest fibre), that is about ten times the yield strain of
2 % at the extreme fibre: the section is fully plastified. Prestressing steel and initial fibre
strains are not admitted in this calculation. The capacity of a reinforced concrete section under a
non-uniform temperature field is not computed through this ratio; it is read from the equilibrium of
the hot frame of the previous section.

## 23.9 Scope

The scope of the fire calculation and its limits are as follows:

- frame bars only, in plane or spatial modelling; grillage modelling is refused, as is an exposed
bar resting on an elastic foundation;

- in plane modelling, the section is a slab or a rectangle;

- secant method: the result is an equilibrium state at one fire duration, not a load-displacement
history; no unloading, no plastic memory, no explicit creep at elevated temperature;

- one strain plane per bar, taken from its mean internal forces;

- no spalling, no moisture transport, no conduction along the bar;

- no prestressing steel in fire: neither the factors of EN 1992-1-2 Table 3.3, nor expansion, nor
tendons in the hot section;

- polygonal outline represented as a staircase by the grid;

- shear and torsional stiffnesses reduced in the ratio of the axial stiffnesses, not integrated over
the hot section.

# Chapter 24 Shells

This chapter deals with shell elements: slabs, deck slabs, walls, box-girder walls, curved shells.
A shell is a thin solid, whose thickness $t$ is small compared with its other dimensions; it
carries load both in membrane action (forces in its plane) and in bending (moments and shear forces).
keta represents it by flat three-node triangular facets, which share with the bars the six degrees of
freedom of their nodes: a slab connects directly to its beams, its piers and its cables. The chapter
describes the element (membrane, bending, enriched facets), its assembly with the bars and the meshing
of slabs, the loads it receives, the prestress that passes through it, the internal forces it returns
and its plastic behaviour.

Plane and solid continuum elements are described in chapter 25. Shells take part in static,
modal, dynamic, buckling and second-order analyses (chapters 4, 15 and 17), in staged construction
(chapter 10) and in influence surfaces (chapter 11).

## 24.1 Assumptions

- each facet is flat, with constant thickness (or linear over the facet for an enriched facet); a
curved surface is approximated by facets;

- bending follows Mindlin-Reissner theory: normals remain straight but not necessarily normal to
the deformed surface, which gives transverse shear; the shear correction factor is
$5/6$;

- the material is linear elastic, isotropic by default, in plane stress
($\sigma_z = 0$);

- small strains and displacements within the element; large displacements are treated by the
corotational analyses (chapter 17), which carry each facet in a frame that follows its
rotation;

- the geometric stiffness contains only the term of the membrane forces acting on the slope of the
deflection;

- the internal forces are returned at the centroid of each facet.

## 24.2 The facet

### 24.2.1 Local axes and degrees of freedom

Each node carries three translations $(u, v, w)$ and three rotations
$(\theta_x, \theta_y, \theta_z)$ in the global axes, giving an $18\times 18$ stiffness
matrix per facet. The local axes are built from the order of nodes 1, 2, 3: the $z$ axis is the
normalised normal $(\mathbf{p}_2 - \mathbf{p}_1)\times(\mathbf{p}_3 - \mathbf{p}_1)$; the
$x$ axis is the projection of the global $X$ axis onto the plane of the facet (of the
$Y$ axis if the normal is parallel to $X$, or of a direction given for the slab, for example
that of a reinforcement layout); $y = z\times x$. With the rotation $\mathbf{R}$ whose rows
are the local axes, repeated over the six triplets of the facet in $\mathbf{T}$,

$$ \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{T}^{\mathsf T}\,\mathbf{K}_\ell\,\mathbf{T},\qquad
\mathbf{T} = \operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{R}) $$ (24.1)

In the local axes, the stiffness $\mathbf{K}_\ell$ is the sum of a membrane block on
$(u, v, \theta_z)$ and a bending block on $(w, \theta_x, \theta_y)$, uncoupled for a
homogeneous facet. A degenerate triangle (area less than $10^{-12}$ times the square of its
longest side) is refused.

**Figure 24.1** — Triangular facet: local axes and degrees of freedom (left); quadratic normal displacement of an edge due to the z-axis rotations of its ends (right)

### 24.2.2 Allman membrane

A constant-strain membrane triangle has no stiffness in rotation about its normal; assembled into
non-coplanar facets or connected to a bar, it leaves mechanisms or forces the addition of a fictitious
spring. keta uses the Allman triangle, which gives a true stiffness to the rotation
$\theta_z$. Following Cook, it is written as the six-node quadratic triangle whose mid-side
displacements are tied to the degrees of freedom of the vertices. On side $i \to j$, with
midpoint $m$:

$$ u_m = \frac{u_i + u_j}{2} + \frac{(y_j - y_i)(\theta_j - \theta_i)}{8},\qquad
v_m = \frac{v_i + v_j}{2} - \frac{(x_j - x_i)(\theta_j - \theta_i)}{8} $$ (24.2)

The side therefore takes a parabolic normal displacement of amplitude $L(\theta_j - \theta_i)/8$
at its midpoint. The strain $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = \mathbf{B}_m\mathbf{d}_m$ is linear over the
facet, and the membrane stiffness
$\mathbf{K}_m = \int t\,\mathbf{B}_m^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{D}_m\mathbf{B}_m\,\mathrm{d}A$, of degree 2, is
integrated exactly by the three mid-side points (weights $A/3$), with
$\mathbf{D}_m = \frac{E}{1-\nu^2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & \nu & 0\\ \nu & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & (1-\nu)/2\end{bmatrix}$.

One zero-energy mode remains: the three rotations $\theta_z$ equal, translations zero. It is
stabilised by a penalty on the difference between the mean rotation of the vertices and the rotation
of the linear field of the vertices (Hughes and Brezzi):

$$ E_\text{stab} = \tfrac12\,\gamma\,G\,t\,A\,\bigl(\bar\theta_z - \omega\bigr)^2,\qquad
\bar\theta_z = \frac{\theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_3}{3},\qquad \omega = \frac12\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right),\qquad \gamma = 1 $$ (24.3)

This energy is zero for a rigid-body motion and for any constant-strain state whose nodal rotations
are the rotation of the continuum: the patch test remains satisfied, and no returned internal force
depends on it. It is the only fictitious stiffness of the element. The choice $\gamma = 1$
(modulus $G$) makes twisted shells converge monotonically, where the rotation mode couples with
the bending of neighbouring non-coplanar facets.

### 24.2.3 Mindlin-Reissner bending

The rotations $\theta_x$, $\theta_y$ are the components of the rotation vector of the
normal. A fibre at height $z$ moves in the plane by $(z\theta_y, -z\theta_x)$, hence the
curvatures and the transverse shear strains

$$ \kappa_x = \frac{\partial\theta_y}{\partial x},\quad \kappa_y = -\frac{\partial\theta_x}{\partial y},\quad
\kappa_{xy} = \frac{\partial\theta_y}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial\theta_x}{\partial x},\qquad
\gamma_{xz} = \frac{\partial w}{\partial x} + \theta_y,\quad \gamma_{yz} = \frac{\partial w}{\partial y} - \theta_x $$ (24.4)

and the forces per unit width

$$ \mathbf{m} = \frac{t^3}{12}\,\mathbf{D}_m\,\boldsymbol{\kappa},\qquad
\mathbf{q} = \tfrac56\,G\,t\,\boldsymbol{\gamma} $$ (24.5)

With linear rotations and deflection, transverse shear interpolated directly locks the element as
the thickness decreases: a thin plate becomes infinitely stiff. keta uses the MITC3 element of Lee
and Bathe: the covariant shear strains $e_{rt}$, $e_{st}$, computed from the
displacements, are sampled at points $A = (\frac12, 0)$, $B = (0, \frac12)$ and
$C = (\frac12, \frac12)$ of the reference triangle, and replaced by the assumed field

$$ \tilde e_{rt} = e_{rt}^A + c\,s,\qquad \tilde e_{st} = e_{st}^B - c\,r,\qquad
c = e_{rt}^C - e_{st}^C - e_{rt}^A + e_{st}^B $$ (24.6)

constant along each side. The curvature is constant over the facet: bending is integrated exactly
at one point; shear, of degree 2, by the three mid-side points.

The figure below shows the convergence of the central deflection of a square plate simply
supported on its four sides, under uniform load, meshed in $n\times n$ squares cut into two
triangles (alternating diagonals), with $t/a = 0.01$. The Mindlin reference is the Kirchhoff
deflection of the Navier series, $0.0040624\,qa^4/D$, increased by the shear deflection
$\mathcal{M}/(\frac56 Gt)$ (relation of Wang, Reddy and Lee between simply supported Kirchhoff
and Mindlin plates), where $\mathcal{M} = (m_x + m_y)/(1+\nu)$ is the sum of the Kirchhoff
moments at the centre: $0.0040645\,qa^4/D$. With the “hard” support, keta's deflection differs
from it by less than $2\cdot10^{-4}$ in relative value at $n = 128$. The “soft” support,
where only the deflection is fixed, gives a shear boundary layer along the edges and a slightly more
flexible plate: this is a fact of Mindlin theory, not a defect of the element, but the choice of
support matters for thick plates.

**Figure 24.2** — Simply supported square plate under uniform load (t/a = 0.01, ν = 0.3): central deflection from keta relative to the Mindlin solution, as a function of the number n of divisions per side

### 24.2.4 Enriched facets

A facet can carry additional data. As soon as it carries one, all its integrals are computed by
the 7-point Dunavant rule, exact to degree 5:

- a different thickness at each vertex, linear over the facet (haunches, deck slabs of variable
thickness): membrane in $t(\xi)$, bending in $t(\xi)^3/12$;

- an offset $e$ of the mid-surface relative to the plane of the nodes, along the normal,
treated as a rigid arm: $u_m = u + e\,\theta_y$, $v_m = v - e\,\theta_x$;

- an orthotropic material (moduli $E_x$, $E_y$, $\nu_{xy}$, $G_{xy}$,
$G_{xz}$, $G_{yz}$, axes rotated by a given angle), bending being that of the homogeneous
plate $t^3\mathbf{Q}/12$;

- a laminate: stacked orthotropic plies, with given thicknesses and orientations, according to
classical lamination theory,

$$ \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{n}\\ \mathbf{m}\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B}\\ \mathbf{B} & \mathbf{D}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\\ \boldsymbol{\kappa}\end{bmatrix},\qquad
(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{D}) = \sum_k \bar{\mathbf{Q}}_k\left(z_{k+1} - z_k,\ \frac{z_{k+1}^2 - z_k^2}{2},\ \frac{z_{k+1}^3 - z_k^3}{3}\right) $$ (24.7)

- with a transverse shear $\sum_k t_k\mathbf{G}_k$ (oriented) and the factor $5/6$; the
ply thicknesses must add up to that of the facet;

- a Winkler elastic foundation normal to the facet, of stiffness $k$ (N/m³), which adds
$k\,A(1 + \delta_{ij})/12$ on the nodal deflections, the exact stiffness for a linear
deflection.

### 24.2.5 Mass and geometric stiffness

The consistent mass comprises the translational mass $\rho t A$, distributed according to the
consistent matrix of the linear triangle
$\frac{A}{12}\left[\begin{smallmatrix}2&1&1\\1&2&1\\1&1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right]$
in each direction, and the rotary inertia $\rho t^3/12$ on $\theta_x$ and
$\theta_y$. The rotation $\theta_z$ has no mass; as it has a stiffness, it is condensed by
the modal analysis and creates no spurious mode. The lumped mass puts a third of the masses of
the facet on each node: $\rho t A/3$ on each translation and $\rho t^3 A/36$ on
$\theta_x$ and $\theta_y$.

Under membrane forces $(n_x, n_y, n_{xy})$ of a prestressed state, the geometric stiffness is
the von Kármán term

$$ \mathbf{K}_g = \int_A \nabla w^{\mathsf T}\begin{bmatrix} n_x & n_{xy}\\ n_{xy} & n_y\end{bmatrix}\nabla w\;\mathrm{d}A $$ (24.8)

exact at one point since $\nabla w$ is constant over the facet. It returns the plate buckling
coefficient $k = 4$ of the simply supported plate in compression and the second-order
amplification $1/(1 - P/P_\text{cr})$. The in-plane and rotational couplings of the initial
state are not represented.

## 24.3 Assembly with the bars

Since the facet has six degrees of freedom per node, including a true stiffness in
$\theta_z$, a bar that arrives at a shell node connects to it without artifice, whatever its
orientation. A beam offset below a slab (rigid arm, chapter 3) whose line of nodes lies in the plane
of the slab acts compositely with it, provided that the beam and the slab share their nodes over their
common length.

### 24.3.1 Meshing of slabs

A slab is described by its outline, its holes, its thickness, its material and a target mesh size
$h$. Its conversion into facets follows deterministic steps (same model, same mesh, same
numbers):

- the plane of the slab passes through the first vertex of the outline, with the Newell normal of
the outline; all vertices must lie within the merge tolerance of it ($10^{-6}$ m by
default);

- the frame bars whose two nodes lie in the plane and whose midpoint is strictly inside the slab are
detected; two such bars that intersect elsewhere than at a common node are refused; a bar lying on
the edge is not integrated;

- the existing nodes inside the slab (pier heads) become imposed vertices of the mesh;

- the domain is triangulated by a constrained Delaunay triangulation (Bowyer and Watson insertion,
recovery of the imposed sides by edge flips), then refined by Ruppert's algorithm: the sides are
first divided to length $h$, then every triangle that is too large or too flat receives a new
vertex at its circumcentre;

- the mesh nodes are merged with the nearest existing nodes within the tolerance;

- the detected bars are split at the mesh vertices lying on their axis, keeping their material,
their section, their offset (interpolated) and their loads (redistributed without changing their
resultant).

A triangle is too large or too flat if

$$ R > \frac{h}{\sqrt3}\qquad\text{or}\qquad \frac{R}{\ell_\text{min}} > \frac{1}{2\sin\theta_\text{min}} $$ (24.9)

where $R$ is the radius of the circumscribed circle, $\ell_\text{min}$ the shortest side
and $\theta_\text{min}$ the target minimum angle (30° by default, between 20 and 34°). Termination
of the algorithm is proven up to 20.7°; beyond, it is observed. A refinement that does not finish is
an error or, if accepted, an explicit warning.

## 24.4 Loads

### 24.4.1 Pressures

A uniform pressure on a slab is expressed in three ways: a force vector per unit of true area in
the global axes; a scalar pressure along the local normal of each facet; a force vector per unit of
area projected onto the horizontal plane (snow, carriageway loads), which gives a facet inclined at
$\beta$ the force $q\,A\cos\beta$ and nothing to a vertical facet. In all three cases, the
force of the facet is shared in three equal thirds among its nodes, which is the consistent vector of
a uniform load on a linear triangle; the consistent nodal moments are neglected. Self-weight follows
the same rule; for a linear thickness, node $i$ receives
$\rho g A(2t_i + t_j + t_k)/12$.

A pressure applied over an arbitrary polygon (a wheel contact area, a storage area), possibly with
holes, is projected along a given direction onto the facets. For each facet, the area $A_c$ of
the intersection of the polygon and the projected triangle (Sutherland and Hodgman clipping) and its
centroid $\mathbf{c}$ are computed exactly; the force $\mathbf{q}A_c$ is distributed
according to the barycentric coordinates of $\mathbf{c}$, which is exact for a uniform pressure
over part of the triangle:

$$ \mathbf{f}_i = \mathbf{q}\int_{A_c} N_i\,\mathrm{d}A = \mathbf{q}\,A_c\,N_i(\mathbf{c}) $$ (24.10)

The hydrostatic pressure $p = \gamma\,d$, where $d$ is the depth below a water level,
zero above it, is applied along the normal with its consistent nodal forces, the facet being cut at
the water line.

When the slab is not modelled, a surface load on a panel bounded by bars is transferred directly
to these bars by the geometric rules described in chapter 3.

### 24.4.2 Thermal effects

A uniform temperature change $\Delta T$ and a gradient $\partial T/\partial z$ through
the thickness enter as initial strains, $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_0 = \alpha\Delta T\,(1, 1, 0)$
and $\boldsymbol{\kappa}_0 = \alpha\,\partial_z T\,(1, 1, 0)$. The equivalent nodal forces
are

$$ \mathbf{f} = t\,A\,\mathbf{B}_m^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{D}_m\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_0 + A\,\mathbf{B}_b^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{D}_b\boldsymbol{\kappa}_0 $$ (24.11)

exact since $\mathbf{B}_m$ is linear and $\mathbf{B}_b$ constant. The returned internal
forces subtract these initial strains: a slab free to expand has no internal forces.

## 24.5 Prestressing in shells

A prestressing tendon in a slab (post-tensioned slab, deck slab) is a polyline at its actual
position in the thickness. It can be built from a plan layout and a longitudinal profile: between two
extreme points (high and low points, with zero slope), two parabolas join at a given fraction of the
interval; between an extreme point and a free point, a parabola with its vertex at the extreme point;
between two free points, a straight line. Each interval is divided into 16 chords by default. The
force along the tendon is

$$ P(s) = P_0\,e^{-\mu\,\alpha(s) - k\,s} $$ (24.12)

from the stressed end, $\alpha(s)$ being the cumulative angular deviation; a tendon stressed
at both ends takes at each point the larger of the two values. The equivalent forces on the concrete
are the force $P\mathbf{t}$ at the live anchorage (and $-P\mathbf{t}$ at the other
anchorage), the deviation force
$P_\text{after}\mathbf{t}_\text{after} - P_\text{before}\mathbf{t}_\text{before}$ at each vertex,
and the friction force per unit length $P'(s)\,\mathbf{t}$ along each segment, integrated by
8 Gauss points on each piece of segment contained in a facet. Each force is transferred to the facet
that contains the orthogonal projection of its point of application, with the moment
$\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}$ of its eccentricity relative to the mid-surface, and shared among
the nodes by the linear shape functions. The system of forces is exactly self-equilibrated. In staged
construction, the steel area, the modulus and the relaxation of the tendon are used to compute its
time-dependent losses (chapters 8 and 10).

## 24.6 Supports and edge springs

A line support is a support applied to each node lying within a tolerance of a segment. A spring
distributed along a line of nodes (slab edge on an elastic support, semi-rigid joint between two
slabs) has a stiffness per unit length $\mathbf{k}$ ($6\times 6$), expressed in the axes of
each segment ($x$ along the segment, $z$ towards a given direction). It is lumped at the
nodes: each node receives half of each of its two segments,

$$ \mathbf{K}_\text{node} = \sum_{\text{adjacent segments}} \mathbf{R}^{\mathsf T}\,\frac{\mathbf{k}\,L}{2}\,\mathbf{R} $$ (24.13)

in the form of elastic links to the ground or to the facing line of nodes, so that all the analyses
that take links (including their nonlinear laws) take them. This lumping is exact for a uniform
relative displacement along the line. A hinge line is built by doubling the nodes and tying their
translations. Because the edge of an Allman facet bends with the rotations $\theta_z$ of its ends
(24.2), keta can tie these rotations along a line of nodes (the normal of the facets
must then be a global axis), so that a supported or loaded edge remains straight between its
nodes.

## 24.7 Returned internal forces

For each facet and each case, the forces per unit width are computed at the centroid, in the local
axes, by subtracting the initial strains:

$$ \mathbf{n} = t\,\mathbf{D}_m\bigl(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} - \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_0\bigr),\qquad
\mathbf{m} = \mathbf{D}_b\bigl(\boldsymbol{\kappa} - \boldsymbol{\kappa}_0\bigr),\qquad
\mathbf{q} = \tfrac56\,G\,t\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} $$ (24.14)

that is $n_x$, $n_y$, $n_{xy}$ (N/m), $m_x$, $m_y$, $m_{xy}$ (N·m/m) and
$q_x$, $q_y$ (N/m). The moment $m_x$ is the one that produces the stresses
$\sigma_x$; it is positive when it puts the $+z$ face in tension. The principal values and
their direction are computed by

$$ m_{1,2} = \frac{m_x + m_y}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{m_x - m_y}{2}\right)^2 + m_{xy}^2},\qquad
\tan 2\varphi = \frac{2m_{xy}}{m_x - m_y} $$ (24.15)

(likewise for $\mathbf{n}$). Principal values are never combined: in a combination or an
envelope, the components are combined, then the principal values recomputed. keta does not smooth
the internal forces at the nodes: the value at the centre of the facet is the most accurate value of
the element, and the mesh must be fine enough where the internal forces vary quickly. The
reinforcement design moments (Wood and Armer) are deduced from the combined $(m_x, m_y, m_{xy})$,
according to the directions of the reinforcement (chapter 21).

## 24.8 Plasticity of shells

### 24.8.1 Layered law

For a collapse analysis of a wall or a steel plate, keta integrates an elastic-plastic law through
the thickness of each facet. At each in-plane integration point (the three mid-side points, or the
seven Dunavant points of a variable-thickness facet) and at each height $z$, the strain is the
Kirchhoff-Love strain $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}(z) = \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_0 + z\boldsymbol{\kappa}$
and the transverse shear is distributed according to $f(z) = \frac54(1 - 4z^2/t^2)$, a profile
whose energy returns the factor $5/6$. The criterion is von Mises in plane stress on
$(\sigma_x, \sigma_y, \tau_{xy}, \tau_{xz}, \tau_{yz})$, with linear isotropic hardening:

$$ f = \tfrac12\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{P}\,\boldsymbol{\sigma} - \tfrac13\,R(\alpha)^2 \le 0,\qquad R = f_y + H\,\alpha $$ (24.16)

where $\mathbf{P}$ is the plane-stress deviatoric projector and $\alpha$ the cumulative
plastic strain. The return to the yield surface is the implicit Euler scheme of Simo and Taylor:
since $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{P}$ have the same eigenvectors, the stress is written in
closed form

$$ \boldsymbol{\sigma}(\Delta\gamma) = \bigl(\mathbf{C}^{-1} + \Delta\gamma\,\mathbf{P}\bigr)^{-1}\mathbf{C}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\sigma}_\text{trial} $$ (24.17)

and the consistency condition is a single equation in $\Delta\gamma$, solved by Newton's
method to rounding. The consistent tangent matrix

$$ \mathbf{C}_{ep} = \boldsymbol{\Xi} - \frac{(\boldsymbol{\Xi}\mathbf{P}\boldsymbol{\sigma})(\boldsymbol{\Xi}\mathbf{P}\boldsymbol{\sigma})^{\mathsf T}}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{P}\boldsymbol{\Xi}\mathbf{P}\boldsymbol{\sigma} + \beta},\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Xi} = \bigl(\mathbf{C}^{-1} + \Delta\gamma\,\mathbf{P}\bigr)^{-1},\qquad
\beta = \frac{\frac23 H\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{P}\boldsymbol{\sigma}}{1 - \frac23 H\,\Delta\gamma} $$ (24.18)

gives quadratic convergence of the global equilibrium. Hill's orthotropic criterion (ratios of the
yield strengths along the material axes) is also available, with the same algorithm; laminates and
orthotropic facets integrate each ply separately. The thickness is integrated by a composite 4-point
Gauss-Lobatto rule over 40 layers by default, exact to degree 5 per layer and whose end points are the
faces: the surface stresses are read, not extrapolated. The stabilisation of the rotation
$\theta_z$ remains elastic.

### 24.8.2 Analysis

The load of the case is applied in 20 equal increments by default; each increment is solved by
Newton's method with the consistent tangent (24.18):

$$ \mathbf{K}_t(\mathbf{u}_i)\,\Delta\mathbf{u} = \lambda_k\mathbf{F} - \mathbf{f}_\text{int}(\mathbf{u}_i),\qquad
\lambda_k = \frac{k}{20},\qquad \|\lambda_k\mathbf{F} - \mathbf{f}_\text{int}\| \le 10^{-10}\,\|\lambda_k\mathbf{F}\| $$ (24.19)

with at most 50 iterations per increment. The bars of the model remain elastic, unless they are
given fibre sections or plastic hinges (chapter 18). As an option, the facets and the bars are
treated in large displacements, in a corotational frame, with small strains. A load that exceeds the
limit load finds no equilibrium: the calculation stops with an explicit error or, on request, divides
the increment up to six times and returns the converged steps, which brackets the limit load. Cables
are not admitted in this calculation.

## 24.9 Scope

- flat facets: a curved shell is approximated by facets, and its accuracy depends on the
mesh;

- internal forces at the centre of the facets, without smoothing at the nodes;

- geometric stiffness limited to the membrane term acting on the slope of the deflection;

- pressures distributed in thirds to the nodes, without consistent nodal moments;

- automatic meshing of flat slabs only; a bar whose chord leaves the domain (concave outline, hole)
makes the meshing fail; a bar on the edge is not integrated into the mesh;

- plasticity of shells by the von Mises or Hill criterion: no cracked-concrete law in shells;
cables refused in the plastic calculation.

# Chapter 25 Continuum elements

This chapter deals with continuum finite elements: plane elements in plane stress or plane strain,
axisymmetric elements and solid elements. They are used where beam and shell theory no longer
applies: end block and diffusion zone of a concentrated force, anchorage block, abutment and ground,
thick member, tank of revolution. The problem posed is that of linear elasticity, or of plasticity
for metals and soils, in small strains. The chapter describes the elements (shape functions,
integration), the loads they receive, their connection to bars and shells, the nonlinear laws and
their integration, heat conduction in these elements and the meshing tools.

Shells are described in chapter 24; heat conduction in the section of a bar exposed to fire, in
chapter 23.

## 25.1 Assumptions

- small displacements and small strains, except for the elastic large-displacement option of the
nonlinear analysis;

- isoparametric elements: the geometry and the displacements are interpolated by the same shape
functions;

- plane and axisymmetric elements lie in the global $XY$ plane; for axisymmetry,
$r = X$ is the radius and $Y$ the axis, and all quantities (forces, masses, stiffnesses) are
counted per radian: a load over the circumference is $2\pi$ times the load per radian;

- the nodes of continuum elements carry only translations;

- isotropic elastic material, defined by $E$ and $\nu$; von Mises, Drucker-Prager and
Mohr-Coulomb plastic laws, and creep, in the nonlinear analysis;

- no mesher for continuum elements: the elements are given node by node.

## 25.2 Elements

### 25.2.1 Families and shape functions

keta offers seven elements:

| element | nodes | use | stiffness rule | mass rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T3 | 3 | plane, axisymmetric | 1 point (axisym.: 3) | 3 points (axisym.: 7) |
| T6 | 6 | plane, axisymmetric | 3 points (axisym.: 7) | 7 points |
| Q4 | 4 | plane, axisymmetric | 2 × 2 | 2 × 2 |
| Q8 | 8 | plane, axisymmetric | 2 × 2 (reduced) | 3 × 3 |
| T4 | 4 | solid | 1 point | 4 points |
| H8 | 8 | solid | 2 × 2 × 2 | 2 × 2 × 2 |
| H20 | 20 | solid | 3 × 3 × 3 | 3 × 3 × 3 |

The vertices are numbered anticlockwise (bottom face then top face for hexahedra), then the
mid-side nodes side by side. The shape functions are the classical ones. For triangles, with the area
coordinates $L_1 = 1 - \xi - \eta$, $L_2 = \xi$, $L_3 = \eta$:

$$ \text{T3:}\ N_i = L_i,\qquad \text{T6:}\ N_i = L_i(2L_i - 1)\ \text{(vertices)},\quad N_{ij} = 4L_iL_j\ \text{(mid-side nodes)} $$ (25.1)

For quadrilaterals, with $(\xi_i, \eta_i) = (\pm1, \pm1)$ at the vertices:

$$ \begin{aligned}
\text{Q4:}\ &N_i = \tfrac14(1 + \xi_i\xi)(1 + \eta_i\eta)\\
\text{Q8:}\ &N_i = \tfrac14(1 + \xi_i\xi)(1 + \eta_i\eta)(\xi_i\xi + \eta_i\eta - 1),\qquad
N_m = \tfrac12(1 - \xi^2)(1 + \eta_m\eta)\ \text{or}\ \tfrac12(1 + \xi_m\xi)(1 - \eta^2)
\end{aligned} $$ (25.2)

and likewise in three dimensions for H8 (product of three linear factors) and H20 (“serendipity”
family, without nodes at the centre of the faces). The derivatives of the shape functions are computed
by automatic differentiation, exact for these polynomials.

**Figure 25.1** — T6 and Q8 elements in their natural coordinates: node numbering and Gauss points of the stiffness

### 25.2.2 Isoparametric mapping

The position and the displacement at a point with natural coordinates $\boldsymbol{\xi}$ are
$\mathbf{x} = \sum_i N_i(\boldsymbol{\xi})\,\mathbf{x}_i$ and
$\mathbf{u} = \sum_i N_i(\boldsymbol{\xi})\,\mathbf{u}_i$. The Cartesian derivatives are obtained
through the Jacobian matrix:

$$ \mathbf{J} = \frac{\partial\mathbf{x}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\xi}} = \sum_i \frac{\partial N_i}{\partial\boldsymbol{\xi}}\,\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T},\qquad
\frac{\partial N_i}{\partial\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{J}^{-\mathsf T}\frac{\partial N_i}{\partial\boldsymbol{\xi}},\qquad
\mathrm{d}V = \det\mathbf{J}\,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\xi} $$ (25.3)

An element whose Jacobian is negative or zero at an integration point (nodes in the wrong order,
element too distorted) is refused. A plane element whose nodes do not all lie in one plane
$Z$ = constant is refused, as is an axisymmetric element that contains a point of zero or
negative radius at an integration point.

### 25.2.3 Strains and elastic laws

The strain is $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = \mathbf{B}\,\mathbf{u}_e$. In plane problems, it has three
components $(\varepsilon_x, \varepsilon_y, \gamma_{xy})$; in axisymmetry, four, with the
circumferential strain due to the radial displacement:

$$ \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = \left(\frac{\partial u_r}{\partial r},\ \frac{\partial u_z}{\partial z},\ \frac{u_r}{r},\ \frac{\partial u_r}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_z}{\partial r}\right) $$ (25.4)

in solids, six components $(\varepsilon_x, \varepsilon_y, \varepsilon_z, \gamma_{xy}, \gamma_{yz}, \gamma_{zx})$.
The elasticity matrices are those of isotropic elasticity: in plane stress,
$\mathbf{D} = \frac{E}{1 - \nu^2}\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1 & \nu & 0\\ \nu & 1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & (1-\nu)/2\end{smallmatrix}\right]$;
in plane strain, in axisymmetry and in solids, with $c = E/[(1+\nu)(1-2\nu)]$,

$$ D_{ii} = c\,(1 - \nu),\qquad D_{ij} = c\,\nu\ (i \ne j,\ \text{normal components}),\qquad D_{\gamma\gamma} = c\,\frac{1 - 2\nu}{2} $$ (25.5)

Plane elements have a thickness $t$ (in plane strain, an arbitrary thickness, generally
1 m).

### 25.2.4 Stiffness, mass and integration rules

The stiffness and the consistent mass of the element are

$$ \mathbf{K}_e = \int_V \mathbf{B}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{D}\,\mathbf{B}\;\mathrm{d}V,\qquad
\mathbf{M}_e = \int_V \rho\,\mathbf{N}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{N}\;\mathrm{d}V,\qquad
\mathrm{d}V = t\,\mathrm{d}A\ \text{(plane)},\quad r\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}z\ \text{(axisymmetry)} $$ (25.6)

integrated by the Gauss rules of the table. On a straight-sided element, the rules of the triangles
and of the tetrahedron are exact for the stiffness; axisymmetry, which introduces $r$ and
$1/r$, takes one order more (3 points for T3, 7 Dunavant points for T6). The Q8 is integrated by
the reduced $2\times2$ rule, which avoids locking and gives better stresses; the H20 by the full
$3\times3\times3$ rule, because the $2\times2\times2$ rule leaves spurious modes in a column
of a single element. The mass rules are exact for affine elements.

The stresses are returned at any natural point of the element, generally at the Gauss points or at
the nodes: $(\sigma_x, \sigma_y, \tau_{xy}, \sigma_z)$ in plane problems, with
$\sigma_z = \nu(\sigma_x + \sigma_y)$ in plane strain and 0 in plane stress;
$(\sigma_r, \sigma_z, \sigma_\theta, \tau_{rz})$ in axisymmetry; the six components in solids.
Nodal averaging of the values of neighbouring elements is left to the user.

The thick cylinder under internal pressure $p$ (radii $a$ and $b = 2a$, plane
strain) has the Lamé solution
$\sigma_{r,\theta} = \frac{pa^2}{b^2 - a^2}\left(1 \mp \frac{b^2}{r^2}\right)$. With four
axisymmetric Q8 elements through the thickness, keta returns its nodal displacements to within
$10^{-13}$; the stresses, continuous within each element, show small jumps between elements,
which disappear with mesh refinement (circumferential stress at the inner wall: 1.6889 instead of
1.6667 times $p$ at the nodal point, with four elements; 1.6684 with sixteen).

**Figure 25.2** — Thick cylinder under internal pressure (b = 2a, ν = 0.3): stresses from four axisymmetric Q8 elements and Lamé solution

## 25.3 Loads

A traction $\mathbf{t}$ (force per unit area, global vector) on a side or a face gives the
consistent nodal forces

$$ \mathbf{f}_i = \int_\Gamma N_i\,\mathbf{t}\;\mathrm{d}\Gamma $$ (25.7)

where $\mathrm{d}\Gamma$ is $t\,\mathrm{d}\ell$ in plane problems, $r\,\mathrm{d}\ell$
in axisymmetry (force per radian), $\mathrm{d}A$ in solids. A side runs from vertex $k$ to
vertex $k+1$, mid-side node included; the faces of a hexahedron are numbered bottom, top, then
$\eta = -1$, $\xi = +1$, $\eta = +1$, $\xi = -1$. A traction can vary linearly
along a side. A pressure acts along the local inward normal, exactly, even on a curved side.
Self-weight gives the forces $\mathbf{M}_e\,\mathbf{g}$, with the consistent mass.

A nodal temperature field $T$ gives an initial strain
$\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_0 = \alpha(T - T_0)$ on the normal components, and the nodal
forces

$$ \mathbf{f} = \int_V \mathbf{B}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{D}\,\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_0\,\mathrm{d}V,\qquad
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_0 = \alpha\,\Delta T\,(1, 1, 0)\ \text{(plane stress)},\quad (1+\nu)\,\alpha\,\Delta T\,(1, 1, 0)\ \text{(plane strain)} $$ (25.8)

(in plane strain, the factor $1 + \nu$ expresses the restrained expansion through the
thickness; in axisymmetry, the circumferential component is included).

**Important.**

These forces are nodal loads: the returned stresses are $\mathbf{D}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{u}$,
without subtracting $\mathbf{D}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_0$. For a thermal case, the true stress is
$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{u} - \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_0)$: a plate free to expand under
$\Delta T = 100$ K is returned with $E\alpha\Delta T/(1 - \nu)$ instead of zero. The
correction is left to the user.

## 25.4 Conduction and seepage

The same elements solve a scalar field problem: temperature (heat conduction) or hydraulic head
(groundwater flow), which obey the same equation

$$ \nabla\cdot\bigl(\mathbf{k}(u)\,\nabla u\bigr) + s = c\,\frac{\partial u}{\partial t},\qquad
k_i(u) = k_i + k_1\,u $$ (25.9)

with a conductivity that is orthotropic along the global axes and linear in $u$, and a
volumetric capacity $c$. The boundary conditions are values imposed at the nodes, incoming
fluxes and exchanges $h(u - u_\text{env})$ on the sides or faces, point sources and conductances
between two nodes or between a node and the surrounding medium. In steady state, keta solves
$\mathbf{K}(u)\,\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{f}$ by Newton's method with the exact tangent (including the
term in $k_1$), to rounding; in transient state, by the implicit Euler scheme with the consistent
capacity matrix and a Newton iteration at each step. The fluxes supplied by the imposed nodes (the
inflow into an excavation, the heat extracted) are returned as reactions. The temperature field
obtained can be used as a thermal loading (25.8).

## 25.5 Connection to bars and shells

Continuum elements are assembled with bars, shells, springs and links in a single stiffness
matrix, through their common nodes. Their nodes carry only the translations they use ($u_x$,
$u_y$ in plane problems and in axisymmetry, all three in solids); the other degrees of freedom of
a node that belongs only to continuum elements are restrained automatically, like those of a truss
node. A bar or a shell that arrives at a node of a continuum element transmits its forces to it, but
not its moments: the node has no rotational stiffness, and the bar is in effect hinged there. To fix a
bar into a solid block, it must be connected by a rigid link to several nodes of the element. For the
same reason, a plane element connects only to the translations in its plane. The table below
summarises the active degrees of freedom according to the elements that meet at a node.

| elements meeting at the node | active degrees of freedom |
|---|---|
| plane or axisymmetric elements only | $u_x$, $u_y$ |
| solid elements only | $u_x$, $u_y$, $u_z$ |
| continuum elements and a bar or a shell | all six, the rotations having only the stiffness of the bar or the shell |

Linear static, modal and dynamic analyses take continuum elements; buckling, second order, large
displacements of bars, staged construction and strain-energy-weighted damping refuse them.

## 25.6 Nonlinear laws

### 25.6.1 Von Mises plasticity

In plane strain, in axisymmetry and in solids, each Gauss point carries the three-dimensional state
(six components): plastic strain $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_p$ and equivalent plastic strain
$\bar\varepsilon_p$. The elastic predictor is
$\boldsymbol{\sigma}^\text{tr} = \mathbf{D}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} - \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_p)$, with
deviator $\mathbf{s}^\text{tr}$. With the von Mises criterion with linear isotropic hardening
$\|\mathbf{s}\| \le \sqrt{2/3}\,(\sigma_y + H\bar\varepsilon_p)$, the radial return of Simo and
Hughes is exact in one step:

$$ \Delta\gamma = \frac{\|\mathbf{s}^\text{tr}\| - \sqrt{2/3}\,(\sigma_y + H\bar\varepsilon_p)}{2G + \frac23 H},\qquad
\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \boldsymbol{\sigma}^\text{tr} - 2G\,\Delta\gamma\,\mathbf{n},\qquad
\bar\varepsilon_p \mathrel{+}= \sqrt{2/3}\,\Delta\gamma $$ (25.10)

with $\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{s}^\text{tr}/\|\mathbf{s}^\text{tr}\|$. The consistent tangent
matrix

$$ \mathbf{D}_{ep} = K\,\mathbf{1}\otimes\mathbf{1} + 2G\beta\,\mathbf{P} - 2G\bar\gamma\,\mathbf{n}\otimes\mathbf{n},\qquad
\beta = 1 - \frac{2G\Delta\gamma}{\|\mathbf{s}^\text{tr}\|},\qquad \bar\gamma = \frac{1}{1 + H/(3G)} - (1 - \beta) $$ (25.11)

($\mathbf{P}$ deviatoric projector, $K$ bulk modulus) gives quadratic convergence of the
equilibrium at each increment. Plane stress is refused for a plastic material: its return is a
different algorithm (that of the shells, chapter 24).

A thick cylinder ($b/a = 2$) in plane strain, perfectly plastic, has the limit pressure
$p_\text{lim} = \frac{2}{\sqrt3}\,\sigma_y\ln(b/a) = 0.80038\,\sigma_y$. With sixteen
axisymmetric Q8 elements, the last load step converged by keta is $0.800375\,\sigma_y$, the next
one having no equilibrium.

### 25.6.2 Creep

A von Mises material can also creep, according to a time-hardening power law, possibly thermally
activated (Norton-Arrhenius law):

$$ \varepsilon_c = A\,q^n\,t^m\,e^{-Q/T} $$ (25.12)

where $q$ is the von Mises stress, $t$ the time since the start of the calculation and
$T$ the absolute temperature at the Gauss point, interpolated from the nodal temperatures and
constant in time. The flow is deviatoric, along the von Mises normal. It is integrated implicitly
together with plasticity: over a step $[t_0, t_1]$,
$\Delta\varepsilon_c = A\,q_1^n\,(t_1^m - t_0^m)\,e^{-Q/T}$, where $q_1$ is the end-of-step
stress, the root of an increasing scalar equation solved by a Newton method safeguarded by bisection.
The scheme is unconditionally stable, exact under constant stress and first-order under varying
stress. With $\sigma_y = 0$, the material is purely viscous.

### 25.6.3 Drucker-Prager and Mohr-Coulomb

For soils (tension positive), keta offers two frictional criteria, with constant cohesion or with
linear hardening of the cohesion $c = c_0 + H\bar\varepsilon_p$, with an angle of friction
$\varphi$ and an angle of dilatancy $\psi \le \varphi$ (non-associated plastic potential if
$\psi < \varphi$). The Mohr-Coulomb criterion, in principal stresses
$\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \sigma_3$, and the Drucker-Prager criterion are written

$$ (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3) + (\sigma_1 + \sigma_3)\sin\varphi = 2c\cos\varphi,\qquad
\sqrt{J_2} + \eta\,p - \xi\,c = 0 $$ (25.13)

The Drucker-Prager cone is matched to the Mohr-Coulomb hexagon in three ways: by its compressive
meridian (outer cone), by its tensile meridian (inner cone), or so as to give the same limit load in
plane strain:

$$ \eta = \frac{6\sin\varphi}{\sqrt3\,(3 \mp \sin\varphi)},\quad \xi = \frac{6\cos\varphi}{\sqrt3\,(3 \mp \sin\varphi)}\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\eta = \frac{3\tan\varphi}{\sqrt{9 + 12\tan^2\varphi}},\quad \xi = \frac{3}{\sqrt{9 + 12\tan^2\varphi}} $$ (25.14)

**Figure 25.3** — Mohr-Coulomb criterion and Drucker-Prager cones in the deviatoric plane (φ = 30°, zero mean pressure)

The Drucker-Prager return is in closed form on the smooth part of the cone,
$\Delta\gamma = f/(G + K\eta\bar\eta + \xi^2 H)$ ($\bar\eta$ computed with $\psi$), or on
the apex. The Mohr-Coulomb return is performed in principal stress space, following de Souza Neto,
Perić and Owen: return to the main plane, otherwise to the right or left edge (two active planes),
otherwise to the apex; each is a linear system that is exact for linear hardening, and the first that
gives positive multipliers and respects the order of the principal stresses is retained. The
consistent tangent comprises, in addition to the principal part, the terms of rotation of the
principal directions $(\sigma_i - \sigma_j)/(\varepsilon_i - \varepsilon_j)$. It is not symmetric
when $\psi \ne \varphi$: the global system is then solved by a sparse LU factorisation. In a
triaxial compression test ($\varphi = 30°$, $c$ = 10 kPa, proportional loading,
lateral stress one fifth of the axial stress), the limit load found by keta coincides with that of
(25.13) to within $10^{-5}$ for both criteria (outer cone for Drucker-Prager); this
case passes through the Mohr-Coulomb edge ($\sigma_1 = \sigma_2$).

### 25.6.4 Global algorithm

The load case is multiplied by a sequence of factors $\lambda_k$; each interval is divided
into equal substeps (4 by default), and each substep is solved by Newton's method from the accepted
state of the previous step:

$$ \mathbf{K}_t(\mathbf{u}_i)\,\Delta\mathbf{u} = \lambda\,\mathbf{F} - \mathbf{f}_\text{int}(\mathbf{u}_i),\qquad
\|\lambda\mathbf{F} - \mathbf{f}_\text{int}\| \le 10^{-10}\,\max(\|\lambda\mathbf{F}\|, \|\mathbf{r}_\text{supports}\|) $$ (25.15)

(at most 60 iterations; convergence is also accepted when the correction falls below
$10^{-13}$ times the displacement, the limit of rounding for stiff materials). The imposed support
displacements of the case are multiplied by the factor. The Gauss point states are accepted only at
convergence of the substep. A substep without equilibrium (beyond the limit load) stops the calculation
with an error or, on request, is halved from the last converged state, up to six times, and the
calculation returns the factors reached. Each converged factor supplies the displacements, the
reactions and, at the end, the stresses and the equivalent plastic strain at the Gauss points. A time
can be associated with each factor; it is required as soon as a material creeps (a factor repeated at
a later time is a creep hold).

As an option, the analysis is carried out in large displacements, in a total Lagrangian
formulation: the strain is the Green-Lagrange strain
$\mathbf{E} = \frac12(\mathbf{H} + \mathbf{H}^{\mathsf T} + \mathbf{H}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{H})$,
$\mathbf{H} = \partial\mathbf{u}/\partial\mathbf{X}$, the material is Saint-Venant-Kirchhoff
($\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{D}\mathbf{E}$), and the tangent includes the geometric stiffness of the
Piola-Kirchhoff stresses. This option is restricted to elastic plane and solid elements; the loads
keep their direction.

The nonlinear analysis takes only models made of continuum elements: bars, shells, links and
kinematic relations are refused there.

## 25.7 Meshing

keta does not generate meshes of continuum elements: the nodes and the elements are supplied by
the user, in the numbering order described above. keta's plane mesher is used for slabs (chapter 24)
and for arbitrary sections (chapter 20). It is a constrained Delaunay triangulation: a triangle is
accepted if no other vertex lies strictly inside its circumscribed circle, a criterion written, for a
triangle $abc$ traversed anticlockwise and a point $d$, as

$$ \begin{vmatrix}
x_a - x_d & y_a - y_d & (x_a - x_d)^2 + (y_a - y_d)^2\\
x_b - x_d & y_b - y_d & (x_b - x_d)^2 + (y_b - y_d)^2\\
x_c - x_d & y_c - y_d & (x_c - x_d)^2 + (y_c - y_d)^2
\end{vmatrix} > 0 \iff d \text{ lies inside the circle} $$ (25.16)

except across an imposed side (outline, hole, internal bar), which cannot be flipped. Ruppert's
refinement then gives the requested size and minimum angle (chapter 24). The result is deterministic:
the same data give the same nodes and the same triangles, in the same order.

## 25.8 Scope

- no mesher for continuum elements; no 10-node tetrahedral element, nor prismatic element;

- stresses returned without subtracting the thermal strains; nodal averaging left to the
user;

- connection to bars and shells through the translations only;

- continuum elements refused by buckling, second order, large displacements of bars and staged
construction;

- nonlinear analysis restricted to models made of continuum elements only; plasticity refused in
plane stress; frictional laws in small displacements; large displacements in elasticity only.

# Appendix A Verification of results

A result of keta is said to be verified when it has been compared with a value that does not come
from keta. This value is of three kinds: a closed form of mechanics (a strength-of-materials formula,
a solution of elasticity, a series or an integral worked out by hand); a published value (a worked
example from a reference book, a table of a standard, a benchmark problem from the literature such as
those of MacNeal and Harder); a reference solution obtained by an independent route, for example the
step-by-step integration of a formula carried out separately or the limit of a sequence of
increasingly fine meshes. The chapters give examples along the way: the catenary of chapter 7, the
resistant moment of a rectangle in chapter 21, the deflection of a simply supported plate in
chapter 24, the Lamé cylinder in chapter 25. The accepted difference depends on the comparison:
rounding when keta must reproduce a formula, the expected discretisation error when it approximates
a continuous solution, the accuracy of the source when the value is read from a publication.

Verification establishes that the calculation is correct in the cases compared; it does not prove
that it is correct in all others, and the rarest combinations of options are the least tested. It
bears on the solution of the problem posed, not on the choice of that problem: it does not say whether
the model represents the structure (supports, stiffnesses, staged construction, material laws,
loads), nor whether the assumptions stated at the head of each chapter suit the case in hand. The
scopes and the refusals described in the chapters bound what has been verified; outside these bounds,
a result has not been verified.

keta computes; it does not validate a structure. The engineer who uses its results in a design
remains responsible for them: the engineer chooses the model, the assumptions, the partial factors and
the code checks, and checks the results by an order of magnitude, by the global equilibrium of loads
and reactions, by a simplified model or by examining the deformed shapes. An unexplained difference
between these checks and keta must be resolved before any use of the result, and deserves to be
reported.

Returns the dict of build_suspension plus l0 (corrected lengths, those of the model's cables), deviation_stage1 and deviation [m] (largest node deviation before and after), iterations."""
        ...
    def build_suspension_on_towers(self, case: int, left: tuple[float, float, float], right: tuple[float, float, float], hanger_x: Sequence[float], hanger_load: Sequence[float], hanger_deck_nodes: Sequence[int], *, left_node: int, right_node: int, cable_material: int, cable_section: int, hanger_material: int, hanger_section: int, target_sag: Optional[float] = ..., target_h: Optional[float] = ..., hanger_kind: str = ..., deck_bars: Sequence[int] = ..., back_left: object = ..., back_right: object = ..., hanger_deck: Sequence[tuple[float, float]] = ..., saddle_tol: float = ..., max_iterations: int = ..., hanger_weight: float = ...) -> dict:
        """Suspension on flexible towers (arguments of build_suspension; left_node and right_node are the existing tower-top nodes at left and right): the cable is form-found with its saddles where the tower tops stand under the permanent case `case`, which also receives the lack of fit of the hangers — a fixed point between the form finding and the solve of the whole, until the saddles move by less than saddle_tol [m]. Returns the dict of build_suspension plus saddle_disp_left, saddle_disp_right (the tower-top displacements under the permanent case), saddle_gap (last update) and iterations."""
        ...
    def suspension_response(self, suspension: dict, case: int) -> dict:
        """Response of a suspension (the dict returned by build_suspension, build_suspension_on_towers or solve_uelm) under case `case`, by the cable statics of the whole: dict(cable_H, cable_Tmax, segment_H, hanger_tension, deck_my_max, deck_my_min, deck_dz_min, deck_dz_max, backstay_H, backstay_Tmax) — horizontal and largest tension of the main cable, tension of each hanger, extreme moment and vertical displacement of the deck (deck_bars and hanger_deck_nodes of the assembly)."""
        ...
    def suspension_live_response(self, suspension: dict, dead_case: int, live_case: int) -> dict:
        """Effect of a live load on a suspension: cables do not superpose, so the dead case alone and the dead and live loads in one case are both solved. Returns dict(dead, total — two dicts of suspension_response —, hanger_delta, cable_H_delta, deck_my_max_delta, deck_my_min_delta), the differences total - dead."""
        ...

class RcSection:
    """Rectangular or T reinforced-concrete section, EN 1992-1-1. z downward from the top fibre; N tension-positive at the gross centroid; M > 0 sagging; stresses tension-positive."""
    def __init__(self, *, b: float, h: float, d: float, As: float, fck: float, bf: float = ..., hf: float = ..., d2: float = ..., As2: float = ..., fctm: float = ..., Ecm: float = ..., gamma_c: float = ..., alpha_cc: float = ..., fyk: float = ..., Es: float = ..., gamma_s: float = ...) -> None:
        """b web width, h depth, d / As tension steel, d2 / As2 compression steel, bf x hf top flange [m, m^2]; fck, fctm (0 = Table 3.1), Ecm (0 = EN value), fyk, Es [Pa]; partial factors."""
        ...
    def uncracked(self, N: float, M: float, phi: float = ...) -> dict:
        """SLS state I (transformed uncracked section, alpha_e = Es (1 + phi) / Ecm)."""
        ...
    def cracking_moment(self, N: float = ..., phi: float = ..., fct_eff: float = ...) -> float:
        """Sagging moment bringing the bottom fibre of the state-I section to fct_eff (0 = fctm)."""
        ...
    def cracked(self, N: float, M: float, phi: float = ...) -> dict:
        """SLS state II (concrete in tension ignored, linear concrete in compression)."""
        ...
    def crack_width(self, N: float, M: float, phi: float = ..., cover: float = ..., bar_dia: float = ..., spacing: float = ..., k1: float = ..., k2: float = ..., k3: float = ..., k4: float = ..., kt: float = ..., fct_eff: float = ...) -> dict:
        """Crack width §7.3.4: wk = s_r,max (eps_sm - eps_cm), eq. 7.8, 7.9, 7.11 (7.14 when the spacing exceeds 5 (c + phi/2))."""
        ...
    def curvature(self, N: float, M: float, phi: float = ..., beta: float = ...) -> dict:
        """Tension-stiffening curvature §7.4.3 eq. 7.18 / 7.19 (beta 1 short-term single load, 0.5 sustained)."""
        ...
    def deflection_ss(self, L: float, M_of_x: Callable[[float], float], N: float = ..., phi: float = ..., beta: float = ..., n_per_half: int = ..., eps_cs: float = ..., phi_cr: float = ...) -> float:
        """Mid-span deflection of a simply supported beam under M(x) with the eq. 7.18 curvature (unit-load integral); eps_cs != 0 adds the shrinkage curvature, interpolated by the same zeta (N = 0 then)."""
        ...
    def shrinkage_curvature(self, eps_cs: float, phi: float = ..., cracked: bool = ...) -> float:
        """Eq. 7.21: 1/r_cs = eps_cs alpha_e S / I (state I or II), sagging-positive."""
        ...
    def mrd(self, N: float = ...) -> dict:
        """ULS sagging resistance with the rectangular block §3.1.7(3) at the axial force N (tension +), about the gross centroid."""
        ...
    def interaction(self, n: int = ...) -> list[tuple[float, float]]:
        """Sagging branch of the N-M interaction curve: (N, M_Rd) at n axial forces spread between the squash and the tension capacities (points with no equilibrium are skipped)."""
        ...

class Results:
    """All analysis results (every case and combination)."""
    def save(self, path: str, note: str = ...) -> None:
        """Write the results to a JSON store (schema version, provenance with this note, sign convention, every case and combination); Model.read_results reads it back bit for bit."""
        ...
    def case(self, id: int) -> CaseResult: ...
    def combo(self, id: int) -> CaseResult: ...
    @property
    def case_ids(self) -> list[int]: ...
    @property
    def combo_ids(self) -> list[int]: ...
    def __repr__(self) -> str: ...
    def envelope(self, cases: Optional[Sequence[int]] = ..., combos: Optional[Sequence[int]] = ...) -> tuple[Bound, Bound]:
        """Envelope of results (default: every case and combination): (minimum, maximum), each component taken independently (displacements, reactions, forces at every study section)."""
        ...
    def envelope_factored(self, terms: Sequence[tuple[int, float, float]]) -> tuple[Bound, Bound]:
        """Envelope of factored cases: terms = [(case, c_min, c_max)]; for each component every case is taken ALONE with the factor of [c_min, c_max] that makes it largest (resp. smallest), and the bound is the extreme over the cases. It is not a combination (add_combination / generate_combinations sum the cases). Returns (minimum, maximum)."""
        ...
    def concomitant(self, what: str, bar: int = ..., station: int = ..., comp: int = ..., node: int = ..., cases: Optional[Sequence[int]] = ..., combos: Optional[Sequence[int]] = ...) -> dict:
        """Extremes of one component and the complete states that go with them: what = 'bar_force' (bar, station index, comp 0..5 = N Vy Vz T My Mz), 'reaction' or 'displacement' (node, comp 0..5). Returns dict(max, min, source_max, source_min, state_max, state_min) — the states give every other result of the source that governs."""
        ...

class Tangent:

        ...

        """Displacement of a node in the state (6-tuple)."""
        ...
    def modal(self, n_modes: int = ..., lumped: bool = ...) -> Modal:
        """Modal analysis on the saved tangent: the modes of the loaded (or staged) structure. Tension stiffens, compression softens; the shapes are per node of the linearized structure."""
        ...
    def buckling(self, model: Model, case: int, n_modes: int = ...) -> Buckling:
        """Buckling of the ADDITIONAL loads of case `case` of `model` about the saved state: K_T + lambda Kg(N_case) singular (factors scale the additional case only; the state stays as it is). `model` is the model the state came from (its structure is checked by fingerprint; its cases may have grown)."""
        ...
